docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 18 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra: Polity and Law. It surveys Indian traditions of political thought and law from the Vedic period to the Constitution of the Republic of India: the Arthaśāstra and the later literature on polity; the theory of kingship in the śāstras and the epics; Buddhist and Jain ideas of the righteous ruler and the law of the monastic order; the Dharmaśāstra literature, from the Dharmasūtras and the Manusmṛti to the medieval commentaries and digests; courts, procedure, contract, property, inheritance, crime and the family in classical law; custom, caste and village institutions; the charters, scribes and statecraft of the medieval kingdoms; Islamic law and the Indo-Persian state of the Sultanate and the Mughals; the making of “Anglo-Hindu” and “Anglo-Muhammadan” law under British rule; and the Constitution’s encounter with this inheritance.

After an introduction, the chapters fall into four groups: the foundations of Indian political thought, the Arthaśāstra’s science of the state and the Buddhist and Jain alternatives to it (Chapters 2–8); the Dharmaśāstra literature (Chapters 9–11); the classical law of procedure, property, crime, the family and custom (Chapters 12–16); and the history of law and government from the medieval regional kingdoms and the Delhi Sultanate to the Republic (Chapters 17–20). Primary texts are quoted only where both the wording and the reference could be confirmed against a standard edition; elsewhere they are paraphrased, with the reference given. Dates follow current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such; in particular, the Arthaśāstra is treated as a composite text of c. 50 BCE–300 CE and the Manusmṛti as a work of about the second century CE, following Patrick Olivelle. The volume does not claim that the classical texts “anticipated” modern constitutions, welfare states or human rights; comparisons with other traditions are presented as comparisons.

The texts discussed here are, among other things, charters of social hierarchy, and the volume does not hide this. It sets out their provisions on varṇa, untouchability and women with references to the primary sources, and it gives space to the critics — from the Buddha to B. R. Ambedkar and modern feminist and Dalit scholars — who exposed and opposed them. It also tries to give due weight to the real intellectual achievements of the traditions: the Arthaśāstra’s analysis of the state, the Dharmaśāstras’ law of procedure and property, and the many forms of local self-government recorded in inscriptions.

References to standard editions, translations and studies — among others by P. V. Kane, Robert Lingat, J. D. M. Derrett, Ludo Rocher, Richard Lariviere, Patrick Olivelle, Donald Davis, R. P. Kangle, Thomas Trautmann, Mark McClish, R. S. Sharma, Romila Thapar, Upinder Singh, Uma Chakravarti, Muzaffar Alam and Marc Galanter — are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography, which is meant as a guide to further reading. A list of abbreviations follows the table of contents; a glossary, a chronology, brief notes on persons and a guide to the principal sources are provided at the end. No survey of this size can be exhaustive or free of error, and every quotation should, before scholarly use, be checked against a critical edition.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Polity and Law in Indian Traditions
docs.text:
This volume is about how people in the Indian subcontinent, over some two and a half thousand years, thought about political power and about law: what kings were for and how they should rule; how states should be organised, financed and defended; how disputes should be settled and wrongs punished; how families, castes, guilds and villages should govern themselves; and how all of this related to the order of the world and to the good life. Its main sources are the Sanskrit treatises on polity (arthaśāstra, nītiśāstra) and on dharma (dharmaśāstra), together with the Sanskrit epics, Buddhist and Jain texts, inscriptions, Islamic legal and political writings, colonial law reports and the Constitution of independent India.

The subject has been surrounded by two opposed distortions. One, common in popular and some nationalist writing, treats the classical texts as a storehouse of timeless wisdom that “anticipated” modern constitutional government, welfare states, human rights, consumer protection and international law, and passes quickly over their hierarchy of caste and gender. The other, found in colonial and some later writing, treats the same texts as evidence of an unchanging, despotic and priest-ridden society. This book tries to avoid both. It follows the texts closely and dates them according to current scholarship; it presents their intellectual achievements, which are considerable; and it states plainly what they prescribed for Śūdras, Dalits and women, and what modern critics — above all B. R. Ambedkar — made of those prescriptions. It also places the Brahmanical śāstras in a wider landscape that includes Buddhist and Jain political thought, customary and local law, Islamic law and Mughal administration, and the transformations of the colonial period.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Rājanīti, Arthaśāstra, Daṇḍanīti
docs.text: Rājanīti means “royal policy” or “the conduct of kings”, and is used here, as in modern Indian languages, for the whole field of political thought and statecraft. The classical Sanskrit name for the discipline was arthaśāstra, “the science of artha” — material well-being, wealth and power, and above all the territory and people from which a king’s power derives (Chapter 3). It was also called daṇḍanīti, “the policy of the rod”, because its central concern was the king’s coercive power (daṇḍa) and its proper use, and nītiśāstra, “the science of policy”, a term that covers later verse manuals and collections of maxims. The one complete surviving treatise of the discipline is the Arthaśāstra ascribed to Kauṭilya, a composite work of c. 50 BCE–300 CE.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Dharma and Dharmaśāstra
docs.text: Dharma is notoriously difficult to translate. Derived from the root dhṛ, “to hold, support”, it came to mean the order that upholds the world and society, and the duties, rights and rules of conduct that sustain that order: religious obligations, moral virtues, the duties of one’s varṇa and stage of life, the customs of one’s community, and law in the sense of rules applied in courts (Chapters 2 and 9). Dharmaśāstra is the Sanskrit scholarly literature on dharma, from the Dharmasūtras of the last centuries BCE to the medieval commentaries and digests. In it, dharma is above all svadharma, one’s own particular duty, which differs according to varṇa, āśrama, gender and circumstance.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Vyavahāra, Daṇḍa, Prāyaścitta
docs.text: Within Dharmaśāstra, vyavahāra (“transaction”, hence “lawsuit”) is the part dealing with courts, procedure and the titles of law (Chapters 12 and 13); daṇḍa is punishment by the king (Chapter 14); prāyaścitta is penance for sin. Ācāra, “conduct”, covers the rites of passage, daily duties, purity and the rules of the varṇas and āśramas (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 1.1.4 Varṇa and Jāti
docs.text: Two terms for social groups recur throughout. Varṇa refers to the fourfold scheme of the texts — Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya and Śūdra — in which the first three are “twice-born” and the Śūdra is assigned to their service, with groups regarded as untouchable placed below or outside the four. Jāti, “birth”, refers to the many endogamous hereditary groups of social life, which the English word “caste” usually denotes. The texts tried to map jātis onto varṇas and to rank them (Chapter 10). The relation between these textual schemes and social reality is a major problem of Indian history; this book uses “varṇa” for the textual categories and “caste” in the ordinary modern sense, and does not assume that either was static.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The Śāstras
docs.text: The core sources are the śāstras: technical treatises in Sanskrit, written by and largely for Brahmin specialists, which set out the rules of a discipline. They are normative texts: they say how things ought to be done. They draw on and sometimes record practice, but they cannot be read as descriptions of how any particular kingdom was governed or any particular court decided cases. The relationship between śāstra and practice is one of the main themes of modern scholarship (Chapters 9 and 16) (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 1.2.2 The Epics and Other Literature
docs.text: The Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, composed over several centuries around the turn of the era, contain long discussions of kingship and dharma, and their stories of good and bad kings, of war and its moral costs, shaped Indian political imagination more than any treatise (Chapter 5). Story literature such as the Pañcatantra, framed as instruction for princes, taught political maxims to a wide audience. Tamil literature contributed its own tradition of political ethics in the Tirukkuṟaḷ.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Buddhist, Jain and Islamic Texts
docs.text: The Pali canon of the Theravāda Buddhists and other Buddhist literature contain accounts of the origin of kingship, ideals of the righteous ruler and the most detailed procedural law of early India in the monastic code (Chapter 8). Jain authors wrote on polity and adapted Brahmanical social theory. From the thirteenth century, Arabic and Persian works of Islamic jurisprudence and political ethics, and the records of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal empire, provide another major body of evidence (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 1.2.4 Inscriptions and Records
docs.text: Inscriptions on stone and copper plate — from Aśoka’s edicts in the third century BCE to the land grants and temple records of the medieval period — are the most important evidence for how kings presented their rule and how local institutions worked. Later, Mughal and colonial archives, court records and law reports document legal practice in detail.

docs.title: 1.3 Chronology
docs.text:
Dating Indian texts is difficult, and older books often give dates that current scholarship has revised. This volume follows the series standard: academic ranges are given first, and traditional dates are labelled as traditional. The most important dates for this volume are:

  • Ṛgveda, c. 1500–1200 BCE (core); later Vedic texts c. 1200–500 BCE (Chapter 2).

  • The Buddha, c. 480–400 BCE on the short chronology now widely accepted (traditional Theravāda dates 624–544 BCE); Mahāvīra an older contemporary.

  • Aśoka, r. c. 268–232 BCE (Chapter 8).

  • Dharmasūtras, c. 3rd–1st centuries BCE (Chapter 9).

  • Arthaśāstra, a composite text of c. 50 BCE–300 CE (Olivelle); its attribution to Kauṭilya or Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya (c. 300 BCE), is traditional (Chapter 3).

  • Manusmṛti, c. 2nd century CE (Olivelle) (Chapter 10).

  • Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, composed over several centuries, c. 400 BCE–400 CE.

  • Yājñavalkyasmṛti, c. 4th–5th century CE; Nāradasmṛti, c. 5th–6th century; Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana, c. 6th–7th century (Chapter 11).

  • Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra, c. 500–700 CE.

  • Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara, c. 1100–1120; Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana, c. 12th century.

  • Mānasollāsa, 1131; Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī, 1148–49; Vijayanagara, c. 1336–1565 (Chapter 17).

  • Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1526; Mughal empire, from 1526; Fatāwā-i ʿĀlamgīrī, compiled in the 1660s and early 1670s (Chapter 18).

  • Hastings’s Judicial Plan, 1772; Indian Penal Code, 1860; Constitution of India, 1950; Hindu Code, 1955–56 (Chapters 19 and 20).

A fuller chronology is given at the end of the volume.

docs.title: 1.4 Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra: Two Traditions
docs.text: The two halves of this volume’s title name two Sanskrit traditions that overlapped and argued with each other: one written for the king and his ministers and judging policy by its effects on power and prosperity, the other written for Brahmin experts and householders and judging conduct by its conformity to dharma. Both took a hierarchical society for granted, and the Yājñavalkyasmṛti ruled that where they conflict, dharmaśāstra prevails (Yājñ 2.21). Their shared ground and their differences are discussed in Chapter 9; the Mahābhārata, which incorporates both, dramatised the tension between them in the figure of a king who must use violence to protect dharma and is tormented by the cost (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 1.5 A Vocabulary of Rule
docs.text:
Sanskrit political writing has a rich vocabulary, and several words recur so often that it is useful to introduce them here. The ruler is rājan (king), nṛpa or narapati (“lord of men”), bhūpati or pṛthivīpati (“lord of the earth”) and, in the Arthaśāstra’s analysis, svāmin, “owner” or “lord”. The ruled are prajā, a word that means both “subjects” and “offspring”, so that the king’s relationship to his people is constantly compared to a father’s to his children. The territory is rāṣṭra, janapada or deśa; the kingdom as a whole is rājya. The king’s officials are amātya or mantrin, and his chaplain the purohita. Political action is described in terms of nīti (policy, leading), naya (prudence), upāya (means) and yoga (application); its goals are the protection (rakṣaṇa, pālana) of the subjects and the “acquisition and secure possession” of good things (yogakṣema); its instrument is daṇḍa.

Legal vocabulary is equally developed. A lawsuit is vyavahāra; its parties are the plaintiff (vādin, arthin) and the defendant (prativādin, pratyarthin); the judge is the prāḍvivāka or dharmastha, the assessors the sabhya; evidence is pramāṇa; witnesses are sākṣin; documents lekhya; possession bhukti; ordeals divya. The texts distinguish ownership (svatva, svāmya) from possession, debt (ṛṇa) from deposit (nikṣepa), and the property of women (strīdhana) from that of the family. A glossary at the end of the volume lists the most important terms.

These words did not have fixed meanings across two millennia. Dharma, as Chapter 2 shows, had a long history before it became the name of a science; rājan meant a tribal chief in the Ṛgveda and an imperial monarch in the Gupta inscriptions; sabhā could mean a Vedic gathering, a royal court of justice or the assembly of a Brahmin village. Reading the sources historically means paying attention to such changes.

docs.title: 1.6 Beyond the King
docs.text:
Indian political thought is often equated with the theory of kingship, and the texts on which this book is based were indeed written for or about kings. But monarchy was not the only form of rule in early India, and kings were not the only holders of authority. The gaṇa or saṅgha polities of the Buddha’s time, governed by assemblies of the heads of ruling clans, survived in parts of northern and western India for several centuries, and the Arthaśāstra devotes a book to them (Chapter 8). Within kingdoms, guilds, merchant associations, temple bodies, caste councils and village assemblies regulated much of social and economic life, and inscriptions record their rules and decisions (Chapters 13 and 16). Brahmin scholars, Buddhist and Jain monastic communities and, later, Muslim jurists exercised a different kind of authority, based on learning and religious prestige rather than force.

The texts were also written in many languages. Sanskrit dominates this book because the major treatises on polity and law were written in it; but Pali Buddhist texts, Prakrit inscriptions, the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ and Caṅkam poetry, Persian works on statecraft and ethics, and Arabic works of Islamic jurisprudence are equally part of the history of Indian political and legal thought. The volume gives them a place, though it cannot treat them all at the length they deserve.

docs.title: 1.7 Voices of Dissent
docs.text: The hierarchical vision of the Brahmanical texts did not go unchallenged within Indian traditions. The Buddha and Mahāvīra rejected the claim that birth determined worth (Chapter 8). In the twelfth century, the Vīraśaiva poet-saint Basavaṇṇa and his companions in the Kannada country composed devotional sayings (vacana) that mocked caste pride and ritual purity and welcomed devotees of every caste into their community. Bhakti poets in many languages — among them the Tamil Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs, Cokhāmeḷā and Tukārām in Marathi, Kabīr and Ravidās in the north — proclaimed that devotion, not birth, made a person acceptable to God, and several of them came from castes regarded as low or untouchable. The Sikh Gurus, from Guru Nānak (1469–1539) onwards, rejected the authority of caste in religious life and instituted the common kitchen (laṅgar) in which all ate together. These movements did not abolish caste in society, and many of them were later absorbed into caste structures; but they show that the language of equality before God was available in Indian traditions long before modern constitutional law. Volumes 4 and 8 of this series discuss them further.

docs.title: 1.8 How Modern Scholarship Came to These Texts
docs.text:
The modern study of Indian polity and law began in the colonial courts. From the 1770s the East India Company commissioned digests of Hindu and Islamic law and translations of the Manusmṛti and other texts, in order to administer “native law” in its courts (Chapter 19). William Jones, H. T. Colebrooke and their successors created the first European scholarship on Dharmaśāstra, and their translations shaped both colonial law and European ideas of India. In the later nineteenth century, philologists such as Georg Bühler and Julius Jolly published translations of the main smṛtis in the Sacred Books of the East (Bühler 1886; Jolly 1889), and Jolly’s Recht und Sitte (1896) was the first scholarly history of Hindu law.

The discovery of the Arthaśāstra in 1905 transformed the field (Chapter 3). It seemed to show that ancient India had possessed a secular, practical science of government, and Indian historians of the nationalist period — K. P. Jayaswal, N. N. Law, R. C. Majumdar, A. S. Altekar and others — used it, together with the epics and inscriptions, to argue that India had a tradition of constitutional government, representative assemblies and corporate self-rule comparable to that of Europe (Jayaswal 1924; Majumdar 1918; Altekar 1958). Their work was a response to colonial claims of “oriental despotism”, and it collected much valuable evidence, but it often read modern institutions into ancient texts. U. N. Ghoshal and, later, R. S. Sharma subjected these claims to critical scrutiny; Sharma in particular related political ideas to the social and economic history of the periods that produced them (Ghoshal 1959; Sharma 1959). A. L. Basham’s general survey of 1954, written for a wide readership, gave a generation of students outside India a sympathetic but measured account of ancient Indian kingship and law (Basham 1954).

The history of Dharmaśāstra was transformed by P. V. Kane’s History of Dharmaśāstra (1930–62), an encyclopaedic survey of the entire literature, and by the work of Robert Lingat, J. D. M. Derrett and Ludo Rocher, who studied the relation between śāstra, custom and colonial law (Kane 1930; Lingat 1973; Derrett 1968; Rocher 2012). Since the 1990s, critical editions and translations by Patrick Olivelle and others have revised the dates and the textual history of the main works, and scholars such as Donald Davis and Mark McClish have proposed new ways of understanding the relation between the śāstras and legal and political practice (Olivelle 2005, 2013; Davis 2010; McClish 2019).

A second line of critical scholarship came from those whom the texts placed at the bottom of society. Jotirao Phule in the nineteenth century and B. R. Ambedkar in the twentieth read the Brahmanical texts as instruments of caste domination, and Ambedkar’s historical studies of the Śūdras and of untouchability remain important works of scholarship as well as of politics (Ambedkar 1946). After Ambedkar, Dalit and Dalit-Bahujan writers and scholars — among them Gopal Guru, Kancha Ilaiah and Anand Teltumbde — carried this critique into political theory, sociology and the study of constitutional practice (Section 20.2). From the 1980s, feminist historians such as Uma Chakravarti examined the same texts as sources for the history of patriarchy (Chakravarti 1993, 2003), and Kumkum Roy studied how the Brahmanical ritual and legal texts recorded the emergence of monarchy in north India (Roy 1994). Historians of Islamic India — among them Irfan Habib, Muzaffar Alam and John Richards — have shown how the Sultanate and Mughal states governed a plural society (Habib 1963; Alam 2004; Richards 1993), and historians of colonial law, such as Bernard Cohn, Marc Galanter and Radhika Singha, have shown how the British transformed what they claimed to preserve (Cohn 1996; Galanter 1989; Singha 1998). This volume draws on all these traditions of scholarship.

docs.title: 1.9 A Note on Translation and Citation
docs.text:
Every translation of these texts involves choices that shape how they are understood. Dharma has been rendered as “law”, “duty”, “religion”, “righteousness”, “virtue” and “order”; each captures part of its meaning and each misleads if taken alone. This book usually leaves the word untranslated, and specifies the sense intended where the context requires it. Varṇa is rendered “class” and jāti “caste”, following common scholarly practice; the English word “caste” itself comes from the Portuguese casta, “lineage” or “breed”, applied by sixteenth-century Portuguese observers to the communities they encountered, and it does not correspond exactly to either Indian term. Rājan is translated “king”, although the Vedic rājan was often a tribal chief rather than a monarch in the later sense; rājya and rāṣṭra are rendered “kingdom” or “realm”, and “state” is used, with caution, where the Arthaśāstra’s conception of an organised apparatus of government justifies it. The phrase “Hindu law” is itself an English creation of the colonial period: the Sanskrit texts speak of dharma and vyavahāra, not of a law belonging to a religious community called Hindus (Rocher 2012; Davis 2010).

Citations of primary texts follow the usual conventions. The Arthaśāstra is cited by book, chapter and sentence in Kangle’s numbering, which Olivelle’s translation retains (thus AŚ 1.19.34). The Manusmṛti is cited by chapter and verse in Olivelle’s critical edition, which differs only slightly from the older vulgate numbering. The Yājñavalkyasmṛti is cited in the vulgate numbering used by the Mitākṣarā, which differs from that of the older commentary of Viśvarūpa. The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa are cited by book, chapter and verse of the critical editions prepared at Poona and Baroda; many older works cite them from the vulgate editions, whose numbering differs considerably. Aśoka’s inscriptions are cited by edict (Rock Edict, Pillar Edict) in the edition of Hultzsch (1925). The abbreviations used for texts in references are listed after the table of contents; note that MīS is the Mīmāṃsāsūtra, while the Manusmṛti is cited simply as “Manu”. Where the numbering of a verse is uncertain or varies between editions, this is noted, and readers who check a quotation against another edition should expect occasional discrepancies.

Translations are based on the published translations listed in the bibliography, especially those of Olivelle for the Arthaśāstra, the Dharmasūtras and the Manusmṛti and of Lariviere for the Nāradasmṛti, sometimes adapted for consistency of terminology. Diacritics follow the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration for Sanskrit and Pali, and the usual scholarly systems for Tamil, Persian and Arabic; modern Indian personal and place names are given in their familiar English spellings.

docs.title: 1.10.1 Texts in Context
docs.text: This volume treats its sources as historical documents. Each was written at a particular time, by particular kinds of people, for particular purposes. The Manusmṛti was composed by Brahmin authors in the second century CE, in a world of foreign dynasties and powerful heterodox movements; the Arthaśāstra was compiled from earlier sources and revised over several centuries; the Mitākṣarā was written at a Deccan court in the twelfth century. Reading them in context means neither condemning them for failing to hold modern values nor exempting them from judgement by those values.

docs.title: 1.10.2 Quotations
docs.text: Quotations from primary texts are given only when their wording and reference could be checked against standard editions and translations, and they are kept short. Many passages that circulate in popular books as quotations from the śāstras are garbled, misattributed or invented, and they are not used here. Where a passage is paraphrased, the reference is given. Verse numbers follow the editions cited (for the Manusmṛti, Olivelle’s critical edition; for the Arthaśāstra, Kangle and Olivelle); numbering in other editions may differ slightly. Readers who wish to use any passage for scholarly purposes should consult the editions themselves.

docs.title: 1.10.3 Modern Comparisons
docs.text: Comparisons between Indian and other political and legal traditions — with Greek and Roman thought, Machiavelli, Hobbes, the Geneva Conventions or modern constitutional, company and criminal law — can be illuminating, and they are made here where they help. Every such comparison in this book is a comparison by modern readers, not a claim that the Indian texts “anticipated” later ideas or were their source; nor does a resemblance between particular rules imply that two systems served the same ends. The policy is stated once, here, and the later chapters take it for granted rather than repeat it. Where earlier writers have claimed priority or influence, the book says briefly why the claim fails.

docs.title: 1.10.4 Caste, Gender and Critique
docs.text: The classical texts on polity and law are, among other things, charters of hierarchy. They assign rights, duties and punishments by varṇa and sex; they exclude Śūdras and women from Vedic learning; they describe some groups as untouchable; and they make women perpetual dependants of men. These features are not marginal; they are central to the texts’ vision of the good society, and they shaped Indian law until the twentieth century. The volume treats them openly, with the primary references, and it gives space to the critics who exposed them: the Buddha’s challenge to Brahmin claims of birth, the bhakti poets, Jotirao Phule, Tarabai Shinde, Pandita Ramabai, E. V. Ramasamy, B. R. Ambedkar and modern feminist and Dalit scholars (Ambedkar 1936; Chakravarti 2003; Sharma 1958).

docs.title: 1.11 Indian Traditions in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Readers coming to this subject from other traditions of political and legal thought will find much that is familiar and much that is not. Like the political philosophers of classical Greece and China, Indian writers asked what makes a ruler legitimate, how a state should be organised, and how justice can be secured. Like Roman jurists and the scholars of Islamic and Jewish law, Indian jurists developed elaborate classifications of obligations, rules of evidence and methods of interpreting authoritative texts. These parallels are instructive, and comparison can help to bring out the distinctive features of each tradition.

Several features of the Indian materials deserve emphasis. First, political theory and law were developed largely by Brahmin scholars within a religious framework, in which the king’s duty was to uphold an order of varṇas and āśramas believed to be grounded in the cosmos and the Veda. Deliberation was not unknown — the assemblies of the gaṇa-saṅghas, the formal procedure of the Buddhist order, debates at royal courts and the village assemblies of the Cōḷa country all record it (Chapters 2, 8 and 16) — but no literature of political philosophy arising from such public debate survives, as it does from the Greek city-states. Second, the most systematic work on statecraft, the Arthaśāstra, was a technical manual for rulers rather than a philosophical inquiry into the best form of government; it does not ask, as Plato and Aristotle did, which constitution is best, but how a king can preserve and enlarge his power. Third, legal thought was organised around the duties of particular persons rather than general rights, and its central institutions — the household, the caste, the guild — were corporate. Fourth, the tradition was plural in its sources of authority: Veda, smṛti, custom and the king’s command each had a place, and their relationship was a matter of continuing debate.

These features have led some writers to describe Indian political thought as “duty-based” rather than “rights-based”, and to present it as a corrective to modern individualism. The contrast contains some truth, but it can easily become a caricature. Classical Indian law recognised many entitlements — of creditors and debtors, owners and heirs, wives and widows — and protected them through courts; and modern rights-based constitutions, including India’s, impose duties as well as conferring rights. The more useful contrast is between a legal order in which entitlements depended on birth, sex and status, and one in which they belong equally to all citizens. Chapter 20 returns to this question.

docs.title: 1.12 The Plan of the Book
docs.text:
The book has twenty chapters, in four groups.

Foundations and statecraft.

Chapter 2 traces the Vedic background: ṛta, truth, the early history of dharma and the Vedic assemblies. Chapter 3 introduces the Arthaśāstra as a text: its date, structure, method and reception, including Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra, the principal later treatise of the discipline. Chapters 4–7 examine its theory of the state’s seven constituents, the theory of kingship (rājadharma) in the śāstras and the epics, the political economy of revenue and administration, and the theory of the circle of kings, diplomacy, espionage and war. The chapter on rājadharma (Chapter 5) draws more on the epics and the Dharmaśāstras than on the Arthaśāstra, but it is placed immediately after the theory of the seven constituents because it treats the first and most important of them, the king, and because the later Arthaśāstra chapters on revenue and foreign policy presuppose the account of his duties that it gives. Chapter 8 turns to Buddhist and Jain political and legal thought, including Aśoka’s dhamma and the monastic law of the saṅgha; it closes the first group because it offers the main early alternatives to the Brahmanical theories of kingship set out before it.

The Dharmaśāstra tradition.

Chapter 9 surveys the Dharmaśāstra literature, its sources of authority and its methods of interpretation. Chapter 10 is devoted to the Manusmṛti, including its provisions on varṇa and women and their modern critics. Chapter 11 discusses Yājñavalkya, Nārada and the later smṛtis, and the Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga.

Law.

Chapters 12–15 examine the main areas of classical law: courts, procedure and proof; debt, contract, property and inheritance; crime, punishment and penance; and family, saṃskāra and the position of women. Chapter 16 turns to custom and local justice: the authority of custom, village and caste assemblies, matriliny and tribal law.

From the regional kingdoms to the Republic.

Chapter 17 reads the records of the regional kingdoms of c. 500–1700 — copper-plate charters, scribes’ formularies, the medieval treatises on kingship, Kalhaṇa’s history of Kashmir, Vijayanagara and the Ahom state — for what they show of law and government in practice. Chapter 18 describes Islamic law and the Indo-Persian state: the jurists’ method, criminal law, the qāḍī’s court, Persian political ethics, the Sultanate and Mughal empire, the Deccan, Malabar and Awadh, and the Maratha and Sikh states that succeeded the Mughals. Chapter 19 describes the making of Anglo-Hindu and Anglo-Muhammadan law under British rule. Chapter 20 considers the Constitution of India and the classical legacy, including the Dalit legal and political thought that has grown from Ambedkar’s critique.

A glossary of key terms, a chronology, notes on persons and a guide to the principal sources follow the select bibliography. Each chapter ends with a short summary and suggestions for further reading.

docs.title: 1.13 Summary
docs.text:
• Rājanīti (royal policy) and dharmaśāstra (the science of dharma) were two overlapping Sanskrit traditions of thought about political power and law. The first is represented above all by the Arthaśāstra, the second by the Dharmasūtras, the smṛtis of Manu, Yājñavalkya and Nārada, and the medieval commentaries and digests.

  • Their texts are normative śāstras written by Brahmin specialists. They must be dated carefully — the Arthaśāstra c. 50 BCE–300 CE, the Manusmṛti c. 2nd century CE — and read in context; they are not descriptions of how particular states were governed.

  • The volume places these traditions alongside Buddhist and Jain political thought, Tamil literature, customary and local law, Islamic law and the Mughal state, and the colonial and constitutional transformations of the last two and a half centuries.

  • The classical texts combine real intellectual achievements with an explicit hierarchy of varṇa and gender. Both are presented here, with the primary references and the work of modern critics.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For general introductions see Lingat (1973) and Davis (2010) on Dharmaśāstra, Olivelle (2013) on the Arthaśāstra, Sharma (1959) and Ghoshal (1959) on political ideas, and Singh (2017) on political violence. Kane (1930) remains the indispensable reference work, and Olivelle and Davis (2018) summarises current scholarship on Dharmaśāstra.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Ṛta, Satya and Dharma: The Vedic Foundations
docs.text:
The classical Indian traditions of law and statecraft did not invent their vocabulary from nothing. Their key terms — dharma, satya, daṇḍa, rājan, sabhā — already have a history in the Vedic corpus, and the authors of the Dharmasūtras and Dharmaśāstras claimed the Veda as the first source of their own authority. This chapter traces that background: the Ṛgvedic idea of ṛta, the place of truth and of the gods who guard it, the slow rise of the word dharma, and the assemblies and rituals of early kingship. It also marks the limits of what the evidence allows. The Vedic texts are liturgical poetry and ritual prose, not law books; the institutions they mention are known from scattered allusions, and much of what was once written about “Vedic democracy” or “Vedic courts” goes far beyond them.

On dates: the core of the Ṛgveda is generally placed c. 1500–1200 BCE; the later Vedic texts (the other Saṃhitās, the Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and early Upaniṣads) c. 1200–500 BCE. The Dharmasūtras, in which dharma first becomes the subject of a dedicated literature, belong to the last three centuries BCE (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Word and Its Range
docs.text:
Ṛta is a past participle formed from the root ṛ, “to move, to fit, to join”; its sense is close to “what is fitted, what is in its right place and course”. It has an exact Avestan cognate, aša (older arta), and the pair shows that an idea of right order goes back to the common Indo-Iranian inheritance. In the Ṛgveda ṛta is one of the most important abstract notions. It names the regular course of nature — the dawns that never fail to arrive, the rivers that flow, the year that turns — and, at the same time, the correct course of the sacrifice, which the poets understood as keeping that larger order going. The gods are “born of ṛta” or “grow strong through ṛta”; the sacrificial fire is its charioteer; the dawns follow its “path” (ṛtasya panthāḥ).

The moral sense grows out of the cosmic and ritual ones. To speak falsely, to break an agreement, or to fail the gods in ritual is to act against ṛta; its opposite is anṛta, “untruth, disorder”. Jan Gonda stressed that ṛta is less a fixed “law” than the condition of right and effective functioning in which each part of the world, including the ritual, performs as it should (Gonda 1963). This is a helpful caution. Ṛta is not a code of rules that a court could apply; it is a vision of a world held in order, within which human truthfulness and correct ritual have their place.

Ṛgveda 10.190.1

ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata tato rātry ajāyata tataḥ samudro arṇavaḥ “Order and truth were born from heat kindled to its height; from that was born night, and from that the billowing sea.”

In this late cosmogonic hymn ṛta and satya stand at the very beginning of the created world, before night and the ocean. The pairing is characteristic. Satya (“what is real, true”) is in many contexts the human, spoken face of ṛta: the true word that matches what is.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Varuṇa and Mitra
docs.text:
The guardians of ṛta among the gods are above all the Ādityas, and especially Varuṇa and Mitra, often invoked together as the dual deity Mitrāvaruṇā. Varuṇa watches human conduct with his spies (spaśaḥ) and binds wrongdoers in his fetters (pāśa); the poets of the hymns to him (notably Ṛgveda 1.24–25, 2.28 and 7.86–89) ask to be released from guilt (āgas) they may have committed knowingly or unknowingly. In Ṛgveda 7.86, attributed to the poet Vasiṣṭha, the speaker asks Varuṇa what his chief offence has been, that the god should wish to destroy a praiser who is his friend, and begs to be told so that he may come to the god free of guilt. The tone is that of a man before a superior whose anger he does not understand, and it is easy to see why modern readers have spoken of Varuṇa as a “judge”. The image should not be pressed too far: there is no procedure, no plaint and no verdict in these hymns, only guilt, confession and the hope of release.

Mitra, whose name is also an ordinary noun meaning “contract, alliance” and then “friend” (it is cognate with Avestan Mithra), is the god of agreements between people. Paul Thieme and others showed how closely the Indo-Iranian Mitra is tied to the binding force of the pact. Georges Dumézil made the pair Mitra–Varuṇa the centre of his theory of the “sovereign function” in Indo-European ideology, with Mitra standing for the contractual, benevolent side of sovereignty and Varuṇa for its awesome, binding side (Dumézil 1988). Dumézil’s wider tripartite scheme is much debated, but the observation that early Indian ideas of rule join cosmic order, binding agreement and royal power remains useful. It is a modern scholarly construction, however, not a doctrine stated in the hymns.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Anṛta and the Weight of Truth
docs.text:
The Vedic poets treat untruth as a serious fault, and later law inherited this attitude in its treatment of testimony. In the Dharmaśāstras perjury is among the gravest offences a witness can commit, and Manu devotes a long passage (8.60–123) to the examination of witnesses, warning that the false witness falls into hell and destroys the merit of his ancestors (Chapter 12). Manu also prescribes how witnesses are to be put on oath according to their varṇa: a Brahmin by his truthfulness, a Kṣatriya by his mount and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain and gold, and a Śūdra by all the grievous sins (8.113). The rule shows both continuities — truth as the core of legal process — and the way in which the later texts graded every procedure by social rank.

It is tempting to read a straight line from Varuṇa’s fetters to the courtroom oath, but the connection is one of shared vocabulary and attitude, not institutional descent. The Vedic texts themselves contain no classification of kinds of falsehood with graded penalties; tables of such “Vedic” offences in popular books have no basis in the sources.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Dharman in the Ṛgveda
docs.text: The word dharma (Vedic dhárman) derives from the root dhṛ, “to hold, support, uphold”. A verse found in the Mahābhārata gives the classic later etymology: dharma is so called because it “upholds” (dhāraṇa) creatures. In the Ṛgveda, however, dhárman is a relatively uncommon word. Joel Brereton’s study of its occurrences concludes that it means something like “foundation” or “support”, the base on which a thing stands, and in some contexts the “ordinances” that establish and maintain order; it is closely associated with ṛta and with the Ādityas, but it is not yet the master concept it later became (Brereton 2004).

docs.title: 2.2.2 From the Brāhmaṇas to the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
In the middle and late Vedic texts the word appears more often, and frequently in connection with the king. Patrick Olivelle has shown that in this period dharma is associated especially with royal power and with Varuṇa, the divine king; the king is the “protector of dharma” (Olivelle 2004). A well-known passage in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.4.14) makes the point in a striking way. After the creation of the social orders, the creator “brought forth a form superior to himself, dharma”; dharma is “the ruling power of the ruling power” (kṣatrasya kṣatram), and “there is nothing higher than dharma”. Through dharma “a weak man can prevail over a strong one, as with the help of a king”. The same passage identifies dharma with truth: what is dharma is truth, and so people say of one who speaks truth that he speaks dharma. This is perhaps the earliest Indian statement of the idea that a principle of right stands above even the power of the ruler — though it is a theological statement, not a constitutional one.

The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (2.23.1) speaks of three “branches” (skandha) of dharma: sacrifice, study and giving; austerity; and the life of the student living in his teacher’s house. Here dharma is already the sum of a person’s religious duties according to his way of life — the sense it has in the Dharmasūtras.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Why Dharma Became Central
docs.text: Olivelle has argued that the sudden prominence of dharma after the Vedic period owes much to its adoption by the new religious movements and by the Mauryan state. The Buddha’s teaching is dhamma; Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) made dhaṃma the watchword of his inscriptions (Chapter 8). On this view the Brahmanical Dharmasūtras, which appear in the following centuries, are in part a response: they claim the term for the Vedic tradition and define it as the duties of the varṇas and āśramas, grounded in the Veda (Olivelle 2004; Olivelle and Davis 2018). Not every scholar accepts every step of this argument, but it is an important corrective to the assumption that dharma had always been the central concept of Brahmanical thought.

docs.title: 2.3 Satya and the Social Order
docs.text:
Truth appears again and again in later Vedic teaching as the foundation of right conduct. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s instruction to the departing student begins: “Speak the truth; practise dharma” (satyaṃ vada, dharmaṃ cara, 1.11.1). The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad’s satyam eva jayate (3.1.6), “truth alone conquers”, became the national motto of the Republic of India. Both are moral and religious teachings; their later use in public life is a matter of reception, discussed in Chapter 20.

The same Vedic sources that exalt truth also lay the foundations of social hierarchy. The Puruṣasūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90.12), a late hymn, describes the Brahmin as the mouth of the cosmic Person, the Rājanya as his arms, the Vaiśya as his thighs and the Śūdra as born from his feet. In the Brāhmaṇas, the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya are repeatedly described as the two powers (brahman and kṣatra) that together rule over the others, and the Vaiśya and Śūdra as their subordinates. The later law books take this ranking as given; it is the starting point of the varṇa provisions discussed honestly in Chapters 10 and 14 (Sharma 1958).

docs.title: 2.3.1 Truth in Later Tradition
docs.text: The Vedic exaltation of truth had a long afterlife in Indian moral and political imagination. The legend of King Hariścandra, told in the Purāṇas, presents a king who gives up his kingdom, his wife and his son and becomes the servant of a cremation-ground keeper rather than break his word; it became one of the most popular stories in Indian literature and drama. M. K. Gandhi recorded in his autobiography that a play about Hariścandra, seen in his childhood, made a deep impression on him, and he made truth (satya) the centre of his political method, which he called satyāgraha, “holding fast to truth”. These modern uses, like the choice of the Muṇḍaka’s phrase as the national motto, are part of the reception of the Vedic idea, not evidence of continuity of institutions; but they show how the conviction that truth upholds the world could be given new political meanings.

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Śūdra and the Woman in Vedic Texts
docs.text:
The later Vedic texts already show the subordination that the law books would systematise. A passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.29), describing the characteristics of the varṇas, says that the Śūdra is “the servant of another, to be expelled at will, to be slain at will”. The Śūdra was excluded from the solemn Vedic sacrifices, and the Brāhmaṇas debate whether he may even be present at them. R. S. Sharma used such passages, together with the evidence of the Dharmasūtras, to trace the progressive degradation of the Śūdras from the late Vedic period onwards (Sharma 1958).

Women’s position in Vedic ritual was more complex. The wife of the sacrificer was a necessary participant in the solemn rites, which a man could not perform without her, and some hymns of the Ṛgveda are attributed by tradition to women poets. Stephanie Jamison’s study of the sacrificer’s wife shows that her ritual role was real and significant, while also being defined by her relation to her husband (Jamison 1996). The idea of a Vedic “golden age” of women’s freedom, popularised by nationalist historians, has been criticised by feminist historians as an idealisation that served to present later subordination as a decline from an Aryan norm (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 2.3.3 The Doctrine of the Debts
docs.text: Another Vedic idea with long legal consequences is that of the debts (ṛṇa) with which a man is born. The Taittirīya Saṃhitā (6.3.10.5) says that a Brahmin is born with three debts: to the seers, paid by Vedic study as a student; to the gods, paid by sacrifice; and to the ancestors, paid by begetting offspring. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.7.2.1–5) adds a debt to men, paid by hospitality. The doctrine expressed the householder’s obligations, and the Dharmaśāstras later used it to argue against renouncing the world before marrying and having a son (Olivelle 1993). The need for a son to pay the debt to the ancestors through the offerings of the ancestral rite (śrāddha) also underlies the law of adoption and inheritance (Chapters 13 and 15). The doctrine tells us about Brahmanical religious obligation; it is not, as is sometimes claimed, a theory of political duty.

docs.title: 2.4 Kingship and Assemblies in the Vedic Texts
2.4.1 The Rājan
docs.text:
The Ṛgvedic rājan was the leader of a clan or tribe (jana, viś), above all a war leader and protector of the people’s cattle. His position was hereditary in some cases and perhaps elective in others; the evidence is too thin for certainty. By the later Vedic period, as settlements spread in the Gaṅgā–Yamunā region, kingship became more elaborate. The Brāhmaṇas describe great royal consecrations such as the rājasūya and the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), in which the king’s power is ritually constituted and displayed. Romila Thapar has described this period as a transition “from lineage to state”: chiefdoms based on kinship gave way, gradually and unevenly, to kingdoms with more permanent authority, revenue and administration (Thapar 1984).

The ritual texts already associate kingship with protection and with the support of the Brahmin. In the rājasūya, the king is presented to the people as their ruler and the priest declares that Soma is the king of the Brahmins; the “jewels” (ratnin) of the court — the general, the chief queen, the charioteer, the collector and others — receive offerings in their houses. These rites show a court with differentiated officers, but they are rituals; they do not describe a governmental system in detail (Heesterman 1985; Gonda 1966).

docs.title: 2.4.2 Sabhā, Samiti and Vidatha
docs.text:
Three kinds of gathering appear in the Vedic texts: the sabhā, the samiti and the vidatha. Their nature has been argued over for a century. The sabhā seems to have been both a building and a gathering of notables, a place of deliberation, of gaming with dice and of social prestige; a man “worthy of the assembly” (sabheya) is a respected figure. The samiti appears as a larger assembly of the people or the clan, which a king might attend. The vidatha is the most obscure; it may have been a gathering connected with ritual and the distribution of goods (Sharma 1959).

Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 7.12.1

sabhā ca mā samitiś cāvatāṃ prajāpater duhitarau saṃvidāne “May the assembly (sabhā) and the gathering (samiti), the two daughters of Prajāpati, in accord, help me.”

The Ṛgveda closes with a hymn (10.191) of concord addressed to an assembly: “Come together, speak together, let your minds be of one accord” (saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ saṃ vo manāṃsi jānatām, 10.191.2). These passages show that collective deliberation was valued. Nationalist historians of the early twentieth century, above all K. P. Jayaswal, read them as evidence for a “Hindu” constitutional tradition of popular assemblies, a parliament and a judiciary (Jayaswal 1924). That reading answered a colonial claim that India had known only despotism, and it was understandable in its time; but it goes far beyond the evidence. The texts say nothing about how membership was determined, how decisions were taken or what powers the assemblies had over a king, and there is no evidence that they exercised anything like judicial review. R. S. Sharma’s study remains the most careful survey (Sharma 1959). The sabhā of the later law books is something different again: the court of the king or of his judge, with assessors (sabhya) chosen for learning in the Veda (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 2.4.3 Hymns for the King
docs.text: Some Vedic hymns were composed for use in royal rites. Ṛgveda 10.173, a hymn for the installation or confirmation of a king, prays that he may stand firm and unshaken “like a mountain”, that all the clans (viśaḥ) may want him, and that the kingdom may not slip from him; it calls on Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, Indra and Agni to hold his kingship firm. The Atharvaveda contains several hymns for kings: for their consecration, for victory, for the return of an exiled king, and for success in the assembly. Nationalist historians read the phrases in which the people “choose” or “want” the king as evidence of election. The hymns certainly express the ideal that a king should have the support of his people, but they are prayers and spells, not records of elections, and they do not tell us how kings were actually chosen (Sharma 1959).

docs.title: 2.4.4 Kings and Gods in the Brāhmaṇas
docs.text:
The Brāhmaṇas also contain myths about the origin of kingship. In one well-known passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (1.14), the gods are defeated by the demons and conclude that this is because they have no king; “let us make a king”, they say, and they make Soma their king, after which they are victorious. The story presents kingship as a remedy for weakness in conflict, an idea that the later mātsyanyāya theory would develop in a different direction (Chapter 5). Other passages explain the king’s power as conferred by the gods in the rituals of consecration, or describe the king as the visible form of Indra, the warrior king of the gods.

The royal rituals themselves are described at length. In the rājasūya, the king was anointed with waters from many sources; he made offerings in the houses of the “jewels” (ratnin) of his court; he played a ritual game of dice; and he took symbolic steps in the four directions to show his rule over the earth. In the aśvamedha, the horse sacrifice, a consecrated horse was allowed to wander for a year, guarded by armed men, and any ruler through whose land it passed without challenge was taken to acknowledge the sacrificer’s supremacy. The vājapeya included a chariot race that the sacrificer won. These rites, which later kings sometimes revived — several Gupta and other kings boasted of performing the horse sacrifice — show how closely kingship was bound to Brahmanical ritual. They also show the dependence of the king on the priest, a theme that J. C. Heesterman explored in his studies of the “inner conflict” between royal power and Brahmanical authority (Heesterman 1985).

docs.title: 2.4.5 The Gambler and the Assembly
docs.text: The Vedic sabhā was not only a place of deliberation. The famous “gambler’s hymn” of the Ṛgveda (10.34), the lament of a man ruined by dice, describes him going to the sabhā to gamble, his body burning with hope, and losing everything, while his wife is abandoned and his family disowns him. The hymn reminds us that the assembly was a place of sociability and play as well as of counsel. The dice game reappears in the royal rituals and, most famously, in the Mahābhārata, where Yudhiṣṭhira gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadī in the assembly hall of the Kauravas — an episode that raises, in dramatic form, questions about the legality of a wager and the rights of a wife that the later law books also discussed (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 2.4.6 Kings in the Upaniṣads
docs.text: The early Upaniṣads show kings in another light: as patrons and participants in philosophical debate. Janaka of Videha presides over the great debate in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad in which Yājñavalkya defeats the Brahmins of the Kuru-Pañcāla country and answers the questions of Gārgī Vācaknavī. In several dialogues a Kṣatriya king teaches a Brahmin — Ajātaśatru of Kāśī instructs the proud Brahmin Gārgya (BU 2.1), and Pravāhaṇa Jaivali teaches the doctrine of the “five fires” and rebirth, remarking that this knowledge had previously been the possession of Kṣatriyas (BU 6.2; CU 5.3). In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.11), King Aśvapati Kaikeya receives a group of learned householders with the declaration that in his realm there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no man who does not keep the sacred fire, no ignorant man and no adulterer, let alone an adulteress. The boast is the earliest Indian statement of the ideal kingdom as a moral community in which the king’s virtue is reflected in the conduct of his subjects — an ideal that the epics and the śāstras would develop at length.

docs.title: 2.4.7 From Vedic Kingship to the Śāstras
docs.text: Between the Vedic rituals and the śāstric theory of kingship lies a long and poorly documented history. The rise of territorial kingdoms and cities in the Gangetic plain from about the sixth century BCE, the formation of the Magadhan state, the Mauryan empire and the kingdoms that followed it created new forms of government that the Vedic texts do not describe. The śāstras inherited from the Vedic world the vocabulary of kingship, the association between king and Brahmin, and the ideal of the king as protector; they added a theory of the state, of law and of administration that belongs to the later period (Thapar 1984; Sharma 1959). Kumkum Roy’s study of the emergence of monarchy in north India between the eighth and fourth centuries BCE reads the later Vedic ritual texts and the early law books for this transition, showing how the Brahmanical sources represented, and helped to legitimate, the growth of royal power over the clan (Roy 1994).

docs.title: 2.5 Ritual Forms of Proof
docs.text: Vedic literature contains the first Indian references to ordeals and solemn oaths, which later became formal modes of proof (divya). The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.16) describes a man accused of theft who is made to grasp a heated axe: if he has spoken the truth he is not burnt, and is released; if he lied, he is burnt and executed. The passage is used as an illustration of the power of truth, but it shows that the fire ordeal was a known procedure. Fire (Agni) was also invoked as a witness to agreements and above all to marriage, in which the couple circle the fire. In the Dharmaśāstras, oaths and ordeals are carefully regulated as evidence of last resort when human proof fails (Chapter 12). Nothing in the Vedic texts amounts to a law of evidence, but the conviction that a truthful person is protected by the gods underlies these later procedures.

docs.title: 2.6 Gift, Fee and the Ritual Economy
docs.text:
The Vedic sacrifice was also an economic institution. Its performance required the payment of a fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests, and the larger śrauta rites prescribed fees of hundreds or thousands of cattle, together with gold, horses and cloth. Several hymns of the Ṛgveda, known as dānastuti (“praises of the gift”), celebrate the generosity of named patrons who rewarded the poets with cattle, horses, chariots and, in some cases, slave women; these passages are among the earliest Indian evidence for the relationship between poets, priests and chiefs (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The patron who sponsored the sacrifice (yajamāna) gained prestige and divine favour; the priests gained wealth; and the exchange bound together the two groups whose alliance would later be expressed in the doctrine that the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya together uphold the world.

The ideology of the gift (dāna) that grew out of this relationship became central to later Dharmaśāstra and to the history of Indian kingship. The texts teach that gifts to worthy Brahmins bring merit to the donor, specify the proper recipients, times and objects of gifts, and condemn those who withhold the fee. Medieval kings and nobles made grants of land and villages to Brahmins and temples, recorded on copper plates that end with verses cursing anyone who confiscates the grant; thousands of these grants survive and are a principal source for the history of land rights (Chapter 5; on the law of gift, Section 13.2.4). J. C. Heesterman and others have analysed the Dharmaśāstra theory of gift as part of a wider system of exchange in which the Brahmin’s acceptance of gifts was both a privilege and, in some texts, a source of ritual danger (Heesterman 1985).

Gift and fee also defined the boundaries of the community. Only those entitled to sacrifice — the initiated men of the three higher classes — could be patrons, and only Brahmins could officiate and receive the fee. The Śūdra was excluded from both roles. The ritual economy thus encoded the hierarchy that the Puruṣasūkta expressed in myth.

docs.title: 2.7 Comparative Perspective
docs.text: Many ancient societies grounded human order in a cosmic one. The Egyptian maat, the Greek dikē and themis, and the Avestan aša (the cognate of ṛta) all join the order of nature, the duties of kings and the truthfulness of persons. These parallels suggest that the Vedic case is one instance of a widespread pattern of archaic thought, not a unique achievement. What is distinctive in India is the later history: the development, from the Dharmasūtras onwards, of a specialised scholarly literature on dharma, written and transmitted by Brahmin experts, which claimed Vedic authority while dealing increasingly with matters — property, debt, procedure, punishment — that the Veda itself did not address (Chapter 9). The idea that this literature simply “unfolded” the Vedic vision of ṛta is a theological claim of the tradition itself; historians see instead a long and contested process in which Brahmin authors adapted older ideas to new social and political conditions.
