docs.title: 3.12 Summary
docs.text:
• The Arthaśāstra is the only complete surviving treatise of the Indian science of politics. It defines its subject as the means of acquiring and protecting the earth, and it treats economics, administration, law, foreign policy and war as parts of a single science.

  • Its attribution to Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya, Viṣṇugupta), minister of Candragupta Maurya, is traditional. Trautmann’s statistical study showed that it is the work of several hands; Olivelle dates the Kauṭilya recension to c. 50–125 CE and a later redaction to c. 175–300 CE. The text is best dated c. 50 BCE–300 CE.

  • It was rediscovered by R. Shamasastry in 1905 and published in 1909 (text) and 1915 (translation); Kangle’s critical edition (1960–65) and Olivelle’s translation (2013) are now standard.

  • Its fifteen books move from the training of the king through administration and law to foreign policy, war and secret practices; Book 15 explains its method of composition.

  • It was praised and criticised by later Sanskrit authors and condensed into verse by Kāmandaka, whose Nītisāra kept its theory of the king, the constituents and foreign policy but dropped its administration and law; it was followed by a long tradition of works on polity in Sanskrit, Tamil and other languages; the Śukranīti, often cited as ancient, is a late work.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The standard translation is Olivelle (2013), with an important introduction on date and composition; McClish and Olivelle (2012) is a good selection for students. Kangle (1960) remains the basic critical edition and study, and Rangarajan (1992) a readable topical version. On authorship and date see Trautmann (1971), McClish (2019) and the short book by Trautmann (2012). Boesche (2002) and Singh (2017) discuss the text’s political thought, the latter with particular attention to violence; Singh (2010) is the best short study of Kāmandaka. Scharfe (1989) places it in the wider history of the Indian state.

docs.title: Chapter 4: The Saptāṅga Theory of the State
docs.text: Indian political theorists did not write about “the state” as an abstraction. They wrote about the kingdom (rājya) and its “constituent elements” (prakṛti), and from the Arthaśāstra onwards the standard analysis lists seven of them. The doctrine came to be called the theory of the seven-limbed (saptāṅga) kingdom. It appears in the Arthaśāstra, the Manusmṛti, the Mahābhārata, the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra and many later works, and it gave Indian political writers a shared vocabulary for analysing the strength and weakness of kingdoms. This chapter sets out the seven elements, the debates about their relative importance and about the calamities that afflict them, and the uses to which historians have put the scheme.

docs.title: 4.1 The Seven Elements
docs.text:
Book 6 of the Arthaśāstra opens with a terse list: “The king, the minister, the countryside, the fort, the treasury, the army and the ally are the constituent elements” (svāmy-amātya-janapada-durga-kośa-daṇḍa-mitrāṇi prakṛtayaḥ, AŚ 6.1.1). The Manusmṛti gives the same seven in verse and introduces the image of limbs:

Manusmṛti 9.294

svāmyamātyau puraṃ rāṣṭraṃ kośadaṇḍau suhṛt tathā sapta prakṛtayo hy etāḥ saptāṅgaṃ rājyam ucyate “The lord, the minister, the fort, the realm, the treasury, the army and the ally — these are the seven constituents; a kingdom is said to have seven limbs.”

The list is ordered: each element is, by default, more important than the one after it. The order follows the logic of a monarchical state seen from the top. The king (svāmin, “lord, owner”) rules through his ministers (amātya); together they govern a populated territory (janapada, “countryside, realm”); the territory is defended by fortified centres (durga); its resources fill the treasury (kośa); the treasury pays for the army (daṇḍa, literally “the rod”); and allies (mitra) extend the king’s power beyond his frontiers. The enemy (amitra) is sometimes counted as an eighth element, since a king’s policy is defined in relation to him, but he is not a “limb” of one’s own kingdom. Figure 4.1 sets out the scheme.

Figure 4.1. The seven constituent elements (prakṛti) of the kingdom, numbered in the Arthaśāstra’s order (AŚ 6.1.1). The arrows show the order of precedence, each element being by default weightier than the next; the Manusmṛti gives the same seven but names the fort before the realm (Manu 9.294). The dashed spokes express Manu’s qualification that the elements, held together like the three staves of an ascetic’s triple staff, support one another, so that none is absolutely superior (Manu 9.296).

docs.title: 4.1.1 Elements, Not Institutions
docs.text: It is important to see what the scheme is and is not. It does not distinguish legislative, executive and judicial functions, nor does it describe any body with power over the king. Its unit of analysis is the king’s resources: human (the king himself, the ministers, the people), material (the territory, the forts, the treasury) and military (the army, the allies). It is a theory of power and its sources, written for a ruler who wishes to preserve and increase his power — which is exactly what the Arthaśāstra says it is (Chapter 3). Each element has its ideal “excellence” (sampad), and the king’s task is to cultivate the excellences of his own elements and exploit the weaknesses of his enemy’s.

docs.title: 4.2 The King
docs.text:
The king is the first element, and the Arthaśāstra lists the qualities of an ideal ruler at length (AŚ 6.1.3–6). They fall into four groups:

  • Qualities that attract (ābhigāmika): high birth, good fortune, intelligence, courage, respect for elders, righteousness, truthfulness, keeping promises, gratitude, generosity, energy, firmness, a council of good quality, and a wish to be trained;

  • Qualities of intellect (prajñā): the desire to learn, attentive listening, grasping, retention, understanding, reflection, and the ability to reject what is false and hold to what is true;

  • Qualities of energy (utsāha): bravery, resentment of injury, speed and skill;

  • Personal excellence (ātmasampad): eloquence, boldness, memory, strength, self-control, and freedom from the vices of lust, anger, greed, obstinacy, fickleness and the like.

The list repeats the teaching of Book 1 that the king’s self-discipline is the foundation of government (Chapter 3). It also explains why the king’s calamities are the gravest of all: in the Arthaśāstra’s words, the king “appoints the minister, the chaplain and the rest” and, being himself endowed with excellences, makes the other elements excellent (AŚ 8.1.13, 8.1.16). The Mahābhārata and Kāmandaka say the same in many forms: as the king is, so are his people.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Princes, Succession and the Royal Household
docs.text:
Because the king is the first element, his safety and the succession are matters of state. The Arthaśāstra devotes chapters to the guarding of princes and to the conduct of a prince out of favour (AŚ 1.17–18). It reports a teacher’s opinion, attributed to Bhāradvāja, that princes are like crabs, which devour their begetter, and should therefore be watched closely or even done away with if they show disaffection; other teachers object that such killing is cruel and destroys the royal line, and recommend confinement or banishment to the frontier. Kauṭilya rejects these harsher proposals and recommends instead careful education, the use of secret agents to test their loyalty and to steer them away from vices, and the appointment of a worthy prince as heir. A prince who falls under suspicion is to submit patiently and seek reconciliation, unless his life is threatened. Book 5 discusses what ministers should do if the king falls mortally ill or dies: they should conceal his death until the succession is secured and the heir installed.

The royal residence itself is a place of danger. The text describes the layout of the palace with escape routes and secret passages, the precautions against fire and poison, and the testing of food and medicines; it advises the king to meet his queens only after their attendants have been checked, citing legendary kings killed by wives in their own chambers (AŚ 1.20–21). These chapters, more than any others, show the climate of suspicion in which the text imagines royal power to operate.

docs.title: 4.3 The Ministers
docs.text: The second element covers the senior officers through whom the king governs. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes the counsellors (mantrin), with whom the king deliberates on policy, from the wider body of ministers (amātya) who head the administration, and from the council of ministers (mantripariṣad). It discusses how many counsellors a king should consult and reports the opinions of earlier schools on the size of the council — twelve according to the Mānavas, sixteen according to the Bārhaspatyas and twenty according to the Auśanasas — before concluding that it should be “according to capacity” (AŚ 1.15). It warns that secret deliberation must be protected from leaks and that the king should not deliberate alone or with too many.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Counsel
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra gives great importance to counsel (mantra). All undertakings, it says, should be preceded by deliberation, and the place of deliberation should be secluded, so that not even birds can see it; it records stories of secrets betrayed by parrots and mynas, and by people who overheard or read signs (AŚ 1.15). Deliberation has five aspects: the means of starting an undertaking, the resources of men and material, the determination of place and time, provision against failure, and accomplishment. The king should consult his counsellors singly and together, weigh their opinions, and act promptly once a decision is made, for delay allows secrets to leak. A well-known verse observes that rulership can be accomplished only with assistance, for a single wheel does not turn; the king should therefore appoint counsellors and listen to their opinions (AŚ 1.7.9). The Manusmṛti likewise remarks that even an easy task is hard to accomplish alone, how much more a kingdom (7.55).

docs.title: 4.3.2 The Secret Tests
docs.text:
Ministers are appointed after their qualities have been examined and are tested through secret trials called upadhā (AŚ 1.10):

  • the test of righteousness (dharmopadhā): the chaplain, pretending to have been dismissed for refusing to officiate for an unworthy person, tries to persuade each minister to join in overthrowing the “unrighteous” king;

  • the test of wealth (arthopadhā): an army officer, pretending to have been dismissed, tempts them with money to join a plot;

  • the test of lust (kāmopadhā): a female ascetic in the king’s service tells each minister that the chief queen desires him;

  • the test of fear (bhayopadhā): the ministers are imprisoned on a pretext, and an agent among the prisoners then tries to incite them to rise against the king.

Those who pass are assigned to posts suited to the test they passed. The text records the objection that a king should not corrupt innocent men by suggesting treason to them, and it insists that the king should never make himself or his queen the object of such a test; the tests are carried out through agents. The passage shows both the sophistication of the text’s thinking about loyalty and the climate of suspicion in which its ideal court operates.

docs.title: 4.4 The Countryside and Its People
docs.text:
The janapada is the populated territory, the source of produce, revenue and soldiers. Its excellences include a good location, capacity to support the population and the army, defensibility, fertile land, mines, forests and pasture, good communications, and a population that is industrious, loyal and composed largely of cultivators and of “low” (avara) varṇas who can be made to work — a frank statement of the text’s assumption that a strong kingdom rests on a subordinate labouring population (AŚ 6.1).

Book 2 describes the settlement of new territory (janapadaniveśa): the king should found villages of 100 to 500 families, “consisting mostly of Śūdra cultivators”, by bringing people from elsewhere or by drawing off surplus population from his own land; he should grant tax remissions to new settlers, give land to those who will cultivate it and take it away from those who do not (AŚ 2.1). The territory is organised in a hierarchy of administrative centres: a sthānīya for 800 villages, a droṇamukha for 400, a khārvaṭika for 200 and a saṃgrahaṇa for every 10 (AŚ 2.1.4). The collector (samāhartṛ) divides the countryside into four divisions, each under an officer (sthānika), with accountants (gopa) responsible for groups of five or ten villages who keep records of land, households, livestock, income and expenditure (AŚ 2.35). Whether any historical kingdom ever administered its villages in this way is unknown; the scheme is the author’s ideal.

docs.title: 4.5 The Fort
docs.text:
The fort (durga) is both the fortified capital and the network of strongholds that protect the frontier. The Arthaśāstra (2.3) classifies forts by their natural defences into four kinds: water forts (audaka), on islands or surrounded by water; mountain forts (pārvata); desert forts (dhānvana); and forest forts (vanadurga). It gives detailed instructions on moats, ramparts, walls, towers and gates, and on the layout of the fortified city with its royal palace, its quarters for officials, artisans and the different varṇas, its temples and its markets (AŚ 2.3–4).

The Greek envoy Megasthenes described Pāṭaliputra, the Mauryan capital, as a city stretching along the Ganges, surrounded by a moat and by a timber wall with 570 towers and 64 gates; his account survives in the Indica of Arrian (2nd century CE). Excavations at Patna have found remains of timber palisades. Megasthenes’ Pāṭaliputra and the Arthaśāstra’s model fort share some features, but the text does not describe that city, and the resemblance should not be used to date the text (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 4.6 The Treasury
docs.text:
“All undertakings depend on the treasury” (kośapūrvāḥ sarvārambhāḥ, AŚ 2.8.1): the Arthaśāstra’s realism about money is one of its best-known features. The treasury is filled from the land tax, customs and tolls, fines, the profits of state enterprises, and a range of other levies (Chapter 6). Its excellence lies in being acquired lawfully, being full of gold, silver, gems and coin, and being able to sustain the state through a long calamity (AŚ 6.1).

The texts urge moderation in filling it — Manu’s king takes his tax little by little, like the leech, the calf and the bee (Manu 7.129) — but the advice is prudential, and the Arthaśāstra pairs it with methods of extracting money by deceit in an emergency (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 4.7 The Army
docs.text: Daṇḍa means both coercive power and its main instrument, the army. The traditional Indian army had four arms (caturaṅga): elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry. The Arthaśāstra classifies troops by their origin (AŚ 9.2): hereditary troops (maula), hired troops (bhṛta), troops supplied by corporations or guilds (śreṇī), troops of an ally (mitra), troops won over from an enemy (amitra) and forest troops (aṭavī). Each earlier type is preferable to the later, because more reliable. The ideal army is hereditary, loyal, well paid, obedient, used to hardship and mainly of Kṣatriyas, though the text also considers armies of other varṇas. War and military organisation are treated in Chapter 7 and, for military history, in Volume 20 of this series.

docs.title: 4.8 The Ally
docs.text: The last element is the ally. The best ally is one whose friendship is hereditary rather than recent, who is constant, under the king’s control, powerful, and able to mobilise quickly — an ally who will not turn against one when one is in difficulty (AŚ 6.1). The Arthaśāstra knows that alliances are interested: in its theory of the circle of kings, the neighbour is a natural enemy and the neighbour’s neighbour a natural ally, and an ally may himself become a rival if he grows too strong (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 4.9 The Calamities of the Elements
docs.text: Book 8 of the Arthaśāstra analyses the “calamities” (vyasana) that can afflict each element: a king’s vices, illness or captivity; disaffection or treachery among ministers; famine, epidemic, flood or revolt in the countryside; a damaged fort; a depleted treasury; a defeated, unpaid or mutinous army; an unreliable ally. The book is constructed as a series of debates in which earlier teachers argue that, in a given pair, the calamity of the later element is worse than that of the earlier. Bhāradvāja, for example, holds that a calamity of the minister is worse than one of the king, because the minister does the actual work of government. Kauṭilya generally answers that the canonical order holds — a calamity of the king is worse, because the king appoints and controls the minister — while accepting that the gravity of a calamity depends on its kind and extent. Book 8 also discusses the king’s vices in detail: hunting, gambling, women and drink, the “vices born of desire”, and verbal abuse, physical violence and the destruction of property, the “vices born of anger” (Kangle 1960; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 4.9.1 Calamities of the Countryside and the Army
docs.text: The later chapters of Book 8 discuss the calamities of the other elements. Among the afflictions of the countryside, the text weighs the relative gravity of fire, flood, disease, famine and plagues of rats, insects and other pests, and debates whether a calamity affecting the leaders of the country or one affecting its people is worse. Among the calamities of the army it lists, in a long series of pairs, troops that are unpaid, sick, newly arrived, exhausted by long marches, dispirited after defeat, cut off from supplies, mixed with traitors or led by a disaffected commander, and asks which is easier to remedy. It also considers the calamities of the ally and of the treasury. The method throughout is comparative and practical: the king is to know which weaknesses can be tolerated and which must be repaired first.

docs.title: 4.10 The Enemy and the Three Powers
docs.text:
The saptāṅga analysis was a tool for comparing kingdoms. The Arthaśāstra describes the “excellences of the enemy” that make him easy to overcome: an enemy who is not of royal family, greedy, with a disaffected council and subjects, unrighteous, given to vices, lacking energy, trusting to fate, without allies and with a weak army is easy to defeat, whereas a powerful enemy with loyal subjects should be resisted only with allies (AŚ 6.1). The point of knowing the elements of one’s own state was to weigh them against those of others.

The same book introduces the “three powers” (śakti) of a king: the power of counsel (mantraśakti), which consists in knowledge and good advice; the power of might (prabhuśakti), consisting of the treasury and the army; and the power of energy (utsāhaśakti), the king’s personal drive and courage (AŚ 6.2; 9.1). The teachers are reported as ranking energy highest, but Kauṭilya argues that might is superior to energy and counsel superior to might, since a king who excels in counsel can overreach even an energetic and mighty opponent by intelligence. Success (siddhi) is correspondingly of three kinds. The doctrine reappears in Kāmandaka and in later works, and it shows the Arthaśāstra’s preference for intelligence over force.

docs.title: 4.11 The Saptāṅga in Other Traditions
docs.text:
The seven-element analysis was shared by other Indian traditions. The Śānti Parvan of the Mahābhārata discusses the seven limbs of the kingdom in several places, and Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra, the most widely read verse digest of the Arthaśāstra’s teaching, devotes chapters to each element. Jain authors on polity adopted it (Chapter 8).

The Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ (c. 5th century CE) offers a related but distinct analysis. Its book on polity opens with a couplet that names six things a king must possess — an army, a people, wealth, ministers, allies and a fortress — and calls the king who has all six “a lion among kings” (Kuṟaḷ 381). The Kuṟaḷ then devotes chapters to each, and to the qualities of the king himself: learning, the avoidance of faults, the seeking of counsel from the wise, a just sceptre (ceṅkōl) and the avoidance of a cruel one. The parallel with the Sanskrit scheme is clear, but the Kuṟaḷ’s emphasis on the king’s ethical character and on the welfare of the people gives it a voice of its own; it belongs to a Tamil tradition of political ethics that also finds expression in the Caṅkam poems addressed to kings (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 4.12 An Organic Image
docs.text:
The image of the kingdom as a body with limbs recalls the organic theories of the state in European political thought, from Plato and Aristotle to medieval and early modern writers. The Indian texts, however, use the image sparingly, and their emphasis is on mutual dependence rather than on any idea of the state as a living whole with its own purposes. The Manusmṛti, after stating that each earlier element is weightier than the later, adds a qualification:

Manusmṛti 9.296

saptāṅgasyeha rājyasya viṣṭabdhasya tridaṇḍavat anyonyaguṇavaiśeṣyān na kiṃ cid atiricyate “In this seven-limbed kingdom, held together like the triple staff of an ascetic, no element is superior, because their qualities are of particular importance to one another.”

Each element is supreme for its own purpose, the text continues; the king must know the strength of each. Kāmandaka likewise describes the seven elements as mutually supporting. The doctrine therefore had a built-in tension: the order of the list expresses a hierarchy with the king at the top, while the image of the triple staff expresses mutual dependence.

docs.title: 4.13 The Saptāṅga in Later Thought and in Historiography
docs.text:
Besides the works just named, the law book of Yājñavalkya and the medieval digests of royal policy repeat the seven-element analysis, and inscriptions sometimes praise kings for the excellence of their seven limbs — a good example of the way a technical analysis from the śāstras passed into general political language.

Modern historians have used the scheme in two ways. Some, beginning with nationalist scholars in the early twentieth century, used it to argue that ancient India possessed a fully developed theory of the state comparable to that of Greece or Europe (Jayaswal 1924; Altekar 1958). Others have treated it as a heuristic for analysing how real kingdoms worked. R. S. Sharma used it to examine changes in the relative weight of the elements from the Mauryan to the post-Gupta period, and to argue that the growth of land grants to Brahmins and officials weakened the treasury and the army in early medieval kingdoms (Sharma 1959). Hartmut Scharfe’s history of the Indian state organises much of its material around the same elements (Scharfe 1989).

Such uses need care. The Mauryan state, as known from Aśoka’s inscriptions and from Megasthenes, had officials (mahāmātra, rajjuka, prādeśika) and practices that only partly match the Arthaśāstra; the Gupta kingdoms had provincial governors (uparika), district officers (viṣayapati) and village headmen known from inscriptions, but there is no evidence that they consciously applied the saptāṅga model; and the Cōḷa kingdoms of the ninth to thirteenth centuries combined royal government with powerful local assemblies (Chapter 16) that have no place in the scheme at all. The seven elements are best read as the categories through which Indian writers thought about royal power — a theory of the king’s resources — rather than as a description of how Indian states were organised.

Comparison: Modern Definitions of Statehood

The Montevideo Convention of 1933 defines a state in international law by four criteria: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. A modern reader can map these onto the janapada, the svāmin and amātya, and the mitra of the Indian scheme. The purposes differ entirely: the Convention defines who counts as a subject of international law; the saptāṅga analyses the resources of a king for the purpose of increasing them.

docs.title: 4.14 Summary
docs.text:
• The Arthaśāstra (6.1) and the Manusmṛti (9.294) analyse the kingdom into seven constituent elements: king, minister, countryside, fort, treasury, army and ally. The order is hierarchical, each element being normally more important than the next.

  • The scheme is a theory of the king’s resources, not a description of governmental institutions; it contains no element of popular representation or constitutional restraint.

  • Each element has its “excellences”; the text lists the qualities of the ideal king, the tests for ministers, the features of a good countryside, the kinds of fort, the qualities of a good treasury, army and ally.

  • Book 8 analyses the calamities that can afflict each element and debates their relative gravity; Book 6 adds the three powers of counsel, might and energy.

  • The Manusmṛti qualifies the hierarchy with the image of the triple staff: the elements support one another, and none is absolutely superior. The scheme passed into the epics, Kāmandaka, Jain works and inscriptions, and the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ has a related six-element analysis.

  • Modern historians have used the scheme to analyse historical states, with mixed success; it should be treated as an Indian way of thinking about royal power rather than as a blueprint of actual administration.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The basic texts are AŚ Books 6 and 8, in Kangle (1960) and Olivelle (2013), and Manu 9.294–297 in Olivelle (2005). Sharma (1959) offers the most searching historical analysis of the saptāṅga theory; Scharfe (1989) and Ghoshal (1959) survey its place in Indian political thought; Spellman (1964) and Drekmeier (1962) discuss it in the context of theories of kingship.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Rājadharma: Kingship in the Epics and the Śāstras
docs.text:
Arthaśāstra 1.19.34

prajāsukhe sukhaṃ rājñaḥ prajānāṃ ca hite hitam nātmapriyaṃ hitaṃ rājñaḥ prajānāṃ tu priyaṃ hitam “In the happiness of his subjects lies the king’s happiness, in their welfare his welfare. The king’s good is not what pleases himself; his good is what pleases his subjects.”

Rājadharma, “the dharma of the king”, is the name the Brahmanical tradition gave to its teaching on kingship. It is found in the Dharmasūtras and Dharmaśāstras, which devote a chapter or more to the king; in the Arthaśāstra, which treats the king’s duties from the standpoint of policy; and above all in the two Sanskrit epics, whose heroes are kings and whose long didactic sections are among the richest sources for Indian political thought. This chapter examines how these texts explained the origin of kingship, what they required of kings, what they thought about the limits of royal power, and how kings themselves presented their rule. It follows the texts closely, because the subject has suffered from two kinds of distortion: a romantic one, which turns rājadharma into a doctrine of constitutional monarchy and welfare government, and a dismissive one, which reduces it to priestly legitimation of despotism. Neither does justice to sources that combine high ideals of protection and justice with an uncompromising defence of social hierarchy and royal coercion.

docs.title: 5.1.1 The “Law of the Fish”
docs.text: The most widespread Indian account of why kings exist begins with the image of mātsyanyāya, “the law of the fish”, in which the big fish eat the small. The Arthaśāstra states it in a definition of the function of punishment: “For when the rod is not used, it gives rise to the law of the fish; for the stronger swallows the weaker in the absence of a wielder of the rod” (AŚ 1.4.13–14). The Manusmṛti uses a related image: “If the king did not tirelessly inflict punishment on those who deserve it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit” (Manu 7.20). Kingship, on this view, exists because human beings left to themselves would destroy one another; the king’s coercive power (daṇḍa) is the remedy.

docs.title: 5.1.2 The Divine Creation of the King
docs.text:
The Manusmṛti couples this argument from necessity with a theology of kingship. “When this world was without a king and people fled in all directions out of fear, the Lord created a king for the protection of this whole world” (arājake hi loke ’smin sarvato vidrute bhayāt / rakṣārtham asya sarvasya rājānam asṛjat prabhuḥ, Manu 7.3). He made him from eternal particles of Indra, the Wind, Yama, the Sun, Fire, Varuṇa, the Moon and Kubera, the guardians of the world; therefore the king surpasses all beings in splendour (7.4–5). “Even a boy king must not be disregarded as a mere human; he is a great deity in human form” (7.8). The king is to be feared as fire; whoever hates him perishes (7.9–12).

This passage has often been called a “divine right” theory. The comparison with early modern Europe is loose, but the text plainly makes the king’s person sacred and obedience to him a religious duty. It is balanced, in the same chapter, by the insistence that the king himself is subject to daṇḍa: punishment “destroys the king who deviates from dharma, together with his relatives” (7.28).

docs.title: 5.1.3 The Mahābhārata’s Narratives
docs.text:
The Śānti Parvan (Book 12) of the Mahābhārata contains the fullest narratives. In 12.59, Yudhiṣṭhira asks Bhīṣma how the word rājan arose, and Bhīṣma begins: “At first there was no kingdom and no king, no rod and no wielder of the rod; all creatures protected one another by dharma alone” (naiva rājyaṃ na rājāsīn na daṇḍo na ca dāṇḍikaḥ / dharmeṇaiva prajāḥ sarvā rakṣanti ca parasparam, 12.59.14). But in time people grew weary of this mutual protection; delusion, greed and desire overtook them, the Veda and dharma perished, and the gods, alarmed, went to Brahmā. Brahmā composed a vast treatise on dharma, artha and kāma, which was then abridged in turn by Śiva, Indra, Bṛhaspati and Kāvya (Uśanas), and a series of rulers was created. One of them, Vena, was a tyrant who was killed by the seers; from his body they produced Pṛthu, who swore to protect the earth and to uphold dharma and the rule of the rod, and to keep the Brahmins exempt from punishment. Because he “delighted” (rañjita) the people, he was called rājan.

A second narrative, in 12.67, comes closer to what modern readers call a contract. People living without a king made agreements (samaya) among themselves to expel anyone who was violent, harsh of speech, adulterous or a thief; when this failed, they went to Brahmā and asked for a lord. Brahmā appointed Manu, who was reluctant to rule people who always behave falsely. The people promised him a share of their cattle, gold and grain and the service of their best warriors, and that a portion of the merit they earned would go to him; Manu then accepted and went about subduing evildoers.

Scholarly Note: Is This a “Social Contract”?

Modern scholars have often compared the Mahābhārata’s story of Manu (12.67), the Buddhist story of the “Great Elect” (Mahāsammata, Chapter 8) and the Arthaśāstra’s story told by spies (below) with the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau. The texts themselves, however, do not develop a theory of contract. In the Brahmanical versions kingship is instituted by the creator god, and the people’s “agreement” consists in accepting a king and paying him; nothing in these stories gives the people a right to revoke the arrangement or to judge the king’s performance. The Buddhist story is different in emphasis, since its first king is chosen by the people, but it too is a myth of origins, not a constitutional doctrine (Spellman 1964; Drekmeier 1962; Collins 1993).

docs.title: 5.1.4 The Arthaśāstra’s Use of the Myth
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra shows how such stories could be put to political use. In a chapter on controlling factions in the king’s own territory (AŚ 1.13), it recommends that secret agents, posing as quarrelling travellers, discuss the king’s merits in public places. When one complains of taxes and fines, the other is to tell the story: people oppressed by the law of the fish made Manu Vaivasvata their king and allotted him one-sixth of their grain and one-tenth of their merchandise, as well as money, as his share; in return kings provide security; those who do not pay taxes and accept punishment are therefore guilty of ingratitude, and the king, who holds the place of Indra and Yama, rewards and punishes visibly. The text is explicit that this is propaganda, spread by agents to secure obedience. It is a reminder that in the Arthaśāstra, theories of legitimacy are instruments of rule.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Protection
docs.text: All the texts agree that the king’s first duty is protection (rakṣaṇa, pālana) of his subjects. “The highest dharma of a Kṣatriya is the protection of his subjects; a king who enjoys the rewards specified [i.e. taxes] is bound to dharma” (Manu 7.144). Taxes are, in many passages, the king’s wages for protection, and a king who takes taxes without protecting incurs the sins of his subjects. Protection covers defence against external enemies, the suppression of thieves and robbers, and the punishment of wrongdoers — what the Arthaśāstra calls the “removal of thorns” (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 5.2.2 Yogakṣema
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra describes the function of daṇḍa as securing the yogakṣema — the acquisition (yoga) and safe possession (kṣema) of good things — of the other sciences: it is “the means of acquiring what has not been acquired, preserving what has been acquired, augmenting what has been preserved, and bestowing what has been augmented on worthy recipients” (AŚ 1.4.3). The word yogakṣema came to mean general welfare and security, and it is the motto of the Life Insurance Corporation of India; but in the Arthaśāstra it is a technical description of what coercive power does for the economy and for knowledge.

The texts do impose on the king obligations that a modern reader would call welfare duties. The Arthaśāstra (2.1) requires the king to maintain children, the aged, the sick and the helpless who have no one to support them, and to remit taxes and supply seed and cattle to farmers in distress; it gives detailed advice on famine relief, including distributing seed and food from the royal stores and undertaking public works so that people can earn food (AŚ 4.3). The Mahābhārata praises the king who feeds the hungry, protects widows and orphans and digs tanks and wells. The injunctions recur from text to text, and inscriptions show kings claiming to have met them. What they do not amount to is a “welfare state”: they create no rights in the subjects, they are owed above all to the king’s own “protected” population, and in the Arthaśāstra they sit alongside policies designed to extract the maximum revenue consistent with keeping the population from revolt.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Justice
docs.text: The king is the supreme judge. The Dharmaśāstras require him to decide lawsuits each day, either in person or through a learned Brahmin judge, with Brahmin assessors, and to follow the rules of procedure and the law of the texts (Manu 8.1–3; Chapter 12). The Arthaśāstra says that the king’s own dharma, protecting his subjects in accordance with dharma, leads him to heaven, while one who does not protect, or who inflicts unjust punishment, goes to hell (AŚ 3.1). A notable principle of the Manusmṛti makes the king liable to punishment himself: “Where an ordinary man would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king shall be fined one thousand; that is the settled rule” (Manu 8.336). Who could impose such a fine on the king is not said; the commentators explain that the king should pay it himself, by throwing it into water or giving it to Brahmins. The rule expresses the principle that the king is not above the law of dharma, while also showing that no human institution was given the power to enforce it against him.

docs.title: 5.2.4 Upholding Varṇa and Āśrama
docs.text:
The duty that the texts themselves stress most is one that modern summaries often leave out: the king must ensure that each varṇa and each stage of life keeps to its own dharma. The Arthaśāstra lists the “own duties” (svadharma) of the four varṇas — the Śūdra’s being service of the twice-born, and also crafts and trade — and declares that the world, “in which the bounds of Ārya conduct are fixed and the varṇas and āśramas are firmly established, prospers and does not perish” when protected by the triple Veda (AŚ 1.3) — an order that it is the king’s task to maintain. The Manusmṛti makes the king responsible for compelling Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their duties, “for if they deviated from their duties, they would throw this world into confusion” (Manu 8.418). The king’s daṇḍa therefore enforced the hierarchy of varṇa as well as protecting persons and property. Chapters 10 and 14 discuss what this meant in law.

The Rāmāyaṇa contains a stark narrative expression of this duty. In its last book (Uttarakāṇḍa), a Brahmin’s son dies young, and Rāma learns that the cause is a Śūdra, Śambūka, performing austerities that are not permitted to his varṇa; Rāma seeks him out and beheads him, and the boy is restored to life. The episode, generally regarded as a late addition to the epic, was criticised already in classical times by the dramatist Bhavabhūti, who in his Uttararāmacarita makes Rāma express revulsion at the deed, and it has been a focus of modern Dalit and reformist criticism of the ideal of “Rāmarājya”.

docs.title: 5.2.5 Protection of Brahmins and Religious Institutions
docs.text: The texts require the king to honour and support Brahmins, to exempt learned Brahmins from taxation, never to execute a Brahmin, and to make gifts to them and to religious institutions. Inscriptions show that kings across India, of all religious affiliations, did make such gifts on a large scale — land grants to Brahmins and temples, and endowments to Buddhist and Jain monasteries. The relation between king and Brahmin was presented as one of mutual dependence: the Brahmin’s sacred power (brahman) and the king’s ruling power (kṣatra) together sustain the world, but the texts insist that the Brahmin is the superior partner (Heesterman 1985).

docs.title: 5.3 The King’s Self-Discipline
docs.text: Every tradition of rājadharma treats the king’s character as decisive. The Arthaśāstra’s first book teaches the conquest of the senses and the avoidance of the “six enemies” — lust (kāma), anger (krodha), greed (lobha), pride (māna), arrogance (mada) and excessive exhilaration (harṣa) — giving for each the example of a legendary king destroyed by it (AŚ 1.6). The Manusmṛti lists ten vices born of desire (hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, drunkenness, music, singing, dancing and idle wandering) and eight born of anger (calumny, violence, malice, envy, fault-finding, destruction of property, verbal abuse and assault), and calls drink, gambling, women and hunting the worst (Manu 7.45–52). The king’s routine (Chapter 3) is designed to keep him at work and accessible; the Arthaśāstra warns that a king who keeps petitioners waiting at his door is made to do the opposite of what he should by those around him, and provokes the anger of his subjects (AŚ 1.19).

docs.title: 5.4.1 Consecration
docs.text:
Kingship was conferred and renewed through rites of consecration (abhiṣeka). The Vedic rājasūya and the “great consecration of Indra” (aindra mahābhiṣeka) described in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Book 8) include an oath sworn by the king — not to the people but to the officiating priest: should he injure the priest, may the priest take away all the merit of his sacrifices and gifts, his heaven, his life and his offspring, from the night of his birth to the night of his death. Later coronations combined Vedic and Purāṇic elements: the sprinkling with waters from sacred rivers and with substances such as milk, curd and honey; the investiture with the royal umbrella, fly-whisk and throne; and the acclamation of ministers and subjects. Some medieval digests set out the rites in detail. The acclamation was a ritual act, not an election (Gonda 1966; Heesterman 1985). Figure 5.1 shows a palace scene from an Ajanta mural.

Figure 5.1. A palace scene from the Mahājanaka Jātaka, mural in Ajanta Cave 1 (c. 5th century CE), showing a prince and attendants. Royal courts are a frequent subject of the Ajanta narrative paintings, which illustrate Buddhist Jātaka stories. Photo: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.4.2 The Chaplain
docs.text: Every royal court had a purohita, a domestic chaplain who performed the king’s rituals and advised him. The Arthaśāstra requires the king to appoint a chaplain of high family and character, learned in the Veda, in omens and in the science of government, and to follow him “as a pupil his teacher, a son his father, a servant his master”; “kṣatra power made to prosper by the Brahmin, consecrated by the counsel of counsellors, and armed with weapons in accordance with the śāstra, conquers the unconquered” (AŚ 1.9). It is sometimes said that the purohita was a constitutional check on the king. He was a powerful figure and could be a moral counsellor, but he was appointed and could be dismissed by the king, and the Arthaśāstra’s own test of ministers (Chapter 4) begins with a staged dismissal of the chaplain. His influence was personal and religious, not institutional.

docs.title: 5.4.3 Council
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra and the Manusmṛti both require the king to consult his ministers before acting and to deliberate in secret (Manu 7.54–59; AŚ 1.15). The Mahābhārata repeatedly shows kings consulting councils of elders and ministers, and the Rāmāyaṇa’s famous “kaccit” chapter in the Ayodhyākāṇḍa, in which Rāma questions his brother Bharata about the government of Ayodhyā (“Do you take counsel neither alone nor with too many? Do you appoint ministers who are honest and tested? Do you pay your soldiers on time?”, 2.94.13, 21, 26), is a compact handbook of rājadharma in the form of questions. In all these texts, however, the final decision rests with the king.

docs.title: 5.5.1 The Mahābhārata
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata, composed over several centuries (c. 400 BCE–400 CE), is in part a long meditation on kingship. Its central plot turns on disputed succession, the ruin of a dynasty by a gambling match and the moral costs of a war fought for a kingdom. After the war, Yudhiṣṭhira, the new king, is overwhelmed by grief and wants to renounce the throne; he is persuaded to rule, and the dying Bhīṣma instructs him in the duties of a king. This instruction fills most of the Śānti Parvan, whose first two sections are the Rājadharma (12.1–128; Bhīṣma’s teaching begins at 12.56) and the Āpaddharma, “dharma in times of distress” (12.129–167), followed by the Mokṣadharma on liberation (12.168–353). The Anuśāsana Parvan (Book 13) continues the instruction (Fitzgerald 2004).

The Rājadharma sections cover much of the ground of the Arthaśāstra — the origin of kingship, the qualities of king and ministers, taxation, the treasury, spies, diplomacy and war — but in a more varied and often more troubled voice. Bhīṣma tells Yudhiṣṭhira that the king’s dharma is the foundation of all other dharmas, because without protection none can be practised; he also teaches that a king must sometimes be harsh and must use deceit against the deceitful. James Fitzgerald has emphasised that the Śānti Parvan addresses the problem of royal violence head-on: it tries to persuade a reluctant, conscience-stricken king that the violence of rule is necessary and righteous (Fitzgerald 2004).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Āpaddharma: Law for Emergencies
docs.text: The Āpaddharma section develops the idea that in emergencies the ordinary rules may be suspended. A king who has lost his treasury may take wealth from those who are not Brahmins; a Brahmin unable to live by his own occupation may live by those of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya. The most famous illustration is the story of the sage Viśvāmitra, who during a twelve-year famine tries to steal dog’s meat from the hut of a Caṇḍāla; the Caṇḍāla argues with him about dharma, and the sage defends his act on the ground that survival comes first (MBh 12.139). The doctrine of emergency rules is found in the Dharmasūtras and Dharmaśāstras as well; it gave the tradition a principled way of accommodating necessity without abandoning its norms.

docs.title: 5.5.3 The Bhagavad Gītā and the Duty of the Warrior
docs.text:
The most famous discussion of a ruler’s duty in Indian literature is the Bhagavad Gītā, set in the Mahābhārata at the beginning of the great battle. Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers in the opposing army, refuses to fight; Kṛṣṇa persuades him to do so. Among his arguments is the appeal to the warrior’s own duty: “for a Kṣatriya there is nothing better than a battle in accordance with dharma” (BG 2.31), and “better one’s own duty, though imperfect, than another’s duty well performed” (BG 3.35). Kṛṣṇa declares that he created the four varṇas according to the division of qualities and actions (BG 4.13), and later lists the duties of each varṇa, ending with service as the duty of the Śūdra (BG 18.41–44). The Gītā’s teaching that one should act without attachment to the fruits of action gave the doctrine of svadharma a new philosophical depth.

The Gītā has been read in very different ways. Classical commentators such as Śaṅkara (c. 700–750 CE; traditional dates 788–820) read it as a text about liberation through knowledge. In the national movement it became a text of political action: Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s Gītā Rahasya (1915) read it as a gospel of energetic, selfless action in the world, and Gandhi read it as a teaching of non-violent, detached service, interpreting its battle allegorically. Ambedkar, by contrast, criticised the Gītā as a defence of the varṇa order and of the duty to kill. These readings show how a classical text about the duty of a warrior-prince could be made to speak to modern politics.

docs.title: 5.5.4 The Rāmāyaṇa and “Rāmarājya”
docs.text: Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa presents Rāma as the ideal king: obedient to his father, faithful to his word, self-controlled, protective of his people. Its descriptions of Ayodhyā under Rāma’s rule — free from disease, untimely death, widowhood, theft and fear, with everyone content in his own dharma — created the ideal of Rāmarājya, “the rule of Rāma”, which has served for two millennia as a byword for good government. The same text shows a king who, in the Uttarakāṇḍa, banishes his pregnant wife because of popular gossip about her chastity, and who executes Śambūka. Modern uses of Rāmarājya, from Gandhi’s ideal of a just and non-violent polity to its use in contemporary politics, are discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 5.5.5 The King Makes the Age
docs.text: A recurring theme of the Śānti Parvan is that the king is responsible for the moral condition of his time. Bhīṣma asks whether time is the cause of the king or the king the cause of time, and answers that the king is the cause of the age: when the king rules fully according to the science of punishment, the age is the Kṛta, the age of perfection; when he abandons it, the age becomes the Kali (MBh 12.70). The idea, which reverses the usual relation between cosmic time and human action, gave the king’s conduct a cosmic weight and made bad times a judgement on bad rulers. It is echoed in the widespread belief, found in many texts and inscriptions, that a righteous king brings timely rain and abundant harvests, and an unrighteous one brings famine.

docs.title: 5.6 Succession and Regency
docs.text:
The texts assume that kingship passes from father to son, and that the eldest son is the proper heir. The Arthaśāstra, after discussing at length the dangers that princes pose to their fathers (Chapter 4), commends succession by the eldest son except in calamity, and considers what should be done when the king has no fit son: a son begotten on the queen by a kinsman, a daughter’s son, or a prince of the royal family might be installed, and the ministers must manage the transition, if necessary concealing the king’s death, so that the kingdom is not exposed to its enemies (AŚ 1.17; 5.6) — a measure of the vulnerability of every succession.

The epics turn on disputed successions. In the Rāmāyaṇa, King Daśaratha’s decision to consecrate his eldest son Rāma as heir apparent is overturned by the boons he owes to his queen Kaikeyī, who demands the throne for her own son Bharata and the exile of Rāma; Bharata refuses to accept the throne and rules as regent in Rāma’s name, placing Rāma’s sandals on the throne. In the Mahābhārata, Dhṛtarāṣṭra is passed over in favour of his younger brother Pāṇḍu because of his blindness, and the rival claims of their sons lead to the great war. Both epics thus present the rule of primogeniture as normative and explore the moral crises that arise when it is challenged.

Historical practice was more varied. Kings often designated their heirs during their lifetime, sometimes passing over elder sons: the Allahabad inscription describes Candragupta I embracing Samudragupta before the assembled court and choosing him as his successor, and several Cōḷa kings associated their chosen heirs with them as heir apparent (yuvarāja) years before their deaths. Wars of succession were common in many dynasties; among the Mughals, who did not follow primogeniture, the sons of a dying emperor regularly fought for the throne, as in the war of 1657–58 from which Aurangzeb emerged victorious (Chapter 18). Queens and ministers frequently acted as regents for minor kings, and some women, such as the Vākāṭaka queen Prabhāvatīguptā and the Kashmiri queen Diddā, wielded royal power in this way for long periods (see below). The gap between the ideal of orderly succession and the frequency of disputed thrones is one reason why the texts insist so strongly on the protection of the king’s person.

docs.title: 5.7 Kings, Temples and Gods
docs.text:
From about the seventh century, the relationship between kings and temples became a central feature of Indian kingship, especially in the south. Kings built great temples to the gods they worshipped, endowed them with land and revenues, and associated their own names with the deity. The Rājarājeśvara (Bṛhadīśvara) temple at Thanjavur, completed by the Cōḷa king Rājarāja I in about 1010, bears inscriptions recording the king’s gifts, the villages assigned to the temple’s support, and the hundreds of persons — priests, musicians, dancers, accountants, watchmen and craftsmen — employed in its service. Such temples were centres of redistribution as well as of worship, and through them kings bound together the Brahmins, merchants and landholders of their realms (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

In some kingdoms the king presented himself as the servant or deputy of a god who was the true sovereign. The Vijayanagara kings issued their grants in the presence of the god Virūpākṣa at Hampi, whose name appears on their records. In Odisha, the Gajapati kings represented themselves as servants of Jagannātha at Puri and, at the annual chariot festival, ritually sweep the path before the god’s chariot, a rite still performed by the titular king. In Travancore, Mārttāṇḍa Varma dedicated his kingdom to the deity Padmanābha in 1750 and ruled thereafter as the god’s servant (padmanābhadāsa). These arrangements gave religious legitimacy to royal power while also placing it, in principle, under a higher authority.

Kings were also expected to protect and regulate temples. Inscriptions record royal orders settling disputes among temple servants, punishing the misappropriation of temple funds and confirming the rights of temple assemblies. This royal role in the administration of religious institutions was inherited by the colonial state and, after independence, by state governments that administer many Hindu temples through statutory boards — a development discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 5.8 Limits on Royal Power
docs.text:
Did the classical texts recognise any limit on the king’s power? They recognised several, but of a particular kind.

  • Dharma and the śāstras. The king is to judge according to the śāstras and the customs of regions, castes and families (Manu 8.41), and he is not to alter the dharma of the varṇas. In practice, kings issued orders (rājaśāsana) freely, and the Arthaśāstra ranks royal edict highest among the bases of decision (Chapter 12).

  • Counsel. The king should deliberate with ministers and heed the purohita; a king who rejects counsel is a fool.

  • Divine and karmic sanction. The unjust king goes to hell, loses his kingdom, and brings famine and disaster on his land.

  • Deposition and resistance. Stories tell of wicked kings killed or deposed: Vena by the seers; Nahuṣa, cast down from Indra’s throne for his arrogance. The Anuśāsana Parvan contains a striking statement that a king who says “I am your protector” and does not protect should be killed by his subjects acting together, like a mad dog (MBh 13.60.19–20). Such passages provide a theoretical justification of resistance to tyranny, though they are rare and never developed into a doctrine with procedures.

What the texts do not provide is any institution with authority over the king — no court that could judge him, no assembly whose consent he required, no right of subjects to sue him. U. N. Ghoshal and R. S. Sharma, from different perspectives, both concluded that the limits on royal power in the Brahmanical theory were essentially moral and religious; Ghoshal stressed the restraining force of dharma, Sharma the role of the theory in legitimating a social order dominated by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas (Ghoshal 1959; Sharma 1959). To read rājadharma as a doctrine of constitutional monarchy or of the rule of law is to mistake moral exhortation for institutional constraint.

docs.title: 5.9 Women and Kingship
docs.text:
The texts of rājadharma assume a male king. The Manusmṛti excludes women, along with the sick and the foolish, from the king’s secret deliberations (7.149–150), and the Arthaśāstra treats the women of the palace chiefly as a security risk (Chapter 4). The chief queen (mahiṣī) had a ritual role in royal consecrations and sacrifices, and the Arthaśāstra places the king’s mother and chief queen in the highest salary grade (Chapter 6); but the śāstras do not discuss the possibility of a woman ruling in her own right.

History nevertheless records a number of women who exercised royal power. The Gupta princess Prabhāvatīguptā, daughter of Candragupta II, governed the Vākāṭaka kingdom as regent for her sons in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Queen Diddā ruled Kashmir in the late tenth century, first as regent and then in her own name; Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī portrays her as able and ruthless. Rudramā Devī ruled the Kākatīya kingdom of the eastern Deccan in the later thirteenth century, and the Venetian traveller Marco Polo described the kingdom under a queen. In the Delhi Sultanate, Raḍiyya (Raziya) ruled from 1236 to 1240 before being overthrown by nobles who resented a woman’s rule. In the eighteenth century, Ahilyabai Holkar governed the Maratha state of Indore for some three decades and was remembered for her patronage of temples, pilgrim routes and public works across India. These rulers were exceptions, and they usually reached power as widows or regents for minor sons; but their careers show that the śāstric assumption of male kingship was not always borne out in practice.

docs.title: 5.10 The King as Giver
docs.text:
One duty of rājadharma left a vast documentary record: the king’s gifts. The Dharmaśāstras praise the gift of land to Brahmins as the highest of gifts, and from the Gupta period onwards kings, queens, feudatories and officials granted villages and fields to Brahmins and temples, recording the grants on copper plates, whose form and legal force are described in Chapter 17. The charters usually end with imprecatory verses attributed to Vyāsa, the best known of which declares that whoever takes away land given by himself or by others will be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.

Historians have used these grants to study the relationship between kingship and Brahmanical authority. R. S. Sharma argued that the transfer of fiscal and administrative rights to Brahmins and temples contributed to a decentralisation of power in early medieval India, which he described as “feudal”; others have emphasised the role of such grants in extending agrarian settlement and royal legitimacy into new areas. Whatever their interpretation, the grants show rājadharma in action: the king fulfilling his duty to support Brahmins and religious institutions, and acquiring in return the legitimacy that their prayers and praise conferred (Sharma 1959; Singh 2008).

docs.title: 5.11 Kings in History
docs.text:
Historical kings did draw on these ideals in presenting themselves. Aśoka’s inscriptions (Chapter 8) proclaim that “all men are my children” and describe welfare works and officials appointed to promote dhamma. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of Khāravela of Kaliṅga (c. 1st century BCE), a Jain ruler, records year by year his military campaigns, his repair of waterworks, remissions of taxes and patronage of Jain ascetics. Gupta inscriptions, notably the Allahabad pillar inscription of Samudragupta (4th century CE), praise the king as a protector of the good and destroyer of the wicked, and as an equal of the gods. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described the great distributions of wealth made by Harṣa (r. c. 606–647) at Prayāga. Bhoja of the Paramāra dynasty (r. c. 1010–1055) was celebrated as a scholar-king, and the Vijayanagara emperor Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529) included a section of advice on statecraft in his Telugu poem Āmuktamālyada (Chapter 17).

A more critical view of kings is found in Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148–49), a verse history of the kings of Kashmir (see also Chapter 17). Kalhaṇa, a Brahmin poet, judged rulers by the standards of rājadharma and recorded their failures with unusual frankness: rapacious ministers, palace intrigues, the oppression of cultivators by tax-collectors, and the conduct of king Harṣa of Kashmir (r. 1089–1101), who, short of money, appointed an officer to despoil temples of their images. His work shows that the ideals of rājadharma could be used to criticise kings as well as to praise them.

These inscriptions and chronicles are self-representations, court praise or the judgements of court poets; they tell us how kings wished to be seen or how learned men thought they should behave. Inscriptions also show the realities that the texts discuss more abstractly: wars of conquest, the destruction of rival capitals, the transfer of land and its cultivators to Brahmins and temples, and the burdens of taxation and forced labour (viṣṭi) on peasants. Upinder Singh’s study of political violence in ancient India shows how the texts and inscriptions together reveal a persistent tension between the ideal of the protective king and the fact of royal violence (Singh 2017).

Comparison: Rājadharma and Other Traditions

Comparisons are often drawn with the Chinese idea of the Mandate of Heaven, under which a ruler who loses virtue loses the right to rule, and with Mencius’s justification of the removal of tyrants; with the European “mirrors for princes”; and with Machiavelli. Each brings out a different side of the Indian material. Mencius developed an explicit argument that killing a tyrant is not regicide, which the Indian texts state only occasionally; the European mirrors, like the Indian ones, combine moral counsel with practical advice; and Machiavelli shares the Arthaśāstra’s frankness about deceit, but not the epics’ preoccupation with the moral costs of rule.

docs.title: 5.12 The Tamil South and the Early Medieval State
docs.text: The śāstras describe kingship from the king’s side: one ruler, his ministers and his rod. Historians who have tried to reconstruct how actual states worked, especially from the abundant poetry and inscriptions of the Tamil country, have reached a more complicated picture, and their debates are a useful test of how far the theory of rājadharma describes Indian polities.

docs.title: 5.12.1 Kingship in Tamil Poetry and the Kuṟaḷ
docs.text: The Tamil literary tradition offers a distinct and early voice on kingship. The Caṅkam anthologies (c. 1st–3rd centuries CE in their core) include many poems addressed to kings, praising their generosity and martial prowess and sometimes admonishing them. A poem of the Puṟanāṉūṟu (186) declares that rice is not the life of the world, nor is water: the king is the life of the world, so a king must know that he is the life of his people. Other poems remind kings that their glory depends on their gifts to poets and on the welfare of their subjects. The Tirukkuṟaḷ’s book on polity (Chapter 4) devotes chapters to the just sceptre (ceṅkōl), which it says is the support of the Brahmins’ Veda and of dharma, and to the cruel sceptre (koṭuṅkōl), whose wielder is likened to a robber. These texts share many ideals with Sanskrit rājadharma, but they developed in a different literary culture, and they emphasise the reciprocal bond between the king and his people more than his divine status.

docs.title: 5.12.2 Crowned Kings and Chiefs in the Caṅkam Poems
docs.text: Beyond these ideals, the Caṅkam anthologies show a political world of many ranks. At the top stood the three “crowned kings” (mūvēntar) — the Cēra, Cōḷa and Pāṇṭiya — called vēntaṉ, kō or maṉṉaṉ; beside and beneath them were numerous chieftains (vēḷir) and lords of hill and forest tracts; and around them all moved bards and poets (pāṇar, pulavar) who praised their patrons and expected gifts in return. The puṟam poems celebrate cattle raids, sieges and the burning of enemy lands (Chapter 7), and above all the generosity of the victor, who redistributed plunder to warriors and poets. Brahmanical kingship is present but not dominant: the Pāṇṭiya Mutukuṭumi Peruvaḻuti, for instance, is praised as a performer of many Vedic sacrifices. George Hart has examined how these poems conceive the king and how they relate to Sanskrit literature, arguing that much in them belongs to an indigenous Tamil culture rather than to a borrowed Brahmanical model (Hart 1975). Historians still disagree whether the polities of the poems were kingdoms with officials and regular land revenue, or chiefdoms held together by kinship, warfare and the circulation of gifts, in which such structures were only beginning to form.

docs.title: 5.12.3 The Cōḷa State: Centralised or Segmentary?
docs.text: From the Pallavas (c. 6th–9th centuries) to the imperial Cōḷas (c. 850–1279), copper plates and temple inscriptions record land grants, royal orders, temple endowments and the decisions of local assemblies (Chapter 16). K. A. Nilakanta Sastri read this evidence as the record of a strong and centralised monarchy, with a large body of officials, royal surveys of land under Rājarāja I and Kulottuṅga I, and a hierarchy of provinces (maṇṭalam), districts (vaḷanāṭu) and localities (nāṭu), combined with vigorous village self-government (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). Burton Stein challenged this picture. Adapting the anthropologist Aidan Southall’s model of the “segmentary state”, he argued that the Cōḷa king exercised full political control only in a core around the Kāviri (Kaveri) delta, and elsewhere enjoyed a ritual sovereignty acknowledged by largely self-governing peasant localities, dominated by landholding cultivating groups allied with Brahmins and temples (Stein 1980). Noboru Karashima and Y. Subbarayalu, analysing large numbers of inscriptions systematically, found more evidence of royal intervention — in revenue assessment, in the appointment of officials and in changing patterns of landholding — than Stein allowed, and most historians now take a position between the two models (Karashima 1984).

docs.title: 5.12.4 Feudal, Segmentary or Integrative?
docs.text:
The southern debate is part of a wider argument about the early medieval state in India (c. 600–1200). R. S. Sharma and D. N. Jha described the period as one of “Indian feudalism”, in which grants of land and fiscal rights to Brahmins, temples and officials fragmented royal authority and bound peasants more tightly to landlords (Section 5.10). B. D. Chattopadhyaya and Hermann Kulke, among others, proposed instead an “integrative” or “processual” model: the spread of land grants, Brahmin settlements and temples carried state society into new regions and absorbed local lineages and cults into regional kingdoms, so that the same evidence records the formation of states rather than their decline (Chattopadhyaya 1994; Kulke 1995). Kulke’s own studies of Odisha, where the kings came to rule as servants of Jagannātha (Section 5.7), are a leading example.

These debates do not settle what rājadharma meant to those who professed it, but they show its limits as a description. The śāstras locate all coercive authority in the king; the inscriptions show authority shared, negotiated and ritually expressed among kings, temples, Brahmin assemblies, landholding groups and local chiefs. Rājadharma supplied the language in which that shared power was legitimated — protection, gift, the upholding of dharma — rather than a blueprint of its structure.

docs.text:
Table 5.1 lists the principal passages discussed in this chapter.

docs.title: 5.14 Summary
docs.text:
• Brahmanical texts explain kingship as a remedy for the “law of the fish”: without the king’s coercive power the strong would devour the weak. The Manusmṛti adds that the creator made the king from particles of the gods; the Mahābhārata tells of Pṛthu and of the people’s agreement with Manu, which confers no right to revoke the king.

  • The king’s duties were protection, justice, the welfare (yogakṣema) of his subjects, and — stressed in every text — the maintenance of the order of varṇas and āśramas. Welfare duties were enjoined, but they created no rights in the subjects.

  • Self-discipline, counsel and the guidance of the chaplain were the main checks on the king. The texts know of the deposition and even killing of tyrants, but they provide no institution with authority over the king.

  • The Mahābhārata’s Śānti Parvan is the fullest discussion of kingship, and it treats royal violence as a moral problem. The Rāmāyaṇa created the ideal of Rāmarājya, but also tells of the banishment of Sītā and the killing of Śambūka.

  • Inscriptions and chronicles show kings presenting themselves through these ideals; Tamil poetry and the Tirukkuṟaḷ offer a parallel tradition stressing the bond between king and people.

  • Historians of the Tamil south and of the early medieval state — with models of centralised, segmentary, “feudal” and integrative states — show royal authority shared with temples, Brahmin assemblies and local groups; rājadharma supplied its legitimating language rather than its structure.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the theory of kingship see Spellman (1964), Drekmeier (1962), Gonda (1966) and Ghoshal (1959); on the social basis of political ideas, Sharma (1959); on the emergence of monarchy in the Brahmanical sources, Roy (1994). Fitzgerald (2004) translates and introduces the first part of the Śānti Parvan. Heesterman (1985) discusses the relation between king and Brahmin, and Singh (2017) the problem of royal violence. On Tamil kingship and the south Indian state see Hart (1975), Nilakanta Sastri (1955), Stein (1980) and Karashima (1984); on the early medieval state, Chattopadhyaya (1994) and Kulke (1995). The relevant primary passages are Manu chapter 7 (Olivelle 2005) and AŚ Book 1 (Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: Chapter 6: Revenue, Administration and the Political Economy of the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
“All undertakings depend on the treasury” (AŚ 2.8.1). The Arthaśāstra’s account of government is to a large extent an account of how a king obtains, guards and spends wealth. Its second book, the longest in the work, describes a kingdom run through some thirty departments, each under a superintendent (adhyakṣa), which manage crown lands and workshops, regulate trade, collect tolls and taxes, and keep accounts. This chapter examines that political economy: the place of economics among the sciences, the king’s revenue, the administration of land, labour, markets, money and trade, and the accounting and control of officials. Its focus is on the state; the history of the Indian economy, guilds, coinage and trade in its own right is treated in Volume 19 of this series.

Two cautions apply throughout. First, the Arthaśāstra is a normative text, composed between c. 50 BCE and 300 CE (Chapter 3). It describes what its authors thought a well-run kingdom should do, not the administration of the Mauryan empire or of any other known state. Second, the Arthaśāstra’s aim is the strength and wealth of the king; the prosperity of the subjects matters because, and in so far as, it supports that aim. Labels such as “mixed economy” or “welfare state” fit it badly for that reason (Olivelle 2013; Trautmann 2012).

docs.title: 6.1 Vārttā: Economics among the Sciences
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra counts economics among the four sciences a king must master (Chapter 3). “Agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade constitute vārttā” (kṛṣipāśupālye vaṇijyā ca vārttā, AŚ 1.4.1); it is useful because it yields grain, cattle, money, forest produce and labour, and “by means of it the king brings under his control his own and the enemy’s party, with the help of the treasury and the army” (AŚ 1.4.2). Economics, in other words, is the material basis of power. The same passage presents daṇḍanīti as the science that secures the acquisition and preservation of wealth.

The Dharmaśāstras assign the same three occupations, together with money-lending, to the Vaiśya varṇa (Manu 1.90, 10.79–80), while permitting other varṇas to practise them in times of distress. In practice, as inscriptions and literary sources show, merchants, artisans and cultivators came from many communities, and the rigid scheme of the law books was never a description of economic life.

docs.title: 6.2.1 The Collector and the Treasurer
docs.text: Two high officers manage the state’s finances. The collector (samāhartṛ) is responsible for revenue: he organises the countryside into divisions and supervises the record-keepers who register land, households and livestock (Chapter 4). The treasurer (sannidhātṛ) is responsible for the storehouses: the treasury proper, the granary, the warehouse of forest produce, the armoury and the prison. The Arthaśāstra lists the “bodies” of revenue (āyaśarīra) under seven headings — fort (the capital and its levies), countryside, mines, irrigation works and gardens, forests, herds and trade routes — and gives a detailed scheme for classifying income and expenditure (AŚ 2.6). Its accounts office (akṣapaṭala) keeps registers of every department, and accountants present their accounts annually, on the full-moon day of the month Āṣāḍha (AŚ 2.7).

docs.title: 6.2.2 The Land Tax
docs.text: The principal tax was the king’s share (bhāga) of the harvest. The Dharmaśāstras give it as one-sixth, one-eighth or one-twelfth of grain (Manu 7.130), and “the sixth” became proverbial: the king was often called “the taker of the sixth part”. The Arthaśāstra assumes a share of one-sixth on private land, alongside a variety of other levies on the countryside: a tax in kind (bali), payments in money, contributions for the army, levies on fruits and vegetables, and dues on fisheries, ferries and forests. Crown lands (sītā) were cultivated directly for the king under the superintendent of agriculture, using slaves, hired labourers and convicts working off fines; or they were leased to sharecroppers for half or a lesser share of the crop (AŚ 2.24). Water from state irrigation works was charged for at rates varying with the method of irrigation.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Tolls, Customs and Other Revenue
docs.text: Goods entering the capital or crossing the frontier paid customs and tolls (śulka), collected at the city gate by the superintendent of customs; the rates varied with the kind of goods, and smuggling, false declaration and evasion were heavily fined (AŚ 2.21–22). Further revenue came from fines imposed by the courts; from the mint, which charged fees for coining; from state monopolies and workshops; from mines; and from the property of those who died without heirs. Brahmins learned in the Veda, along with certain others, were exempt from taxation, and land granted to Brahmins (brahmadeya) was to be free of taxes and fines (AŚ 2.1).

docs.title: 6.2.4 Revenue Terms in the Inscriptions
docs.text: Land grants of the Gupta and later periods allow us to see some of these revenues in practice. The grants transfer to the recipient the king’s rights over a village, often listed in standard formulae: the share of the produce (bhāga), periodic payments in kind (bhoga), taxes (kara), payments in cash (hiraṇya) and, in many grants, forced labour (viṣṭi), together with fines and the right to treasure. They also specify immunities: the village is to be free from the entry of royal soldiers and police, and its inhabitants are told to obey the grantee and to deliver to him the dues they formerly paid to the king. The terms differ from those of the Arthaśāstra but reflect a similar range of exactions. Historians have used them to study the burdens on cultivators and the transfer of fiscal rights from the state to Brahmins, temples and officials (Sharma 1959; Singh 2008).

docs.title: 6.2.5 Moderation and Extraction
docs.text: The texts recommend that taxation be moderate and regular. Manu’s image of the leech, the calf and the bee, which take their food little by little (Manu 7.129), was widely repeated, and both the Arthaśāstra and the Mahābhārata warn that excessive exactions drive subjects to flee or revolt. The Arthaśāstra also counsels the king to grant remissions of tax to new settlers and to those who build irrigation works. It is equally clear-eyed, however, about extraction. When the treasury is in difficulty, the king may demand a one-time contribution (praṇaya) from cultivators, merchants and others; may take a share of the property of temples and religious bodies; and may use secret agents to stage miracles, persuade the wealthy to contribute, or seize the property of the disloyal under pretexts (AŚ 5.2). Such advice belongs to the same book as the warning to take only ripe fruit from the garden of the kingdom (AŚ 5.2.70). The modern idea of “canons of taxation” — equity, certainty, convenience and economy — belongs to Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations (1776); attributing it to the Arthaśāstra misreads a text whose concern is to maximise revenue without provoking revolt.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Settlement and Irrigation
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s model kingdom expands by settling new land with villages of cultivators (AŚ 2.1; Chapter 4). The king should also build irrigation works (setubandha) — reservoirs, tanks and channels — either with natural water or with water brought from elsewhere, and assist others who build them with land, roads, timber and implements. Those who construct new tanks receive a remission of taxes for several years; those who damage or neglect irrigation works are fined (AŚ 2.1; 3.9). Inscriptions from many periods show that the construction of tanks was in fact one of the most important forms of royal and private investment and of religious merit in India.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Crown Workshops and Monopolies
docs.text:
The superintendents of Book 2 manage a wide range of state enterprises: mines and metal-working, the mint, salt, forests and forest produce, the armoury, weaving, liquor and slaughter-houses. Mining and salt were state monopolies, worked either directly or by lessees paying a fixed share; liquor was produced in state establishments or under licence and sold only in licensed taverns; and private manufacture of weapons was forbidden. The superintendent of yarn (sūtrādhyakṣa) employed women to spin, especially widows, women with disabilities, women who did not leave their homes, “mothers of courtesans”, retired temple servants and women working off fines, paying them according to the quality and quantity of their work; women who did not leave home were to be sent work through maidservants (AŚ 2.23). The superintendent of courtesans (gaṇikādhyakṣa) regulated prostitutes, who paid the state a share of their earnings (AŚ 2.27). The superintendent of the slaughter-house enforced bans on killing protected animals and animals in sanctuaries (abhayāraṇya) (AŚ 2.26).

The picture is of a state that is a major producer and employer, not merely a regulator. Whether any ancient Indian state ran such a system is uncertain. The Arthaśāstra may reflect, in idealised form, practices of kingdoms in the centuries around the turn of the era, but it is not a description of the Mauryan economy.

docs.title: 6.3.3 The Superintendents
docs.text:
Book 2 describes the duties of more than two dozen superintendents. Table 6.1 lists the principal ones. The list is useful less as a description of any real administration than as a map of what its authors thought a king’s government should control.

Table 6.1. Principal superintendents (adhyakṣa) and officers in Book 2 of the Arthaśāstra Officer Responsibility samāhartṛ Collector: revenue, records of the countryside, secret agents in the countryside sannidhātṛ Treasurer: treasury, granary, storehouses, armoury, prison akṣapaṭalādhyakṣa Records and accounts office kośādhyakṣa Treasury; examination of gems and precious goods ākarādhyakṣa Mines and metallurgy; salt (with the lavaṇādhyakṣa) lakṣaṇādhyakṣa, rūpadarśaka Mint; examination of coins suvarṇādhyakṣa Goldsmiths’ workshop koṣṭhāgārādhyakṣa Granary and stores paṇyādhyakṣa Trade: state goods, prices, demand and supply kupyādhyakṣa Forest produce āyudhāgārādhyakṣa Armoury and weapons pautavādhyakṣa, mānādhyakṣa Weights and measures; measures of space and time śulkādhyakṣa Customs and tolls sūtrādhyakṣa Yarn and weaving sītādhyakṣa Crown agriculture surādhyakṣa Liquor sūnādhyakṣa Slaughter-houses; protected animals gaṇikādhyakṣa Courtesans and entertainers nāvadhyakṣa Shipping, ferries and ports go’dhyakṣa Cattle aśvādhyakṣa, hastyadhyakṣa, rathādhyakṣa, pattyadhyakṣa Horses, elephants, chariots and infantry mudrādhyakṣa Passes for travel vivītādhyakṣa Pasture lands and the safety of roads nāgaraka City superintendent

The superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa) illustrates the level of detail. He is to collect seeds of all kinds, know the science of agriculture and of plants, and supervise the sowing of crown lands in their proper seasons according to the rainfall; the text records the expected rainfall of different regions and describes a vessel for measuring it at the storehouse. He must ensure that slaves, labourers and convicts working the land are supplied with tools and draught animals, and that the work of artisans who make implements is not delayed (AŚ 2.24).
