Similar detail is given for mines (the identification of ores and the processing of metals), for forests (the reservation of forests for elephants and the collection of timber and forest produce), and for the care of cattle, horses and elephants.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The Superintendent of Trade
docs.text: The superintendent of trade (paṇyādhyakṣa) is to ascertain the demand and supply of goods, high and low prices, and the costs of transport, and to arrange for the sale of state goods (AŚ 2.16). Trade in goods produced in the kingdom is to be centralised in one place; foreign goods are to be sold in many places. Merchants bringing goods from abroad are to be encouraged with remissions and protected from suits for debt by local creditors.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Regulation and Penalties
docs.text:
Book 4, on the “removal of thorns”, treats merchants and artisans as potential sources of harm to the public, alongside thieves (AŚ 4.1–2). The superintendent of weights and measures (pautavādhyakṣa) inspects scales and measures every four months, and false weights are fined. Merchants are allowed a fixed margin of profit: the superintendent is to fix “a profit of five per cent on local goods and ten per cent on foreign goods” (AŚ 4.2.28), and those who raise prices beyond this, or who conspire to withhold goods or to fix prices, are fined. Adulteration and the sale of inferior goods as superior are punished; so are artisans who fail to deliver on time or misappropriate materials. The state itself may buy up surpluses and sell when prices are high.

These provisions are sometimes described as “consumer protection” and “anti-cartel” law. Ancient states commonly regulated weights and prices, and the Arthaśāstra’s rules are unusually detailed; but they belong to a system in which the state is itself a merchant and in which the trading community is regarded with suspicion as a source of fraud. They protect the king’s revenue and public order as much as the buyer.

docs.title: 6.4.3 Guilds
docs.text:
Merchants and artisans in early India were organised in guilds and corporations: the śreṇī (guild of artisans or traders), the naigama (association of merchants), the pūga and gaṇa (associations of various kinds), and the sārtha (caravan). Inscriptions from the second century BCE onwards record guilds of weavers, potters, oil-pressers, corn-dealers, bamboo-workers and others making donations to Buddhist monasteries and acting as bankers: an inscription of Uṣavadāta at Nasik (early 2nd century CE) records permanent endowments of money deposited with two weavers’ guilds at Govardhana, the interest of which was to provide robes and other needs for monks (Majumdar 1918; Thapar 2002). The Dharmaśāstras recognise the conventions (samaya, saṃvid) of guilds and require the king to enforce them, and they give guilds judicial authority over their members (Chapters 12 and 13).

The Arthaśāstra is wary of corporate power: it treats armed corporations and confederacies as potential threats (Book 11) and considers how the king may use or divide them. Its attitude to guilds is therefore ambivalent — they are useful sources of troops and revenue, but rival centres of power.

docs.title: 6.5 Money
docs.text: Coinage in India began with silver punch-marked coins, which archaeology dates from about the fifth or fourth century BCE; they continued in use into the early centuries CE, alongside cast and die-struck copper coins and, from the second century BCE, the coinages of Indo-Greek, Śaka, Kuṣāṇa and other rulers (Thapar 2002). The Arthaśāstra describes a mint under the superintendent of coinage (lakṣaṇādhyakṣa) that strikes silver coins — the paṇa and its half, quarter and eighth — and copper coins — the māṣaka and its fractions down to the kākaṇī — specifying their alloy, and an examiner of coins (rūpadarśaka) who certifies coins in circulation and the treasury (AŚ 2.12). Fines, wages and prices throughout the text are reckoned in paṇas. Counterfeiting is punished, and the punishments listed for offences against the coinage are severe.

docs.title: 6.6.1 Salaries of State Servants
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra gives a scale of annual salaries in paṇas for the servants of the state (AŚ 5.3). At the top, the sacrificial priest, the teacher, the counsellor, the chaplain, the commander of the army, the crown prince, the king’s mother and the chief queen receive 48,000 paṇas; the chamberlain, the head of the harem, the commandant, the collector and the treasurer 24,000; princes, the city judge, the director of factories, the members of the council of ministers and the frontier commanders 12,000; and so on downwards through officials, physicians, soldiers and artisans to servants and labourers at 60 paṇas. The ratio of 800 to 1 between highest and lowest is an index of the steep hierarchy that the text takes for granted. It suggests that the king should pay salaries rather than grant land, and that if the treasury is short he may pay in kind — forest produce, cattle or land.

docs.title: 6.6.2 Hired Labour
docs.text: Book 3 regulates the relation of employer and labourer (AŚ 3.13–14). A labourer who does not work as agreed, or an employer who does not pay, is fined; where no wage was agreed, the labourer receives a customary share of the produce — a tenth of the crop for a cultivator, a tenth of the butter for a herdsman, a tenth of the goods for a trader’s assistant. Labourers who are unable to work because of illness or misfortune are to be given time or allowed to substitute another worker. These rules are a precise and interesting record of how labour relations were imagined; they are not a “labour code” in the modern sense, and they apply within a society in which a great deal of labour was unfree.

docs.title: 6.6.3 Slavery and Bondage
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra and the Dharmaśāstras accept slavery (dāsa) as a legal institution. The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on slaves (AŚ 3.13) is notable for its restrictions. “An Ārya shall never be made a slave” — though the same chapter allows an Ārya to be pledged as a bondsman in distress, and to be enslaved as a judicial punishment — while Mlecchas (foreigners or outsiders) may sell or pledge their own offspring without fault. Kinsmen who sell a minor Śūdra who is an Ārya are fined. A slave may keep what he earns without prejudice to his master’s work and inherit from his father, and can regain freedom by paying his value; a master who makes a slave carry corpses or dirt, or abuses a female slave sexually, loses the price paid for the slave; and a female slave who bears her master’s child is to be freed together with the child. The Manusmṛti, by contrast, lists seven kinds of slave — including the man captured in war, the man who serves for his food, the slave born in the house and the man enslaved as a punishment — and declares that a Śūdra, whether bought or not, may be made to perform servile work, “for he was created by the Self-existent to serve the Brahmin” (Manu 8.413–415).

These provisions reveal a society in which slavery, debt bondage and forced labour (viṣṭi) were normal. Modern presentations that highlight only the Arthaśāstra’s restrictions on the enslavement of Āryas, and omit the institution itself, give a misleading picture. Uma Chakravarti and others have shown how slavery and the servile status of the Śūdra were intertwined in the social theory of the period (Chakravarti 1987; Sharma 1958).

docs.title: 6.7 Calamities and Relief
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra lists “eight great perils” that come from fate rather than from human agency: fire, flood, disease, famine, rats, wild animals, snakes and evil spirits (AŚ 4.3). For each it prescribes remedies, practical and ritual. Against fire, villages are to take precautions in summer and the king is to make offerings to Agni; against floods, villagers living near rivers are to move to higher ground and keep boats and rafts ready; against disease, physicians are to treat the sick with medicines while ascetics perform propitiatory rites; against rats and other pests, traps, poison and the protection of granaries. In famine the king should distribute seed and provisions, undertake public works such as the building of forts or waterworks in which people can earn their food, share his own stores, ask his allies for help, or even migrate with his people to another region with good harvests, or settle them near rivers and lakes and have them cultivate grain, vegetables and roots. The chapter combines empirical measures with religious ones, and it shows a realistic awareness that the king’s revenue and security depended on the survival of the cultivators in bad years.

Records from later periods show that famine relief of this kind — remission of revenue, distribution of grain, the employment of the hungry on public works — was practised by many Indian rulers, as it was by the Mughals and, with notorious failures, by the colonial state. The Arthaśāstra’s recommendations are an early chapter in this long history of the state’s response to subsistence crises.

docs.title: 6.8 Forests and Forest Peoples
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s kingdom is surrounded and penetrated by forest, and its attitude to forests and their inhabitants is revealing. Forests are a resource: the king is to establish forests for producing timber and other materials, and reserved forests for elephants, which were essential to his army; whoever kills an elephant in the royal forests is to be put to death (AŚ 2.2). Forests also served as sanctuaries for animals and as places of retreat for ascetics.

The peoples of the forest (aṭavī, aṭavika) appear in the text chiefly as a problem. They are listed among the possible sources of trouble for a kingdom, and their chiefs are to be watched, won over with gifts or set against one another; forest troops are listed, last and least reliable, among the kinds of troops a king may employ (Chapter 4); and the frontier officers (antapāla) and the officers of the pasture lands are to protect travellers and caravans from them. Aśoka’s thirteenth Rock Edict similarly warns the forest peoples within his empire that, though he has renounced conquest, he still has the power to punish them (Chapter 8). The texts thus record, from the side of the state, the long history of tension between expanding agrarian kingdoms and the communities of the forest, whose own traditions of law and governance are discussed in Chapter 16 (Thapar 2002; Singh 2017).

docs.title: 6.9 Trade and the Wider World
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra knows a wide world of trade. It discusses whether the land route to the north or to the south is more profitable — the teachers prefer the northern route, which brings elephants, horses, perfumes, ivory, skins, silver and gold; Kauṭilya prefers the southern route, which brings conch shells, diamonds, gems, pearls and gold, and has many mines (AŚ 7.12). It lists precious goods from many regions, including silk “from the land of China” and coral from Alexandria (AŚ 2.11). The superintendent of ships (nāvadhyakṣa) supervises ferries, river and coastal shipping, port towns and fisheries, levies tolls and port dues, and is to help ships in distress (AŚ 2.28).

Other sources show that the period in which the Arthaśāstra took shape was one of expanding overland and maritime commerce: the routes known as the uttarāpatha and dakṣiṇāpatha linked the Gangetic plain to the north-west and to the Deccan; the Indian Ocean trade connected the ports of western and southern India with the Roman world, the Gulf and East Africa, and the east coast with Southeast Asia. This history belongs to Volume 19.

docs.title: 6.10 Controlling Officials
docs.text: A distinctive concern of the Arthaśāstra is the honesty of its own officials. It lists forty ways in which officials embezzle, from delaying receipts to falsifying accounts (AŚ 2.8), and observes that it is as impossible to know when an official appropriating revenue is doing so as to know when a fish in water is drinking (AŚ 2.9.33). Its remedies are characteristic: frequent transfers so that officials cannot entrench themselves; joint responsibility of several officers for each department; rewards for informers, who receive a share of what is recovered; secret agents who watch officials and test them with temptations; and punishments graded by the amount embezzled. Officials who increase revenue by ruining the countryside are themselves to be punished, because they “eat up” the kingdom. The modern language of “audit”, “whistle-blowing” and “anti-corruption agencies” captures something of this; the system as a whole, however, rests on surveillance and mutual suspicion rather than on public accountability.

docs.title: 6.11 Town and Country
docs.text:
The city superintendent (nāgaraka) keeps registers of the inhabitants of each ward, controls travellers and lodging-houses, enforces a night curfew, and is responsible for fire precautions — each house is to keep pots of water, ladders and hooks, and cooking in summer is restricted — and for sanitation, with fines for throwing dirt or carcasses in the street (AŚ 2.36). On certain festivals and on the king’s birthday, prisoners are to be released. The text’s countryside is similarly ordered, with records of every household, its members, occupations, income, expenditure and livestock.

Such provisions are often cited as evidence of “urban planning” or “public health” in ancient India. They show the Arthaśāstra’s ideal of a closely supervised population, in which the king’s officers know who lives where, what they own and what they do. They should be read alongside the text’s chapters on espionage and coercion (Chapters 3 and 14).

docs.title: 6.12 Assessment
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s political economy is a remarkable intellectual achievement: a systematic treatment of the economic foundations of state power, written with close attention to detail. Thomas Trautmann has described it as the earliest Indian “science of wealth”, and has argued that it presents a distinctive, state-centred theory of economic life that should be understood on its own terms rather than as a forerunner of European economics (Trautmann 2012). Its central idea — that the king’s power rests on a productive, settled and closely administered population, and that the state should actively organise production and trade to fill the treasury — belongs to its own world of competing kingdoms in early historic India.

docs.title: 6.13 Summary
docs.text:
• The Arthaśāstra treats economics (vārttā: agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade) as one of the four sciences and the treasury as the basis of all undertakings.

  • Its kingdom raises revenue from a land tax (customarily a sixth of the crop), crown lands, tolls and customs, fines, mines, monopolies and many other sources, recorded by an elaborate system of accounts; it also describes means of extracting money in emergencies by deceit.

  • Some thirty superintendents manage state enterprises — mines, mint, weaving, liquor, forests, crown agriculture — and regulate trade, weights and measures and prices, with a fixed profit margin for merchants.

  • Labour was hired, bonded and enslaved; the Arthaśāstra regulates slavery, forbidding the enslavement of an Ārya except in specified cases, while Manu regards the Śūdra as created for servitude.

  • The text’s control of officials relies on rotation, joint responsibility, informers and spies. Its forest policy treats forest peoples mainly as a danger and a resource. Throughout, the aim of this political economy is the power and wealth of the king.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: AŚ Books 2 and 5 are translated and annotated in Olivelle (2013) and Kangle (1960). Trautmann (2012) is the best short study of the Arthaśāstra’s economics. On guilds see Majumdar (1918) (dated but still useful); on the social history of labour and slavery, Sharma (1958) and Chakravarti (1987); on the wider economic history, Thapar (2002) and Singh (2008), and Volume 19 of this series.

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Circle of Kings: Diplomacy, Intelligence and War
docs.text:
Books 6 to 14 of the Arthaśāstra — more than half of the work — concern the relations of a king with other kings. They present a theory of the inter-state system, the “circle” (maṇḍala) of kings; a set of six policy options (ṣāḍguṇya) to be chosen according to circumstances; a doctrine of the means (upāya) by which an opponent may be won over or overcome; detailed advice on envoys, spies and covert action; and an account of military expeditions, battle and the capture of forts. The Mahābhārata and the Dharmaśāstras discuss the same subjects from their own perspectives, and their rules of righteous war (dharmayuddha) have attracted particular attention from modern students of the laws of war.

This chapter presents these doctrines, with attention to what the texts actually say. It also notes the tension, present within the tradition itself, between the Arthaśāstra’s frank acceptance of deception and violence and the epic and dharmaśāstric ideal of honourable war. Military history and the technology of war are treated in Volume 20 of this series.

docs.title: 7.1.1 The Conqueror and His Neighbours
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s theory of foreign policy is built around a figure called the vijigīṣu, “one who wishes to conquer”. He is not an emperor but the ruler of a kingdom of middling size, endowed with good personal qualities and good constituent elements, who seeks to increase his power (AŚ 6.2). Around him are other kings, whose attitude to him is determined principally by geography. The king whose territory borders his is his natural enemy (ari); the king beyond the enemy, who borders the enemy, is his natural ally (mitra); beyond him lies the enemy’s ally (arimitra), then the ally’s ally (mitramitra), then the ally of the enemy’s ally (arimitramitra). Behind the conqueror, similarly, there is a “rear enemy” (pārṣṇigrāha, literally “heel-catcher”), a “rear ally” (ākranda) and the allies of each (pārṣṇigrāhāsāra, ākrandāsāra).

Two further kings complete the circle. The “middle” king (madhyama) has territory adjoining both the conqueror and his enemy and is strong enough to help or resist either of them separately but not together. The “neutral” king (udāsīna) lies outside, is stronger than the conqueror, the enemy and the middle king, and is able to help or resist all of them separately. Together these make twelve kings. Each has five material elements of his own (minister, country, fort, treasury, army), so that the full circle has twelve royal and sixty material elements, seventy-two in all (AŚ 6.2). Figure 7.1 sets out the twelve positions.

Figure 7.1. The circle of twelve kings (maṇḍala) of AŚ 6.2, drawn as a line of kingdoms in front of and behind the would-be conqueror, with the middle and neutral kings outside it. Kingdoms coloured red are hostile to the conqueror by position, those coloured green friendly. Each of the twelve kings has five material elements of his own (minister, country, fort, treasury, army), so that the circle comprises seventy-two elements.

docs.title: 7.1.2 What Kind of Theory Is This?
docs.text:
The maṇḍala is an abstract model. Its alternating pattern — “my neighbour’s neighbour is my friend” — follows from the assumption that kings who share a frontier compete for land and resources, so that the enemy of an enemy has an interest in cooperating against him. The text immediately qualifies it: a neighbour may be a “natural” enemy, but there are also enemies by birth (such as kinsmen with claims to the throne) and enemies made by injury, and an ally may become dangerous if he grows too strong. The model is a tool for thinking about a world of many kingdoms of comparable strength, in which none can afford to ignore the others. That is the world of the early historic Gangetic plain and Deccan, or of the regional kingdoms of the early medieval period, rather than of the Mauryan empire.

Modern scholars of international relations have often compared the maṇḍala with the balance-of-power thinking of European statecraft and with the “realist” theory of international politics, in which the structure of the system rather than the character of states determines their conduct. The comparison describes the text’s logic well, and Kauṭilya is now often read in courses on strategic thought (Boesche 2002). What it can obscure is the text’s purpose: the Arthaśāstra’s theory is addressed to a king who wishes to conquer, and it assumes, without argument, that expansion is the natural goal of kingship.

docs.title: 7.1.3 Three Kinds of Conqueror
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra itself distinguishes kinds of conquest. In Book 12, discussing how a weaker king should respond to a stronger, it describes three types of conqueror: the “righteous conqueror” (dharmavijayin), who is satisfied with the submission of the defeated; the “greedy conqueror” (lobhavijayin), who wants land and wealth; and the “demonic conqueror” (asuravijayin), who wants land, wealth, the sons and wives of the defeated and their lives (AŚ 12.1). The weaker king should submit to the first, buy off the second, and resist the third by every means. The idea that a king might conquer and then restore the defeated ruler as a subordinate appears in inscriptions: Samudragupta’s Allahabad pillar inscription (4th century CE) boasts that he captured and then released and reinstated the kings of the south. Aśoka’s dhammavijaya, “conquest by dhamma”, proclaimed in his thirteenth Rock Edict after the bloody conquest of Kaliṅga, is a different and more radical idea (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.2.1 Definitions
docs.text:
Book 7 begins: “The circle of constituent elements is the source of the six measures” (AŚ 7.1.1). The six measures (ṣāḍguṇya) are peace (sandhi), war (vigraha), staying quiet (āsana), marching (yāna), seeking shelter (saṃśraya) and the double policy (dvaidhībhāva). The text records that one teacher, Vātavyādhi, recognised only two measures, peace and war, from which the others derive; Kauṭilya insists that there are six, because the situations differ (AŚ 7.1.2–5). It then defines them tersely:

  • Peace (sandhi) is an agreement with stipulations (paṇabandha);

  • war (vigraha) is doing injury;

  • staying quiet (āsana) is remaining indifferent;

  • marching (yāna) is augmentation of one’s power, the military expedition;

  • seeking shelter (saṃśraya) is submitting oneself to another;

  • the double policy (dvaidhībhāva) is resorting to peace with one and war with another.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Choosing a Policy
docs.text:
The choice among them follows from an assessment of relative strength and of the direction in which one’s power is moving. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes three conditions of a kingdom: decline (kṣaya), stability (sthāna) and growth (vṛddhi); the aim of policy is to move from decline to stability and from stability to growth. Its basic rules are: a king who is declining in comparison with his enemy should make peace; one who is growing should make war; one who thinks that neither he nor his enemy can harm the other should stay quiet; one who has excess of strength should march; one who lacks strength should seek shelter with a stronger king; and one who needs help to achieve his aim should adopt the double policy (AŚ 7.1). If peace and war bring equal advantage, peace is to be preferred, because war brings losses, expenditure, absence from home and other evils (AŚ 7.2).

The remainder of Book 7 works through a long series of cases — whether to march against a weak enemy or a strong one, whether to ally with a weak king or a strong one, what to do when the rear enemy threatens — with a precision that has impressed modern readers. Its method is casuistic: it enumerates possibilities, compares advantages and disadvantages, and reports earlier opinions before giving its own.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Treaties and Hostages
docs.text: Peace is concluded by agreements that may be sealed by oath, by surety or by hostages. The Arthaśāstra prefers agreements backed by hostages or sureties to those resting only on oaths, which it regards as unreliable (AŚ 7.17). It classifies peace treaties by what the weaker party surrenders: troops, treasure or territory, in various forms and on harder or easier terms (AŚ 7.3). It also explains how a king who has made peace may break it when he becomes stronger, and how he can use a treaty to lull an enemy into security. Treaties, in this text, are instruments of policy, binding for as long as they serve the interest of the party bound by them.

docs.title: 7.2.4 The Weaker King
docs.text: Book 12, on the weaker king (ābalīyasa), considers the situation from the other side. Beyond the advice on the three kinds of conqueror given above, it describes the means by which a weak king can defeat a strong one without open battle: sending envoys to divide the enemy’s allies from him, using agents to turn his ministers and commanders against him, poisoning or assassinating him and his chief officers, and inciting his subjects and neighbours against him. Its realism about the resources available to the weak is one reason why the Arthaśāstra has interested modern students of asymmetric conflict.

docs.title: 7.2.5 Expeditions: Power, Place and Time
docs.text: Before marching, the king must weigh his own and his enemy’s strength in terms of the “three powers” — counsel, might and energy (Chapter 4) — and consider the place and the time (AŚ 9.1). Places are to be judged by their suitability for one’s own army: some terrain suits elephants, some horses, some chariots, some infantry. Times are judged by the season — the text recommends particular months for campaigns against particular kinds of enemy, with attention to the harvest, the availability of fodder and water, and the rains — and by the opportunity presented by the enemy’s calamities. The king must also guard against revolts in the rear and against the danger that his own ministers or princes will rise while he is away. Book 9 thus combines the analysis of the maṇḍala with the practicalities of logistics and internal security.

docs.title: 7.3 The Four Means
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra and the Dharmaśāstras recognise four means (upāya) of dealing with an opponent: conciliation (sāman), gifts (dāna, upapradāna), sowing dissension (bheda) and force (daṇḍa) (AŚ 2.10). The scheme became proverbial in Indian languages as “sām–dām–daṇḍ–bhed”. It is applied not only to enemy kings but to rebellious officials, forest peoples and confederacies.

The Manusmṛti expresses a preference for the milder means: the king should try to conquer his enemies by conciliation, gifts and dissension, used together or separately, and never by battle; since victory in battle is uncertain, he should avoid war as far as possible (Manu 7.198–199). Elsewhere it observes that the learned praise conciliation and force above the others for the growth of the kingdom (Manu 7.109). The Arthaśāstra is more pragmatic and more elaborate. In its treatment of confederacies (Book 11), for example, it recommends that agents sow dissension among the leaders by spreading rumours, provoking quarrels over women, and staging insults, so that the confederacy can be broken up and absorbed. The four means are not a moral hierarchy in the Arthaśāstra but a toolkit.

docs.title: 7.4 Envoys
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra distinguishes three kinds of envoy (dūta) according to the powers delegated to them: the plenipotentiary (nisṛṣṭārtha), who has full authority to negotiate; the envoy with a limited mission (parimitārtha); and the bearer of a message (śāsanahara) (AŚ 1.16). The envoy should travel with the permission of the frontier officers, observe the strength of the enemy’s forts and army on the way, deliver his message exactly as given even if threatened with weapons, and avoid drink and women. He should gather information through spies and through the enemy’s disaffected subjects, and stay or leave according to his king’s interest.

Envoys enjoyed a protected status. The Arthaśāstra gives the reason: kings speak through envoys, and envoys must speak as instructed even when weapons are raised against them; “of them, even those of the lowest birth are not to be killed, much less Brahmins” (AŚ 1.16.14–15). The Rāmāyaṇa dramatises the same principle: when Hanumān, Rāma’s envoy, is captured in Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa wishes to kill him, but his brother Vibhīṣaṇa reminds him that envoys may not be killed, and Hanumān’s tail is set on fire instead. The inviolability of envoys is a principle found in many ancient societies, the remote ancestor of modern diplomatic immunity rather than a peculiarly Indian rule.

The epics give the envoy a central place in their plots. In the Mahābhārata’s Udyoga Parvan, Yudhiṣṭhira first sends word through Sañjaya, the envoy of the Kaurava king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that the Pāṇḍavas would be content with five villages (MBh 5.31) — the offer that popular retellings put into Kṛṣṇa’s mouth. Kṛṣṇa then goes in person as envoy of the Pāṇḍavas to the Kaurava court to seek a peaceful settlement that would restore their share of the kingdom; Duryodhana refuses, and plots to seize the envoy, a plan that the elders condemn as a violation of dharma and that Kṛṣṇa foils by a display of divine power. The failure of the embassy makes war inevitable. In the Rāmāyaṇa, Aṅgada goes as Rāma’s envoy to Rāvaṇa before the battle for Laṅkā. These episodes dramatise both the ideal of negotiation before war and the vulnerability of envoys in the court of an enemy.

The Arthaśāstra is also candid that envoys are spies: the envoy is to cultivate the enemy’s officials, learn the disposition of his forces, and sow dissension where he can. Diplomacy and intelligence are not separate activities in this text.

docs.title: 7.5.1 The Network of Agents
docs.text: No feature of the Arthaśāstra is more famous than its system of secret agents (Chapter 3). Book 1 describes “stationary” agents — a fraudulent student (kāpaṭika), an apostate ascetic (udāsthita), a householder (gṛhapatika), a trader (vaidehaka) and a holy man with shaven head or matted hair (tāpasa) — and “roving” agents: the secret operative (sattrin), often an orphan raised by the state and trained in signs, palmistry and other arts; the bravo (tīkṣṇa), ready to fight even an elephant for money; the poisoner (rasada); and the wandering nun (parivrājikā, bhikṣukī), who has access to the houses of high officials (AŚ 1.11–12). Agents are also placed as cooks, bath attendants, servants, entertainers, prostitutes and doorkeepers. They report through a system of signs and codes, and their reports are confirmed only when three independent agents agree.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Purposes
docs.text:
The agents serve three purposes. They watch the king’s own ministers and officials, test their loyalty and report on their conduct. They watch the population, reporting on the contented and the discontented and winning over or eliminating the latter. And they operate in the territory of enemies and allies, gathering intelligence, spreading rumours, corrupting officials and, when ordered, killing. Books 11–14 describe their use against confederacies, against a besieged fort and against enemy kings: agents may poison food and water, set fires, assassinate leaders at festivals, and use magical and medical preparations described in Book 14.

The modern vocabulary of “intelligence cycle”, “counter-intelligence” and “disinformation” has been applied to these chapters, and the text does show a sophisticated understanding of the gathering, verification and use of information. But the Arthaśāstra’s spies are more than an intelligence service: they are an instrument of social control within the kingdom and of covert violence outside it. Upinder Singh has emphasised how central this violence is to the text’s conception of the state (Singh 2017).

docs.title: 7.6 The Maṇḍala after Kauṭilya
docs.text: The theory of the circle of kings was taken up and modified by later writers. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra restates it at length, discussing the various circles of kings and the measures of policy, and it reports alternative schemes in which the circle has different numbers of members. The Manusmṛti summarises the same scheme (7.155–158), and the Śānti Parvan and later works on polity repeat it. Medieval inscriptions sometimes describe kings as having “subdued the circle” of their neighbours, using the vocabulary of the theory to praise military success. The concept also travelled with Indian political ideas to Southeast Asia, and modern historians of that region have used the term maṇḍala to describe the loosely structured, overlapping polities of the first and second millennia, in which a powerful centre was surrounded by tributary states whose allegiance shifted with its strength (Wolters 1982; Tambiah 1976). That modern usage is an analytical borrowing, not evidence that Southeast Asian rulers read the Arthaśāstra.

docs.title: 7.7 Intelligence in Later Indian States
docs.text: Later Indian states maintained systems of intelligence and reporting, though they cannot be shown to have followed the Arthaśāstra. The Mughal empire posted news-writers (wāqiʿa-nawīs) and secret reporters in the provinces, who sent regular reports to the court on the conduct of governors and officials, on events in the towns and on the movements of troops; the emperor and his ministers used these reports to check the power of provincial officers. The Maratha state and the regional kingdoms of the eighteenth century maintained similar networks, and the East India Company built up its own system of intelligence in the course of its wars of conquest. Such institutions show that the problems the Arthaśāstra addressed — the loyalty of officials and the gathering of information in large states — were recurrent ones, solved in each period with the resources available.

docs.title: 7.8.1 Three Kinds of War
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra distinguishes open war (prakāśayuddha), fought at an appointed time and place; concealed war (kūṭayuddha), which uses surprise, ambush, feigned retreat and attacks at night or on troops in difficulty; and “silent war” (tūṣṇīṃyuddha), the use of secret agents to kill or subvert enemy leaders without open hostilities (AŚ 7.6). Open war is the most honourable; the others are the most effective. When the conqueror is superior in strength, he may fight openly; when he is not, he should use concealed or silent war.

docs.title: 7.8.2 The Army and Battle
docs.text:
The traditional army had four arms (caturaṅga): elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry. The Arthaśāstra describes the duties of the commander and of the superintendents of elephants, horses, chariots and infantry, the training and pay of troops, the choice of terrain suitable for each arm, and the order of march (AŚ 2.30–33; Book 10). It describes battle arrays (vyūha), of which four are basic: the staff (daṇḍa), the snake (bhoga), the circle (maṇḍala) and the detached array (asaṃhata), each with variants (AŚ 10.6). The elaborate arrays with names such as cakravyūha, garuḍavyūha and padmavyūha belong chiefly to the Mahābhārata and later literature.

The famous numerical scheme of army units is also epic rather than Kauṭilyan. The Mahābhārata (1.2) defines a patti as one chariot, one elephant, three horsemen and five foot soldiers; three pattis make a senāmukha, three senāmukhas a gulma, three gulmas a gaṇa, three gaṇas a vāhinī, three vāhinīs a pṛtanā, three pṛtanās a camū, three camūs an anīkinī, and ten anīkinīs an akṣauhiṇī — that is, 21,870 chariots, 21,870 elephants, 65,610 horsemen and 109,350 foot soldiers. The Kauravas are said to have fielded eleven akṣauhiṇīs and the Pāṇḍavas seven. These figures are epic idealisations, not records of real armies.

docs.title: 7.8.3 Sieges and Pacification
docs.text:
Book 13 of the Arthaśāstra describes how to take a fort: by sowing dissension within it through agents posing as holy men who claim omniscience or divine powers, by luring the enemy out, by blockade and by assault. It advises the destruction of the enemy’s crops, stores and water before a siege, and the Manusmṛti similarly tells the king besieging an enemy to spoil his fodder, food, water and fuel and to break his tanks, ramparts and moats (Manu 7.195–196). Neither text, therefore, protects the “environment” in war, as is sometimes claimed.

The last chapter of Book 13 concerns the pacification of conquered territory, and it is one of the more humane passages of the text. The conqueror should replace the vices of the defeated king with his own virtues; honour the local deities, festivals and religious leaders; adopt the dress, language and customs of the people; release prisoners and help the distressed; and abolish practices that the people regard as unjust (AŚ 13.5). The motive is stability, but the advice shows a clear understanding that conquest must be followed by legitimacy.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Rules in Manu and the Epic
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras and the Mahābhārata lay down rules of conduct for Kṣatriyas in battle. Manu’s rules are among the most often quoted (Manu 7.90–93). A warrior fighting in battle should not kill his enemies with concealed weapons, or with barbed, poisoned or fire-tipped arrows. He should not kill an enemy who is on the ground when he himself is in a chariot, nor a eunuch, nor one who joins his palms in supplication, nor one whose hair is loose, nor one who is seated, nor one who says “I am yours”; nor one who is asleep, without armour, naked or unarmed, nor a spectator who is not fighting, nor one engaged with another; nor one whose weapons are broken, who is in distress, badly wounded, terrified or fleeing. The Mahābhārata’s Bhīṣma Parvan opens with a similar list of conventions agreed by both sides before the great battle: combatants should fight their equals, chariot against chariot and horse against horse; those who withdraw, who are unarmed or who have surrendered, charioteers, drummers and those carrying weapons for others should not be attacked.

These rules belong to the core of the tradition. The protection of those hors de combat, of the surrendered and of non-combatants, and the prohibition of certain weapons, all have counterparts in the Geneva and Hague Conventions. The differences are as instructive. The Indian rules are a warrior’s code of honour among Kṣatriyas, enforced, if at all, by religious sanction and reputation, not by any inter-state law. They protect combatants of equal standing far more than they protect civilians, and they coexist in the same texts with the advice to destroy the enemy’s supplies and to use stratagem when necessary.

docs.title: 7.9.2 The Epic’s Moral Struggle
docs.text: The Mahābhārata does not present righteous war as easily attained. The Pāṇḍavas, the side of dharma, win the war only by a series of stratagems that break the agreed rules, most of them advised by Kṛṣṇa: Bhīṣma is felled by Arjuna sheltering behind Śikhaṇḍin, whom Bhīṣma will not fight; Droṇa is made to lay down his arms by Yudhiṣṭhira’s half-truth that “Aśvatthāman” (an elephant of that name) has been killed; Karṇa is killed while trying to free his stuck chariot wheel; Duryodhana is struck below the navel in a mace-fight, against the rules. The defeated Kauravas protest each time, and the epic gives their protests weight. Kṛṣṇa’s justification — that against enemies who themselves had broken every rule, and who could not otherwise be defeated, such means were necessary — reproduces in narrative form the Arthaśāstra’s distinction between open and concealed war. The epic’s refusal to resolve this tension is one of its most profound features.

docs.title: 7.9.3 Kauṭilya and the Laws of War
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra does not deny the value of open, honourable battle, but it treats it as one option among several, to be used when one is stronger. Its silent war of assassination and its concealed war of stratagem belong to the same calculus. This frankness is the reason why later literary authors, such as Bāṇa, condemned the text as ruthless (Chapter 3), and why it fascinates modern students of strategy.

docs.title: 7.10 Diplomacy in Practice
docs.text:
Historical sources show Indian rulers practising many of the arts the texts describe. After Seleucus, Alexander’s successor in the east, failed to recover the Indian provinces, he concluded a treaty with Candragupta Maurya (c. 303 BCE) by which he ceded territories in the north-west, received five hundred war elephants, and entered into an agreement on marriage; Megasthenes was sent as his envoy to the Mauryan court. Aśoka’s thirteenth Rock Edict names five Hellenistic kings to whom he had sent his “conquest by dhamma” (Chapter 8).

Marriage alliances were a standard instrument of policy. The Gupta king Candragupta II married his daughter Prabhāvatīguptā to the Vākāṭaka king of the Deccan, and after her husband’s death she ruled as regent, extending Gupta influence southward. The Allahabad inscription of Samudragupta lists rulers who paid him homage, offered daughters in marriage or sought his favour. Harṣa of Kanauj exchanged embassies with the Tang emperor of China in the seventh century. The Cōḷa kings conducted diplomacy and war across the Bay of Bengal. Later, the Mughals combined war, marriage alliances with Rajput houses, the grant of ranks (manṣab) and the confirmation of local rulers in their lands in a policy of incorporation (Chapter 18). These cases illustrate the range of instruments — treaties, marriages, gifts, hostages, the reinstatement of defeated rulers — that the śāstras classify, though no ruler can be shown to have followed the Arthaśāstra as a manual.

docs.title: 7.11 Buddhist and Jain Views of War
docs.text: The Buddhist and Jain traditions, with their ethics of non-violence, viewed war with particular unease. In the Pali canon the Buddha declares that a warrior who dies in battle does not, as was popularly believed, go to a heaven of warriors, because his mind at death is set on killing; Aśoka’s thirteenth Rock Edict expresses remorse for the deaths in Kaliṅga and recommends conquest by dhamma (Chapter 8). Jain narratives send the Vāsudeva heroes who kill their enemies to hell. Yet Buddhist and Jain kings fought wars like other kings, and their traditions found ways to accommodate them. The Sri Lankan chronicle Mahāvaṃsa tells how King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, after defeating the Tamil king Eḷāra in the second century BCE, was troubled by the thousands killed in his war, and how monks consoled him by saying that only one and a half of the slain were true human beings, the rest being unbelievers — a passage often cited in modern discussions of religion and violence in Sri Lanka. The episode shows how religious traditions of non-violence could themselves be bent to justify war (Tambiah 1976).

docs.title: 7.12 War in Tamil Tradition
docs.text: The Tamil Caṅkam poems offer a view of war very different from that of the Sanskrit treatises. The “exterior” (puṟam) poems, concerned with public life, war and kingship, were classified by early Tamil grammarians into situations (tiṇai), many of them military: the cattle raid that opened hostilities (veṭci) and the recovery of the cattle (karantai); the invasion of enemy territory (vañci) and its defence (kāñci); the siege of a fort (uḻiñai) and its defence (nocci); battle (tumpai) and victory (vākai). The poems celebrate the courage of warriors, the generosity of kings to their bards, and the grief of mothers and widows, and they record the custom of erecting memorial stones (naṭukal) for heroes who died in battle, many of which survive with inscriptions. They do not set out rules of war in the manner of Manu or the Mahābhārata; their values are those of a heroic society in which honour, gift and lament were bound together. Volume 8 of this series discusses this poetry, and Volume 20 the history of war.

docs.title: 7.13 Spoils, Captives and the Conquered
docs.text:
The texts that regulate the conduct of battle also regulate its rewards. Manu lays down that chariots, horses, elephants, parasols, money, grain, animals, women, goods of every kind and base metals belong to whoever wins them, but that the warriors should give the king a choice portion, and the king should distribute among them whatever was not won individually (Manu 7.96–97). The inclusion of women among the spoils is a reminder that the warrior’s code did not protect the women of the defeated. Captivity in war was also one of the recognised origins of slavery: Manu’s list of seven kinds of slave begins with the man “captured under a standard” (dhvajāhṛta, Manu 8.415), and the Arthaśāstra discusses the ransom and release of Āryas taken captive (Chapter 13).

Manu also advises the conqueror on how to treat a conquered kingdom. Having learned the wishes of its people, he should install a member of the defeated king’s family on the throne, make a formal agreement with him, honour the conquered king and his chief men with gifts, and make the laws and customs of the conquered land authoritative (Manu 7.201–203). This is close to the Arthaśāstra’s advice on pacification and to its ideal of the “righteous conqueror” (see above). Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa gives the ideal its classic literary form: King Raghu, on his conquest of the four quarters, is a “righteous conqueror” who takes the glory of the defeated king of Mahendra but not his land (Raghuvaṃśa 4.43). Inscriptions such as Samudragupta’s at Allahabad, which distinguish between kings of the north who were “violently uprooted” and kings of the south who were captured and released, show that rulers could practise both kinds of conquest and boast of both.

Aśoka’s thirteenth Rock Edict offers a rare view from the side of the victims: its account of the deportations and deaths in Kaliṅga (Chapter 8) dwells on the suffering of Brahmins, ascetics and householders who had done no wrong (Hultzsch 1925; Thapar 1961). No other ancient Indian text speaks of the victims of war in this way.

docs.title: 7.14 Comparisons and Reception
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s doctrines of war and diplomacy are often compared with Sun Tzu’s Art of War (c. 5th–3rd century BCE), which also recommends the use of spies — it distinguishes five kinds — and prefers victory without battle; with Thucydides’ account of the Peloponnesian War, whose Melian Dialogue is a classic statement of the logic of power; and with Machiavelli. Such comparisons show that early political thinkers in several civilisations reached similar conclusions about the role of power, deception and intelligence in the relations of states. They do not establish that one tradition was more “advanced” than another, and the Arthaśāstra’s distinctive contribution is better described in its own terms: a systematic and casuistic analysis of the options open to a king in a world of competing kingdoms (Boesche 2002).

In modern India, the maṇḍala and the four means have been invoked by commentators on foreign policy, and Kauṭilya’s name has been given to institutions and conferences on strategic affairs. These are uses of a classical text by modern actors (Chapter 20). Historians have also drawn attention to the gap between the Arthaśāstra’s model and the actual conduct of Indian states, whose wars, alliances and marriage diplomacy are known from inscriptions and chronicles; the Cōḷa king Rājendra I’s naval expedition against Śrīvijaya in Southeast Asia (c. 1025 CE), for example, belongs to a world of maritime power that the text barely imagines.

docs.title: 7.15 Summary
docs.text:
• The maṇḍala of twelve kings, in which neighbours are natural enemies and the neighbours’ neighbours natural allies, is the frame for six measures of policy and four means, chosen by relative strength.

  • Envoys are inviolable but also spies, and a network of secret agents serves surveillance at home and covert violence abroad.

  • The Arthaśāstra treats open, concealed and silent war as options to be weighed; Manu and the epic lay down rules of righteous war, which the Mahābhārata shows broken by the side of dharma itself.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: AŚ Books 6–14 are translated in Olivelle (2013) and Kangle (1960); McClish and Olivelle (2012) provides selections. Boesche (2002) discusses the Arthaśāstra as political realism; Singh (2017) examines war and violence in the texts and inscriptions. On the rules of war in the epic, see Fitzgerald (2004); for military history and technology, Volume 20 of this series.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Kingship, Dhamma and Law in the Buddhist and Jain Traditions
docs.text:
The Brahmanical śāstras are not the only Indian sources of political and legal thought. The Buddhist and Jain traditions, which arose in the eastern Gangetic plain in the fifth century BCE, produced their own accounts of the origin of kingship and society, their own ideals of the righteous ruler, and — in the monastic codes — some of the most detailed procedural law to survive from early India. Aśoka, the most powerful king of the period, proclaimed a policy of dhamma in inscriptions across the subcontinent. Jain authors wrote works on polity and adapted the Brahmanical scheme of social orders to their own purposes, and Jain kings and merchants shaped the legal culture of western India for centuries.

This chapter surveys these traditions. It has two aims: to represent them on their own terms rather than as variations on a Brahmanical norm, and to avoid the opposite error of treating them as egalitarian alternatives to Brahmanical hierarchy. The early Buddhist and Jain communities challenged the Brahmins’ claims to superiority by birth, but they did not set out to abolish kingship, social rank or slavery in society at large, and their own institutions had hierarchies of their own (Chakravarti 1987).

docs.title: 8.1 The World of the Śramaṇas
docs.text:
The Buddha (c. 480–400 BCE on the now widely accepted short chronology; the traditional Theravāda dates are 624–544 BCE) and Mahāvīra, the twenty-fourth Jina of the Jains and an older contemporary of the Buddha, belonged to a broad movement of renouncers (śramaṇa) who rejected the authority of the Veda and the efficacy of sacrifice. They taught in a region of new cities and expanding kingdoms — Magadha under Bimbisāra and Ajātaśatru, Kosala under Prasenajit — and of clan-based polities called gaṇa or saṅgha, such as the Śākyas (the Buddha’s own clan), the Mallas and the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, leaders of the Vajjian confederacy.

These gaṇa-saṅghas are sometimes called “republics”. They were governed not by a single hereditary king but by assemblies of the heads of leading Kṣatriya families, each of whom might bear the title rājā; decisions were taken in a hall (santhāgāra) after discussion. They were oligarchies of a ruling clan, which excluded the many dependants, labourers and slaves who lived in their territory, and it is misleading to call them democracies (Sharma 1959; Thapar 1984). They nevertheless show that monarchy was not the only form of government known in early India. The Arthaśāstra’s Book 11 treats such confederacies as dangerous rivals to be divided and absorbed (Chapters 3 and 7), and most of them were absorbed into the Magadhan empire within a few centuries.

docs.title: 8.2 The Buddha and the Vajjian Assembly
docs.text:
The Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 16), which recounts the last months of the Buddha’s life, opens with a political episode. King Ajātasattu of Magadha resolves to destroy the Vajjis and sends his minister to ask the Buddha’s opinion. The Buddha, turning to his attendant Ānanda, asks whether the Vajjis still observe certain practices, and declares that as long as they do so, they may be expected to prosper and not decline. The seven “conditions of non-decline” (aparihāniyā dhammā) are: that the Vajjis meet often and in large numbers in assembly; that they meet, act and disperse in concord; that they do not authorise what has not been authorised nor abolish what has been authorised, but proceed according to the ancient Vajjian law as established; that they honour and listen to their elders; that they do not abduct or coerce the women and girls of their clans; that they honour their shrines and maintain their customary offerings; and that they protect and support the arahants. The Buddha then applies a parallel list of conditions to his own monastic community. Ajātasattu’s minister concludes that the Vajjis cannot be defeated in war — except by diplomacy or by sowing dissension among them.

The passage is often cited as evidence of the Buddha’s sympathy for “republican” government. It certainly shows respect for the governance of the gaṇas and for deliberation, concord and adherence to established custom. It is also a teaching about the conditions for the survival of the saṅgha itself, and it ends with the observation — worthy of the Arthaśāstra — that a confederacy is vulnerable to dissension.

docs.title: 8.3 The Origin of Kingship: The Aggañña Sutta
docs.text:
The Aggañña Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 27), the “discourse on what is primary”, contains the best-known Buddhist account of the origins of society and kingship (Collins 1993). It is addressed to two Brahmin novices who have been reviled by other Brahmins for joining the Buddha’s order. The Brahmins claim, the young men report, that only Brahmins are the best varṇa and the true sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth. The Buddha replies by observing that Brahmin women are seen to menstruate, become pregnant and give birth like any others, and he then tells a story of the world’s evolution.

At the beginning of a cycle, beings are luminous and self-sustaining. Gradually they begin to eat a savoury earth, become coarser, and are differentiated in appearance; pride in beauty appears. Eventually rice grows of itself, and beings take it as needed. When some begin to store rice out of laziness, the rice no longer grows back; the beings divide the land into fields with boundaries. Then one being, greedy, takes rice from another’s field; he is reproached and promises not to do it again, but does so a second and third time; he is beaten. “Thus theft appeared, and censure, and lying, and punishment.” The beings then gather and agree to choose one among them who will be angry with what should provoke anger, censure what should be censured and banish whoever should be banished, in return for a share of their rice. They choose the most handsome, attractive and capable among them. Because he is “agreed upon by the great people” (mahājanasammata), he is called Mahāsammata, the “Great Elect”; because he is “lord of the fields” (khettānaṃ adhipati), he is called khattiya; and because he “delights others with dhamma” (dhammena pare rañjeti), he is called rājā. The text then accounts for the Brahmins, Vessas and Suddas by similar punning etymologies, and concludes that whoever, of any varṇa, lives a good life and becomes an arahant is “foremost”. Even so, it adds that among those who rely on lineage, the khattiya is the best.

Modern readers have often called this a “social contract” theory of kingship and contrasted it with the divine origin of the king in the Manusmṛti (Chapter 5). There is a genuine difference: in the Buddhist story kingship is a human institution, created by agreement to deal with theft, and the king is paid for his services. But Steven Collins, in his annotated translation, argued that the sutta is in large part a parody — a witty retelling, in a Buddhist key, of Brahmanical myths of origin and of the etymologies the Brahmins used to justify their claims — and that its main purpose is to deny that varṇa is a matter of divine creation, not to found a political theory (Collins 1993). Its “contract” gives the people no right to remove the king, and the later Buddhist tradition used the figure of Mahāsammata as the ancestor of royal lineages rather than as a model of popular sovereignty (Tambiah 1976).

docs.title: 8.4.1 The Cakkavatti-sīhanāda Sutta
docs.text:
The ideal Buddhist ruler is the cakkavattin (Sanskrit cakravartin), the “wheel-turning” universal monarch, who conquers the four quarters not by force but by the power of righteousness, symbolised by a divine wheel that rolls before him. The figure is pan-Indian: Jain texts list twelve cakravartins among their great persons, and Brahmanical texts know the cakravartin as a world-ruler. The Cakkavatti-sīhanāda Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 26) gives the fullest Buddhist account.

A cakkavattin named Daḷhanemi rules righteously and, when the wheel slips from its place, hands the kingdom to his son. Each new king must himself earn the wheel by practising the “noble duty of a wheel-turner”: relying on dhamma, honouring it, he provides lawful protection and security to his household, his troops, Kṣatriyas, vassals, Brahmins and householders, townspeople and country people, ascetics and Brahmins, and animals and birds; he lets no wrongdoing prevail in his realm; and “to whoever in the kingdom is poor, give wealth”. A later king fails to give wealth to the poor. Poverty spreads; a poor man steals; the king, when told he stole because he had nothing, gives him wealth to live on and support his family. Others then steal in order to receive wealth, so the king changes policy and has a thief executed. Thieves then arm themselves and kill those they rob; violence, lying, slander, adultery and other evils spread, and the human lifespan declines, generation by generation, from eighty thousand years to ten. Only after a period of mutual slaughter do the survivors turn again to good conduct, and the world gradually recovers, until the future Buddha Metteyya appears in the time of a new wheel-turning king.

The sutta has been read as a theory of the social causes of crime: it is the king’s failure to relieve poverty that sets off the decline, and the resort to execution makes things worse. It is also a myth of cosmic decline and renewal, and it insists, like the Brahmanical texts, that the king must suppress wrongdoing. Its striking feature is the link it makes between the ruler’s economic duty to the poor and the moral condition of society.

docs.title: 8.4.2 Kūṭadanta’s Sacrifice
docs.text: A similar argument appears in the Kūṭadanta Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 5). A Brahmin asks the Buddha how to perform a great sacrifice, and the Buddha tells him of a king of the past who wished to do so. The king’s chaplain advises that the country is troubled by bandits, and that it would be wrong to tax it further; nor will the bandits be suppressed by execution, imprisonment, fines or banishment, since survivors will continue to harass the realm. Instead, the king should give seed and fodder to those who farm and keep cattle, capital to those who trade, and food and wages to those in government service. Then people, intent on their own occupations, will not harass the realm, revenue will increase, and the country will be at peace, “with doors open”. The king follows this advice, and then performs a sacrifice in which no animal is killed and no labour is forced. The story uses the form of a royal sacrifice to teach an argument about economic remedies for disorder — and to criticise Vedic sacrifice.

docs.title: 8.4.3 The Ten Royal Virtues
docs.text: The Jātakas, the stories of the Buddha’s former lives, frequently refer to ten “royal virtues” (dasa rājadhammā): generosity (dāna), moral conduct (sīla), liberality (pariccāga), honesty (ajjava), gentleness (maddava), self-restraint (tapa), freedom from anger (akkodha), non-violence (avihiṃsā), patience (khanti) and non-opposition, that is, not obstructing what is right (avirodhana). The list became a central element of royal ideology in the Buddhist kingdoms of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, where kings were expected to embody these virtues and to protect the Buddhist order (Tambiah 1976).

docs.title: 8.4.4 The Buddha and Kings
docs.text: The Pali canon is realistic about kings. They appear as patrons and devotees, like Bimbisāra of Magadha and Pasenadi of Kosala, but also as dangers: kings are listed with fire, water and thieves among the threats to property, and Ajātasattu came to the throne by having his father killed. The monastic code forbids monks to watch armies and limits their contact with soldiers. Steven Collins has argued that the Pali texts contain two attitudes: an “ethic of reciprocity”, which accepts that kings must punish and fight, and an “ethic of non-violence”, expressed in the monastic ideal, which judges all violence as wrong; Buddhist political thought lives with the tension between them (Collins 1998).

docs.title: 8.5 The Saṅgha as a Legal Community
8.5.1 The Vinaya
docs.text: The Buddhist monastic code, the Vinaya, is one of the largest bodies of early Indian law. It survives in several versions belonging to different schools (Theravāda in Pali; Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka and others in Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan). At its core is the Pātimokkha, the list of rules recited by monks every fortnight, with a longer list for nuns, arranged in classes by gravity. Around the rules the Vinaya builds a large casuistic literature, recording for each rule the case that occasioned it, the definitions of its terms, and the exceptions (Horner 1938).

docs.title: 8.5.2 The Structure of the Code
docs.text:
The Theravāda Pātimokkha for monks contains 227 rules in eight classes: four pārājika offences — sexual intercourse, theft of a certain value, killing a human being and falsely claiming spiritual attainments — entailing permanent expulsion; thirteen saṅghādisesa offences (requiring a meeting of the community and a period of probation); two “undetermined” (aniyata) cases, in which the offence depends on the testimony of a trustworthy laywoman; thirty offences involving forfeiture of an improperly acquired object (nissaggiya pācittiya), such as an extra robe or money; ninety-two offences requiring confession (pācittiya), from lying to drinking alcohol; four offences to be acknowledged (pāṭidesanīya); seventy-five rules of training (sekhiya) concerning deportment; and the seven ways of settling disputes. Each rule is accompanied in the Suttavibhaṅga by a story of the incident that led the Buddha to lay it down, a word-by-word commentary, and a discussion of the cases in which it does or does not apply — a method strikingly similar to the casuistry of legal commentaries elsewhere.

The Vinaya also records disputes within the saṅgha that tested its procedures. The quarrel among the monks of Kosambī, which the Buddha was unable to settle, and the council held at Vesālī about a century after his death to decide whether monks could accept gold and silver, show communities arguing about the interpretation of rules and using formal procedures to resolve disagreements. Disagreements over discipline were among the causes of the schisms that divided the early Buddhist schools (Horner 1938).

docs.title: 8.5.3 Procedure
docs.text:
The Vinaya’s procedure for collective decisions is notably formal. A valid act of the community (saṅghakamma) requires a quorum of fully ordained monks within a defined boundary (sīmā), the consent of absent members, a formal motion (ñatti), and in important cases three further proclamations, with silence taken as assent. The Samatha rules lay down seven ways of settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-samatha): a decision in the presence of the parties and of the relevant rules (sammukhāvinaya); a verdict that a monk is innocent by reason of his mindfulness (sativinaya); a verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya); acting on the confession of the accused (paṭiññātakaraṇa); decision by the majority, determined by voting with tickets (salākā) (yebhuyyasikā); a decision against a monk whose guilt is established but who is evasive (tassapāpiyasikā); and “covering over with grass” (tiṇavatthāraka), a general settlement in which both parties confess and mutual recriminations are dropped.

It is tempting to call this “democracy”. It is better described as a carefully regulated procedure for collective decision within a voluntary religious order: it applied only to fully ordained members, it governed monastic discipline and property, and the ticket vote was a last resort, organised by an appointed officer who could set it aside if he thought the wrong side would win. What the Vinaya does show is that sophisticated procedural thinking — about quorum, notice, motion, evidence and the finality of decisions — was alive in early India outside the Brahmanical tradition.

docs.title: 8.5.4 Exclusions and Hierarchies
docs.text: The saṅgha admitted members of all varṇas, and the texts insist that within it seniority depends on the date of ordination, not on birth. But ordination was refused to certain categories: slaves, debtors, soldiers in royal service, criminals wanted by the king, persons with certain diseases or deformities, and minors without their parents’ consent. Most of these rules protected the saṅgha from conflict with kings, creditors and masters; their effect was that the order did not become a refuge for the unfree. Nuns were admitted, but under eight “weighty rules” (garudhamma) that subordinated the order of nuns to that of monks — a nun of a hundred years’ standing must rise and salute a monk ordained that day. Uma Chakravarti’s study of early Buddhism concluded that the saṅgha offered social mobility within its own walls while accepting the stratified social order outside (Chakravarti 1987).

docs.title: 8.6.1 The Inscriptions
docs.text:
Aśoka, the third Mauryan emperor (r. c. 268–232 BCE), is known above all from his inscriptions: the Major and Minor Rock Edicts, the Pillar Edicts and other records, engraved on rocks and polished stone pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka (Figures 8.1 and 8.2), mostly in Prakrit in the Brāhmī script, but also in Kharoṣṭhī and, in the north-west, in Greek and Aramaic (Hultzsch 1925; Thapar 1961). They are the earliest deciphered royal records in India and the only extended statement of political ideals by an Indian king of antiquity.

Figure 8.1. The find-spots of Aśoka’s major and minor rock edicts and pillar edicts, on a modern map that shades the approximate maximum extent of the Mauryan empire c. 260 BCE. The shading should not be read as uniform rule: the boundaries, especially in the south and east, are uncertain, and historians now distinguish a metropolitan core in the Gangetic plain from regions held more loosely through governors, local rulers and the control of routes, so that the nature and degree of Mauryan control over much of the shaded area is itself debated. Map: Levakpitam, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 8.6.2 Kaliṅga and the Turn to Dhamma
docs.text: The thirteenth Rock Edict records that eight years after his consecration Aśoka conquered Kaliṅga (in modern Odisha), and that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed and many times that number died. Afterwards, the edict says, the king felt remorse, and he now regards “conquest by dhamma” (dhammavijaya) as the best conquest. He claims to have won such conquests among the Greek kings of the west — Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander, whom he names — and among peoples of the south and of the frontiers. The same edict warns the forest peoples (aṭavi) within his dominions that the king, though repentant, still has power, and that they should reform lest they be killed.

docs.title: 8.6.3 The Content of Dhamma
docs.text:
Aśoka’s dhamma, as the inscriptions describe it, is a practical ethic: obedience to parents and elders, generosity to Brahmins and śramaṇas, proper treatment of slaves and servants, abstention from killing living beings, moderation in spending and possessions, and restraint in speech, especially in speaking about other religious groups. Rock Edict XII urges respect for all sects (pāsaṇḍa): whoever honours his own sect while disparaging others injures his own. Rock Edict I prohibits animal sacrifice in the capital and records that the killing of animals for the royal kitchen has been reduced to two peacocks and a deer a day, and will cease. Rock Edict II records the provision of medical treatment for people and animals, the planting of medicinal herbs and the digging of wells along roads, in his own dominions and those of neighbouring kings. Rock Edict V announces the creation, thirteen years after his consecration, of a new class of officials, the “great officers of dhamma” (dhamma-mahāmātra), to promote dhamma among all groups and to look after the welfare of prisoners, the aged and the destitute.

Figure 8.2. The single-lion capital of the Mauryan pillar at Kolhua, Vaishali (Bihar), of the type associated with Aśoka. Aśoka’s Pillar Edicts were inscribed on polished sandstone columns of this kind. Photo: Amitabha Gupta, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 8.6.4 Justice and Punishment
docs.text: Several inscriptions concern justice. The separate edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada in Kaliṅga, addressed to the officials of the region, begin with the declaration that “all men are my children”: just as the king desires every kind of welfare and happiness in this world and the next for his own children, so he desires it for all men. The edicts rebuke officials who imprison or torment people without cause, and announce that inspecting officers will be sent every five years to ensure that the judicial officers are acting fairly. Pillar Edict IV, issued twenty-six years after his consecration, states that the king has given the rajjūka officers authority over judgments and punishments, so that they may act confidently and without fear, and declares that there should be uniformity in judicial procedure (vyavahāla-samatā) and in punishment (daṃḍa-samatā). It grants a respite of three days to prisoners condemned to death, so that their relatives may seek a reconsideration or the prisoners may prepare for the next world by fasts and gifts. Pillar Edict V lists animals that may not be killed and days on which fishing and the castration of animals are forbidden.

docs.title: 8.6.5 Interpretation
docs.text:
Aśoka’s own inscriptions tell us that he became a Buddhist lay follower, and some of them address the saṅgha directly, recommending particular texts and warning against schism. Romila Thapar argued that his dhamma was nevertheless not simply Buddhism: it was a policy of social ethics designed to hold together an empire of great diversity, emphasising tolerance and social responsibility rather than doctrine (Thapar 1961). Other scholars have stressed its religious sincerity, and Nayanjot Lahiri’s biography reconstructs the king’s development over his reign from the inscriptions and from the places where they were set up (Lahiri 2015). The find-spots themselves raise a further question: many lie along routes and in frontier zones rather than in the Gangetic heartland, and historians debate how far the empire they mark was directly administered rather than held through governors, local rulers and the control of communications (Figure 8.1) (Singh 2008). Either way, the inscriptions represent a remarkable attempt by a ruler to make moral persuasion a principle of government, and to announce it publicly in the languages of his subjects.

They also have limits that a balanced account must record. Aśoka retained the death penalty; his edicts regulate it rather than abolish it. The dhamma-mahāmātras were officials who intervened in the lives of subjects in the name of morality, and the Kaliṅga edict’s warning to the forest peoples is a threat. The inscriptions say nothing about the abolition of varṇa or slavery; they ask that slaves and servants be treated properly. And the later Buddhist legend of Aśoka in the Aśokāvadāna, which includes stories of his cruelty before his conversion and of his violence against heretics, shows that the tradition itself remembered a more complicated figure. The modern Indian state’s adoption of the Sarnath lion capital as its emblem and of the dharma-wheel on its flag (Chapter 20) is a modern act of reception.

docs.title: 8.7 Buddhist Kingship beyond India
docs.text:
Buddhist ideas of kingship had their longest life outside India. In Sri Lanka, the Pali chronicles (Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa) present kings as protectors of the Buddha’s teaching and the saṅgha, and the legend of the Buddha’s own visits to the island links political legitimacy with Buddhist sanctity. In Burma, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, kings styled themselves dhammarāja and cakkavattin, supported and purified the saṅgha, and were expected to embody the ten royal virtues. Stanley Tambiah described the resulting order as a “galactic polity”, in which a central king surrounded himself with replicas of his own court in concentric circles of lesser rulers — a structure he compared to the Arthaśāstra’s maṇḍala (Tambiah 1976). Law in these kingdoms drew on Indian models: the Burmese dhammathat law books, for instance, traced their authority to a legendary sage Manu, though their content was adapted to local custom (Section 9.11).

The longest-lived of these legal traditions was in Thailand. After the destruction of Ayutthaya in 1767, King Rama I of the new Chakri dynasty ordered a revision of the kingdom’s laws, completed in 1805 and known as the “Law of the Three Seals”. It opened with a version of the dhammasattham, the law book traced to the sage Manu, adapted to Buddhist cosmology and kingship, followed by royal laws on procedure, property, marriage, slavery and crime. It remained the basis of Thai law until the codifications of the early twentieth century. The case shows how the Indian idea of a law book attributed to Manu could be absorbed into a Buddhist monarchy far from India and transformed in the process.

docs.title: 8.8.1 The First King
docs.text:
Jain universal history begins its account of civilisation with Ṛṣabha (Ṛṣabhadeva), the first Jina of the present age. In the Digambara version told in Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa (9th century), Ṛṣabha was also the first king: when the wish-fulfilling trees of the age of plenty disappeared, he taught people the six means of livelihood — the use of arms, writing, agriculture, learning, trade and crafts — founded villages and towns, and established the social orders, before renouncing the world to become the first Tīrthaṅkara. His son Bharata became the first universal monarch (cakravartin), and in Jinasena’s account it was Bharata who created the Brahmin order from among the most pious Jain laymen (Jaini 1979; Dundas 2002).

This narrative is a striking example of the Jain response to Brahmanical social theory. Jinasena accepted the framework of varṇa, but grounded it in human institution by a Jain king rather than in the body of the creator, and he defined a Jain Brahmin by conduct and initiation. He also composed Jain versions of the life-cycle rites (saṃskāra). Padmanabh Jaini saw this as part of a deliberate “Brahmanisation” of Jain lay life that helped the Jain community to survive as a socially respectable group in medieval India (Jaini 1979).

docs.title: 8.8.2 Great Persons and Kings
docs.text: Jain narrative literature recounts the lives of the sixty-three “illustrious persons” (śalākāpuruṣa): the twenty-four Jinas, twelve cakravartins, and nine each of three classes of heroes (the Baladevas, the Vāsudevas and their antagonists the Prativāsudevas). The most famous telling is Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita (12th century). Kingship in these stories is honourable but spiritually dangerous: Vāsudevas, who kill their enemies in battle, go to hell; cakravartins who renounce their kingdoms attain liberation. Jain texts thus share with the Buddhist ones the tension between the necessary violence of rule and the renouncer’s ideal of non-violence (ahiṃsā).

docs.title: 8.8.3 Somadeva’s Nītivākyāmṛta
docs.text: The most important Jain work on polity is the Nītivākyāmṛta (“Nectar of Aphorisms on Polity”) of Somadeva Sūri (10th century), a Digambara monk who also wrote the Yaśastilaka (959), a romance in mixed prose and verse (campū). Written in short aphorisms, it covers the same ground as the Arthaśāstra and Kāmandaka — the king’s training, the ministers, the constituent elements of the state, envoys, spies, the treasury and war — and draws heavily on the earlier nīti tradition. It frames this material within a Jain ethical outlook, insisting on the king’s self-control and on dharma, but it accepts that the king must punish wrongdoers and wage war when necessary. Its existence shows that the śāstric science of polity was common property, adaptable to different religious frameworks.

docs.title: 8.8.4 Jain Kings and Merchants
docs.text:
Several Indian rulers patronised or professed Jainism. Khāravela of Kaliṅga (c. 1st century BCE), whose Hāthīgumphā inscription opens with a salutation to the Arhats, recorded his campaigns and public works alongside gifts to Jain ascetics. In western and southern India, Jainism enjoyed the patronage of several dynasties, including the Gaṅgas and some Rāṣṭrakūṭa rulers in the south and the Caulukyas of Gujarat. The Caulukya king Kumārapāla (r. 1143–1172) was a patron of the Jain scholar Hemacandra; Jain sources credit him with proclaiming the prohibition of animal slaughter (amāri) in his realm and with abandoning the royal right to seize the property of men who died without sons, which had impoverished their widows. These accounts come from Jain biographers and should be read as such, but they show how Jain ethical ideals could be translated into royal policy.

Jain merchant communities, especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan, developed their own institutions: the mahājan, an association of merchants that regulated trade, settled disputes and administered charities, including animal shelters (pāñjarāpoḷ). Under British rule, Jains were generally governed by Hindu law in matters of family and inheritance, unless they could prove a distinct custom, and the question of a separate Jain law became a subject of litigation and of reformist writing in the early twentieth century.

docs.title: 8.8.5 Jain Ethics and Economic Life
docs.text: Jain teaching shaped legal and economic life less through treatises on polity than through the ethics it required of lay people. The lay vows (aṇuvrata) — limited versions of the ascetic’s great vows of non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, chastity and non-possession — were elaborated in manuals of lay conduct (śrāvakācāra). These manuals forbade occupations that involved great violence to living beings, such as charcoal-burning, clearing forests, draining lakes and trading in weapons, poisons, ivory and lac, and they encouraged honest dealing, the limitation of possessions and generous giving (Jaini 1979). Such rules help to explain why Jain communities in western India came to be concentrated in trade and banking, and why their merchant associations combined commercial regulation with religious charity.

docs.title: 8.9 Later Buddhist Advice to Kings
docs.text:
Buddhist authors continued to write advice for rulers after the canonical period. The Ratnāvalī (“Precious Garland”) attributed to the philosopher Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd century CE), composed as a letter of counsel to a king, urges the ruler to govern with compassion: to care for the sick, the orphaned and the destitute, to build rest-houses and supply water along roads, to treat prisoners humanely, and to punish in a spirit of compassion rather than anger. Āryaśūra’s Jātakamālā retold stories of the Buddha’s former lives as a king who sacrificed himself for his subjects.
