Such texts, widely read in the Buddhist world, kept alive an ideal of the compassionate ruler that complemented, and sometimes challenged, the more coercive vision of the Arthaśāstra.

Buddhist rulers did not, however, abandon the ordinary instruments of government. Kings who patronised Buddhism — from the Kuṣāṇas to the Pālas of Bengal (8th–12th centuries), whose inscriptions combine Buddhist invocations with standard formulae of land grants to Brahmins — waged war, collected taxes and punished offenders like other kings. The Buddhist ideal shaped royal self-representation and patronage more than it transformed the state.

docs.title: 8.10 Monasteries, Patronage and Decline
docs.text:
Buddhist and Jain institutions depended on the patronage of rulers, merchants and lay communities. Inscriptions record gifts to monasteries from kings and queens of many dynasties — Mauryas, Śakas, Sātavāhanas, Kuṣāṇas, Guptas, Maitrakas, Pālas — and from guilds, merchants, monks, nuns and lay men and women. Great monastic universities such as Nālandā (founded in the fifth century CE) and Vikramaśīla (founded by the Pāla king Dharmapāla around 800) were supported by grants of villages whose revenues maintained the monks and their students. Monasteries thus became, like temples, corporate landholders, with their own rules for the management of property.

Buddhism declined in most of India between the seventh and thirteenth centuries, for reasons that historians still debate: the loss of royal and mercantile patronage as political and economic conditions changed; the growth of devotional Hindu traditions that absorbed many of Buddhism’s popular functions; the concentration of Buddhist life in large monasteries dependent on a few patrons; and, at the end, the destruction of the great monasteries of Bihar and Bengal during the Turkish campaigns of c. 1193–1205 associated with Bakhtiyār Khaljī. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited Nālandā in 1234, found it still occupied but much reduced. Buddhism survived in the Himalayan regions and in parts of eastern India, and flourished in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet and East Asia. Jainism, by contrast, survived in western and southern India, sustained by merchant communities and by its accommodation with the social order around it.

docs.title: 8.11 Assessment
docs.text:
Three conclusions emerge. First, the Buddhist and Jain traditions offered genuinely different accounts of political authority: kingship as a human institution created to restrain theft (the Aggañña), the king’s duty to relieve poverty (the Cakkavatti-sīhanāda and Kūṭadanta), and a sustained moral critique of violence. Second, they did not reject kingship, punishment or social hierarchy as such; their sharpest criticism was directed at the Brahmins’ claim to superiority by birth, and their monastic institutions, while open to all varṇas, accommodated rather than challenged slavery and the subordination of women. Third, their most enduring institutional legacy lies in the monastic law of the saṅgha, the Aśokan model of moral government, and the royal ideologies of Buddhist Asia.

In modern India, B. R. Ambedkar turned to Buddhism as a religion of equality. In 1956, shortly before his death, he converted to Buddhism with several hundred thousand followers at Nagpur, and his The Buddha and His Dhamma (published 1957) reinterpreted the Buddha’s teaching as a social gospel of liberty, equality and fraternity (Ambedkar 1957; Zelliot 1992). At the conversion ceremony he administered to his followers twenty-two vows, which included the renunciation of Hindu deities and rituals and the affirmation of the equality of all human beings. Ambedkar’s reading was a new interpretation for a new purpose; it is itself a major chapter in the history of Indian political thought (Chapters 10 and 20).

Table 8.1 lists the principal passages discussed in this chapter.

docs.title: 8.13 Summary
docs.text:
• Early Buddhist texts describe kingship as a human institution created to restrain theft (the Aggañña Sutta), tie the king’s legitimacy to righteousness and to the relief of poverty (the Cakkavatti-sīhanāda and Kūṭadanta Suttas), and list ten royal virtues. Collins reads the Aggañña largely as a parody of Brahmanical claims.

  • The gaṇa-saṅgha polities were governed by assemblies of ruling clans; the Buddha praised the Vajjis’ practice of meeting in concord and following their ancient law.

  • The monastic code (Vinaya) contains detailed procedural law for the saṅgha, including formal motions, majority voting by tickets and seven methods of settling disputes; it excluded slaves, debtors and soldiers from ordination and subordinated nuns to monks.

  • Aśoka’s inscriptions proclaim a policy of dhamma: non-violence towards animals, respect for all sects, welfare works, officers of dhamma and fair judicial procedure. He retained the death penalty and warned the forest peoples of his power.

  • Jain authors adapted the Brahmanical framework of varṇa and the science of polity, and Jain ethics shaped merchant communities. Buddhist kingship had its longest life in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and was reinterpreted in modern India by Ambedkar.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the Pali texts, see the translations of the Dīgha Nikāya and, for the Aggañña Sutta, Collins (1993); for the Vinaya, Horner (1938). Collins (1998) and Tambiah (1976) are the major studies of Buddhist political thought; Chakravarti (1987) examines the social context critically. On Aśoka, see Thapar (1961), Lahiri (2015) and the inscriptions in Hultzsch (1925). On the Jains, Jaini (1979) and Dundas (2002).

docs.title: Chapter 9: The Dharmaśāstra Tradition: Sources, Texts and Interpreters
docs.text:
Dharmaśāstra, “the science of dharma”, is the name of a Sanskrit scholarly tradition that for some two thousand years set out the rules of right conduct for the members of Brahmanical society. Its texts range from the prose Dharmasūtras of the last centuries BCE, through the verse treatises (smṛti) of Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada and others, to the commentaries and the vast topical digests (nibandha) of the medieval period. They deal with ritual and daily conduct, with the stages of life and the duties of the varṇas, with marriage, inheritance and the family, with the king’s duties and the conduct of lawsuits, and with penances for wrongdoing. Under British rule a narrow selection of this literature became the basis of “Hindu law” in the courts (Chapter 19), and it is still read, admired and denounced in modern India.

This chapter introduces the tradition as a whole: what its authors meant by dharma, where they located its authority, how the literature developed, how it was interpreted, and how far it can be called “law”. The Manusmṛti and the later smṛtis are treated in Chapters 10 and 11, and the main areas of legal doctrine in Chapters 12–15.

docs.title: 9.1 Dharma in the Śāstras
docs.text:
In the Dharmaśāstras, dharma is above all a matter of duty specific to one’s position. The texts speak of the dharma of the varṇas (varṇadharma), of the stages of life (āśramadharma), of the king (rājadharma), of women (strīdharma), and of times of distress (āpaddharma). They also recognise a set of virtues common to all (sādhāraṇa dharma) — the Manusmṛti lists non-injury, truthfulness, not stealing, purity and control of the senses as the dharma of all four varṇas in brief (Manu 10.63) — but the weight of the literature lies on the differentiated duties of particular persons. Dharma in this sense is not a universal moral law addressed equally to everyone; it is a highly differentiated order in which a person’s duties depend on varṇa, gender, stage of life and circumstance.

The early history of the word is discussed in Chapter 2. By the time of the Dharmasūtras, it had become the term for the whole body of religiously sanctioned norms that a Brahmin expert could teach. The legal scholar Robert Lingat stressed that dharma combines duty and law, ritual and morality; Donald Davis has argued that the centre of the tradition is the householder and that Dharmaśāstra is best understood as a “theology of the household” that also regulates the institutions — castes, guilds, temples, villages — through which households lived (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 9.2.1 The Canonical Lists
docs.text:
From the beginning the tradition was concerned with the question of authority: how is dharma known? The Dharmasūtras answer with short lists. Gautama names the Veda, the tradition and practice of those who know it (GDh 1.1–2); Āpastamba bases dharma on “the agreement of those who know dharma and on the Vedas” (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2–3); Vasiṣṭha names the Veda, tradition and the practice of cultured people (śiṣṭa). The Manusmṛti gives the most famous formulation:

Manusmṛti 2.6

vedo ’khilo dharmamūlaṃ smṛtiśīle ca tadvidām ācāraś caiva sādhūnām ātmanas tuṣṭir eva ca “The root of dharma is the entire Veda, and the tradition and practice of those who know the Veda, the conduct of good people, and what is pleasing to oneself.”

A few verses later Manu restates the list as four “visible marks” of dharma: the Veda, tradition, the conduct of good people and what is pleasing to oneself (2.12). Later interpreters read the order as hierarchical: where two sources conflict, the earlier prevails.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Veda
docs.text: The Veda is the first source, but it contains few rules of the kind the Dharmaśāstras discuss. The tradition solved this problem by a theory of indirect authority. Smṛti rules, it held, are based on Vedic texts that have been lost or are no longer recited but whose existence can be inferred from the fact that learned people remember and practise the rules. The Mīmāṃsā school of Vedic hermeneutics developed this theory with great care. Its foundational text, the Mīmāṃsāsūtra of Jaimini, argues that a smṛti has authority because it can be presumed to rest on the Veda, but that where a smṛti contradicts an extant Vedic text it is to be disregarded (MīS 1.3.3) (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Smṛti
docs.text: Smṛti, “what is remembered”, means in this context the tradition preserved by those who know the Veda — in practice, the texts of the Dharmasūtras and Dharmaśāstras, which are themselves called smṛtis. They were attributed to sages and divine figures, which gave them authority: Manu was the primordial ancestor of humanity; Yājñavalkya a celebrated Upaniṣadic teacher; Nārada a divine sage. The Yājñavalkyasmṛti lists twenty authors of dharmaśāstras: Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa and Vasiṣṭha (Yājñ 1.4–5). Later lists of eighteen or more “smṛti authors” vary, and many of the texts that circulate under these names are late compositions.

docs.title: 9.2.4 The Conduct of the Good
docs.text: The third source — ācāra, sadācāra or śiṣṭācāra, the practice of good or cultured people — opened the śāstra to custom. The texts define the “cultured” narrowly: for Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha they are Brahmins free from envy and greed, learned in the Veda; Manu speaks of the practice handed down in Brahmāvarta, the land between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers (Manu 2.17–18). But the texts also recognise the customs of regions, castes and families. Gautama declares that the laws of regions, castes and families are authoritative if they do not contradict the Veda, and that cultivators, merchants, herdsmen, money-lenders and artisans are authorities for their own groups (GDh 11.20–21). Baudhāyana lists five practices peculiar to the south — among them marrying the daughter of one’s maternal uncle or paternal aunt — and five peculiar to the north, such as going to sea and dealing in wool, and reports the view that each region should follow its own practice (BDh 1.2.1–4). Custom is the subject of Chapter 16.

docs.title: 9.2.5 What Is Pleasing to Oneself
docs.text: The fourth source, ātmatuṣṭi or “what is pleasing to oneself”, has attracted much modern attention as a recognition of individual conscience. The commentators interpreted it narrowly: Medhātithi, for example, limits it to the satisfaction of a person learned in the Veda in matters where the other sources allow a choice. Davis has argued that it refers to the inner disposition of a learned and virtuous person rather than to private conscience in a modern sense (Davis 2010). It is not a licence to set aside the texts.

docs.title: 9.3.1 The Dharmasūtras
docs.text:
The oldest surviving texts are four Dharmasūtras, composed in the terse prose of the Vedic ancillary sciences and attributed to Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha. Āpastamba and Baudhāyana belong to the Kalpasūtras of schools of the Black Yajurveda, alongside manuals of solemn and domestic ritual; the others were attached to Vedic schools by tradition. Older scholarship placed them as early as 600 or even 800 BCE. Patrick Olivelle’s translation and study have established a much later chronology: Āpastamba, the oldest, belongs to about the early third century BCE, Gautama and Baudhāyana to the following two centuries, and Vasiṣṭha perhaps to the first century BCE or a little later. The Dharmasūtras as a genre thus belong to the third to first centuries BCE — to the time of Aśoka and after, not to the age of the Buddha (Olivelle 1999).

Their contents are already broad: the student’s life, the householder’s duties, marriage, impurity, food, the king’s duties, judicial procedure, inheritance and penance. Each is characterised briefly below.

docs.title: 9.3.2 The Smṛtis
docs.text: The next stage is represented by the great verse treatises, beginning with the Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE; Chapter 10). They are written in the śloka metre, address society as a whole rather than one Vedic school, and organise their material in a more systematic way. Manu introduced the classification of litigation into eighteen titles (vyavahārapada, Manu 8.4–7), which became standard (Chapter 12). The Yājñavalkyasmṛti (c. 4th–5th century CE) arranged its material in three books on conduct, legal procedure and penance; the Nāradasmṛti (c. 5th–6th century) is devoted entirely to law; and the treatises of Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana (c. 6th–7th century), which survive only in quotations, developed the law of procedure and evidence further (Chapter 11). The Viṣṇusmṛti (or Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra), a later work presented as the teaching of the god Viṣṇu to the Earth, and the Parāśarasmṛti, which claims to be the law for the present Kali age, are among the many other smṛtis.

docs.title: 9.3.3 Commentaries and Digests
docs.text:
From the second half of the first millennium CE the creative work of the tradition shifted to commentary. Commentators explained the root texts, resolved contradictions between them, and adapted their rules to new circumstances, often by ingenious interpretation. The great commentaries include those of Medhātithi on Manu and of Vijñāneśvara (the Mitākṣarā) and Aparārka on Yājñavalkya. From the twelfth century, scholars also compiled digests (nibandha), which gathered quotations from all the smṛtis on a topic, arranged them systematically and harmonised them. Many were composed at royal courts or by ministers, and they show how the tradition was organised in different regions. Table 9.1 lists some of the most important works.

docs.title: 9.3.4 The Dharmasūtras in Outline
docs.text:
A brief characterisation of each Dharmasūtra shows the range of the early literature (Olivelle 1999).

  • Āpastamba, the oldest, belongs to the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda. Its first part deals with the student and with the duties of the snātaka; its second with the householder, inheritance, marriage, the king and penance. It is notable for the independence of its views: it rejects some customs approved by other authorities, and in its closing passage it reports the opinion that the remaining dharmas may be learned from women and from people of all varṇas.

  • Gautama, the most systematic, arranges its material by topic and devotes considerable space to the king, witnesses, debts, inheritance and penance. It contains one of the earliest lists of the saṃskāras and of the virtues of the self, and recognises the customs of regions, castes and families.

  • Baudhāyana, also of the Black Yajurveda, survives in a composite text with later additions. It discusses the differing customs of north and south, the mixed classes, inheritance and the āśramas, and preserves much ritual detail.

  • Vasiṣṭha, probably the latest, shows the influence of developing legal procedure: it recognises documents as evidence and has a substantial section on adoption and on the sons of different kinds.

These texts were transmitted in Vedic schools, which explains why they are attached to particular branches of the Veda. Their authors were Brahmin teachers addressing pupils, and their primary concern was the life of the Brahmin householder; the king and the law appear as one topic among many.

docs.title: 9.3.5 Kane’s Survey of the Literature
docs.text: The first volume of Kane’s History of Dharmaśāstra (1930) is a survey of the literature: more than a hundred smṛtis and digests, with their authors, dates, contents and relations. Its later volumes are organised by topic — varṇa and āśrama, the saṃskāras, marriage, daily duties, gifts, the king and the law, penance, funeral rites, pilgrimage, vows and festivals, and the relation of Dharmaśāstra to other disciplines. For many of the texts mentioned in this chapter, Kane remains the only comprehensive account; but his dates, often earlier than those now accepted, must be checked against more recent work (Kane 1930, vol. 1; Olivelle and Davis 2018).

docs.title: 9.4 The Three Divisions
docs.text: From the Yājñavalkyasmṛti onwards, the subject matter of Dharmaśāstra was commonly divided into three: ācāra, “conduct”, covering the saṃskāras, the duties of the varṇas and āśramas, daily rites, food, purity and gifts; vyavahāra, “legal procedure”, covering the courts, evidence and the eighteen titles of litigation; and prāyaścitta, “penance”, covering expiations for sins. The division is useful but should not be read as a modern distinction between private morality, public law and rehabilitation. Many matters crossed the lines: marriage was both a saṃskāra and a subject of litigation; some offences were punished by the king and also required penance; and the king was obliged to enforce the duties of the varṇas.

docs.title: 9.5.1 Mīmāṃsā and Legal Reasoning
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstra commentators borrowed their methods from Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, the school that had developed rules for interpreting the Vedic injunctions governing ritual. Its principles were applied to the smṛtis as if they were Vedic texts. Among the most important were:

  • the distinction between an injunction (vidhi) and an explanatory or laudatory statement (arthavāda), which has no independent force;

  • the distinction between a general rule (utsarga) and an exception (apavāda), the specific overriding the general;

  • the restrictive rule (niyama) and the exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), which govern whether a rule excludes alternatives;

  • the hierarchy of means of determining which rule applies to which act — direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), syntactic connection (vākya), context (prakaraṇa), position (sthāna) and name (samākhyā) — with the earlier prevailing over the later (MīS 3.3.14);

  • and, where two equally authoritative rules conflict, the doctrine of option (vikalpa), under which either may be followed, which Mīmāṃsakas regarded as a last resort.

Commentators used these tools to reconcile apparently contradictory smṛtis, to limit the scope of rules they found objectionable or obsolete, and to extend old rules to new cases. Modern readers have noticed resemblances to the canons of statutory interpretation in common-law systems, such as the maxim that the specific overrides the general; the resemblance reflects the common problem of interpreting authoritative texts, not any historical connection (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 9.5.2 A Debate about Custom
docs.text: The Mīmāṃsā discussion of custom shows how these methods were applied. Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsāsūtra considers whether practices followed by the people of particular regions — the example given in the later literature is a spring festival called holākā, observed by easterners — are authoritative for all, or only for those who observe them. The question is whether such a practice, like a smṛti rule, can be presumed to rest on a lost Vedic text, and if so whether that text would apply universally. The Mīmāṃsakas and later Dharmaśāstra authors debated the matter at length, some arguing that authoritative practices bind everyone, others that regional customs bind only those of the region. Behind this technical debate lay a real problem for a tradition that claimed universal validity while recognising the diversity of customs across the subcontinent; Dharmaśāstra authors generally resolved it by accepting regional custom for the region, provided it did not openly contradict the texts (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 9.5.3 The Commentator as Lawmaker
docs.text: The commentators presented themselves as explaining what the texts had always meant. In fact they often changed the law. Medhātithi treated many of Manu’s rules of royal policy as resting on worldly experience rather than on the Veda; Vijñāneśvara’s doctrine that sons acquire a right in ancestral property by birth (Chapter 11) was a major juristic construction; and the nibandha authors created systems of inheritance and adoption out of scattered verses. Lingat compared their role to that of the jurists of Roman law or the judges of the common law, creating law through interpretation while maintaining the fiction that they were merely expounding a fixed tradition (Lingat 1973).

docs.title: 9.5.4 Law for the Age: Yugadharma and Kalivarjya
docs.text: The tradition also allowed for change through time. The doctrine of the four ages (yuga) held that dharma declines from the perfect Kṛta age to the present Kali age. A verse of the Parāśarasmṛti assigns the laws of Manu to the Kṛta age, those of Gautama to the Tretā, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita to the Dvāpara and those of Parāśara to the Kali (Parāśara 1.24). Medieval authors compiled lists of practices permitted in earlier ages but forbidden in the Kali age (kalivarjya): among them the appointment of a man to beget a son on a widow (niyoga), the remarriage of a woman whose marriage had been consummated, sea voyages, the killing of cattle in sacrifice and the marriage of a man with a woman of a lower varṇa. Such lists could be used to set aside embarrassing older rules; they could equally be used to forbid practices — such as widow remarriage — that older texts had allowed in some circumstances. The doctrine was a mechanism for change, but not necessarily for liberal change.

docs.title: 9.6 Paṇḍits, Assemblies and Written Rulings
docs.text:
Dharmaśāstra was not only written; it was taught, recited and applied by learned Brahmins (paṇḍita, śāstrin) in schools attached to temples, monasteries and royal courts and in the households of scholarly families. The texts themselves provide for an assembly of learned men (pariṣad) to decide doubtful questions of dharma: Manu says that a matter not covered by the texts should be decided by an assembly of at least ten, or in need even of three, learned Brahmins, or even by a single Brahmin who knows the Veda, but not by thousands who are ignorant (12.108–114). Such assemblies prescribed penances, readmitted outcastes, and decided disputes about ritual and caste status.

In the early modern period, written rulings by paṇḍits — often called vyavasthā (“determination”) or nirṇaya (“decision”) — were issued in answer to questions put by individuals, communities or rulers, citing the authorities on which they relied. Collections of such rulings survive from Maharashtra, Banaras and Bengal, and they show the śāstras being applied to concrete questions of inheritance, adoption, marriage, penance and caste. Under the East India Company, the court paṇḍits’ answers to judges’ questions were similarly called vyavasthās, and some were printed for the guidance of the courts (Chapter 19). This living practice of consultation is one reason why historians now see Dharmaśāstra less as a dead letter than as a working tradition of legal expertise (Davis 2010; Rocher 2012).

docs.title: 9.7 Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The relation between the two śāstras has been much debated. They share a great deal: the Dharmaśāstras’ chapters on the king and the courts draw on the same body of political ideas as the Arthaśāstra, and the Arthaśāstra’s Book 3 is a treatise on private law that overlaps closely with the smṛtis. Both texts accept the hierarchy of varṇa and the king’s duty to uphold it. The differences are of emphasis and audience. The Arthaśāstra addresses the king and his ministers, judges institutions by their usefulness, and accepts espionage, deception and covert killing; the Dharmaśāstras address Brahmin experts and the householders they advised, and judge actions by their conformity to dharma. The Yājñavalkyasmṛti states that where dharmaśāstra and arthaśāstra conflict, dharmaśāstra prevails (Yājñ 2.21).

Mark McClish has argued that the surviving Arthaśāstra was itself revised to bring it closer to dharmaśāstric norms, and that the two traditions should be seen as parts of a single developing discourse on royal power and law rather than as opposites (McClish 2019). The Mahābhārata’s Śānti Parvan, which combines both perspectives, shows that the same authors could hold them together (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 9.8 Was Dharmaśāstra Law?
docs.text:
Under British rule, judges treated Dharmaśāstra texts as a code of “Hindu law” to be applied in court (Chapter 19). Modern scholars have asked whether that was a misunderstanding. Three positions can be distinguished.

  • A scholastic tradition of norms. On one view, the texts are the products of Brahmin scholars describing an ideal order; they were studied and transmitted as learning, and their relation to the actual decisions of kings and local bodies was loose. Derrett emphasised the gap between śāstra and practice and the importance of custom (Derrett 1968).

  • A record of customary law. Richard Lariviere argued that the Dharmaśāstras should be read as compendia of what was accepted practice, and that the irony of modern Indian legal history is that judges came to treat these flexible records of custom as binding statutes (Lariviere 1989a).

  • A jurisprudence of institutions. Donald Davis has argued that Dharmaśāstra functioned as a jurisprudence — a theory of law — for the many legal institutions of medieval India (castes, guilds, temples, monasteries, village assemblies and royal courts), which applied their own rules within a framework the śāstras defined and legitimated. Inscriptions and medieval documents show such bodies invoking dharma and the śāstras while deciding cases according to their own customs (Davis 2010).

These views are not mutually exclusive. What is clear is that Dharmaśāstra was never a code enacted by a sovereign and applied uniformly by state courts; it was a learned tradition with great prestige, which shaped how disputes were thought about and decided, alongside custom, royal orders and the rules of corporate groups. It was also, throughout, a Brahmanical tradition: its authors were Brahmins, its norms privileged Brahmins and men, and its prestige helped to entrench varṇa hierarchy and patriarchy (Chapters 10 and 15).

docs.title: 9.9 Regional Traditions
docs.text: Although the smṛtis claimed universal authority, the commentaries and digests reveal regional traditions — the Dāyabhāga and Raghunandana in Bengal, Caṇḍeśvara and Vācaspati Miśra in Mithilā, Nīlakaṇṭha in western India, the Smṛticandrikā and Mādhava in the south, and the Mitākṣarā over much of the subcontinent — which the British courts later hardened into territorial “schools” (Chapter 11). Some communities followed customs that departed sharply from the smṛtis: the matrilineal Nāyars of Kerala are the best-known case (Chapter 16), and cross-cousin marriage, condemned by northern authors, was common in the south and accepted by southern commentators.

docs.title: 9.10 Dharmaśāstra and the State: The Case of Nepal
docs.text:
The one pre-modern state in South Asia that enacted a comprehensive legal code explicitly based on caste hierarchy was not in India but in Nepal. The Mulukī Ain (“Law of the Land”) of 1854, promulgated under the Rana prime minister Jang Bahadur, codified the law of the kingdom in a single text. It classified all the kingdom’s population into a hierarchy of caste groups — “wearers of the sacred thread” at the top, “liquor-drinking” groups below them, and impure and untouchable groups at the bottom — and laid down rules of commensality, marriage, punishment and penance according to rank, drawing on Dharmaśāstric principles while incorporating the diverse peoples of the Himalayan kingdom. Andras Höfer’s study of the code showed how it used the categories of the śāstras to construct a national caste order for a state that had never been organised in that way. The code was replaced in 1963 by a new law that abolished caste discrimination (Höfer 1979).

The Nepalese case shows what Dharmaśāstra could become when adopted as the law of a centralised state. In India, by contrast, no pre-colonial state codified Dharmaśāstra, and the closest approximation was the colonial “Anglo-Hindu law” (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 9.11 Beyond the Subcontinent: Law Books in Southeast Asia
docs.text: Indian political and legal vocabulary travelled to Southeast Asia from the first centuries CE. Sanskrit inscriptions appear in Borneo, Java, Champa and Cambodia from about the fifth century; kings took Sanskrit titles, employed Brahmin chaplains and were consecrated with Indian rites; and local elites adopted the Indian categories selectively for their own purposes, a process that O. W. Wolters called “localisation” (Wolters 1982). Law books were part of this exchange, and their history shows what happened to Dharmaśāstra when it was carried into societies that did not share the varṇa order.

docs.title: 9.11.1 Java and Bali
docs.text: The Old Javanese legal literature, of which the best-known work is the Kuṭāramānava associated with the Majapahit kingdom (fourteenth to fifteenth century), invokes Manu among its authorities and arranges its rules under headings that correspond to the eighteen titles of law (Chapter 12): debt, deposit, sale, boundaries, theft, violence, defamation, the relations of husband and wife, and the rest. Its substance, however, is largely Javanese: fines are stated in local currency, many offences concern local forms of property and status, and Brahmanical rules on varṇa are much reduced. In Bali, where a Hindu courtly culture survived the Islamisation of Java, related texts continued to be consulted by Brahmin judges in the courts of the Balinese kingdoms, and the Dutch colonial government later used them in its own courts for Balinese litigants. The Javanese and Balinese texts are thus the furthest extension of the Dharmaśāstric genre, but they are adaptations, not translations (Hooker 1978).

docs.title: 9.11.2 The Dhammasattha of Burma
docs.text:
In Burma (Myanmar) and the neighbouring Mon, Tai and Lao lands, law books called dhammasattha (Pali for “dharmaśāstra”; Burmese dhammathat) are attested from the thirteenth century, when the word appears in an inscription of the Pagan kingdom. They were written in Pali, Burmese and Mon, often in bilingual form, and survive in hundreds of manuscripts. Their tradition traced their authority to a sage named Manu, but in a Buddhist guise: Manu was a hermit who, having attained supernatural powers, travelled to the wall that encircles the world and found the law written there in enormous letters, which he copied and brought back to the king. The law was thus presented not as the command of a creator god or the teaching of the Veda but as an order inscribed in the structure of the cosmos and discovered by a wise man (Lammerts 2018).

The content of the dhammasattha deals with inheritance, marriage and divorce, debt and pledge, slavery, theft, assault and the procedure of the courts, often grouped in categories that echo the Indian titles of law. Its rules reflect Burmese society and Buddhist ethics more than Brahmanical ones: divorce by mutual consent is permitted, the wife’s share of the marital property is substantial, and there is no varṇa hierarchy, though distinctions of rank, debt-bondage and slavery are prominent. Burmese kings commissioned new compilations, among them the Manusāra of the mid-seventeenth century, composed by a lay jurist and a monk, and the Manugye of the 1750s under the Konbaung dynasty. Christian Lammerts has shown that these texts were the work of an indigenous Buddhist legal scholarship, with its own commentaries and debates, rather than degenerate copies of the Manusmṛti; their relationship to Indian Dharmaśāstra lies in a shared genre and shared categories more than in borrowed rules (Lammerts 2018). Under British rule, an English translation of the Manugye (1847) became an authority for the colonial courts, which applied “Buddhist law” to Burmese Buddhists in matters of succession, marriage and religious usage — a Burmese counterpart of Anglo-Hindu law.

docs.title: 9.11.3 Siam and the Wider Region
docs.text: The Thai Law of the Three Seals (1805), described in Chapter 8, opens with a Phra Thammasat that tells a version of the same story of the hermit Manu, followed by royal laws on procedure, property, family, slavery and crime; related texts circulated in Laos and Cambodia. Across mainland Southeast Asia, then, the name of Manu and the form of the śāstric law book became the vehicle for law codes that were Buddhist in ethics and local in substance. The contrast with Nepal is instructive. The Nepalese code of 1854 took the hierarchy of the śāstras as the organising principle of a national law; the Southeast Asian law books kept the authority of the genre while discarding most of that hierarchy (Hooker 1978; Lammerts 2018).

docs.title: 9.12 From Manuscript to Print
docs.text: Until the nineteenth century Dharmaśāstra texts circulated in manuscripts, copied by hand on palm leaf, birch bark or paper, and studied with teachers. Manuscripts of the same text often differ, and many works survive in only a few copies; others are known only from quotations. The colonial period brought printing. Texts were printed in Calcutta, Bombay, Banaras, Madras and Poona from the early nineteenth century onwards, first for the use of the courts and of colonial scholars and then for Indian readers; series such as the Bibliotheca Indica of the Asiatic Society, the Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series of Poona and the publications of the Nirṇaya Sāgara Press of Bombay made many smṛtis, commentaries and digests available in print. Printing standardised texts that had varied in manuscript, often on the basis of a few manuscripts and without critical method, and it made them available to lawyers and reformers who had not studied with traditional teachers. Modern critical editions, such as Olivelle’s of the Manusmṛti, reconstruct the history of the text from all available manuscripts and commentaries, and sometimes show that the familiar printed text differs from the one the early commentators knew (Olivelle 2005).

docs.title: 9.13 P. V. Kane and Modern Scholarship
docs.text:
The modern study of Dharmaśāstra rests above all on the History of Dharmaśāstra of Pandurang Vaman Kane (1880–1972), published in five volumes (some in several parts) between 1930 and 1962. Kane, a Sanskritist and advocate of the Bombay High Court, surveyed the entire literature — texts, authors, dates and doctrines — with an exhaustiveness that has never been equalled; he received the Bharat Ratna in 1963 (Kane 1930). His work remains indispensable as a reference, though its chronology has been revised and its interpretive stance — sympathetic to the tradition and broadly reformist — reflects its time.

Since Kane, the field has been transformed by critical editions and translations, above all those of Patrick Olivelle (the Dharmasūtras, the Manusmṛti and the Yājñavalkyasmṛti) and Richard Lariviere (the Nāradasmṛti); by Ludo Rocher’s studies, including his translation of the Dāyabhāga; by J. D. M. Derrett’s work on the relation of śāstra, custom and colonial law; by Robert Lingat’s synthesis; and by Donald Davis’s work on Dharmaśāstra as jurisprudence (Olivelle 1999, 2005, 2019; Lariviere 1989b; Rocher 2002, 2012; Derrett 1968; Lingat 1973; Davis 2010). The collective volume edited by Olivelle and Davis, Hindu Law: A New History of Dharmaśāstra (2018), summarises current knowledge (Olivelle and Davis 2018). Critical perspectives from social history, Dalit studies and feminist scholarship — notably the work of B. R. Ambedkar, R. S. Sharma and Uma Chakravarti, and of the Dalit scholars who followed Ambedkar — have also reshaped how the tradition is read (Chapters 10 and 15; Section 20.2).

docs.title: 9.14 Summary
docs.text:
• Dharmaśāstra is the Sanskrit scholarly tradition on dharma: the duties of persons according to varṇa, āśrama and sex, the duties of kings, legal procedure and penance. Its literature runs from the Dharmasūtras (c. 3rd–1st centuries BCE) through the smṛtis to the commentaries and digests of the second millennium.

  • The tradition located the authority of dharma in the Veda, in smṛti, in the practice of the good and, to a limited extent, in what is pleasing to oneself; it recognised the customs of regions, castes and families, within limits.

  • Its interpreters used the methods of Mīmāṃsā to reconcile and apply the texts, and in doing so they made new law.

  • Scholars debate whether Dharmaśāstra was law: a scholastic ideal, a record of custom, or the jurisprudence of a world of corporate legal institutions. It was never a code enacted by a state, and it was throughout a Brahmanical tradition with Brahmanical priorities.

  • Outside India the form of the śāstric law book passed, much transformed, into the law books of Southeast Asia, while Nepal’s code of 1854 made the śāstric caste hierarchy the basis of national law.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The best introductions are Lingat (1973), Davis (2010) and the essays in Olivelle and Davis (2018) and Lubin et al. (2010). Kane (1930) is the indispensable reference. On Southeast Asia, see Hooker (1978) and Lammerts (2018). Olivelle (1999) translates the Dharmasūtras with an introduction on their date. Derrett (1973) surveys the literature; Lariviere (1989a) and Rocher (2012) discuss its relation to practice.

docs.title: Chapter 10: The Manusmṛti
docs.text:
No Indian legal text has been more admired or more hated than the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, the “treatise on dharma of Manu”, better known as the Manusmṛti or, in English, the “Laws of Manu”. For the commentators of the first and second millennia it was the most authoritative of the smṛtis. For the British administrators who sought a “code of the Hindus” it was the obvious first text to translate, and William Jones’s version of 1794 made it one of the best-known Sanskrit works in Europe. For the anti-caste movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it was the charter of Brahmanical oppression, and on 25 December 1927 B. R. Ambedkar and his followers burned it publicly at Mahad. It remains a symbol over which Indians argue.

This chapter tries to read the text as a historian should: to say what it is, when and how it was composed, what it contains and how it was received, and to set out plainly its provisions on varṇa, untouchability and women, which are central to its social vision and cannot be explained away. It draws throughout on Patrick Olivelle’s critical edition and translation (Olivelle 2005).

docs.title: 10.1.1 Frame and Authority
docs.text: The Manusmṛti presents itself as the teaching of Manu, the first human being and ancestor of humanity, son of the self-existent creator. In its opening verses the great seers approach Manu and ask him to teach them the dharmas of all the varṇas and of the intermediate classes. Manu describes the creation of the world and states that he learned the treatise from the creator; he then asks his pupil Bhṛgu to recite it, and the rest of the text is spoken by Bhṛgu (1.1–60). The frame gives the text the highest possible authority: it is not the opinion of a scholar but the primeval law of humanity. It also makes the text a Brahmin’s account of dharma, addressed to Brahmins: the seers ask, Bhṛgu speaks, and the work repeatedly declares that Brahmins are the lords of creation.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Date
docs.text: The text cannot be dated precisely, but its relative position is clear. It is later than the Dharmasūtras and earlier than the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, and it knows the Greeks (yavana), Śakas and Pahlavas as peoples of the north-west, whom it classes, with other peoples on the margins of its world, as Kṣatriyas who have sunk to the status of Śūdras through the neglect of rites (10.43–44); Aloka Parasher has traced such Brahmanical attitudes to outsiders up to c. 600 CE (Parasher 1991). Olivelle places its composition in the second century CE, and the series follows this date; older estimates ranging from the second century BCE to the second century CE are still found in the literature (Olivelle 2005). It is thus a work of the post-Mauryan period, composed in a world of foreign dynasties and powerful Buddhist and Jain communities, when Brahmin authors had reason to restate their vision of a social order headed by Brahmins and protected by a king loyal to them.

docs.title: 10.1.3 Unity of Composition
docs.text: Earlier scholars often treated the text as a stratified compilation, built up by successive authors over several centuries, and used this hypothesis to explain its apparent contradictions — for example, between verses that honour women and verses that subordinate them. Some have hoped that the harshest provisions on caste and gender might prove to be late interpolations. Olivelle’s critical edition, based on a comprehensive study of the manuscripts and commentaries, points the other way. He argues that the Manusmṛti was composed by a single, highly skilled author, or by a strong chairman working with a team, according to a carefully designed plan, and that its structure is deliberate; he identifies relatively few interpolations. The tensions within the text, on this view, are tensions within its author’s vision, not evidence of different hands (Olivelle 2005). The claim, sometimes repeated, that Olivelle showed the restrictive provisions on women or on Śūdras to be later additions is not correct.

docs.title: 10.1.4 Structure
docs.text:
The critical edition has about 2,685 verses in twelve chapters. Olivelle shows that the text is organised in four parts: the creation of the world (chapter 1); the sources of dharma (2.1–24); the dharma of the four varṇas, including the life of the student, the householder, the forest-dweller and the renouncer, the king and the law (2.25–11.266); and the consequences of action and the path to liberation (chapter 12). Table 10.1 summarises the contents chapter by chapter.

Table 10.1. Contents of the Manusmṛti by chapter Ch. Main contents 1 Frame; creation of the world; origin of the varṇas; the ages; praise of the Brahmin and of the treatise 2 Sources of dharma; the sacred land; saṃskāras; the student 3 Marriage and its forms; the householder; the five great sacrifices; ancestral offerings 4 The householder’s livelihood and conduct; the snātaka’s observances 5 Food; impurity; purification; the duties of women 6 The forest-dweller and the renouncer 7 The king: his creation, punishment, ministers, taxation, foreign policy and war 8 The king’s court; procedure; witnesses; the eighteen titles of law (debts to assault) 9 Titles of law continued: husband and wife, inheritance, gambling; the removal of “thorns”; duties of Vaiśyas and Śūdras 10 The mixed classes; occupations in times of distress 11 Gifts; penances (prāyaścitta) 12 Action and its consequences; rebirth; the highest good

docs.title: 10.2 The Householder’s World
docs.text:
Most of the Manusmṛti is not about law in the narrow sense but about the life of the twice-born man, above all the Brahmin householder. Chapter 2 describes the student’s life: his initiation, his duties to his teacher, the rules of begging, celibacy and Vedic recitation. Chapters 3 to 5 describe the householder: his marriage (Chapter 15), the five “great sacrifices” he must perform daily — to the Veda by study, to the ancestors by offerings of water and food, to the gods by oblations in the fire, to beings by scattering food, and to men by hospitality to guests (3.70) — the ancestral rites, and the rules of food, impurity and purification. The householder is praised as the support of all the other orders: as all creatures live by depending on air, so all the orders live by depending on the householder (3.77).

Manu’s account of how a Brahmin should earn his living is revealing. He lists modes of livelihood in descending order of purity: gleaning grain from fields (called ṛta, “truth”); accepting what is given unasked (amṛta, “immortal”); begging (mṛta, “dead”); agriculture (pramṛta, “killing”, because ploughing destroys living beings); and trade (satyānṛta, “truth-and-falsehood”); service of others is “the dog’s way of life” and is to be avoided (4.4–6). In distress a Brahmin may live by the occupations of the Kṣatriya and, failing that, of the Vaiśya, though he should avoid agriculture because it injures living beings (10.81–84). The scheme expresses a Brahmanical ideal of detachment from worldly production; it also shows how the texts ranked occupations, placing agriculture and service low and treating trade with suspicion.

Chapter 6 describes the forest-dweller and the renouncer, who abandon the household and live by alms. Chapter 11 sets out gifts and penances, and chapter 12 the consequences of action: rebirth according to one’s deeds and the three qualities (guṇa) of goodness, passion and darkness, and the path of knowledge that leads to liberation. In this frame, the law of chapters 7 to 9 is one part of a comprehensive account of the right life, which ends not in the court but in release from rebirth.

docs.title: 10.3.1 The Creation of the Varṇas
docs.text: The Manusmṛti grounds the social hierarchy in creation. “For the growth of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra” (1.31), an image derived from the Ṛgvedic Puruṣasūkta (Chapter 2). To each the creator assigned activities: to Brahmins, teaching and study, sacrificing for themselves and others, giving and receiving gifts; to Kṣatriyas, protecting the people, giving, sacrificing and study; to Vaiśyas, cattle, giving, sacrificing, study, trade, money-lending and agriculture; “but the Lord assigned only one activity to the Śūdra: service to these very varṇas without resentment” (1.88–91). Because he was born from the mouth, the Brahmin is the lord of this whole creation (1.93). The text declares that there are only four varṇas: the Brahmin, Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are “twice-born”, the Śūdra “once-born”, “and there is no fifth” (10.4).

docs.title: 10.3.2 The Twice-born and the Śūdra
docs.text: The line between the twice-born and the Śūdra runs through the whole text. Only the twice-born undergo Vedic initiation and study the Veda; a Brahmin must not teach the Veda to a Śūdra, nor give him advice, nor teach him dharma or penance (4.80–81). The Śūdra’s dharma is service, above all service of Brahmins, “which alone is declared to be his highest duty” (10.123). He should not accumulate wealth even if he is able to, “for a Śūdra who has acquired wealth harasses Brahmins” (10.129). A Brahmin may confidently take the property of his Śūdra slave, for the slave has no property of his own (8.417), and a Śūdra, whether bought or not, may be made to do servile work, “for he was created by the Self-existent one for the service of the Brahmin” (8.413). Even if freed by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude, “for it is innate in him” (8.414).

docs.title: 10.3.3 The Mixed Classes and the Caṇḍāla
docs.text:
Chapter 10 explains the many occupational communities (jāti) of the author’s world as the offspring of unions between members of different varṇas. Unions in which the husband is of higher varṇa than the wife (anuloma, “with the grain”) are tolerated; those in which the wife is of higher varṇa (pratiloma, “against the grain”) produce degraded classes, the lowest of all being the Caṇḍāla, the child of a Śūdra man and a Brahmin woman (10.12). The text’s treatment of the Caṇḍālas and similar groups is a classic statement of what would later be called untouchability:

The dwelling of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village; they must use discarded vessels, and their wealth shall be dogs and donkeys. Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; they shall eat from broken dishes; their ornaments shall be of iron; and they must wander constantly. A man who follows the dharma should not seek contact with them. … At night they must not walk about in villages and towns. (Manu 10.51–54, paraphrased after Olivelle)

They are to carry out executions and to take the clothes, beds and ornaments of those executed (10.56).

The chapter assigns occupations to the mixed classes. The Sūta, it says, should look after horses and chariots, the Ambaṣṭha practise medicine, the Vaidehaka serve in the women’s quarters and the Māgadha engage in trade; the Niṣāda should fish; the Āyogava work in wood; the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus and Madgus hunt wild animals; the Kṣattṛs, Ugras and Pukkasas catch and kill animals living in holes; the Dhigvaṇas work leather; and the Veṇas play musical instruments (10.46–49). Several of these names were names of real peoples or occupational groups, and some, like the Andhras, of regions. The text thus attempts to fit the occupations of a complex society, and peoples on its margins, into a scheme of descent from the four varṇas, ranking them by the degree of their supposed mixture and by the impurity of their work. Many of the occupations it degrades — leather-working, hunting, fishing, the handling of the dead — were those of groups later classed as untouchable.

The chapter also sets out what the varṇas may do in times of distress (āpad). A Brahmin who cannot live by his own occupations may adopt those of the Kṣatriya and then the Vaiśya; a Kṣatriya may live as a Vaiśya; a Vaiśya unable to live by his own work may do a Śūdra’s work, but must abandon it when he can; a Śūdra unable to find service may live by crafts (10.81–100). The rules acknowledge economic reality while insisting on the hierarchy: a lower varṇa may never take up the occupation of a higher one, and a man who lives by a higher varṇa’s work is to be punished by the king with confiscation of property and banishment (10.95–96). This taxonomy of mixed classes has no historical value as an account of the origins of real communities; it is a Brahmanical theory designed to fit an existing world of hereditary occupational groups into the four-varṇa scheme, and to rank them. Its importance lies in its later authority. Uma Chakravarti and R. S. Sharma have shown how such texts helped to fix the low status of labouring and “impure” groups, and Ambedkar devoted much of his scholarship to the history of untouchability that they record (Sharma 1958; Chakravarti 2003; Ambedkar 1946).

docs.title: 10.3.4 Varṇa and the Law
docs.text: The varṇa hierarchy shapes Manu’s law at every point. The king is to compel Vaiśyas and Śūdras to do their work (8.418). Witnesses are to be of the same varṇa as the parties and are sworn in different ways according to varṇa (8.68, 8.113; Chapter 12). Interest rates rise as the debtor’s varṇa falls (8.142; Chapter 13). Above all, punishments vary with the varṇa of offender and victim, a principle set out in detail in Chapter 14. A Śūdra who reviles or strikes a twice-born man suffers corporal punishment or mutilation, while a Brahmin who reviles a Śūdra pays a small fine (8.267–283); a Śūdra’s sexual offence against a guarded twice-born woman may cost him his life, a Brahmin’s only a fine (8.374–385); a Brahmin is never to be executed, “for there is no greater injustice on earth than killing a Brahmin” (8.379–381); and even the penance for homicide shrinks as the victim’s varṇa falls (11.127). One principle runs the other way — the heavier guilt of a high-born thief (8.337–338), discussed with the king’s thousandfold fine in Chapter 14 — but it is confined to theft and cannot offset the systematic privileging of Brahmins and degradation of Śūdras in the rest of the law.

docs.title: 10.3.5 Varṇa, Jāti and “Caste”
docs.text: Modern scholars emphasise that varṇa, the fourfold scheme of the texts, and jāti, the many endogamous hereditary groups of social life, are different things, and that the English word “caste” blurs them. That is true, and the history of the caste system cannot be read off the Manusmṛti. But the distinction should not be used to minimise the text’s significance. Manu’s chapter 10 is precisely an attempt to map the jātis onto the varṇas and to rank them, and his rules on purity, commensality, marriage and occupation became, through the commentaries and digests and later through colonial courts, a powerful resource for those who defended hierarchy (Dirks 2001; Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 10.4 Women in the Manusmṛti
docs.text: The Manusmṛti’s provisions on women are the second great focus of modern debate. They must be read together, not selectively.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Honour and Protection
docs.text: The text contains a well-known passage on honouring women: “Where women are revered, there the gods rejoice; but where they are not revered, all rites are fruitless. Where the women of the family grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, it always prospers” (3.56–57). Fathers, brothers, husbands and brothers-in-law who desire prosperity should honour women and give them ornaments, clothes and food (3.55, 3.59). A mother, the text says elsewhere, surpasses a thousand fathers in veneration (2.145). The verses belong to the critical text, and the concern they voice for the welfare of women within the household is not to be dismissed.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Dependence and Control
docs.text: The same text insists that women must never be independent. “Her father guards her in childhood, her husband guards her in youth, and her sons guard her in old age; a woman is not fit for independence” (pitā rakṣati kaumāre bhartā rakṣati yauvane / rakṣanti sthavire putrā na strī svātantryam arhati, 9.3; compare 5.147–148). Men must guard their women day and night, because women are by nature fickle and lustful: the text attributes to them, at its creation, a love of bed and seat and ornament, impure desires, anger, crookedness, malice and bad conduct (9.14–17). Women are excluded from the Vedic rites performed with mantras, and the text declares that marriage is for women the equivalent of Vedic initiation, serving the husband the equivalent of living with a teacher, and housework the equivalent of tending the sacred fires (2.66–67). A virtuous wife should constantly worship her husband as a god, even if he is devoid of virtue, given to lust or without good qualities (5.154).

docs.title: 10.4.3 Widowhood and Remarriage
docs.text: The Manusmṛti opposes the remarriage of widows. After her husband’s death a woman should emaciate her body, living on flowers, roots and fruits, and should never mention the name of another man; a virtuous wife who remains chaste after her husband’s death goes to heaven even without a son, while one who breaks faith with him is reborn in the womb of a jackal (5.157–164). “Nowhere is a second husband prescribed for good women” (5.162). The text describes the older practice of levirate (niyoga), in which a widow or the wife of an impotent man might be appointed to bear a son by a kinsman of the husband (9.59–63), but then condemns it as fit only for animals, a practice introduced in the reign of the wicked king Vena, and states that the marriage formulae nowhere mention niyoga or the remarriage of widows (9.64–68). The text’s waiting periods for a wife whose husband has gone abroad — eight years if he has gone for a religious purpose, six for learning or fame, three for pleasure (9.76) — have sometimes been read as permitting her to remarry afterwards; the text does not say so, and the commentators understood the rule otherwise. Only a virgin widow, whose marriage was not consummated, may undergo the marriage rite again with her husband’s brother (9.69–70).

docs.title: 10.4.4 Property
docs.text: Manu recognises a category of women’s property (strīdhana): what was given before the nuptial fire, at the bridal procession, as a token of love, and by her brother, mother and father (9.194), which passes on her death to her children (Chapter 15). Yet he also states that “a wife, a son and a slave — these three are declared to have no property; whatever they earn belongs to the man to whom they belong” (8.416). Commentators reconciled the two by distinguishing kinds of property and degrees of control. The text gives daughters a share of inheritance only through an “appointed daughter” (putrikā) when there is no son, and recommends that brothers give their unmarried sisters a portion of their own shares (9.118).

docs.title: 10.4.5 Interpreting the Tension
docs.text: The coexistence of these provisions is not a puzzle to be solved by assigning them to different authors. Uma Chakravarti’s analysis of “Brahmanical patriarchy” explains it as a coherent system: the honour paid to women within the household and the control exercised over their sexuality both served to preserve the purity of lineage and thus of caste, which required that women’s sexuality — especially that of upper-caste women — be closely guarded (Chakravarti 1993, 2003). Julia Leslie’s study of a later text, the eighteenth-century Strīdharmapaddhati, shows how such norms were transmitted and elaborated (Leslie 1989). These analyses do not deny that the text expresses concern for women’s welfare; they show that this concern operated within a framework of subordination.

docs.title: 10.5 The King and the Law
docs.text:
Chapters 7 to 9 are the Manusmṛti’s treatise on government and law, and they are discussed in detail in Chapters 5 and 12–14. Their main features may be noted here.

  • The king is created by the Lord from particles of the gods for the protection of all (7.3–8). His instrument is punishment (daṇḍa), which “rules all subjects, protects them, and keeps watch while they sleep” (7.18).

  • Taxation is moderate: one-sixth, one-eighth or one-twelfth of grain, one-fiftieth of cattle and gold; artisans and Śūdras who live by labour owe one day’s work a month; a Brahmin learned in the Veda is never to be taxed (7.130–138).

  • The court is held daily by the king or a Brahmin judge with three assessors (8.1–11). Manu explains that if justice is defeated by injustice, a quarter of the sin falls on the wrongdoer, a quarter on the witness, a quarter on the court and a quarter on the king (8.18).

  • The eighteen titles of law (8.4–7) are listed for the first time in this text and became the standard classification of litigation (Chapter 12).

  • Fines are graded into three levels: 250 paṇas (the lowest “violence fine”), 500 (the middle) and 1,000 (the highest) (8.138).

  • The king is fined a thousand times what an ordinary man would pay for the same offence (8.336; Chapter 5).

Manu’s account of the king (chapter 7) follows the pattern of the Arthaśāstra in compressed form. The king should keep seven or eight hereditary ministers, learned and tested, and a Brahmin of special learning as his chief counsellor; he should appoint an envoy who is learned, honest and skilled in reading gestures (7.54–68). He should live in a fort — a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a fort of men or a mountain fort, the last being the best (7.70–71). He should organise the countryside in units of one, ten, twenty, a hundred and a thousand villages, each under a lord responsible to the next (7.115–120). He should deliberate in secret, on a mountain top or in a lonely place, excluding from his council idiots, the dumb, the blind and the deaf, animals, the very old, women, barbarians, the sick and the maimed (7.147–150). He should know the circle of kings around him — the conqueror, his enemy, the middle king and the neutral — and the six measures of policy (7.155–180), and wage war according to the rules of righteous battle (7.87–98; Chapter 7). His day is divided between the court, counsel, exercise, meals, the inspection of troops and the reports of spies (7.145–226). The chapter shows how thoroughly the Dharmaśāstra absorbed the science of polity, while framing it within the king’s duty to uphold dharma.

The Manusmṛti’s legal sections are technically accomplished. They include rules on the examination and credibility of witnesses, on the oath and ordeals, on interest and pledges, on deposits, partnerships and sales, on boundaries and on inheritance, and they show a concern for orderly procedure and for proportion in punishment. They are achievements of legal thought within a system that is explicitly unequal, and their technical virtues cannot be detached from it.

docs.title: 10.6 Action and Rebirth
docs.text:
The last chapter of the Manusmṛti places the whole of its law within a theory of action (karman) and its consequences. Every action, mental, verbal or bodily, bears fruit, good or bad; from bad actions of the mind a man is reborn in a low station, from bad actions of speech as a bird or beast, from bad actions of the body as an immobile being (12.3–9). The text analyses human character in terms of the three qualities (guṇa) of goodness, passion and darkness, which determine the kind of rebirth one attains (12.24–52), and it lists the rebirths that await particular sinners — the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief of gold, the violator of the teacher’s bed — in the wombs of animals and of despised humans (12.54–72). It ends with the knowledge of the self, which leads to the highest state.

This framework explains a feature of the text that modern readers often find puzzling: its readiness to assign to the next life consequences that a modern law would seek in this one, and its treatment of social position as the result of past deeds. A Śūdra’s birth, on this view, is the consequence of his past actions, and his faithful performance of service is the means to a better birth. Ambedkar singled out this doctrine as one of the ideological foundations of caste, because it made social inequality appear as cosmic justice (Ambedkar 1936). It also made law, penance and rebirth parts of a single moral order, in which the king’s punishment, the Brahmins’ penances and the workings of karma all served to maintain dharma.

docs.title: 10.7 Universal Virtues
docs.text:
The Manusmṛti also contains statements of virtues common to all. In the chapter on the renouncer it lists ten marks of dharma for twice-born men in all the āśramas:

Manusmṛti 6.92

dhṛtiḥ kṣamā damo ’steyaṃ śaucam indriyanigrahaḥ dhīr vidyā satyam akrodho daśakaṃ dharmalakṣaṇam “Resolve, forbearance, self-control, not stealing, purification, mastery of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness and lack of anger: these are the ten marks of dharma.”

In chapter 10 it states the dharma of all four varṇas in brief: “Abstention from injury, truthfulness, not stealing, purification and mastery of the senses” (10.63). These lists are often quoted as evidence of a universal ethic in the text, with good reason; but in the text they stand alongside, not above, the differentiated duties of varṇa and gender.

docs.title: 10.8 Commentaries
docs.text: The Manusmṛti attracted more commentaries than any other smṛti. An earlier commentary by Bhāruci survives only in part; the oldest to survive complete is the Manubhāṣya of Medhātithi (9th–10th century, probably Kashmir), an independent and learned work that applies Mīmāṃsā reasoning and frequently notes alternative views and readings; Ganganatha Jha translated it in full (Jha 1920). Later commentators include Govindarāja (11th–12th century), Sarvajñanārāyaṇa, Rāghavānanda, Nandana and Kullūka Bhaṭṭa, whose Manvarthamuktāvalī (perhaps 13th–15th century) became the most widely used. Olivelle has pointed out that the text known to most modern readers is the vulgate transmitted with Kullūka’s commentary, because it was this version that Jones translated and that Indian printers reproduced (Olivelle 2005).

docs.title: 10.9.1 In India before the Modern Period
docs.text: The Manusmṛti’s authority in the classical tradition was very great. Later smṛtis cite it as the foremost authority; the Bṛhaspatismṛti is quoted as saying that a smṛti contrary to Manu is not approved. Its verses are quoted throughout the commentaries and digests, and inscriptions sometimes praise kings for ruling according to Manu. But its authority was the authority of a learned text within a scholastic tradition; there is no evidence that any pre-colonial state enforced it as a code, and many of its rules were modified or set aside by commentators and by custom (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 10.9.2 Southeast Asia
docs.text: Law books in Burma (the dhammathat), and in the Mon and Thai traditions derived from them, traced their authority to a sage called Manu, and Old Javanese legal literature also invoked Manu. The content of these works was adapted to local custom and to Buddhist ethics, and they should not be read as translations of the Sanskrit text (Chapter 8 and Section 9.11).

docs.title: 10.9.3 Colonial Law and European Reception
docs.text: Under the East India Company, the Manusmṛti was the first Dharmaśāstra text to be translated into English, by Sir William Jones (Institutes of Hindu Law: or, the Ordinances of Menu, Calcutta, 1794) (Jones 1794). Jones believed it to be among the oldest law codes in the world and to have been the law of the Hindus; his translation, together with the later rendering by Georg Bühler in the Sacred Books of the East (1886), gave it a place in European thought far beyond that of any other Indian legal text (Bühler 1886). British judges cited it as a source of “Hindu law”, and its prestige was thereby increased in India itself (Chapter 19). In Europe, it was read as evidence for the early history of law (Henry Maine) and, in a different spirit, by Friedrich Nietzsche, who in his late works praised the “Law of Manu” as a model of an aristocratic order superior to Christian morality — a reading based on a French popular version and coloured by his own polemics.

docs.title: 10.9.4 Manu in the Colonial Courts
docs.text: Although Jones’s translation made the Manusmṛti the best-known Hindu law book in English, the colonial courts relied less on Manu than on the medieval commentaries and digests, especially the Mitākṣarā and the Dāyabhāga, which dealt with inheritance and family property in detail (Chapter 11). Manu was cited as a general authority, often in the translations of Jones and Bühler, on questions of marriage, adoption and caste. Its prestige among British administrators and Orientalists, and the assumption that it represented “the” ancient law of the Hindus, nonetheless gave it a symbolic status out of proportion to its practical role in the courts, and that status explains why it became the principal target of anti-caste critique.

docs.title: 10.9.5 Critique: Phule, Ambedkar and After
docs.text:
The most important modern responses to the Manusmṛti came from Indians who had suffered under the order it defended. Jotirao Phule (1827–1890), in Gulamgiri (“Slavery”, 1873), attacked the Brahmanical texts as instruments by which Brahmins had enslaved the Śūdras and Atiśūdras. E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar) made the critique of Brahmanical scriptures central to the Self-Respect Movement in the Tamil region.

B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956) engaged with the text both as an activist and as a scholar. In March 1927 he led thousands of Dalits to draw water from the Chavdar tank at Mahad, in the Konkan, asserting a right of access that the municipality had recognised on paper but caste Hindus denied in practice. When the tank was ritually “purified” by caste Hindus afterwards, Ambedkar convened a second conference at Mahad in December 1927, at which, on 25 December, a copy of the Manusmṛti was publicly burned. The act repudiated the text’s authority as a charter of untouchability, and 25 December is still observed by many Dalits as Manusmṛti Dahan Din. In Annihilation of Caste (1936), Ambedkar argued that caste could not be reformed while the authority of the śāstras that sanctioned it was accepted, and in Who Were the Shudras? (1946) he offered a historical account of how the Śūdras came to be the lowest varṇa (Ambedkar 1936, 1946; Zelliot 1992). As chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution and as Law Minister, he later led the effort to replace Dharmaśāstra-based personal law with modern legislation (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 10.9.6 Feminist and Historical Scholarship
docs.text: From the 1980s, feminist historians, above all Uma Chakravarti, examined the Manusmṛti as a source for the history of patriarchy and its links with caste; Chakravarti’s essay on “Brahmanical patriarchy” (1993) and her book Gendering Caste (2003) are the most influential statements (Chakravarti 1993, 2003). Historians such as R. S. Sharma used it as a source for the social history of the Śūdras (Sharma 1958). Olivelle’s edition has provided all sides with a reliable text and with an argument about its date and composition that makes it harder to evade its content by attributing unwelcome passages to interpolators (Olivelle 2005).

docs.title: 10.9.7 In Contemporary India
docs.text: The Manusmṛti remains contested. Some Hindu traditionalists continue to regard it as a sacred text, often quoting its verses on honouring women and on universal virtues; Dalit and feminist activists regard it as a symbol of oppression. A statue of Manu installed in the premises of the Rajasthan High Court at Jaipur in 1989 has been the object of protests and litigation ever since. The Constitution’s guarantees of equality before the law (Article 14), its prohibition of discrimination on grounds of caste and sex (Article 15) and its abolition of untouchability (Article 17) are, in substance, the negation of the Manusmṛti’s legal order (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 10.10 Assessment
docs.text: The Manusmṛti is a work of great intellectual ambition: a carefully constructed account of the whole of human life — creation, society, family, kingship, law, penance and liberation — from a Brahmanical point of view. Its legal sections are among the most important sources for the history of Indian law, and its literary skill and influence are beyond doubt. It is also, unmistakably, a charter of hierarchy, which assigns rights and penalties by birth and sex, places Brahmins above all others, condemns Śūdras to service and outcastes to exclusion, and subordinates women to men. A responsible reading must hold both facts together. It should neither sanitise the text by selective quotation or by imaginary interpolation, nor reduce the whole of Indian tradition to it: the Manusmṛti was one Brahmanical text among many, and Indian traditions — Buddhist, Jain, bhakti, Islamic, Sikh and modern — also produced powerful critiques of the order it describes.

docs.title: 10.11 Principal Passages
docs.text:
Table 10.2 lists the principal passages discussed in this chapter.
