docs.title: 10.12 Summary
docs.text:
• The Manusmṛti is a carefully structured Brahmanical treatise of about the second century CE, presented as the teaching of the first man, Manu. Olivelle has argued for its unity of composition; attempts to explain away its harsh provisions as late interpolations are not supported by his edition.

  • It covers the whole of dharma: creation, the sources of dharma, the student and householder, women, the renouncer, the king, law, mixed classes, penance and rebirth.

  • Its social order is explicitly hierarchical: Brahmins are lords of creation, Śūdras exist to serve, and groups such as the Caṇḍālas are excluded; legal penalties are graded by varṇa, with a reverse gradation for theft.

  • It honours women within the household while declaring them unfit for independence, opposes widow remarriage and gives wives no property of their own apart from strīdhana — a combination analysed by Uma Chakravarti as “Brahmanical patriarchy”.

  • It was the most authoritative smṛti for the commentators, the first Dharmaśāstra translated into English, and a model for law books in Southeast Asia. Jotirao Phule, B. R. Ambedkar — who burned it at Mahad in 1927 — and later Dalit and feminist scholars (Section 20.2) made it the central target of their critique of caste and patriarchy.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Olivelle (2005) is the critical edition and translation, with an essential introduction; Doniger and Smith (1991) and Bühler (1886) are earlier translations, and Jha (1920) translates Medhātithi’s commentary. On the text’s social vision and its critics see Ambedkar (1936), Ambedkar (1946), Sharma (1958), Chakravarti (1993), Chakravarti (2003) and Zelliot (1992).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Yājñavalkya, Nārada and the Schools of Hindu Law
docs.text: After the Manusmṛti, the most consequential Dharmaśāstra texts were a shorter and more systematic smṛti attributed to Yājñavalkya; the Nāradasmṛti, the first smṛti devoted wholly to law; the lost treatises of Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana, which survive in quotations; and two medieval works that gave rise to the “schools” of Hindu law recognised by the British courts: the Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara and the Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana. This chapter introduces these texts, their authors and dates, and the doctrines for which they are best known. Their contributions to procedure, evidence and substantive law are taken up in more detail in Chapters 12–15.

docs.title: 11.1.1 Frame, Date and Structure
docs.text:
The Yājñavalkyasmṛti is attributed to Yājñavalkya, the great teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. In its opening verses the sages approach “the lord of yogis” Yājñavalkya, who is in Mithilā, and ask him to teach them the dharmas of the varṇas, the āśramas and the others; he answers by naming the fourteen sciences that are the foundations of knowledge and dharma and the twenty authors of dharmaśāstras (1.1–5; Chapter 9). The attribution is a claim to authority, not a statement of authorship. The text draws extensively on the Manusmṛti and on the Arthaśāstra tradition; it uses technical legal vocabulary more developed than Manu’s; and it was known to authors of the later Gupta period. Patrick Olivelle, whose edition and translation appeared in 2019, places it around the fourth or early fifth century CE; the series uses the range c. 4th–5th century CE (Olivelle 2019).

The text has just over a thousand verses, arranged in three books: ācāra, “conduct” (368 verses in the vulgate), covering the saṃskāras, the student and householder, food, purity, gifts, ancestral offerings, the propitiation of planets and the king; vyavahāra, “legal procedure” (307 verses), covering the courts and the titles of law; and prāyaścitta, “penance” (335 verses), covering impurity, the duties of ascetics and expiation. This threefold arrangement became the standard division of the subject matter of Dharmaśāstra.

docs.title: 11.1.2 Character
docs.text:
Compared with Manu, Yājñavalkya is concise and orderly. Its legal book treats procedure first — the court, the plaint, the answer, the means of proof — and then each title of law in turn, with an attention to documents that reflects the growing use of written instruments in commercial life. It names the means of proof as documents, possession and witnesses, with ordeals to be used only when these are lacking (2.22). It recognises the jurisdiction of guilds, merchant associations, assemblies of villages and families alongside the king’s court, and lays down a hierarchy among them (2.30; Chapter 12). It states that where two smṛtis conflict, reasoning based on legal practice should decide, and that dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra (2.21).

It would be wrong to suppose that Yājñavalkya softened the hierarchy of varṇa. Its rules on witnesses, interest, marriage and punishment, like Manu’s, are graded by varṇa; it prescribes that a Śūdra who abuses a twice-born man be punished severely; and it shares the general Dharmaśāstric picture of women’s dependence. Its importance lies rather in its technical clarity, which made it the natural basis for later commentators.

docs.title: 11.1.3 The Three Books in Outline
docs.text:
The first book, on conduct, begins with the sources of dharma, the fourteen sciences and the twenty authors of dharmaśāstras, and then sets out the saṃskāras, the duties of the student, the rules of marriage, the varṇas and mixed classes, the householder’s daily rites, the rules for a snātaka, food, purification, gifts, ancestral offerings and the rites to propitiate the planets. It closes with a long section on the king: his qualities, ministers, chaplain, taxes, forts, foreign policy and the administration of justice — a compressed version of the Arthaśāstra’s teaching.

The second book, on legal procedure, is the core of the text for the history of law. It describes the court and the judge; the plaint, the answer, proof and decision; the means of proof (documents, possession, witnesses and ordeals); and then each title of law, from debts and deposits to partition, boundary disputes, assault, theft, violence, sexual offences, gambling and miscellaneous matters. Its treatment of documents and of ordeals is much fuller than Manu’s, and its arrangement of the titles became the model for later works.

The third book, on penance, covers impurity after birth and death, the duties of the forest-dweller and the renouncer, a summary of the doctrine of the self and rebirth, and the penances for the various sins. Its combination of practical law with ritual and soteriology shows that, for Yājñavalkya as for Manu, law remained one part of dharma rather than a separate discipline.

docs.title: 11.1.4 Commentaries
docs.text: The Yājñavalkyasmṛti attracted several important commentaries. The earliest surviving is the Bālakrīḍā of Viśvarūpa (9th century, probably in the south). The Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara (c. 1100–1120) became the most influential legal text of medieval and colonial India. Aparārka, a twelfth-century Śilāhāra king of the north Konkan, wrote a voluminous commentary that is a mine of quotations; Śūlapāṇi wrote a commentary in Bengal in the fifteenth century (Kane 1930; Derrett 1973).

docs.title: 11.2.1 The First Juridical Smṛti
docs.text:
The Nāradasmṛti, attributed to the divine sage Nārada, is unique among the major smṛtis in dealing only with law. It contains no rules on ritual, purity, the stages of life or penance; it is a treatise on vyavahāra. Its date is uncertain; it is later than Manu and Yājñavalkya, and is generally placed in the fifth or sixth century CE. It survives in a shorter and a longer recension, and an early commentary by Asahāya is known; Richard Lariviere’s critical edition and translation (1989) is the standard version (Lariviere 1989b). Julius Jolly had translated the text in the Sacred Books of the East in 1889 (Jolly 1889).

The text opens with a long introduction on procedure (the mātṛkā, “matrix”), discussing the nature of lawsuits, the court, the plaint and answer, the means of proof and the qualities of the judge. It then treats the eighteen titles of law in an order and with names somewhat different from Manu’s, adding a title on “miscellaneous” matters (prakīrṇaka), which includes offences against the king’s commands, and an appendix on theft.

docs.title: 11.2.2 Distinctive Doctrines
docs.text:
Several features of the Nāradasmṛti have attracted attention.

  • Procedure. Nārada’s account of the four parts of a lawsuit — plaint, answer, proof and decision — and of the kinds of answer and proof is the most developed among the smṛtis that survive complete (Chapter 12).

  • Capacity. Nārada sets out who may validly transact: transactions by those who are not independent (minors, sons under their father’s authority, slaves) or by the intoxicated, the insane, the afflicted and those acting under fear or compulsion are invalid. Later commentators drew on this in their law of contract (Chapter 13).

  • Remarriage. Nārada allows a woman to take another husband in five calamities: when her husband is missing, dead, has become an ascetic, is impotent or has fallen from caste (naṣṭe mṛte pravrajite klībe ca patite patau / pañcasv āpatsu nārīṇāṃ patir anyo vidhīyate, Nārada 12.97). The same verse appears in the Parāśarasmṛti. It is the clearest classical text permitting remarriage, and it was cited by Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar in the nineteenth-century campaign for widow remarriage (Chapter 15), though medieval commentators generally held that it did not apply in the Kali age.

  • Royal authority. Nārada gives the king’s command great weight. It adopts the Arthaśāstra’s four “feet” or bases of decision, with royal edict at their head (Chapter 12); and in its final title it insists that the king must be honoured and obeyed by his subjects even if he lacks good qualities.

Lariviere has argued that the Nāradasmṛti reflects actual legal practice more closely than the earlier smṛtis, and that it represents a stage at which law had become a specialised field within Dharmaśāstra (Lariviere 1989b, 1989a).

docs.title: 11.3 Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana
docs.text:
Two further law books, attributed to Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana, are lost as independent texts but survive in hundreds of verses quoted by the commentators and digests. Both are generally placed in the sixth or seventh century CE. Their quotations were collected into reconstructed texts: Bṛhaspati by K. V. Rangaswami Aiyangar (1941), Kātyāyana by P. V. Kane (1933); Jolly translated the Bṛhaspati fragments then known in 1889 (Jolly 1889).

They represent the most developed stage of the smṛti law of procedure and evidence. Kātyāyana, in particular, deals at length with the plaint and answer, with documents and their authentication, with possession and with the burden of proof. Bṛhaspati is credited with a well-known warning that a decision should not be made by relying on the letter of the śāstra alone, for when a case is decided without reasoning, dharma is lost. Both treat custom as authoritative in many matters. The digests quote them constantly, and much of what later writers called “Hindu law” on procedure and evidence derives from these fragments (Kane 1930).

docs.title: 11.4 Other Smṛtis
docs.text: Many other smṛtis circulated, most of them short and many late. The Viṣṇusmṛti (or Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra), a Vaiṣṇava reworking of an older dharmasūtra presented as the teaching of Viṣṇu to the Earth, contains a substantial section on the king and the law. The Parāśarasmṛti, which claims to be the dharmaśāstra for the Kali age, is concerned mainly with conduct and penance; its importance owes much to the fourteenth-century commentary-digest of Mādhava at Vijayanagara. Works attributed to Atri, Dakṣa, Devala, Hārīta, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Saṃvarta and others are known in full or in fragments; some of them, such as Devala’s rules on readmitting people forcibly converted, reflect the circumstances of particular periods. Kane’s History remains the guide to this large and uneven literature (Kane 1930).

docs.title: 11.5.1 Vijñāneśvara
docs.text: Vijñāneśvara composed the Mitākṣarā (“concise words”) at the court of the Western Cālukya king Vikramāditya VI (r. 1076–1126) at Kalyāṇa (modern Basavakalyan, Karnataka), probably between about 1100 and 1120. Despite its title, the work is a large commentary on the whole Yājñavalkyasmṛti, which it uses as a framework for a systematic exposition of Dharmaśāstra, citing a wide range of smṛtis and earlier commentators and applying Mīmāṃsā reasoning to reconcile them. Its section on inheritance became the most important single source of “Hindu law” in British India, and through the British courts it governed the family property of most Hindus outside Bengal and Assam until 1956, and in part until 2005 (Derrett 1968; Lingat 1973).

docs.title: 11.5.2 Ownership by Birth
docs.text: The Mitākṣarā’s most famous doctrine is that a son acquires ownership of ancestral property by birth (janmanā svatvam). Its starting point is a verse of Yājñavalkya: “In land acquired by the grandfather, in a corrody or in movable property, father and son have equal ownership” (Yājñ 2.121 in the vulgate numbering). Vijñāneśvara argued that ownership (svatva) is a worldly matter, known from ordinary experience and usage rather than solely from scripture, and that the texts treating sons as owners show that ownership in ancestral property arises at birth, not at the father’s death. From this followed the institution that British lawyers called the Mitākṣarā coparcenary: the father and his sons, grandsons and great-grandsons in the male line hold ancestral property jointly, with rights that arise at birth; a son may demand partition even during his father’s lifetime; and the father’s power to alienate ancestral property is restricted. A widely quoted text allowed a single member to alienate immovable property only in times of distress, for the needs of the family, or for pious purposes. On a member’s death his interest passed to the surviving coparceners by survivorship rather than to his own heirs (Derrett 1968; Rocher 2012).

docs.title: 11.5.3 Inheritance by Consanguinity
docs.text: For property not held jointly — the separate property of a man who died without male issue — the Mitākṣarā established an order of heirs based on nearness of blood. It read the relationship of sapiṇḍas as one of blood rather than of shared ancestral offerings (Section 11.10), and ranked heirs accordingly. Following Yājñavalkya 2.135–136, the widow, then the daughters, the daughter’s son, the parents, the brothers and their sons and so on inherit the estate of a sonless man who had separated from his coparceners. The widow thus inherited only in limited circumstances, and as a rule a woman took a limited estate, which passed on her death not to her own heirs but to the next heirs of her husband (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 11.6.1 Jīmūtavāhana
docs.text: The Dāyabhāga (“partition of inheritance”) of Jīmūtavāhana, a Bengali jurist probably of the twelfth century, is not a commentary but an independent treatise on inheritance, partition, women’s property and related matters. It became the leading authority on these subjects in Bengal, together with the later works of Raghunandana (16th century), and the British courts applied it there and in Assam. Ludo Rocher’s annotated translation (2002) has replaced Colebrooke’s translation of 1810 as the standard version (Rocher 2002; Colebrooke 1810).

docs.title: 11.6.2 Ownership on Death
docs.text:
Jīmūtavāhana rejected the doctrine of ownership by birth. Sons, he argued, acquire ownership of their father’s property only when the father’s ownership ceases — through death, through becoming an ascetic or through loss of caste. During his lifetime the father is the owner of both ancestral and self-acquired property and can dispose of it; there is no coparcenary of father and sons in the Mitākṣarā sense. After the father’s death the brothers may hold the property jointly, but each holds a definite share, which on his death passes to his own heirs rather than by survivorship to the others.

Jīmūtavāhana also formulated a principle that later lawyers called factum valet (“the deed stands”): even if a father acts against the precepts of the texts in disposing of property — for instance, by giving away ancestral land without his sons’ consent — the transaction is valid, though the father may incur sin, because “a fact cannot be altered by a hundred texts”. The principle distinguishes between moral injunction and legal effect, and it was much used by British courts.

docs.title: 11.6.3 Inheritance by Spiritual Benefit
docs.text:
The Dāyabhāga’s order of heirs rests on the capacity to confer spiritual benefit on the deceased through the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) in the ancestral rites: those who offer, or whose offerings benefit, the deceased and his ancestors inherit in order of the benefit they confer. On this principle, the widow of a man who died without a son inherited his whole estate even if he had been living jointly with his brothers — a significant difference from the Mitākṣarā, which allowed her to inherit only if he had separated. Some historians have connected the Bengal rule with the relatively high incidence of widow-burning (satī) recorded in Bengal in the early nineteenth century, on the hypothesis that relatives had an interest in removing a widow who had inherited property; the connection has been suggested but not demonstrated. Table 11.1 summarises the main differences between the two schools.

Table 11.1. Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga compared (as applied by the Anglo-Indian courts) Question Mitākṣarā Dāyabhāga When does a son acquire rights in ancestral property? At birth On the father’s death (or renunciation, or loss of caste) Father’s power to alienate ancestral property Restricted Full Joint family property Coparcenary of father and male descendants; devolution by survivorship Joint holding of brothers after the father’s death, each with a definite share passing to his heirs Basis of the order of heirs Consanguinity Spiritual benefit (piṇḍa offerings) Widow of a sonless man Inherits only if her husband had separated Inherits even if her husband was joint Region (British India) Most of India Bengal and Assam

docs.title: 11.7 Partition and the Joint Family in Practice
docs.text:
The commentators devoted much attention to partition (vibhāga), the division of family property among its members. Under the Mitākṣarā, partition could take place during the father’s lifetime, at his wish or, in certain circumstances, at the demand of a son; after the father’s death the brothers could partition whenever they chose. Property acquired by a member through his own efforts, without the use of family funds, was his separate property and not divisible; so were gifts of affection and certain gains of learning — a doctrine that occupied later lawyers greatly when educated men began to earn salaries in professions. The question became acute in the colonial period, when courts had to decide whether the earnings of a member of a joint family who had been educated at the family’s expense belonged to him or to the family; the Hindu Gains of Learning Act of 1930 settled it in favour of the individual. The Mitākṣarā required that, before division, provision be made for the debts of the family, for the marriage of unmarried daughters and for the maintenance of dependants. Under the Dāyabhāga, partition among brothers after the father’s death followed similar rules, but each brother’s share was his own from the start.

Medieval documents and colonial records show that joint families were common among landholding and commercial castes, but that partition was also frequent, and that the size and composition of households varied widely by region and caste. The model of the large, stable joint family living under a patriarch was in part an ideal of the texts and of the colonial courts; the reality was more fluid (Derrett 1968; Newbigin 2013).

docs.title: 11.8 Women’s Property in the Commentaries
docs.text: The commentators’ treatment of women’s property shows how much interpretation mattered. Vijñāneśvara read Yājñavalkya’s definition of strīdhana broadly enough to include property a woman inherited; Jīmūtavāhana confined it to property over which she had independent power of disposal. The British courts preferred the narrower view for inherited property and so created the “woman’s limited estate” that the Hindu Succession Act abolished in 1956. The texts and the litigation are discussed in Chapter 15.

docs.title: 11.9 Daughters as Heirs
docs.text: The rights of daughters illustrate the differences between the schools. Both recognised daughters as heirs of a man who left no son, widow or son’s son, but with restrictions. Under the Mitākṣarā as applied by the courts, unmarried daughters took precedence over married ones, and among married daughters those who were poor over those who were well off. Under the Dāyabhāga, a daughter could inherit only if she had a son or might bear one, since the basis of inheritance was the capacity to benefit the deceased through the offerings of a male descendant; a widowed daughter without sons, or a daughter who was barren, was excluded. In both schools a daughter, like a widow, took a limited estate that passed on her death to the next heirs of her father. These rules, which put daughters far behind sons, were among the main targets of the reformers whose work culminated in the Hindu Succession Act of 1956 and its amendment in 2005.

docs.title: 11.10 Sapiṇḍa Relationship
docs.text:
The commentators also differed on the meaning of a term central to both inheritance and marriage: sapiṇḍa. In the older texts, sapiṇḍas are those connected by the ancestral offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa): a man offers piṇḍas to his father, grandfather and great-grandfather, and those who share in such offerings are sapiṇḍas of one another. Vijñāneśvara reinterpreted the term in the Mitākṣarā to mean those connected by particles of the same body, that is, by blood, through either parent. Jīmūtavāhana retained the older sense based on offerings, which was the foundation of his theory of inheritance by spiritual benefit (see above). The difference had practical effects: the Mitākṣarā’s definition made the circle of sapiṇḍas wider, including relatives through the mother, and the two schools consequently ordered the heirs differently.

In marriage, sapiṇḍa relationship defined the prohibited degrees. Yājñavalkya forbids marriage with a girl within the fifth degree on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s (Yājñ 1.53), and similar rules appear in other smṛtis. These rules were in tension with the customs of much of southern India, where marriage with the daughter of one’s mother’s brother was common and often preferred. Baudhāyana already notes this southern custom among the practices peculiar to particular regions (BDh 1.2.1–4), and later authorities debated whether it could be accepted as a regional custom or was to be condemned; most southern commentators accepted it (Kane 1930; Trautmann 1981). The Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 adopted a shorter definition of sapiṇḍa relationship — three generations in the line of ascent through the mother and five through the father — and prohibited marriages within it and within listed degrees of relationship, unless a custom governing both parties permits such a marriage. The saving clause for custom preserved the legality of cross-cousin marriage in the south, and is a modern statutory form of the old śāstric recognition of regional usage.

docs.title: 11.11 The “Schools” of Hindu Law
docs.text:
Medieval jurists did not belong to “schools” in any formal sense; they wrote within regional traditions of learning in which some authorities were more respected than others — the works that local paṇḍits consulted most readily. The British courts, needing to decide which texts to apply, systematised these preferences into a map of schools with defined territories, so that the law of inheritance came to depend on where a family was domiciled (Chapter 19). The Dāyabhāga school governed Bengal and Assam; the Mitākṣarā school the rest of India, divided into sub-schools according to the supplementary authorities preferred in each region (Figure 11.1):

Figure 11.1. The “schools” of Hindu law as systematised by the Anglo-Indian courts, with the supplementary authorities that the courts of each region preferred. The territorial scheme was a colonial construction from regional traditions of learning; within each area, proven custom could override the texts.

  • the Banaras school, in much of northern India, relying on the Mitākṣarā and on the Vīramitrodaya of Mitra Miśra;

  • the Mithilā school, in north Bihar, relying also on the digests of Caṇḍeśvara and Vācaspati Miśra;

  • the Bombay (Mahārāṣṭra) school, relying also on Nīlakaṇṭha’s Vyavahāramayūkha (17th century), which the Bombay courts sometimes followed in preference to the Mitākṣarā where the two differed — for example, in allowing sisters to inherit in certain cases;

  • the Madras (Drāviḍa) school, relying also on the Smṛticandrikā of Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa (c. 1200), Mādhava’s Parāśaramādhavīya (14th century, Vijayanagara) and other southern works.

Within each area, the courts also recognised proven customs that departed from the texts — among them the matrilineal systems of Kerala and the customs of many agricultural communities of Punjab (Chapter 16). J. D. M. Derrett and Ludo Rocher emphasised how much this system of schools was a product of colonial jurisprudence, which turned flexible scholarly traditions into territorially defined bodies of law (Derrett 1968; Rocher 2012; Kane 1930).

docs.title: 11.12 The Smṛtis in the Reform Debates
docs.text:
In the nineteenth century the smṛtis became weapons in public debates about social reform. Because the colonial courts treated the śāstras as law, reformers and their opponents argued about what the texts actually required. Rammohun Roy argued from Manu that satī was not enjoined, and the orthodox Dharma Sabha of Calcutta, founded in 1830, replied with texts of its own in petitioning against the Bengal Sati Regulation. Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar’s two tracts on widow remarriage (1855) built their case on the Parāśarasmṛti’s claim to be the law for the Kali age and on its verse permitting remarriage in five calamities; his opponents answered with the Manusmṛti and the medieval lists of practices forbidden in the Kali age (Chapter 9). In the debate over the Age of Consent Bill (1891), Bal Gangadhar Tilak opposed the legislation, not least as an intrusion by a foreign government into Hindu religious life, while reformers cited texts and medical evidence in its support. The campaigns themselves are described in Chapter 15.

These debates made the interpretation of the smṛtis a matter of public, and often bitter, controversy among educated Indians, and they confirmed the colonial state’s practice of legislating on Hindu personal law only when it could claim support from within the tradition — a pattern that recurred in the debates over the Hindu Code after independence (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 11.13 From Commentary to Statute
docs.text: The Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga remained the basis of Hindu family property law until independence. The Hindu Succession Act of 1956 replaced the textual law of succession with a statutory scheme, giving daughters and widows rights of inheritance and abolishing the widow’s limited estate; but section 6 of the Act preserved the Mitākṣarā coparcenary, with survivorship among male coparceners, subject to a notional partition when a coparcener left female heirs. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act of 2005 made daughters coparceners by birth in their own right, with the same rights and liabilities as sons. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) the Supreme Court held that a daughter’s right under the amended section arises by birth and does not depend on her father having been alive in 2005 (Chapter 20). The doctrine of ownership by birth that Vijñāneśvara constructed for sons in the twelfth century has thus been extended by Parliament and the courts to daughters — a striking example of the way modern Indian law has transformed rather than simply abolished its classical inheritance.

docs.title: 11.14 Summary
docs.text:
• The Yājñavalkyasmṛti (c. 4th–5th century CE) arranged Dharmaśāstra in three books — conduct, legal procedure and penance — and gave the law of procedure and documents a clearer form than Manu.

  • The Nāradasmṛti (c. 5th–6th century) is the first smṛti devoted entirely to law; it develops procedure, defines capacity to transact, gives great weight to the king’s command, and permits a woman to remarry in five calamities.

  • Vijñāneśvara’s Mitākṣarā (c. 1100–1120) held that sons acquire ownership of ancestral property by birth; Jīmūtavāhana’s Dāyabhāga (12th century) held that they acquire it only on the father’s death, and based inheritance on spiritual benefit. The colonial courts turned their regional authority into territorial “schools”.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Olivelle (2019) translates the Yājñavalkyasmṛti; Lariviere (1989b) edits and translates the Nāradasmṛti; Jolly (1889) translates Nārada and the Bṛhaspati fragments. Rocher (2002) translates the Dāyabhāga with a full introduction, and Colebrooke (1810) the inheritance sections of both schools. On the schools and their colonial transformation see Derrett (1968), Lingat (1973) and Rocher (2012); on the texts in general, Kane (1930).

docs.title: Chapter 12: Vyavahāra: Courts, Procedure and Proof
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word vyavahāra means, in ordinary usage, “dealing, transaction, business”. In the Dharmaśāstras it became the technical term for a lawsuit and for legal procedure, and by extension for the whole body of rules applied in litigation — what we would call law in the narrow sense. The smṛtis of Manu, Yājñavalkya and Nārada and the fragments of Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana contain a detailed and increasingly sophisticated account of how disputes were to be brought before a court, how the parties were to state their cases, how facts were to be proved, and how judgments were to be given. The Arthaśāstra describes a parallel system of royal courts. This chapter sets out these rules: the courts and judges, the classification of lawsuits into eighteen titles, the stages of a trial, and the means of proof.

Two cautions apply. First, these are normative texts written by Brahmin scholars; they tell us how procedure was imagined, and only indirectly how cases were actually decided. Inscriptions and the few surviving records of medieval courts show a world of village assemblies, caste and guild bodies, temple authorities and royal officers who applied their own rules and customs alongside or instead of the śāstras (Chapter 16) (Davis 2010). Second, the procedural law of the śāstras, like their substantive law, was graded by varṇa and gender. Its technical achievements are considerable; equality before the law was no part of them, and to call the system one of “due process” is anachronistic (Lingat 1973).

docs.title: 12.1.1 The King’s Court
docs.text:
In the Dharmaśāstras the king is the source of judicial authority. Manu instructs the king, wishing to examine lawsuits, to enter the court (sabhā) with Brahmins and experienced counsellors, and to decide the cases of the litigants each day, on the basis of the reasons that arise from the customs of regions and from the treatises (Manu 8.1–3). If he does not hear cases himself, he should appoint a learned Brahmin to do so, who should sit with three assessors (sabhya); such a court is called “the court of Brahmā” (8.9–11). The judge came to be called prāḍvivāka (“one who asks and decides”) and the assessors sabhya or sabhāsad. The court was attended by a clerk (lekhaka), an accountant (gaṇaka) and a bailiff or summoner (sādhyapāla), and the texts describe its sacred character: it was to be held in a hall facing east, and the judge and assessors were to be impartial.

The texts are explicit about who may judge. Manu states that a king may let even a Brahmin who lives only on his birth expound the law, but “never a Śūdra”; a king who looks on while a Śūdra decides the law finds his kingdom sinking “like a cow in the mud” (8.20–21). The assessors, like the judge, are to be learned Brahmins.

docs.title: 12.1.2 A Hierarchy of Tribunals
docs.text: The later smṛtis recognise that most disputes were settled not by the king but by other bodies. Yājñavalkya lists, in ascending order of authority, the family (kula), the guild (śreṇī), the association (pūga) and the officials appointed by the king (Yājñ 2.30); Nārada gives a similar sequence — family, guild, corporation, the appointed judge and the king — each later body being superior to the earlier (Nārada 1.7). A case that had been decided by a lower body could be reconsidered by a higher one. The ordering does not describe a system of appellate courts in the modern sense; it records a hierarchy of authorities, each competent for its own community, under the ultimate authority of the king (Lingat 1973; Davis 2010).

docs.title: 12.1.3 The Arthaśāstra’s Courts
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra describes royal courts organised territorially. Courts of “judges” (dharmastha), each composed of three judges and three ministers, are to be held in the frontier posts, the centres for groups of ten villages, and the district and provincial headquarters (AŚ 3.1.1); they decide private disputes under the titles of Book 3. A separate set of magistrates (pradeṣṭṛ), also sitting in threes, deals with the “removal of thorns” — the suppression of crime and of harmful conduct by artisans, merchants and officials — using secret agents and interrogation (AŚ 4.1). The text declares invalid transactions made in secret, inside a house, at night, in a forest, through fraud or in seclusion, except where such circumstances are inherent in the transaction, and it fines the parties and witnesses involved in them (AŚ 3.1). It also lays down that a lawsuit has four bases — dharma, transaction (vyavahāra), custom (caritra) and royal edict (rājaśāsana) — each later one overriding the earlier (AŚ 3.1.39); the Nāradasmṛti repeats the formula. In this hierarchy the king’s command stands above the texts — a point that sits uneasily with the claim that the king was always “under dharma” (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 12.2 The Eighteen Titles of Law
docs.text:
The classification of lawsuits into eighteen titles (vyavahārapada, “feet” or “grounds” of litigation), first found in the Manusmṛti (8.4–7), became standard in the later literature. The list, in Manu’s order, is given in Table 12.1.

Table 12.1. The eighteen titles of law (Manu 8.4–7) Sanskrit Meaning 1 ṛṇādāna Non-payment of debts 2 nikṣepa Deposits 3 asvāmivikraya Sale by one who is not the owner 4 saṃbhūya-samutthāna Partnership (joint undertakings) 5 dattasyānapakarma Non-delivery or resumption of gifts 6 vetanādāna Non-payment of wages 7 saṃvid-vyatikrama Breach of agreement or convention 8 krayavikrayānuśaya Rescission of sale and purchase 9 svāmipāla-vivāda Disputes between the owner of cattle and the herdsman 10 sīmāvivāda Boundary disputes 11 vākpāruṣya Verbal assault (abuse, defamation) 12 daṇḍapāruṣya Physical assault 13 steya Theft 14 sāhasa Violence (robbery, homicide and other violent crime) 15 strīsaṃgrahaṇa Sexual offences against women (including adultery) 16 strīpuṃdharma The law concerning husband and wife 17 vibhāga Partition (inheritance) 18 dyūta and samāhvaya Gambling and betting (on animal contests)

Several observations follow. The first eight titles, which concern debts, deposits, sales, partnership, gifts, wages and agreements — eight of eighteen, or about 44 per cent — show how large commercial and contractual disputes loomed in the authors’ minds. The list mixes what modern law would separate into civil and criminal matters: theft, violence and sexual offences sit alongside debts and partition. Title 15 concerns sexual relations with women “belonging” to other men and is graded by varṇa (Chapter 14); title 16, on husband and wife, is less a law of marriage than a code of women’s duties. Later texts rearranged and renamed the titles: Nārada separates the breach of a contract of service from the non-payment of wages, adds a title on “miscellaneous” matters (prakīrṇaka) that includes offences against the king’s commands, and treats theft in an appendix. Bṛhaspati distinguishes fourteen titles “arising from wealth” and four “arising from injury”. The scheme was a teaching device for organising the material, not a code of causes of action (Olivelle 2005; Lariviere 1989).

docs.title: 12.3.1 The Four Parts
docs.text:
The later smṛtis describe a lawsuit as having four “feet” (pāda) or stages: the plaint (pūrvapakṣa, also pratijñā or bhāṣā); the answer (uttara); the proof (kriyā); and the decision (nirṇaya). This is a different use of the expression “four feet” from the four bases of decision (dharma, transaction, custom and edict) mentioned above, and the two should not be confused. Figure 12.1 shows how the four stages and the four kinds of answer fit together.

Figure 12.1. The course of a lawsuit (vyavahāra) in the later smṛtis: the four stages (pāda) of plaint, answer, proof and decision, and the four kinds of answer, which determine whether proof is needed and who must give it. Compiled from Yājñavalkya, Nārada and the fragments of Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana; the constructed example in Section 12.3.6 follows the same steps.

docs.title: 12.3.2 The Plaint
docs.text: A suit begins when a person who has been wronged, or who claims a right, approaches the court. In civil matters the king or judge was not to start proceedings on his own initiative, though in certain grave offences he could act without a complainant. The plaintiff’s statement was to be precise: Kātyāyana and Bṛhaspati require that it state the matter in dispute, the amount, the place and time and the names of the parties, and that it be free of ambiguity, irrelevance and contradiction. It was first written provisionally (on a board or on the ground), corrected, and then recorded on a leaf or cloth. A plaint that was vague, that combined unrelated claims, or that concerned something impossible was to be rejected.

docs.title: 12.3.3 The Answer
docs.text:
The defendant, once summoned, gave his answer in the presence of the plaintiff. The smṛtis recognise four kinds of answer:

  • denial (mithyā): the defendant denies the claim;

  • admission (saṃpratipatti): he admits it, in which case the suit ends;

  • special plea (kāraṇa or pratyavaskandana): he admits the facts but pleads a circumstance that defeats the claim — for instance, that he received the money but has repaid it;

  • former judgment (prāṅnyāya): he pleads that the matter has already been decided in an earlier suit, in which he was successful.

An answer that was evasive, partial, contradictory or irrelevant was defective. The defendant was not allowed to bring a counter-suit against the plaintiff until the first suit was decided, with some exceptions (Yājñ 2.9). Parties who failed to appear, who fled, or who were shown to have lied were to lose the case and be fined; the Arthaśāstra lists a series of conduct that makes a party lose (AŚ 3.1).

docs.title: 12.3.4 Proof
docs.text: Once the plaint and answer had fixed the issue, the court determined which party must prove his case. In a simple denial the burden lay on the plaintiff; in a special plea, on the defendant; with a plea of former judgment, on the defendant to prove the earlier decision. The means of proof are described below.

docs.title: 12.3.5 Decision
docs.text:
After weighing the evidence, the judge and assessors gave their decision, and the successful party received a written decree (jayapatra, “document of victory”), which was to record the plaint, the answer, the evidence, the reasoning and the result, and to be signed by the judge and assessors and sealed. The texts allow for the review of a decision that has been wrongly given: Yājñavalkya states that the king should review lawsuits badly decided and fine the assessors and the successful party (2.305). Manu holds that a matter once lawfully decided should be regarded as settled and not reopened (9.233), and that whatever has been given, enjoyed or written under compulsion is void (8.168).

Manu describes the moral weight of judgment in vivid terms. When justice is defeated by injustice, a quarter of the guilt falls on the wrongdoer, a quarter on the witness, a quarter on all the members of the court and a quarter on the king (8.18). “Justice, when violated, destroys; justice, when protected, protects” (dharma eva hato hanti dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ, 8.15). Judges who decide cases for bribes are to have their property confiscated (9.231).

docs.title: 12.3.6 An Illustration
docs.text: The working of these rules can be shown by a simple, constructed example of the kind the commentators themselves used. A merchant (the plaintiff) claims before the court that a cultivator owes him a hundred paṇas, lent a year earlier at a stated rate of interest. His plaint must state the amount, the date, the rate and the fact that the sum has not been repaid. If the cultivator answers that he never borrowed the money (denial), the merchant must prove the loan, by a written document attested by witnesses or by the testimony of witnesses present at the transaction. If the cultivator answers that he borrowed it but has repaid it (special plea), the burden passes to him to prove the repayment, for example by a receipt or an endorsement on the document. If he answers that the same claim has already been decided in his favour by a guild court or the village assembly (former judgment), he must prove that decision. If he admits the debt, the court orders payment, with interest within the limits allowed by law. In each case the judgment is written down and given to the successful party. The example shows how the classification of answers determined the burden of proof, an idea that the smṛtis expressed with considerable clarity.

docs.title: 12.4.1 Human and Divine Proof
docs.text: Yājñavalkya states: “Document, possession and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof; in the absence of any of these, one of the ordeals is prescribed” (Yājñ 2.22). The later literature systematises this into human proof (mānuṣa) — documents, witnesses and possession — and divine proof (daiva), the ordeal and oath. It also allows for inference from circumstances (yukti, anumāna), especially in criminal cases.

docs.title: 12.4.2 Documents
docs.text: The use of written documents (lekhya, likhita) is one of the most notable developments of the post-Manu period. Yājñavalkya and the later texts distinguish royal documents, such as land grants engraved on copper plates and royal decisions, from private documents written by the parties or by a scribe and attested by witnesses. They describe how a document recording a loan should be drawn up — with the names of the parties, the date, the amount and the rate of interest, the signatures of debtor and witnesses — and how a disputed document is to be tested by comparing handwriting, examining the witnesses and considering the circumstances. Kātyāyana and Bṛhaspati discuss forgery and the treatment of documents that have been lost or damaged. The prominence of documents in these texts reflects the growing use of writing in commerce and land transactions, also attested by inscriptions.

docs.title: 12.4.3 Possession
docs.text: Long possession (bhukti, bhoga) was evidence of ownership, especially of land. Yājñavalkya lays down that an owner who watches his land being enjoyed by another for twenty years without objection loses it, and in the case of movables, ten years (Yājñ 2.24); Manu gives ten years for movables (8.147–148). These rules do not apply to pledges, boundaries, deposits, the property of minors, the king’s property and the property of women and learned Brahmins (8.149). Later texts distinguish possession with a title (āgama) from possession without one, and hold that possession for three generations is valid even without proof of title. These rules, which modern writers compare with prescription and limitation, were designed to settle titles to land in a society where written title was often lacking.

docs.title: 12.4.4 Witnesses
docs.text:
The longest discussions concern witnesses (sākṣin). Manu requires at least three witnesses in a lawsuit, who should be householders with sons, natives of the place, trustworthy and free from greed, and drawn from the same group as the parties: “Women should be witnesses for women; twice-born men of the same kind for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and men of the lowest birth for those of the lowest birth” (8.68). Many persons are disqualified: those with an interest in the suit, friends, associates and enemies of the parties, persons previously convicted of perjury, the sick, the very old and the very young, and so on (8.64–67). Women are generally excluded as witnesses for men: “a single man free from greed may be a witness, but not many women, even if they are pure, because women’s understanding is unsteady” (8.77). Some later texts relax these rules: Nārada and others admit any person as a witness in cases of violence, theft, assault and adultery, where the event may have been seen only by a few.

Witnesses were examined in the court, before the parties, and exhorted to tell the truth with solemn warnings about the consequences of perjury in this world and the next (8.79–101). They were sworn according to varṇa (8.113; Chapter 2). Manu fixes graded fines for false testimony, ending with banishment (8.120–123). It also allows a witness to depart from the truth in one situation: where telling the truth would lead to the death of a man of any varṇa, a false statement is permitted, and the witness should afterwards perform a penance (8.103–105). Elsewhere it lists situations in which a false oath is not sinful, including in dealings with women, at marriages and to protect a Brahmin (8.112).

docs.title: 12.4.5 Interrogation and Torture
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras’ procedure is essentially for civil suits and for crimes prosecuted by a complainant. The Arthaśāstra’s procedure for suspected criminals is different: its magistrates arrest suspects on reports by secret agents and on circumstantial grounds, and may torture those who will not confess, within limits that the text sets out (AŚ 4.8). This procedure is described in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 12.5 Ordeals and Oaths
docs.text:
When human evidence was lacking, the texts allowed recourse to ordeals (divya). Yājñavalkya describes five: the balance (tulā), in which the accused was weighed twice and declared guilty if he was heavier the second time; fire (agni), in which he carried a heated iron ball across a series of circles; water (jala), in which he remained submerged while an arrow was shot and retrieved; poison (viṣa); and the sacred libation (kośa), in which he drank water in which images of a deity had been bathed and was judged guilty if he suffered misfortune within a fixed period (Yājñ 2.95ff.). Nārada and later texts add others, such as chewing rice grains and taking a coin out of hot oil. The Arthaśāstra, notably, does not rely on ordeals. The ordeal is the part of classical procedure that modern readers find hardest to take seriously, and it is often described as if it were an arbitrary appeal to chance. The texts present it instead as a closely regulated procedure, hedged with conditions of gravity, consent and status. Yājñavalkya restricts the five ordeals to grave accusations, and only where the accuser undertakes to bear the “head” (śīrṣaka) of the suit — that is, to suffer the penalty himself if the accused is cleared; only in cases of treason against the king and of grave sin may an ordeal be imposed without this undertaking (Yājñ 2.95–96). The ordeal is to be performed at sunrise, after the accused has fasted and bathed in his clothes, in the presence of the king and of Brahmins (2.97). The choice of ordeal depends on the person: the balance is prescribed for women, children, the aged, the blind, the lame, Brahmins and the sick, while a Śūdra is to undergo fire or water or a measured dose of poison (2.98); and the heated iron, the poison and the balance are not to be used where the sum in dispute is less than a thousand paṇas (2.99). The rules thus graded the risk of the ordeal by the gravity of the case and by the status of the accused — with the familiar consequence that the harshest forms fell on the Śūdra.

For lesser matters the texts prescribe oaths (śapatha), likewise graded by varṇa: Manu has a Brahmin swear by his truthfulness, a Kṣatriya by his mount and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, seed and gold, and a Śūdra by all the grave sins (Manu 8.113). An oath was not a mere formality. A witness or party who swore falsely was expected to suffer misfortune, and some texts set a period within which such misfortune would reveal the perjurer — the same logic that underlies the ordeal of the sacred libation. The later digests devoted whole treatises to ordeals: Raghunandana’s Divyatattva in sixteenth-century Bengal sets out the procedure for each in detail, with the mantras to be recited and the signs of guilt and innocence (Kane 1930).

Ordeals are sometimes said to have “declined” as procedure was rationalised, but the medieval digests discuss them at great length, and there is evidence that they were actually used. Al-Bīrūnī, writing in the early eleventh century, describes Indian ordeals by poison, water, the balance and hot iron in his account of Indian lawsuits. The first volume of the Asiatick Researches, the journal of the Asiatic Society founded at Calcutta by William Jones, printed an account of trial by ordeal among the Hindus by ʿAlī Ibrāhīm Khān, the chief magistrate of Banaras, which shows that ordeals were still known and occasionally performed there in the late eighteenth century. In Travancore, Brahmins accused of grave offences could clear themselves by plunging a hand into boiling ghee at the temple of Śucīndram, a practice abolished by the Travancore government in the nineteenth century. The Company’s courts did not admit ordeals as proof, and colonial legislation replaced the religious oath — Hindus had at first sworn on Ganges water and Muslims on the Qurʾān — with the oath or affirmation prescribed by the Indian Oaths Act of 1873.

Medieval Europe also used ordeals of fire and water as “judgements of God” until the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 forbade the clergy to take part in them. The parallel suggests a common function: where documents and witnesses failed, the ordeal produced a decision that the community could accept as final, and the long preparation it required gave room for confession, compromise or the withdrawal of the charge. In India it also expressed the conviction, already present in the Vedic literature (Chapter 2), that the gods protect the truthful.

docs.title: 12.6 Courts in Practice
docs.text: How far did actual courts follow the procedure of the śāstras? Direct evidence is scarce before the second millennium CE, but inscriptions and later records give glimpses.

docs.title: 12.6.1 Inscriptions
docs.text: Medieval South Indian inscriptions record the decisions of village and temple assemblies and of royal officers in disputes over land, temple property and offences. Several Cōḷa-period inscriptions record cases of accidental homicide — for example, a man killed by a stray arrow in a hunt — in which the assembly, after inquiry, required the person responsible to endow a perpetual lamp in a local temple rather than suffer a penalty; the transaction combined compensation, expiation and public record. Royal courts are also mentioned: Cōḷa inscriptions refer to a dharmāsana, a royal seat of justice, and to Brahmin experts (dharmāsana-bhaṭṭa) who sat in it (Nilakanta Sastri 1955). Donald Davis’s study of medieval Kerala records shows temple authorities and local assemblies deciding cases according to their own rules and customs, while using the vocabulary of dharma (Davis 2004).

docs.title: 12.6.2 Documents of Decision
docs.text: A few later documents preserve the decisions of assemblies of Brahmins (dharmasabhā) and other bodies on questions of caste status, penance, inheritance and marriage. In Maharashtra under the Peśvās, for example, disputes were frequently referred to pañcāyats of the parties’ peers, whose decisions were recorded and enforced by government officers (Chapter 16). Such records show the śāstras being invoked, interpreted and sometimes set aside in favour of custom, and they show that procedure in practice was often more informal and more consensual than the texts’ model of plaint, answer, proof and decision.

docs.title: 12.6.3 Islamic and Colonial Courts
docs.text: From the thirteenth century, qāḍīs’ courts and the courts of royal officials operated in much of northern India, and many Hindus as well as Muslims used them to register transactions and settle disputes (Chapter 18). The colonial courts established from 1772 introduced a new procedure based on English models; their rules of pleading and evidence, codified in the Code of Civil Procedure and the Indian Evidence Act of 1872, owed nothing directly to the śāstras, although colonial judges sometimes noted resemblances.

docs.title: 12.7 Bringing a Defendant to Court
docs.text:
A lawsuit could not proceed without the defendant, and the texts discuss how he was to be brought before the court. The ordinary means was a summons issued by the king’s court, delivered by an officer or conveyed by a seal. Nārada also describes a form of private restraint (āsedha) by which a plaintiff could, in the king’s name, forbid a defendant to leave a place, to depart on a journey or to carry on an activity until he had answered the claim; a defendant who disobeyed a lawful restraint was punishable, while a plaintiff who imposed an unlawful one was himself liable (Lariviere 1989). The texts exempt certain persons from being summoned or restrained at particular times: among others, those about to marry, those afflicted by illness or grief, those engaged in sacrifice, and cultivators at the time of harvest.

To secure the parties’ continued presence and the execution of the judgment, the courts required sureties (pratibhū). The smṛtis distinguish sureties for appearance, sureties for good faith and sureties for payment, with different degrees of liability, and discuss whether the sons of a deceased surety are bound to pay (Kane 1930). Sureties appear frequently in medieval documents, which suggests that the institution was in common use.

docs.title: 12.8 Representation and Costs
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras do not know a profession of advocates in the modern sense. Parties were expected to plead in person. The later smṛtis, however, allow a party who is unable to plead — because of youth, illness, absence or inexperience — to be represented by a relative or an appointed agent, whose acts bind the principal; Kātyāyana discusses such representatives and their remuneration (Kane 1930; Lingat 1973). Under the Mughals, agents called vakīl represented parties before the qāḍī and other officials, and the East India Company’s courts licensed Indian pleaders, also called vakīls, from the late eighteenth century; the modern Indian legal profession, with its advocates trained in English law, grew out of these colonial institutions (Chapter 19).

The classical courts were not free to litigants. The king took a share of the sum recovered in a suit for debt, and the losing party paid a fine in addition to what he owed; a defendant who falsely denied a debt that was then proved against him paid more than one who admitted it. The texts justify these payments as compensation to the king for the labour of justice and as a deterrent to false claims and false denials. They also show awareness that litigation could be used to harass: a plaintiff who brought a false suit was to be fined, and a case once properly decided was not to be reopened, although a judgment obtained by force, fraud or the corruption of the judges could be set aside and heard again (punarnyāya) (Davis 2010).

docs.title: 12.9 The Language of the Courts
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras were written in Sanskrit, but the courts they describe heard litigants who spoke the languages of everyday life. The texts assume that the plaint was recorded in writing by a scribe, and the surviving legal documents of medieval India are written in Sanskrit, in regional languages such as Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and Marathi, or in mixtures of these; the records of the Peśvā period in Maharashtra mentioned above, for example, are in Marathi. Law was thus applied through a constant process of translation between the learned language of the śāstras and the spoken languages of the parties.

Under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, Persian became the language of administration and of the higher courts, and Islamic legal texts were in Arabic. The East India Company at first continued to use Persian in its courts. Act XXIX of 1837 ended the official use of Persian and allowed the regional languages to replace it in the lower courts, while English became the language of the higher courts. The choice of script then became a political question: in the North-Western Provinces, the order of 1900 permitting petitions in the Devanāgarī script as well as the Persian script used for Urdu was a milestone in the Hindi–Urdu controversy, which contributed to the separation of Hindu and Muslim political identities.

The Constitution of India provides that the proceedings of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, and the authoritative texts of laws, shall be in English until Parliament provides otherwise (Article 348), while the lower courts use the official languages of the states. The question of the language of justice — whether litigants can follow the proceedings that decide their rights — thus remains a live issue, as it was when Sanskrit-trained judges heard disputes among villagers who knew no Sanskrit.

docs.title: 12.10 The Judge
docs.text:
All the texts stress the qualities of the judge and assessors: learning in the Veda and the treatises, truthfulness, impartiality, freedom from anger and greed, and courage. Nārada and Kātyāyana describe how the assessors should speak out if the king or judge is about to decide wrongly, and say that an assessor who remains silent, or speaks falsely, incurs sin. Judges are not to hold private conversations with a party, and those who take bribes or decide out of partiality are to be punished. Bṛhaspati’s warning that a decision should not be made by the letter of the śāstra alone, because a judgment devoid of reasoning destroys dharma, was often quoted.

These are serious ideals, and they show a developed understanding of the conditions of fair adjudication. Like other features of the tradition, they assume a court of Brahmin experts applying a law that gave different weight to the testimony and interests of different varṇas and of men and women.

docs.title: 12.11 Assessment
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstra law of procedure is one of the most technically developed parts of classical Indian learning. Its analysis of the stages of a suit, of the kinds of plea and of the burden of proof, its rules for documents and possession, and its insistence on written decisions show a mature legal culture. Modern writers have drawn parallels with Roman civil procedure, with the English forms of pleading and with the Indian Code of Civil Procedure of 1908; none of them implies historical continuity, for the modern Indian law of procedure and evidence was built on English models (Chapter 19). The classical system was also bound up with the hierarchy of varṇa and gender, which determined who could judge, who could testify for whom and how witnesses were sworn. A balanced account must recognise both its technical achievement and the social order it served.

docs.title: 12.12 Principal Passages
docs.text:
Table 12.2 lists the principal passages discussed in this chapter.
