docs.title: 12.13 Summary
docs.text:
• In the Dharmaśāstras the king is the source of judicial authority; he decides cases himself or through a learned Brahmin judge with Brahmin assessors. Śūdras may not judge. Families, guilds and associations decide cases within their own spheres, under the king’s authority.

  • A lawsuit has four parts — plaint, answer, proof and decision; the kind of answer decides who must prove what. Proof is by documents, possession and witnesses, with ordeals and oaths in their absence; the rules on witnesses are graded by varṇa and sex.

  • Inscriptions and later records show local assemblies, temple bodies, royal officers and qāḍīs deciding cases in ways that drew on, but did not simply apply, the śāstric model.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The main texts are Manu chapter 8 (Olivelle 2005), Yājñavalkya Book 2 (Olivelle 2019), and the Nāradasmṛti (Lariviere 1989); AŚ Books 3–4 (Olivelle 2013). Kane (1930), vol. 3, gives a detailed account of procedure and evidence; Lingat (1973) and Davis (2010) discuss the relation between procedure and practice.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Debt, Contract, Property and Inheritance
docs.text:
Most of the eighteen titles of law concern what modern lawyers would call private or civil law: debts and their recovery, deposits and pledges, sales, partnerships, gifts, wages, agreements, boundaries and inheritance. The Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstra treat these subjects in considerable detail, and they are among the parts of the tradition that most impress modern readers with their technical precision. They also show the economic world in which the texts were written: a world of money-lenders and merchants, guilds and caravans, cultivators, herdsmen and labourers, slaves and bonded servants, and of joint families holding land across generations.

This chapter surveys the main areas of this law. It follows the order of the titles only loosely, and it notes, where relevant, how the rules depended on varṇa and gender. Inheritance is treated here in outline; the schools of the Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga are described in Chapter 11, and women’s property in Chapter 15. Kane’s third volume remains the fullest survey of the titles discussed here (Kane 1930, vol. 3; Lingat 1973).

docs.title: 13.1.1 The First Title
docs.text: The non-payment of debts (ṛṇādāna) is the first of the eighteen titles in every list, and the texts discuss it at greatest length. Manu’s treatment (8.47–178) is the longest of any title, partly because he uses the suit for debt as the model case in which to set out the rules on witnesses; Yājñavalkya and Nārada also give it long sections. The word ṛṇa also carried a religious meaning — every man is born with debts to the seers, the gods and the ancestors (Chapter 2) — and the idea that debts must be paid, in this life or the next, gave the law of debt a moral weight. A debtor who died without paying, Nārada says, would be reborn as the creditor’s slave or animal.

docs.title: 13.1.2 Interest
docs.text:
The texts regulate interest (vṛddhi, “growth”) in detail. Manu permits a lender to take one-eightieth of the principal per month — one and a quarter per cent — a rate he attributes to Vasiṣṭha, or two per cent per month “remembering the dharma of good people”; but he also allows rates of two, three, four and five per cent per month according to the varṇa of the borrower, from Brahmin to Śūdra (Manu 8.140–142). Yājñavalkya gives the same scheme: one-eightieth per month when there is a pledge, and otherwise two, three, four or five per cent according to varṇa (Yājñ 2.37). The graded rates are sometimes explained as reflecting differences in risk; whatever their rationale, they meant that the poorest and lowest-ranked borrowers paid the most.

Two important limits protected debtors. First, the total interest collected on a loan of money, when paid at one time, could not exceed the principal — so that the debt could at most double — while on grain, fruit, wool and draught animals the limit was five times the principal (Manu 8.151). This rule, known in later Indian law as dāmdupat, was applied by British courts in parts of India into the twentieth century. Second, Manu forbids several kinds of oppressive interest: interest for more than a year at a time, interest not agreed, compound interest (cakravṛddhi), and “corporal” interest exacted in labour (8.153). For loans on sea voyages and on long journeys, where risk was high, the rate was to be fixed by people experienced in such voyages (8.157) — a provision often compared with the Roman fenus nauticum, the high-interest maritime loan.

docs.title: 13.1.3 Recovery
docs.text: Manu describes five ways in which a creditor may recover a debt: by persuasion (dharma), by suit at law (vyavahāra), by stratagem (chala), by customary pressure (ācarita) — such as sitting fasting at the debtor’s door — and by force (bala) (8.49). A creditor who recovers his money by these means is not to be blamed by the king (8.50). Self-help, in other words, was legitimate. A debtor who could not pay might be made to work off the debt: Manu says that a debtor of the same or lower varṇa may be made to pay by labour, while a debtor of higher varṇa should pay gradually (8.177). The texts thus recognise a form of debt bondage, graded by varṇa, which the Arthaśāstra also regulates (Chapter 6). Nārada adds that a debtor who denies a debt proved against him must pay it with a fine.

docs.title: 13.1.4 Liability for a Father’s Debts
docs.text: The smṛtis require sons, and in some cases grandsons, to pay the debts of a father who has died, gone abroad or become incapable; Yājñavalkya excepts debts incurred for liquor, lust or gambling, unpaid fines and tolls, and idle promises (Yājñ 2.47–50). The colonial courts made this into the doctrine of the “pious obligation” of sons to pay their father’s debts not incurred for illegal or immoral purposes, which allowed creditors of a Mitākṣarā father to proceed against the ancestral property held jointly with his sons.

docs.title: 13.1.5 Sureties and Pledges
docs.text: A creditor could secure a loan by a surety (pratibhū) or by a pledge (ādhi). Yājñavalkya distinguishes three kinds of suretyship: for the appearance of the debtor, for his honesty, and for payment; only the surety for payment, and in some cases his sons, could be made to pay the debt itself (Yājñ 2.53–54). Pledges were either merely held as security or used and enjoyed by the creditor. An enjoyed pledge, such as a field or a cow whose produce the creditor took, earned no further interest (Manu 8.143); a pledge merely held had to be preserved, and the creditor was liable if it was damaged through his fault. Yājñavalkya states that a pledge is forfeited to the creditor if it is not redeemed when the debt has doubled, except a pledge that is being enjoyed (Yājñ 2.58). These rules, the precursors of the forms of usufructuary and simple mortgage known to later Indian law, show the importance of land and cattle as security in an agrarian credit economy.

docs.title: 13.1.6 Documents
docs.text: The later texts give particular attention to documents of debt. Yājñavalkya and Kātyāyana describe how a loan document should be written — with the names of the parties and their fathers, the date, the amount, the rate of interest and the signatures of the debtor and witnesses — and how payments should be endorsed on it, or a receipt given. A debt proved by a document could be recovered from the debtor’s heirs; disputes over documents were resolved by the methods described in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 13.1.7 Debt in Colonial India
docs.text: The classical rules on debt had a long afterlife. Under British rule, the courts applied the rule of dāmdupat — that interest could not exceed the principal — to Hindus in the Bombay and Calcutta presidencies, while elsewhere English rules of contract prevailed. The enforcement of debts through civil courts, and the sale of land for debt, contributed to the transfer of land from cultivators to moneylenders in many regions. In 1875 peasants in the Deccan attacked moneylenders and destroyed their account books; the government responded with the Deccan Agriculturists’ Relief Act of 1879, which allowed courts to examine the history of transactions and reduce excessive claims, and later laws restricted the alienation of agricultural land. These measures were colonial responses to colonial problems, but they echo the classical concern to limit the creditor’s power over the debtor’s livelihood.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Deposits
docs.text: The title of deposits (nikṣepa) covers property entrusted to another for safe keeping. The texts distinguish an open deposit, counted or described in the presence of witnesses, from a sealed deposit (upanidhi), handed over in a sealed container. The depositary must return the deposit on demand. He is not liable if it is lost through the action of the king, through fate or through thieves, unless the loss occurred after the owner had demanded it back or through the depositary’s own fault; but if he uses the deposit without permission, he must pay it back with interest and is fined (Manu 8.179–196; Yājñ 2.65–67). The same rules apply, with variations, to property lent for use, property handed to an artisan to be worked, and property entrusted to a messenger.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Sale by a Non-owner
docs.text: The third title concerns sale by one who is not the owner (asvāmivikraya). Manu declares such a sale invalid: the true owner may recover his property, and the seller who is not the owner is to be treated as a thief (8.197–198). A buyer who bought openly, in the market or before witnesses, is free from blame and may seek recompense from the seller; a buyer who bought secretly or at an unreasonably low price is under suspicion (8.201–202). The rule that one cannot give a better title than one has is familiar in many legal systems; the Dharmaśāstra version combines it with the practical recognition that open purchase in a market was evidence of good faith.

docs.title: 13.2.3 Rescission
docs.text: Manu allows either party to a sale or purchase who repents of the transaction to cancel it within ten days; after ten days, the transaction stands (8.222–223). Nārada sets different periods for the inspection of different kinds of goods and provides that goods found defective may be returned. The Arthaśāstra fixes periods within which merchants, cultivators, herdsmen and artisans may withdraw from a sale, and regulates the conduct of merchants and artisans as part of its “removal of thorns” (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 13.2.4 The Law of Gift
docs.text:
Giving (dāna) was at the centre of Brahmanical religion and of kingship: the Vedic fee to the priest (Chapter 2), the king’s grants of land (Chapter 5), the marriage of a daughter conceived as a gift (Chapter 15). The title on gifts (dattasyānapakarma, “non-delivery” or “resumption” of gifts; in Nārada, dattāpradānika) is the part of the law that regulated this practice, and it is less a law of charity than a law of who may alienate what.

The basic rule is stated by Yājñavalkya: a man may give what is his own, without detriment to his family, but not his wife or son, nor his whole property if he has descendants, nor what he has already promised to another (Yājñ 2.175); the acceptance of a gift, above all of land, should be made openly (2.176). Nārada’s title on gifts (Nārada 4) adds property that is not one’s own to give — a deposit, a pledge, property held jointly with others or borrowed — and distinguishes valid gifts from void ones: gifts made under fear, in anger or grief, in jest, by mistake, by a minor or by an insane or intoxicated person are invalid and may be recovered, as are gifts made in return for a service that was not performed. The commentators analysed a gift as the giver’s relinquishing of his own ownership and the creation of the recipient’s, completed by acceptance; once so completed it could not be resumed, which is what the name of the title expresses. The rules therefore protected two interests at once: the family’s claim on its property, against a donor’s piety or folly, and the recipient’s title, against a donor’s change of mind.

Beside this law of alienation stood an immense religious literature on the merit of giving. It specified the worthy recipient (pātra), above all the learned Brahmin, the proper times and places, the right objects and the disposition of the giver, and it described “great gifts” (mahādāna), such as the weighing of a king against gold that was then distributed to Brahmins (tulāpuruṣa), which inscriptions show rulers actually performing. The medieval digests gave the subject whole books — the Dānakāṇḍa of Lakṣmīdhara’s Kṛtyakalpataru, the Dānasāgara of the Bengal king Ballālasena, the Dānakhaṇḍa of Hemādri’s Caturvargacintāmaṇi — and Kane’s survey of them remains the standard account (Kane 1930, vol. 2).

The two literatures met in the gift of land. The charters by which kings granted villages to Brahmins and temples (Chapter 17) are legal instruments of gift: they name the donor’s title, define the object, record the acceptance and declare the gift perpetual, and their imprecatory verses add a religious sanction to the legal rule that a completed gift may not be taken back. What a royal gift transferred was in most cases the king’s revenue and rights over a village rather than the soil itself, a limit that Mīmāṃsā authors expressed in their argument that even a universal monarch cannot give away the earth (Section 13.5). The law of gift also shaped women’s property, much of which consisted of gifts made at and after marriage (Chapter 15), and it supplied the framework within which temples, monasteries and Brahmin settlements accumulated the endowments on which so much of medieval religious and economic life depended.

docs.title: 13.3.1 Partnership
docs.text: The title of partnership (saṃbhūya-samutthāna, “rising up together”) covers joint undertakings by merchants, artisans, cultivators and also priests who perform a sacrifice together. The general rule is that profits and losses are shared in proportion to each partner’s contribution, unless otherwise agreed; a partner who causes loss through negligence or acts without the agreement of the others must make good the loss, while one who saves the common property from danger is entitled to a reward (Nārada; Yājñ 2.259–265). Manu discusses at length how priests who officiate jointly at a sacrifice should share the fee (8.206–211). The rules show the importance of collaborative enterprise in trade and crafts.

docs.title: 13.3.2 Caravans and Sea Trade
docs.text: Long-distance trade raised its own legal problems. Merchants travelled in caravans (sārtha) under a leader (sārthavāha), and the texts discuss the sharing of profits and losses among the members, the responsibility of the leader, and the liability of merchants whose goods were lost to robbers, to the king’s officials or to accident. Nārada and Yājñavalkya hold that a partner who saves the common goods from danger — from fire, robbers or the king — is entitled to a tenth of what he saves, and that goods lost without anyone’s fault are a common loss. Sea voyages, which the Dharmaśāstras regarded with suspicion as polluting for Brahmins, were nonetheless undertaken by merchants of many communities, and the texts’ provision for special rates of interest on sea loans (Manu 8.157) shows that lenders financed them. Inscriptions and the accounts of foreign observers describe the ports and the merchant communities of the Indian Ocean in detail; that history belongs to Volume 19.

docs.title: 13.3.3 Guilds and Corporate Bodies
docs.text:
The title “breach of conventions” (saṃvid-vyatikrama) concerns the agreements (saṃvid, samaya) of villages, guilds (śreṇī), merchant associations (naigama), corporations (pūga) and other groups. The king is to enforce such agreements: a member who breaks the convention of his group, or who steals or misappropriates its common property, is to be banished and his property confiscated (Manu 8.219–221; Yājñ 2.186–192). Yājñavalkya and Bṛhaspati describe the officers who manage a group’s affairs, and require that they be honest, learned in the Veda and of good family; they forbid actions by the officers that harm the group and require that the group’s decisions be followed. These rules, together with the evidence of inscriptions, show that guilds and similar bodies made their own rules, held property, received endowments and settled their members’ disputes (Majumdar 1918).

Inscriptions give life to these texts. At Nasik, in the early second century CE, Uṣavadāta deposited money with two weavers’ guilds as a permanent endowment, the interest of which was to clothe the monks of a cave monastery (Chapter 6). At Mandasor in western Malwa, an inscription of the fifth century CE records how a guild of silk-weavers who had migrated from Lāṭa (southern Gujarat) built and later restored a temple of the Sun. Medieval South Indian inscriptions record merchant associations, such as the “Five Hundred” (Ayyāvoḷe), operating across regions and overseas. Tamil inscriptions of merchant associations have been found outside India — at Takua Pa in southern Thailand (associated with the Maṇigrāmam, 9th century) and at Barus in Sumatra (of the Five Hundred, dated 1088) — showing that these bodies carried their organisation and their record-keeping across the Bay of Bengal. Modern writers sometimes describe the śreṇī as a “corporation” with “legal personality” and “perpetual succession”. The texts do treat the guild as a body that holds property and makes binding rules; the categories of company law are nonetheless not those of the śāstras, and the guild is better described in its own terms.

docs.title: 13.4 Wages, Service and Slavery
docs.text:
The titles on non-payment of wages (vetanādāna) and, in Nārada, on breach of a contract of service (abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā) regulate the relation between master and worker. A hired servant who abandons his work without cause forfeits his wages and is fined; a master who refuses to pay is compelled to pay and fined. Where no wage was agreed, the servant receives a customary share — a tenth of the produce for a cultivator, a tenth of the profit for a trader’s assistant, as the Arthaśāstra also provides (AŚ 3.13; Chapter 6). Herdsmen’s wages and liabilities are treated under the title of disputes between owner and herdsman (below).

Nārada distinguishes five kinds of dependent worker: the student, the apprentice, the hired servant, the overseer and the slave. The first four do “pure” work; the slave does “impure” work, such as sweeping, cleaning latrines and removing refuse. The apprentice (antevāsin) lives with his master for an agreed period, receives instruction and maintenance, and may be compelled to complete his term. Nārada lists fifteen kinds of slave, among them those born in the house, bought, received as a gift, inherited, maintained in a famine, pledged, released from a heavy debt, captured in war, won in a wager, self-sold and enslaved for a fixed period; and he describes the ceremony of manumission, in which the master breaks a jar of water carried by the slave and sprinkles him with water (Nārada 5). A slave could be freed if he saved his master’s life; those who had sold themselves could not easily recover their freedom. These rules, like Manu’s seven kinds of slave and the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on slaves, show that slavery was an established legal institution in classical India (Chakravarti 1987).

docs.title: 13.4.1 The End of Legal Slavery and the Persistence of Bondage
docs.text: Slavery remained a legal institution in India until the colonial period. The East India Company at first tolerated it; under pressure from the abolitionist movement in Britain, the Indian Slavery Act of 1843 provided that slavery would no longer be recognised by the courts, and the Indian Penal Code of 1860 made the buying, selling and holding of slaves criminal offences. These measures ended legal slavery but not unfree labour: agrarian servitude, often hereditary and tied to caste, and debt bondage persisted in many regions. Independent India’s Constitution prohibits forced labour (Article 23), and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act of 1976 declared all bonded-labour agreements void; but bonded labour has continued to be documented in agriculture, brick-kilns and other industries. The classical texts’ regulation of slavery and debt bondage thus has a long and troubling sequel.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Who Owned the Land?
docs.text: Whether the king owned all the land of his kingdom was a question much debated in the colonial period, when the East India Company claimed the rights of the Mughal state and argued that cultivators held land only at the sovereign’s pleasure. Classical Indian thinkers had already discussed the question. In the Mīmāṃsā, a sacrifice called the viśvajit required the sacrificer to give away “everything”; Jaimini and his commentator Śabara argued that even a universal monarch could not give away the earth, because it is common to all, and that the king’s right was a right to a share of the produce in return for protection (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 6.7.3). The Dharmaśāstras assume private ownership of fields, which could be sold, mortgaged, given and inherited, while recognising the king’s right to taxes and his ownership of mines, treasure-trove and ownerless property. Medieval inscriptions show layered rights: those of the king to revenue, of grantees (often Brahmins or temples) to the king’s share, of village communities over common land, and of cultivators to their fields (Kane 1930; Sharma 1959).

docs.title: 13.5.2 Ownership in Theory
docs.text: Medieval jurists also debated the nature of ownership (svatva) itself: was it a relation known only from the śāstras, so that property acquired by means the texts forbade was not truly owned, or a worldly relation known from ordinary usage? The Mitākṣarā argued that ownership is a worldly (laukika) matter, and that a man who acquires property by a forbidden means is guilty of a sin but is still its owner. The distinction between moral fault and legal effect, which the Dāyabhāga expressed in its principle that a fact cannot be altered by a hundred texts (Chapter 11), is one of the more sophisticated achievements of the tradition (Derrett 1968; Rocher 2012).

docs.title: 13.5.3 Boundaries
docs.text: Boundary disputes (sīmāvivāda) were among the commonest lawsuits in an agrarian society. Manu recommends that villages mark their boundaries with trees, tanks, wells, shrines and mounds, and with hidden markers — stones, bones, cow’s hair, chaff, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, pebbles and sand — buried along the line so that the boundary can be proved later (8.245–251). Where there is doubt, the neighbours and the elders of the villages are to be examined; if they are lacking, people who know the forest — hunters, fowlers, herdsmen, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers and gleaners — may be called as witnesses (8.258–260). If no evidence exists, the king himself fixes the boundary (8.265).

docs.title: 13.5.4 Owners and Herdsmen
docs.text: The title on disputes between the owner of cattle and the herdsman (svāmipāla-vivāda) allocates responsibility for animals. By day the herdsman is responsible for the safety of the herd, by night the owner if the animals are in his house; a herdsman must make good animals lost through his negligence but not those killed by robbers he has reported or by unavoidable accidents. Around every village a strip of common land is to be left for pasture, and cattle that damage unfenced crops on it are not to be fined (Manu 8.229–244). These rules show a careful attention to the practical problems of a mixed farming and pastoral economy.

docs.title: 13.6 Lost Property, Treasure and Escheat
docs.text: Several rules concern property without an evident owner. Lost property found by royal officials is to be kept in safe custody by the king for three years; the owner who proves his claim within that time recovers it, though the king takes a share — a sixth, a tenth or a twelfth, according to the circumstances — and after three years the king may take it (Manu 8.30–34). Treasure found buried in the ground belongs in principle to the king, who as the protector of the land is its “lord”, but a learned Brahmin who finds treasure may keep the whole of it, and others must give the king a share; the king who finds ancient treasure should give half to Brahmins (8.35–39). The property of a man who dies without heirs goes to the king, except the property of a Brahmin, which goes to other Brahmins (9.188–189). These rules show the king’s position as the residual owner of property in his realm, qualified, characteristically, by special privileges for Brahmins.

docs.title: 13.7 Gambling and Betting
docs.text: The last of the eighteen titles concerns gambling with dice (dyūta) and betting on animal contests (samāhvaya). The texts take two different attitudes. Manu regards gambling as a form of open theft that destroys kingdoms: the king should suppress it, punish gamblers and those who keep gambling houses corporally, and banish them (9.220–228). Yājñavalkya and Nārada, like the Arthaśāstra, take a regulatory view: gambling should be conducted in licensed halls under a supervisor, who provides the dice, takes a percentage of the winnings for the king and enforces the payment of debts; gambling outside such halls is forbidden and cheating with false dice is punished (Yājñ 2.199–203; AŚ 3.20). The contrast illustrates the difference between the moralising and the fiscal approaches to the same social fact, and between Manu and the later, more practical smṛtis.

docs.title: 13.8 Houses and Neighbours
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s Book 3 includes a chapter on disputes about dwellings and buildings (vāstuka), which shows the attention of its authors to urban life. It regulates the distance to be left between houses, the placing of drains, latrines, wells and fireplaces so as not to harm a neighbour, the obstruction of light and air, the use of common walls and the right of way; and it fixes fines for damage to a neighbour’s property, for blocking a path or a water channel, and for nuisances (AŚ 3.8). The Dharmaśāstras treat many of these matters under the title of boundaries. Such rules are among the most practical in the texts, and they remind us that the law of the śāstras was concerned with the ordinary frictions of village and town life as well as with grand questions of varṇa and kingship.

docs.title: 13.9.1 The Joint Family
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras assume that property is held by families, and that sons inherit from their fathers. Manu states that after the death of the father and mother the brothers may divide the paternal property among themselves, or the eldest may take the whole and support the others as a father would (9.104–105). Yājñavalkya allows a father to partition his property among his sons during his lifetime, and gives the mother a share equal to a son’s when the sons partition after the father’s death (Yājñ 2.114–123). The British courts’ later doctrines of the Mitākṣarā coparcenary and of the Dāyabhāga’s absolute paternal ownership grew out of the commentators’ interpretations of these and related verses (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 13.9.2 Shares and Exclusions
docs.text: The earlier texts give the eldest son an extra share (uddhāra) and allow unequal partition according to the varṇa of the mothers when a man has wives of different varṇas: the son of a Brahmin wife takes more than the son of a Kṣatriya wife, and so on, while the son of a Śūdra wife takes little or nothing (Manu 9.149–157). Later texts, and the commentators, prefer equal partition among sons. Unmarried sisters are to receive a quarter of a brother’s share for their marriage (Manu 9.118; Yājñ 2.124). Certain property is impartible: Manu lists clothes, vehicles, ornaments, cooked food, water, women (that is, slave women), the means of livelihood and pasture (9.219). Persons suffering from certain disabilities and those who have fallen from caste are excluded from inheritance but are to be maintained (Manu 9.201–203).

docs.title: 13.9.3 Sons and Adoption
docs.text: Because the continuation of the family and of the ancestral offerings required a son, the texts recognise twelve kinds of son, including, besides the son born of a man’s lawful wife, the son begotten on his wife by another through niyoga, the adopted son (dattaka), the son made (kṛtrima), the son born secretly, the son of an unmarried girl, the son bought and the son of a remarried woman (Manu 9.158–180). Six of these are heirs; the others are kinsmen but not heirs. In later centuries only the natural and the adopted son remained important; the law of adoption is described in Chapter 15. A daughter could be “appointed” (putrikā) to bear a son for her father if he had no son.

docs.title: 13.9.4 Order of Heirs
docs.text: Where a man died without male issue, the texts give an order of heirs. Yājñavalkya’s list — wife, daughters, parents, brothers and their sons, more distant kinsmen, pupil and fellow-student (2.135–136) — became the basis of the Mitākṣarā scheme; the Dāyabhāga ranked heirs by their capacity to benefit the deceased through ancestral offerings (Chapter 11). Women generally took a limited estate in property they inherited from men, with the right to its income but restricted power to alienate it; their own property (strīdhana) followed separate rules (Chapter 15). In the absence of any heir, the property went to the king, except the property of a Brahmin, which went to other learned Brahmins.

docs.title: 13.10 The Arthaśāstra’s Private Law
docs.text: Book 3 of the Arthaśāstra is a treatise on the same titles of law, written from the perspective of the royal courts (Chapter 12). It covers marriage, the duties of spouses, inheritance, property in houses and fields, boundaries, debts, deposits, slaves and labourers, partnerships, sales, gifts, theft, assault and gambling. Its rules are often close to those of the smṛtis, sometimes more detailed, and in places notably different: it is more permissive on divorce and remarriage than the Dharmaśāstras (Chapter 15); it imposes fines more consistently than corporal punishments; and it frames its rules with an eye to public order and the king’s revenue. It also invalidates transactions made by dependants — sons dependent on their fathers, slaves, those under another’s authority — and by the intoxicated, the insane and the distressed, except in recognised cases (AŚ 3.1). McClish has argued that the presence of this dharmaśāstric material in the Arthaśāstra is in part the result of its later redaction (Chapter 3) (McClish 2019; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 13.11 Assessment
docs.text: The civil law of the Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstra is technically accomplished and closely engaged with economic life. Its rules on interest and its limits, on pledges and sureties, on deposits, sales and partnerships, on boundaries and on the joint family reflect the needs of a society of cultivators, traders and creditors, and many of them continued to be applied by Indian courts until well into the twentieth century. Comparisons with Roman law — the societas, depositum, fenus nauticum — or with Islamic law — the muḍāraba partnership, the prohibition of ribā — can illuminate common solutions to common problems. But this was not a law of free and equal contracting parties. Interest rates, debt bondage, the capacity to own property, the shares of sons and the inheritance of women all depended on varṇa and gender; slavery was regulated, not questioned. The technical achievements and the social hierarchy belong to the same system.

docs.title: 13.13 Summary
docs.text:
• The law of debt regulated interest — graded by the varṇa of the borrower — and limited it: the total interest on money could not exceed the principal, and compound and other oppressive forms of interest were forbidden. Creditors could recover debts by suit or by self-help; debtors of lower varṇa could be made to work off their debts.

  • Sureties, pledges, deposits, sales, partnerships and the conventions of guilds were each regulated in detail; the law of gift defined who might alienate what, and underlay the land grants of kings.

  • Hired labour, apprenticeship and slavery were legal institutions; land was held privately, subject to the king’s right to revenue.

  • Inheritance and partition were organised around the joint family and the male line, reflecting the importance of sons and of the ancestral rites.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The primary texts are Manu chapters 8–9 (Olivelle 2005), Yājñavalkya Book 2 (Olivelle 2019), the Nāradasmṛti (Lariviere 1989) and AŚ Book 3 (Olivelle 2013). Kane (1930), vol. 3, discusses each title in detail; Lingat (1973) and Derrett (1968) analyse property and inheritance; Rocher (2002) translates the Dāyabhāga. On guilds, see Majumdar (1918); on slavery and labour, Chakravarti (1987) and Sharma (1958).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Crime, Punishment and Penance
docs.text:
Manusmṛti 7.18

daṇḍaḥ śāsti prajāḥ sarvā daṇḍa evābhirakṣati daṇḍaḥ supteṣu jāgarti daṇḍaṃ dharmaṃ vidur budhāḥ “Punishment disciplines all the subjects, punishment alone protects them, punishment stays awake while they sleep; the wise know punishment to be dharma.”

The Sanskrit word daṇḍa means a staff or rod, and by extension the coercive power of the king, the army, and punishment. Indian political theory gave it a central place: the science of government was called daṇḍanīti, “the policy of the rod”, and the texts are unanimous that without punishment the strong would devour the weak (Chapter 5). This chapter examines what the Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstra say about the justification of punishment, the classification of offences, the forms and measure of punishment, the treatment of suspects and prisoners, and the relation between royal punishment and religious penance (prāyaścitta).

It is in criminal law that the hierarchical character of the classical legal order is most visible. The punishments of the Dharmaśāstras depended on the varṇa of offender and victim and on the sex of the offender and victim; the Arthaśāstra prescribed torture in interrogation and cruel forms of execution. The same texts also insist on proportion and on weighing the circumstances of an offence. Both sides are set out here (Singh 2017; Kane 1930, vols. 3–4).

docs.title: 14.1.1 Manu
docs.text:
Manu’s chapter on the king contains an extended praise of punishment (Manu 7.14–31). The creator produced punishment, his own son, as the protector of all beings and as dharma itself; through fear of it all beings, moving and unmoving, are kept to their duties. Properly used, after due consideration, it makes all people happy; used without consideration, it destroys everything. “If the king did not tirelessly inflict punishment on those who deserve it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit” (7.20); crows would eat the sacrificial cake, dogs would lick the oblations, no one would have ownership, and everything would be turned upside down (7.21). Punishment is “a great power, difficult to wield by those of untrained mind”; it destroys the king who deviates from dharma, together with his kin (7.28).

The texts thus justify punishment primarily by its effects — deterrence and the protection of the social order — while also presenting it as the embodiment of dharma. Manu adds a religious motive for the offender: men who have committed crimes and have been punished by kings go to heaven, cleansed, like those who have done good deeds (8.318). Punishment by the king thus also had an expiatory function.

docs.title: 14.1.2 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s justification is more purely political. Daṇḍa secures the acquisition and preservation of wealth and the stability of the sciences (AŚ 1.4.3–4). Its measure is decisive: “a king severe with the rod terrifies people; a king mild with the rod is despised; a king who metes out just punishment is honoured”. Punishment properly applied after full consideration endows subjects with dharma, wealth and pleasure; used wrongly, out of passion, anger or contempt, it enrages even forest-dwellers and ascetics; not used at all, it gives rise to the law of the fish (AŚ 1.4.7–14).

docs.title: 14.1.3 The Measure of Punishment
docs.text: Both traditions insist that punishment must be proportionate. Manu instructs the king to consider the motive, the time and place, the capacity of the offender and the nature of the offence before inflicting punishment (8.126). He describes a gradation of measures: first a verbal reprimand, then a stern rebuke, third a fine, and after that corporal punishment; and if even corporal punishment does not restrain an offender, all four together (8.129–130). Repeat offenders are to be punished more heavily, and a first offence committed without intent more lightly. In the Dharmaśāstras, however, “the capacity of the offender” and “the nature of the offence” were both understood in terms of varṇa, so that proportion and inequality were combined in the same calculation.

docs.title: 14.2.1 The Titles of Criminal Law
docs.text: Among the eighteen titles of law (Chapter 12), five concern what we would call criminal matters: verbal assault (vākpāruṣya), physical assault (daṇḍapāruṣya), theft (steya), violence (sāhasa) — a category that includes robbery, homicide, arson and other crimes committed openly by force — and sexual offences against women (strīsaṃgrahaṇa). Theft was distinguished from violence by its secrecy: what is done openly by force is sāhasa, what is done secretly is theft. The Arthaśāstra’s Book 4 adds a wide range of offences against public order: offences by artisans and merchants, by officials and judges, by counterfeiters and adulterators, by those who harbour criminals, and by those who conspire against the king.

docs.title: 14.2.2 Grave Sins
docs.text: The legal categories were paralleled by the religious category of “grave sins” (mahāpātaka): killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft (of a Brahmin’s gold), sexual intercourse with the wife of one’s teacher, and associating with those who commit these sins (Manu 11.55). The list reflects Brahmanical priorities: the killing of a Brahmin heads it, and the drinking of liquor is a grave sin for Brahmins in particular. Lesser sins (upapātaka) include killing a cow, usury, adultery, the sale of a wife or child, and teaching or learning the Veda for pay. These categories governed the penances described below, but they also affected punishment by the king, who was to brand those guilty of grave sins and banish them (Manu 9.235–239).

docs.title: 14.2.3 Intention and Accident
docs.text: The texts distinguish intentional and unintentional acts. Penances for unintentional sins are lighter than for intentional ones, and some authorities hold that intentional sins cannot be expiated at all (Manu 11.45–46). In criminal law, accidental injury — for example by a driver of a cart whose animals run out of control — is treated differently from intentional assault, and the texts discuss at length the responsibility of drivers, owners of animals and persons who cause injury unknowingly (Manu 8.290–298). Modern writers have compared these distinctions with the common-law concept of mens rea, although the Indian texts never develop a general theory of criminal intent.

docs.title: 14.3.1 The Dharmaśāstric Principle
docs.text:
The most important feature of Dharmaśāstric criminal law is that the punishment for a given act depended on the varṇa of the offender and of the victim. The principle runs through every title of criminal law in the Manusmṛti and, with variations, the other smṛtis (Chapter 10):

  • Verbal abuse (Manu 8.267–272): A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brahmin is fined 100 paṇas, a Vaiśya 150 or 200, and a Śūdra is to receive corporal punishment; a Brahmin who reviles a Kṣatriya pays 50, a Vaiśya 25, a Śūdra 12. A Śūdra who insults twice-born men with gross abuse has his tongue cut out; one who mentions their names and castes contemptuously has a red-hot iron nail ten fingers long thrust into his mouth; one who presumes to instruct Brahmins in their dharma has hot oil poured into his mouth and ears.

  • Physical assault (8.279–283): A low-born man who strikes a superior loses the limb with which he struck; one who raises his hand or stick has his hand cut off; one who kicks has his foot cut off; one who sits on the same seat as a superior is branded on the hip and banished, or has his buttocks cut; one who spits on him loses his lips.

  • Sexual offences (8.359–385): Penalties vary with the varṇas of the man and woman and with whether the woman is “guarded”. A Śūdra who has intercourse with a guarded woman of a twice-born varṇa loses his limb and all his property, or his life (8.374); a Brahmin who does the same with a guarded woman pays a fine (8.378–385).

  • Capital punishment (8.379–381): A Brahmin is never to be executed. Shaving his head is the equivalent of execution for him; at most he is banished with his property intact, “for there is no greater injustice on earth than killing a Brahmin”.

  • Places of punishment (8.124–125): The ten “places” on which punishment may be inflicted — the genitals, belly, tongue, hands, feet, eyes, nose, ears, property and body — apply to the three lower varṇas; a Brahmin should depart unharmed.

The one important exception is theft, where the texts reverse the gradation: Manu makes the guilt and fine of a thief eightfold for a Śūdra, sixteenfold for a Vaiśya, thirty-twofold for a Kṣatriya and sixty-four-fold or more for a Brahmin, because the higher-born man knows the gravity of what he does (8.337–338); the verse before them fines the king a thousandfold (8.336; Chapter 5). These rules express a principle that knowledge and status bring responsibility, and they show that the texts did not simply exempt the high-born. But they are exceptions within a system whose general rule protected Brahmins and degraded Śūdras.

docs.title: 14.3.2 Interpretation
docs.text: Defenders of the tradition have sometimes argued that the varṇa-graded penalties expressed a rational differentiation of responsibility, or that they were rarely applied. The first argument is not supported by the texts, whose penalties for offences by Śūdras against Brahmins are the most severe in the whole law; the second cannot be tested, because we have so little evidence of actual criminal trials before the medieval period, but it does not change what the texts prescribe and what their authority later legitimated. B. R. Ambedkar singled out these provisions as proof that the śāstras could not be the basis of a just society (Ambedkar 1936); R. S. Sharma used them to reconstruct the legal disabilities of the Śūdras (Sharma 1958); and the Constitution’s guarantee of equality before the law (Article 14) is in direct contradiction with them.

docs.title: 14.3.3 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra also grades penalties by varṇa in some places — for example, in its rules on verbal abuse and sexual offences — but it relies more consistently on fines and treats many offences without reference to varṇa. It exempts Brahmins from torture: for any crime, a Brahmin is not to be tortured, but is to be branded on the forehead with a mark indicating his crime — a dog for theft, a headless body for murder, and so on — proclaimed, and banished or sent to the mines (AŚ 4.8). Its frequent use of fines for offences that the smṛtis punish corporally reflects, in part, its interest in revenue.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Fines
docs.text: Fines were the commonest punishment. The texts define three standard levels of the “violence fine” (sāhasa): in Manu, 250 paṇas for the lowest, 500 for the middle and 1,000 for the highest (8.138); in the Arthaśāstra, 48 to 96 paṇas for the lowest, 200 to 500 for the middle and 500 to 1,000 for the highest (AŚ 3.17). Many penalties are expressed by reference to these levels. Fines went to the king’s treasury; compensation to the victim was also required in cases of injury and damage to property.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Corporal Punishment and Mutilation
docs.text: Corporal punishment ranged from flogging to branding and the cutting off of limbs — fingers, hands, feet, tongue, nose, ears or lips. The Arthaśāstra provides for the redemption of mutilation by the payment of fines on a fixed scale — so many paṇas for the tip of a finger, more for a hand or foot (AŚ 4.10) — which made mutilation a punishment chiefly for those who could not pay.

docs.title: 14.4.3 Execution
docs.text: Death was prescribed for grave offences: murder, robbery with violence, certain thefts, sexual offences by men of low varṇa against women of high varṇa, treason and conspiracy against the king, and some offences against public works such as breaking a dam. The Arthaśāstra describes methods of execution that include impalement, burning and being torn apart by animals, and distinguishes execution with and without torture (AŚ 4.11). It prescribes death for anyone who kills an elephant in the royal forests (AŚ 2.2). The texts that exempt Brahmins from execution substitute shaving of the head, branding and banishment.

docs.title: 14.4.4 Banishment and Loss of Caste
docs.text: Banishment from the kingdom, and expulsion from the caste by its own members, were severe punishments in a society in which a person’s livelihood and identity depended on membership of a group. Loss of caste (patitatva) entailed exclusion from commensality, marriage and inheritance, and the texts describe the ritual by which the kinsmen of a fallen man overturn a water pot to signify his social death (Manu 11.183–185) and the procedure for readmitting him after penance.

docs.title: 14.4.5 Imprisonment
docs.text: Imprisonment was used chiefly for detaining suspects, debtors and those awaiting punishment, rather than as a sentence in its own right. The Arthaśāstra describes a prison (bandhanāgāra) with separate wards for men and women (AŚ 2.5), and punishes prison officials who torment prisoners, deny them food or water, or sexually abuse women in their custody (AŚ 4.9). It also provides that prisoners — the young, the old, the sick and the helpless among them — be released on the day of the king’s birth constellation and on full-moon days, and that prisoners be released on the occasion of a conquest or the installation of a crown prince (AŚ 2.36). Aśoka records that he released prisoners on the anniversaries of his consecration (Chapter 8). These provisions show concern for the conditions of detention; they do not amount to a theory of rehabilitation through imprisonment, which was a nineteenth-century European idea.

docs.title: 14.5 The Arthaśāstra’s “Removal of Thorns”
docs.text:
Book 4 of the Arthaśāstra, “The Removal of Thorns” (kaṇṭakaśodhana), is the fullest account of crime control in classical Indian literature. Its magistrates (pradeṣṭṛ) deal with artisans and merchants who cheat, with officials who embezzle or take bribes, and with criminals of all kinds. Their main tools are secret agents. Agents posing as holy men are to identify those who are living beyond their means, consorting with prostitutes, or seeking magical help; agents are also to provoke crimes — for instance by tempting a suspected official with a bribe or a seditious proposal — and then expose those who succumb (AŚ 4.4–5). Suspects are to be arrested on circumstantial grounds: unexplained wealth, a change of residence, signs of injury, possession of stolen goods.

Suspects may be interrogated, and where the evidence is strong but the suspect will not confess, tortured. The text describes a graded series of tortures (karma), including beating, flogging, suspension and the water-tube, and lays down that they are not to be applied to pregnant women, to women within a month of childbirth, to minors, the aged, the sick, the intoxicated, the insane, those exhausted by hunger, thirst or travel, and some others (AŚ 4.8). It also warns that innocent persons under torture may confess to crimes they did not commit, giving examples, and requires that a confession be corroborated. The cautions are notable, but the procedure as a whole is the opposite of a presumption of innocence and of a prohibition of torture (Olivelle 2013; Singh 2017).

docs.title: 14.6.1 Theft
docs.text: Manu treats theft at length (8.301–343). The king is to make special efforts to suppress thieves, for by protecting his subjects from them his fame and his kingdom grow; a king who takes taxes but does not suppress thieves takes on their sins. Punishments are graded by the value and kind of property stolen: small thefts of grain or goods are punished with fines several times the value, theft of larger amounts, of precious metals, of men and women of good family, or of important animals with mutilation or death. A thief caught with the stolen property, or with the instruments of burglary, is to be punished, and whoever gives food, shelter or help to thieves is to be punished like a thief. A thief who confesses and approaches the king with a club, asking to be punished, is either killed or released; in either case he is purified (8.314–316). Some takings are excused: a twice-born traveller who has run out of provisions and takes two stalks of sugarcane or two radishes from another’s field is not to be fined (8.341).

docs.title: 14.6.2 Violence
docs.text: The category of sāhasa, “violence”, covers offences committed openly by force: robbery, homicide, assault on women, arson and the destruction of property. Nārada divides it into three degrees according to the object — fruits and similar goods, clothes and animals, and human life or wives — and Manu states that the man who commits violence is worse than a slanderer, a thief or one who strikes with a stick, and that a king must never pardon him (8.344–347). In self-defence, in protecting women and Brahmins, or in a war undertaken for dharma, a man who kills commits no offence; and one may kill without hesitation an assailant (ātatāyin) who comes with intent to murder, even if he is one’s teacher or a learned Brahmin (8.348–351).

docs.title: 14.6.3 Insult and Defamation
docs.text: Verbal assault (vākpāruṣya) covered abuse, insult and defamation. Apart from the varṇa-graded penalties described above, Manu fines a man who calls another one-eyed, lame or the like — even if it is true — and imposes a larger fine on one who reviles another’s mother, father, wife, brother, son or teacher, or who refuses to make way for his teacher (8.274–275). Fines between persons of equal varṇa are lower than those across varṇas. Nārada distinguishes degrees of verbal assault according to the gravity of the words used — harsh speech, obscene speech and speech imputing grave sins — and treats false accusation of a grave crime as particularly serious. These rules reflect a society in which honour and reputation were valuable and fragile, and in which insult across lines of rank was treated as a threat to the social order.

docs.title: 14.6.4 Harm to Animals and Plants
docs.text: The criminal law also protected animals and plants, in a manner that reflects both their economic value and religious sentiment. Manu prescribes fines for damaging trees according to their use — fruit trees, flowering trees, creepers and shrubs — and for injuring men and animals according to the pain caused, with compensation for the cost of treatment (8.285–287). Killing large domestic animals, and above all cows, attracted heavy penalties and penances; the killing of a cow is listed among the lesser sins (upapātaka) and required an elaborate penance (11.109–117). The Arthaśāstra fines those who kill protected animals or animals in sanctuaries, and those who injure cattle (Chapter 6). These provisions protected property, livelihood and religiously valued beings within a hierarchy of value that placed the cow above most humans of low status.

docs.title: 14.6.5 Investigating Sudden Death
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra contains a chapter on the investigation of sudden deaths (AŚ 4.7). The magistrate is to examine the body of a person who has died suddenly for signs of strangulation, hanging, drowning, poisoning or beating — swollen hands and feet, protruding eyes, marks on the neck, discoloration and so on — and to inquire into the dead person’s quarrels, debts and relationships in order to discover whether the death was caused by another. The chapter is a striking example of the text’s empirical approach to crime, written as practical guidance for officials.

docs.title: 14.6.6 Offences by Officials
docs.text: Both traditions treat crimes by officials severely. The Arthaśāstra lists punishments for judges who threaten, abuse or silence litigants, ask irrelevant questions, delay cases, or decide unjustly; for clerks who falsify records; and for prison officials who abuse prisoners (AŚ 4.9). Manu requires the king to confiscate the property of officials who take bribes from litigants and banish them (9.231). These rules show an awareness that the agents of justice could themselves be sources of injustice.

docs.title: 14.7.1 Prāyaścitta
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras’ third division, after conduct and law, is prāyaścitta, penance or expiation. Wrongdoing, in this view, produces sin (pāpa), which brings suffering in this life and the next, including rebirth in lower forms; penance removes or reduces it. The penances range from fasts, recitations of Vedic texts and gifts to Brahmins to severe austerities. For the killing of a Brahmin, Manu prescribes that the killer live for twelve years in a hut in the forest, carrying the skull of the dead man as a banner and living on alms (11.73), or undergo other equally severe penances. For lesser sins there are graded fasts, of which the best known are the kṛcchra and the cāndrāyaṇa, in which the amount of food eaten is increased and decreased with the phases of the moon.

docs.title: 14.7.2 Penance and the Social Order
docs.text: Penance was not only a private religious matter. It was imposed by assemblies of learned Brahmins (pariṣad), which decided what penance a sinner should perform, and it was the condition of readmission to the caste for those who had been outcast. In this sense prāyaścitta was a form of social discipline administered by the Brahmin community, alongside the king’s daṇḍa. Its penances, too, were graded by varṇa: the penance for killing a Kṣatriya was a quarter of that for killing a Brahmin, for killing a Vaiśya an eighth, and for killing a Śūdra a sixteenth (Manu 11.127), and the killing of a Śūdra was placed on a level with the killing of certain animals.

docs.title: 14.7.3 Readmission and Reconversion
docs.text: Penance was also the means by which those who had lost caste could be readmitted. Some later smṛtis, such as the one attributed to Devala, prescribe penances for persons who had been forcibly carried off or converted by foreigners and wished to return to their community — a sign that such situations were known in the period of the texts’ composition. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the Ārya Samāj and other Hindu organisations developed rites of “purification” (śuddhi) to receive converts to Hinduism and to readmit those who had converted to other religions, sometimes also to raise the status of low castes; these campaigns became entangled with the communal politics of the period. The history illustrates how a classical institution of caste discipline was adapted to new social and political purposes.

docs.title: 14.7.4 Punishment and Penance Compared
docs.text: Scholars have discussed how far the domains of punishment and penance overlapped. The texts envisage both for many offences: the king punishes, and the offender also performs a penance for the sin. Some authorities held that a person who had been punished by the king was thereby purified (Manu 8.318). The relation between the two is better described as a coordination of royal and Brahmanical authority than as a “dual-track” system of punishment and rehabilitation in a modern sense (Kane 1930, vol. 4; Olivelle and Davis 2018). The system was centred on purity and status rather than on the victim.

docs.title: 14.8 Punishment in Later Indian States
docs.text:
What is known of punishment in practice in medieval and early modern India suggests both continuity and change. Inscriptions record fines, confiscation and banishment, and the endowment of temple lamps or other gifts as a form of compensation and expiation for offences such as accidental homicide (Chapter 12). Chroniclers describe kings inflicting mutilation and cruel executions on rebels and traitors, and travellers report harsh punishments for theft and robbery. Under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, Islamic criminal law distinguished fixed penalties for certain offences, retaliation or compensation for homicide and injury at the choice of the victim’s heirs, and discretionary punishments by the judge or ruler; in practice much criminal justice was administered by governors and police officials exercising the ruler’s discretionary authority (Chapter 18). In the Maratha and other regional states, fines and confiscation were common, and caste and village councils punished breaches of caste rules by fines and outcasting.

The varṇa-graded penalties of the Dharmaśāstras were thus never the whole of Indian penal practice, and for long periods they were not the law of the state at all. But the principle that status should affect liability, and the exemption of Brahmins from corporal and capital punishment, were widely respected by Hindu rulers, and the idea that caste councils could punish their members persisted into the colonial period and beyond.

docs.title: 14.9 From Daṇḍanīti to the Penal Code
docs.text:
Islamic criminal law, administered in the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal empire, and the criminal law of the East India Company, which retained Islamic criminal law in modified form in Bengal until the nineteenth century, replaced the Dharmaśāstric penal law in most of India long before independence (Chapters 18 and 19). The Indian Penal Code, drafted by a Law Commission under Thomas Babington Macaulay in the 1830s and enacted in 1860, owed nothing to Dharmaśāstra and was based on English and continental models; it applied the same penalties to all, regardless of caste or religion, though the colonial state also enacted discriminatory laws such as the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871. Claims that the Penal Code’s structure “parallels” the Arthaśāstra, or that it adopted a three-tier classification derived from the sāhasa fines, have no basis. In 2023 the Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Evidence Act were replaced by new statutes (Chapter 20).

Independent India retained the death penalty, but the courts have narrowed its use. In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality while holding that it should be imposed only in the “rarest of rare” cases, after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances relating both to the crime and to the criminal. The classical texts, too, prescribed death for grave crimes while exempting Brahmins and urging the weighing of circumstances; the modern doctrine differs fundamentally in that it applies the same standard to every person, whatever his birth.

docs.title: 14.10 Principal Passages
docs.text:
Table 14.1 lists the principal passages discussed in this chapter.

Table 14.1. Principal passages on crime, punishment and penance discussed in this chapter Passage Subject Manu 7.14–31 The praise of punishment (daṇḍa) Manu 8.124–130 The ten places of punishment; the measure and gradation of punishment Manu 8.267–283 Verbal and physical assault, graded by varṇa Manu 8.285–298 Injury to trees, men and animals; accidents with carts Manu 8.301–343 Theft; the thief who confesses (8.314–316); the reverse gradation (8.337–338) Manu 8.318 Those punished by the king are purified Manu 8.344–351 Violence; self-defence and the assailant (ātatāyin) Manu 8.359–385 Sexual offences, graded by varṇa Manu 8.379–381 No execution of a Brahmin Manu 9.231, 9.235–239 Corrupt officials; branding and banishment of grave sinners Manu 11.45–46, 11.55 Intentional and unintentional sins; the grave sins Manu 11.73, 11.127 Penance for killing a Brahmin; penances graded by varṇa Manu 11.183–185 The overturned water pot: exclusion of an outcaste AŚ 1.4.7–14 The just measure of the rod; the law of the fish AŚ 2.5, 2.36, 4.9 Prisons, release of prisoners, offences by officials AŚ 3.17 The three levels of the sāhasa fine AŚ 4.4–5, 4.7, 4.8 Secret agents; sudden death; interrogation, torture and the branding of Brahmins AŚ 4.10–11 Redemption of mutilation; forms of execution

docs.title: 14.11 Summary
docs.text:
• Punishment (daṇḍa) was justified as the protector of order and as dharma itself, and was to be measured to the offence and the offender.

  • In the Dharmaśāstras, punishments depend on the varṇa of offender and victim, with Brahmins exempt from execution and corporal punishment; theft is the main exception. The Arthaśāstra relies more on fines but prescribes torture for suspects and cruel executions.

  • Penance (prāyaścitta), administered by Brahmin assemblies and graded by varṇa, worked alongside royal punishment; classical penal law was later displaced by Islamic and then colonial criminal law.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The principal texts are Manu chapters 7–9 and 11 (Olivelle 2005) and AŚ Books 3–4 (Olivelle 2013). Kane (1930), vols. 3–4, surveys punishment and penance. Singh (2017) is the best study of violence and punishment in early India; Sharma (1958) and Ambedkar (1936) discuss the varṇa provisions critically. Singha (1998) examines the transition to colonial criminal law.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Family, Saṃskāra and Women in Dharmaśāstra
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras devote more space to the life of the household than to any other subject. Their rules on the rites of passage (saṃskāra), the stages of life (āśrama), marriage, the duties of husband and wife, adoption, maintenance and women’s property were the parts of the tradition that touched most people most directly, and they were the parts that British courts and, later, the Indian Parliament took over as “Hindu personal law”. They are also the parts in which the texts’ hierarchies of varṇa and gender are most consequential for ordinary lives.

This chapter surveys the main institutions of family law in the śāstras: the saṃskāras and their exclusions, the āśramas, marriage and its forms, the position of wives and widows, women’s property and inheritance, and the controversial practices of child marriage and widow-burning. It then turns to women’s own voices and to the reform of family law in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It draws on the critical scholarship of Uma Chakravarti, who described the system as “Brahmanical patriarchy” — a structure in which the control of women’s sexuality was the means of maintaining the purity of caste — and on studies of particular texts and practices (Chakravarti 1993, 2003; Leslie 1989).

docs.title: 15.1 The Stages of Life
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras organise a man’s life in four stages (āśrama): the Vedic student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the renouncer (saṃnyāsin). Patrick Olivelle has shown that this scheme had a history. In the Dharmasūtras the āśramas were four alternative ways of life, among which an adult who had completed his studies could choose; only in the Manusmṛti and later texts did they become successive stages through which a twice-born man should pass in order (Olivelle 1993). Throughout, the texts give pre-eminence to the householder, on whom all the other orders depend “as all creatures depend on the air” (Manu 3.77). The scheme was addressed to twice-born men; women’s stages of life were defined by their relation to men — daughter, wife, widow — and Śūdras were excluded from Vedic studentship.

docs.title: 15.2.1 Purpose and Number
docs.text:
Saṃskāra means “making perfect” or “preparing”: the rites of passage were believed to remove impurities and to qualify a person for the next stage of ritual and social life. The domestic ritual manuals (Gṛhyasūtras) and the Dharmaśāstras describe them, and their number varies. Gautama lists forty saṃskāras, including many Vedic sacrifices (GDh 8.14–24); later authors settled on a list of sixteen, the form in which they are usually presented today (Pandey 1969; Kane 1930). Table 15.1 gives this list.

Table 15.1. A common list of sixteen saṃskāras (after Pandey 1969) Saṃskāra Occasion garbhādhāna Rite for conception puṃsavana Rite in early pregnancy, intended to secure a male child sīmantonnayana Parting of the pregnant woman’s hair jātakarman Birth rites nāmakaraṇa Naming, usually on the tenth or twelfth day niṣkramaṇa First outing of the child annaprāśana First feeding with solid food cūḍākaraṇa First cutting of the hair karṇavedha Piercing of the ears vidyārambha Beginning of learning the alphabet upanayana Initiation into Vedic study (“investiture with the sacred thread”) vedārambha Beginning of Vedic study keśānta First shaving of the beard samāvartana Return home at the end of studentship vivāha Marriage antyeṣṭi Funeral rites

The table conceals important differences in who could receive these rites. The rites of pregnancy and childhood were performed for the children of the twice-born; for girls, the texts prescribe them without Vedic mantras (Manu 2.66). The puṃsavana, despite modern euphemistic descriptions, was a rite intended to secure the birth of a son.

docs.title: 15.2.2 Upanayana and Its Exclusions
docs.text:
The most important saṃskāra before marriage was upanayana, the initiation of a boy into Vedic study, which made him “twice-born” (dvija). Manu prescribes it in the eighth year from conception for a Brahmin, the eleventh for a Kṣatriya and the twelfth for a Vaiśya, with outer limits of sixteen, twenty-two and twenty-four years respectively (Manu 2.36–38). The materials of the boy’s girdle differ by varṇa, and his sacred cord is to be of cotton for a Brahmin, hemp for a Kṣatriya and wool for a Vaiśya (2.42–44). Those who are not initiated in time become “fallen from the Sāvitrī” (vrātya) and are excluded from Vedic learning until they perform a penance (2.39–40).

Upanayana was denied to Śūdras and, in the Dharmaśāstras, to women. Manu states that for women the marriage ceremony takes the place of initiation, serving the husband takes the place of residence with a teacher, and household work takes the place of the care of the sacred fires (2.67). A few later texts recall a former age in which girls too were initiated and studied the Veda, and the Upaniṣads mention women such as Gārgī and Maitreyī who debated with male teachers; but by the time of the Dharmaśāstras Vedic learning had become a male, twice-born preserve. The exclusion of Śūdras and women from Vedic learning, and therefore from the most prestigious forms of knowledge and ritual, is one of the foundations of the hierarchy the texts describe (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 15.2.3 The Student’s Life
docs.text: After initiation, the student (brahmacārin) lived in his teacher’s house, learning the Veda by heart. Manu describes his discipline: he should beg for food each day and offer it to his teacher, tend the sacred fire, bathe, avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, women, gambling and idle talk, sleep on the ground, and obey and honour his teacher as a father (2.175–201). The period of study was ideally twelve years for each Veda, though shorter periods were common; it ended with a ritual bath (samāvartana) after which the young man, now a snātaka (“one who has bathed”), could marry. The initiation itself taught the boy the Sāvitrī verse (the “Gāyatrī”) and invested him with the girdle, staff and sacred cord. In practice, Vedic study of this kind was confined to Brahmin families of scholarly lineage; for most twice-born men, initiation became a short ritual followed by an ordinary education.

docs.title: 15.2.4 Impurity
docs.text: Birth and death produced a temporary impurity (aśauca) in the family, during which relatives were excluded from rites and from contact with others. The texts grade its duration by closeness of kinship and by varṇa: Manu prescribes ten days for a Brahmin, twelve for a Kṣatriya, fifteen for a Vaiśya and a month for a Śūdra after the death of a close relative (5.83). Women were also regarded as impure during menstruation and after childbirth. These rules, which modern readers may find marginal to law, were central to the texts’ vision of social order: they reinforced the boundaries of kinship and caste, and they made purity, graded by varṇa, a matter of continual observance.

docs.title: 15.2.5 Funeral and Ancestral Rites
docs.text: The last saṃskāra, the funeral (antyeṣṭi), was followed by a period of impurity for the relatives, graded by closeness of kinship and by varṇa, and by a series of ancestral offerings (śrāddha) in which rice-balls (piṇḍa) were offered to the deceased, his father and grandfather. About a year after death the deceased was united with his ancestors in the rite of sapiṇḍīkaraṇa. These rites had legal consequences: the relationship of sapiṇḍa, “sharing the rice-ball”, defined the circle of kin within which marriage was forbidden and, in the Dāyabhāga, the order of inheritance (Chapter 11). They also made the birth of a son, who could offer the piṇḍa, a religious necessity.

docs.title: 15.3.1 A Sacrament and a Gift
docs.text: For the Dharmaśāstras, marriage (vivāha) was a saṃskāra and the foundation of the householder’s life. In its approved forms it was conceived as the gift of a girl (kanyādāna) by her father to the groom. The ceremony, described in the Gṛhyasūtras, included the taking of the bride’s hand (pāṇigrahaṇa), the circumambulation of the sacred fire, and the seven steps (saptapadī) taken together by bride and groom. Manu states that the marriage mantras are the definitive mark of a wife, and that the marriage is complete at the seventh step (8.227). The Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 still provides that where the saptapadī is part of the ceremony, the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken. The ideal of the relationship is expressed in a verse of Manu: “Let mutual fidelity continue until death; this, in brief, is the highest dharma of husband and wife” (9.101).

docs.title: 15.3.2 The Marriage Rite
docs.text: The domestic ritual manuals describe the wedding in detail, and many of its elements survive in contemporary Hindu weddings. After the bride’s father has given her to the groom, the groom takes her right hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) with verses from the Ṛgvedic wedding hymn (10.85); the bride steps on a stone, to be firm like it; the couple offer parched grain into the fire; they circle the fire, keeping it to their right; and they take seven steps together, each step accompanied by a wish — for food, strength, wealth, happiness, offspring, the seasons and lifelong friendship. In the evening the groom shows the bride the pole star (dhruva), a symbol of constancy. The rites vary between the ritual schools and between regions; in much of southern India, for example, the tying of a pendant (tāli) around the bride’s neck became the essential act.

docs.title: 15.3.3 The Eight Forms
docs.text:
The texts list eight forms of marriage (Manu 3.21–34):

  • Brāhma: the father gives his daughter, adorned, to a learned man of good conduct whom he has invited;

  • Daiva: the gift of a daughter to the officiating priest at a sacrifice;

  • Ārṣa: the gift of a daughter after receiving a cow and a bull from the groom “in accordance with dharma”;

  • Prājāpatya: the gift of a daughter with the injunction “May you both practise dharma together”;

  • Āsura: the groom gives wealth to the bride’s kin and to the bride and takes her — marriage by bride-price;

  • Gāndharva: the union of a girl and a man by mutual desire;

  • Rākṣasa: the forcible abduction of a girl from her home, after killing or wounding her kin;

  • Paiśāca: the seduction or rape of a girl who is asleep, intoxicated or out of her senses — “the most evil” form.

The first four were approved, especially for Brahmins; the Rākṣasa form was allowed to Kṣatriyas; the Āsura and Paiśāca were condemned, though the texts differ in detail (3.23–26). The list is often cited as evidence that the tradition recognised love marriage (the Gāndharva form). That is true, and the Gāndharva marriage of Duṣyanta and Śakuntalā is celebrated in literature; but the texts rank it low, and their inclusion of abduction and rape among the “forms of marriage” shows that the purpose of the classification was to regularise the status of the woman and her children after the event, not to recognise women’s choice. Consent of the bride plays no part in the approved forms, which are all gifts by her father.

docs.title: 15.3.4 Rules of Eligibility
docs.text: A man should marry a girl of his own varṇa who is not a sapiṇḍa of his mother nor of his own gotra (patrilineal clan) on his father’s side (Manu 3.4–5). Twice-born men may also take wives from lower varṇas in descending order (anuloma), but a Brahmin who takes a Śūdra wife is condemned (3.12–19); a woman’s marriage to a man of lower varṇa (pratiloma) is the gravest violation of the order of varṇas and produces the most degraded offspring (Chapter 10). Polygyny was permitted and polyandry was not (Section 15.13). Northern authorities condemned the marriage of cross-cousins, which was customary and accepted in the south (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 15.3.5 The Age of Marriage
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras increasingly recommended that girls be married before puberty. Gautama advises giving a daughter in marriage before she reaches puberty; Manu suggests that a man of thirty should marry a girl of twelve, and a man of twenty-four a girl of eight (9.94), and later authorities treated it as a sin for a father to allow his daughter to menstruate unmarried. These norms, combined with the prohibition of widow remarriage, produced the problem of child widowhood that became a central concern of nineteenth-century reformers.

docs.title: 15.3.6 Divorce
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstras, which regarded marriage as an indissoluble sacrament, did not recognise divorce in the approved forms of marriage. A husband could, however, take another wife (“supersede” his first wife) on grounds discussed below (Section 15.13). Nārada permits a woman to take another husband in five calamities (Chapter 11), and the Arthaśāstra allows the dissolution of marriages contracted in the unapproved forms by mutual consent, and permits a wife to leave a husband who has been long absent (AŚ 3.3–4). Many castes, especially among cultivating, artisan and lower-status communities, recognised divorce and remarriage by custom; these customs were often recognised by the colonial courts (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 15.4.1 The Duties of Wives
docs.text:
The “dharma of women” (strīdharma) in the śāstras is above all the duty of a wife to her husband. Manu’s statement of it is unambiguous: a woman should do nothing independently, even in her own house; she should always be cheerful, skilful in household work and frugal; she should serve her husband as a god even if he is of bad character (5.147–156; 9.2–3). The Strīdharmapaddhati of Tryambakayajvan, an eighteenth-century treatise from the Thanjavur court studied by Julia Leslie, shows how these norms were elaborated into a detailed daily discipline for wives (Leslie 1989).

The texts also impose obligations on husbands: to maintain their wives, to honour them, not to abandon a wife without cause, and to give a superseded wife compensation. A wife who was abandoned could seek maintenance. These obligations belong, however, to a framework of guardianship rather than equality.

docs.title: 15.4.2 Widowhood
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras of Manu and his successors forbid the remarriage of widows (Manu 5.157–162, 9.64–68; Chapter 10). A widow was to live a life of austerity, often with shaved head, plain clothes and restricted diet, and to devote herself to her husband’s memory. Among higher castes the result was a large population of widows, including child widows, dependent on their husbands’ families and subject to severe social restrictions. Among many other communities, widow remarriage — often with the deceased husband’s younger brother — was customary.

The exception provided by Nārada and Parāśara, which allow a woman to remarry if her husband is missing, dead, has become an ascetic, is impotent or has fallen from caste (Nārada 12.97; Parāśara 4.30), became the textual basis for the reformers’ campaign. Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar (1820–1891) argued from Parāśara, which claims authority for the Kali age, that widow remarriage was permitted by the śāstras; his campaign led to the Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act of 1856. The Act removed the legal bar on remarriage, but it also provided that a remarrying widow forfeited her rights in her deceased husband’s property — a provision that, among communities that had previously allowed remarriage, could worsen a widow’s position.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Satī
docs.text:
The burning of a widow on her husband’s funeral pyre (satī, “the virtuous woman”, a name applied to the woman and, in English, to the practice) is the most notorious practice associated with Hindu law. The early Dharmaśāstras do not prescribe it; Manu prescribes chaste widowhood. Later texts praise it: the Viṣṇusmṛti offers the widow the choice of chastity or “ascending the pyre after him” (25.14), and several Purāṇas and later smṛtis promise great rewards to the widow who dies with her husband. Some commentators rejected it: Medhātithi regarded it as a form of suicide forbidden by the Veda, and the dramatist Bāṇa condemned it in the seventh century. Historical evidence for satī comes from inscriptions and memorial stones from about the sixth century CE, from the accounts of foreign observers, and from the records of the East India Company; it was practised especially among some ruling and warrior groups and, in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, among several castes in Bengal (Mani 1998).

Rammohun Roy campaigned against satī from 1818, arguing from the śāstras that it was not obligatory; the Bengal Sati Regulation of 1829, issued under the governor-general William Bentinck, declared it illegal. Lata Mani’s study of the debate showed that both the reformers and their orthodox opponents argued mainly about what the scriptures prescribed, and that the women who died were largely absent from the debate as subjects (Mani 1998). The practice did not disappear entirely: the death of Roop Kanwar at Deorala, Rajasthan, in 1987 led to the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act of 1987, which prohibits the glorification of satī as well as its commission.

docs.title: 15.5 Women in the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra’s treatment of marriage and women differs in several respects from the Dharmaśāstras, and the differences are instructive. Its chapters on marriage, the duties of spouses and women’s property (AŚ 3.2–4) accept the eight forms of marriage and the authority of fathers and husbands; but they also regulate the relationship in practical terms that give women more room than Manu allows.
