The text defines a wife’s property as consisting of maintenance (vṛtti) and ornaments, fixes a maximum amount of maintenance that may be settled on her, and allows her to use it for herself, her son and her daughter-in-law if her husband is absent and has made no provision. A widow who wishes to live a religious life may keep it; if she remarries, she may keep what her father-in-law and husband gave her only if she marries with her father-in-law’s consent, and loses it otherwise. The text thus assumes that widows may remarry, while protecting the interests of the husband’s family.

The Arthaśāstra also allows the dissolution of marriage. Marriages in the four unapproved forms may be dissolved by mutual consent of husband and wife, though marriages in the approved forms may not (AŚ 3.3). It lays down periods for which the wife of an absent husband should wait — longer if he is a Brahmin who has gone for study, shorter for a short journey, and differing according to whether she has children and whether he has left provision for her — after which she may take another husband, preferably a kinsman of her husband, with the permission of the judges (AŚ 3.4). It regulates a husband’s right to punish his wife and imposes fines on wives who are disobedient or who leave the house without permission, and on husbands who are cruel or who neglect their wives.

These rules are not egalitarian: they assume the authority of husbands and the control of women’s sexuality, and they treat women’s property as limited and contingent. But they show that the Brahmanical opposition to widow remarriage and divorce was not universal even among learned authors, and they are closer to the practices of many communities recorded in later centuries than are the rules of Manu (Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 15.6.1 Strīdhana
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras recognise a category of women’s own property (strīdhana). Manu lists six kinds: what was given before the nuptial fire, at the bridal procession and as a token of affection, and what she received from her brother, her mother and her father (9.194). Yājñavalkya adds what was given by her husband, gifts on supersession, the bride-price and later gifts from her husband’s family, and ends with the word “and the like” (Yājñ 2.143–144). On this last word the Mitākṣarā built an expansive interpretation: strīdhana, Vijñāneśvara argued, includes all property a woman acquires by inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure or finding. The British courts did not follow him: the Privy Council held that property a woman inherited from a male was not her strīdhana but a “limited estate”, which passed on her death to the heirs of the last male owner.

A woman’s control of her strīdhana had limits. Yājñavalkya allows a husband to take his wife’s strīdhana in a famine, for a religious duty, in illness or when he is imprisoned, without being obliged to return it (Yājñ 2.147). Kātyāyana distinguishes gifts from her own relatives, over which she has full power of disposal, from gifts made by her husband, over some of which her power was restricted. On her death strīdhana passed to her daughters and children; if she died childless, to her husband or her parents according to the form of her marriage (Manu 9.195–197).

docs.title: 15.6.2 Inheritance
docs.text:
The classical law gave women limited rights of inheritance. Daughters inherited from their fathers only in the absence of sons, or through the device of the appointed daughter (putrikā); unmarried sisters were to receive a share for their marriage. Widows inherited the separate property of sonless husbands under Yājñavalkya’s list of heirs, but under the Mitākṣarā not their husbands’ interest in joint family property, and in either case usually as a limited estate (Chapters 11 and 13). Mothers took a share equal to a son’s when sons partitioned after their father’s death, and widows and unmarried daughters had a right of maintenance charged on the family property.

In the colonial period, the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act of 1937 gave widows a right to their husbands’ share in joint family property, but only as a limited estate. The Hindu Succession Act of 1956 made women absolute owners of property they possessed (section 14), made daughters, widows and mothers heirs of the first class to a man’s separate property, but preserved the male coparcenary; the Amendment of 2005 made daughters coparceners by birth (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 15.6.3 Women as Witnesses and Litigants
docs.text: Manu excludes women as witnesses except for other women, on the ground that “women’s understanding is unsteady” (8.68, 8.77); some later texts admit women as witnesses in cases of violence and in matters concerning women (Chapter 12). Women could be parties to lawsuits, particularly about their strīdhana and maintenance, though they were generally represented by male relatives. Inscriptions show many women — queens, wives of merchants and officials, temple women — making gifts of land and money and endowing temples, which implies that they controlled substantial property in practice (Davis 2010).

docs.title: 15.7 Women in the Buddhist and Jain Orders
docs.text:
Buddhism and Jainism offered women an alternative to the household: the life of a nun. Buddhist tradition holds that the Buddha agreed, after initial reluctance and at the request of his foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the intercession of Ānanda, to admit women to the order, subject to the eight “weighty rules” that subordinated nuns to monks (Chapter 8). The Therīgāthā, the verses of the early nuns, include poems in which women celebrate their release from domestic drudgery, from husbands and from grief. The order of fully ordained nuns died out in the Theravāda countries in the medieval period, though it survived in East Asia.

The Jain community has had nuns throughout its history, and nuns have often outnumbered monks. The two main Jain traditions differed over women’s spiritual capacity: the Digambaras held that women cannot attain liberation in a female body, because they cannot practise the complete nudity required of the highest ascetics, while the Śvetāmbaras held that they can, and revered the nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, Mallī, as a woman (Jaini 1979; Dundas 2002). Monastic life thus gave some women independence from the household and access to learning, within institutions that also maintained hierarchies of gender.

docs.title: 15.8 Devadāsīs
docs.text: The devadāsīs (“servants of the god”) were women dedicated to temple service, especially in southern India, where they danced and sang in temple rituals and at royal courts. Inscriptions from the Cōḷa period onwards record their appointment, their endowments and their gifts; they were often well-to-do, could own and dispose of property, and were not bound to a husband. They also stood outside the norms of marriage, and in many places their status was linked to sexual relations with patrons. In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, reformers — among them Muthulakshmi Reddy, the first woman legislator in the Madras presidency — campaigned against temple dedication as a form of prostitution, and laws such as the Bombay Devadasis Protection Act (1934) and the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act (1947) prohibited it. Historians have since debated the consequences of these laws: they ended a practice that exposed girls to exploitation, but they also stripped a community of women of its livelihood, property and artistic role, while the dance associated with them was reinvented as “Bharatanatyam” by upper-caste performers (Soneji 2012).

docs.title: 15.9 Adoption and Maintenance
docs.text:
The need for a son to continue the lineage and perform the ancestral rites made adoption an important institution. Of the twelve kinds of son listed in the early texts (Chapter 13), only the adopted son (dattaka), “given” by his natural parents, remained widely recognised in later centuries. The law of adoption was elaborated in two late treatises, the Dattakamīmāṃsā of Nanda Paṇḍita (17th century) and the Dattakacandrikā, which the British courts treated as authoritative. They laid down, among other rules, that the adopted boy should ideally be of the same caste and close kin, that he should be one who could have been born to the adopter (so that, for instance, a sister’s son was excluded in some schools), and that a woman could adopt only with her husband’s authority. The question whether a widow could adopt a son to her deceased husband, and with whose permission, produced much litigation in the colonial courts. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act of 1956 replaced these rules, permitting the adoption of girls as well as boys and allowing women to adopt in their own right.

The texts recognise duties of maintenance. A man must maintain his aged parents, his wife and his minor children; a verse attributed to Manu in the commentaries (it is quoted in the Mitākṣarā on Yājñ 2.175, but is not in the Manusmṛti itself) declares that aged parents, a virtuous wife and an infant son must be supported even at the cost of doing a hundred wrongs. Widows and unmarried daughters, and members excluded from inheritance by disability, were entitled to maintenance from the family property. These obligations were enforced by the colonial courts as rights of maintenance and were codified in the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act; the general law also provides, since the nineteenth century, a summary remedy for maintenance of wives, children and parents, which became the subject of the Shah Bano case (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 15.10 Women’s Voices
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras were written by men. Women’s own perspectives survive in other sources. The Therīgāthā, verses attributed to early Buddhist nuns, include poems of release from domestic servitude (Chapter 8). Women poet-saints of the bhakti movements — Āṇṭāḷ, Akkā Mahādevī, Lal Ded, Mīrābāī and Bahiṇābāī, among others — defied the expectations of wifely obedience in the name of devotion (Volume 8 of this series).

In the nineteenth century, women began to write directly about law and custom. Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) opened, with her husband Jotirao Phule, one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848, and wrote poetry against caste and the subordination of women. Tarabai Shinde’s Marathi tract Strī-Puruṣ Tulanā (“A Comparison of Women and Men”, 1882) attacked the double standards by which women were blamed for vices tolerated in men. Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), a Sanskrit scholar from a Brahmin family, criticised the treatment of high-caste widows in The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887), founded a home for widows, and became a Christian. Rukhmabai, married as a child, refused in the 1880s to join the husband to whom she had been married, and the litigation that followed — in which she was ordered to join him or go to prison — became a cause célèbre; she later qualified as a physician. Her case and the death of the child bride Phulmoni contributed to the Age of Consent Act of 1891, which raised the age of consent for girls from ten to twelve. The Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929 (the Sarda Act) set minimum ages of marriage (Kumar 1993; Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 15.11 Women as Patrons, Authors and Reformers
docs.text:
The exclusion of women from Vedic study did not mean that women had no part in public, religious and literary life. Inscriptions show women of royal and merchant families acting as donors and patrons. The Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāyanikā records the great Vedic sacrifices performed by her husband and the fees paid for them, and the Nāsik inscription of Gautamī Balaśrī, mother of King Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi, records her gift of a cave to the Buddhist community and celebrates her son’s achievements. At the Buddhist sites of Sāñcī and Bhārhut, many of the donative inscriptions on railings and gateways name women, lay and monastic, as donors. Such records show women controlling wealth and making religious gifts in their own names, in ways the normative texts do not always lead one to expect (Singh 2008).

Women also wrote. Sanskrit anthologies preserve verses attributed to women poets, and the bhakti poets mentioned above composed in the regional languages. The nineteenth-century writers discussed in the previous section — Savitribai Phule, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai, who had been given the title paṇḍitā in Calcutta for her Sanskrit learning — drew on, criticised and sometimes turned against itself the textual tradition discussed in this chapter (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 15.12 From Strīdhana to Dowry
docs.text:
The gifts that the Dharmaśāstras classed as a woman’s own property — what she received at her wedding from her parents and kin — were the historical basis of the institution later called dowry. In the classical texts, such gifts belonged to the bride; the bride-price (śulka) paid by the groom’s family was condemned in the Āsura form of marriage. Over the centuries, and especially among higher castes in northern India, gifts at marriage increasingly took the form of payments demanded by the groom’s family and controlled by it, and the practice spread to many communities in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Dowry became a major cause of the indebtedness of brides’ families and of violence against married women.

Independent India responded with legislation: the Dowry Prohibition Act of 1961 forbade the giving and taking of dowry; later amendments, and the addition to the Penal Code in 1983 and 1986 of offences of cruelty by a husband or his relatives and of “dowry death”, sought to protect married women. The persistence of the practice, despite the law, shows how deeply marriage payments are embedded in social expectations. It also shows that the history of women’s property in India runs from the strīdhana of the śāstras through the changing customs of communities to the problems of the present (Agnes 1999; Kumar 1993).

docs.title: 15.13 Polygyny, Supersession and Monogamy
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras permit a man to have more than one wife, while requiring a woman to have only one husband. Manu allows a man of a higher class to take wives of lower classes in addition to a wife of his own class, and ranks the wives by class, the wife of equal class having precedence in religious rites (Manu 3.12–13; 9.85–87). The texts also allow a husband to take another wife — to “supersede” (adhivedana) his first wife — in specified circumstances. Manu permits a barren wife to be superseded in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the tenth, one who bears only daughters in the eleventh, and one who speaks unpleasantly immediately (Manu 9.81). Yājñavalkya lists grounds such as drinking, chronic illness, barrenness, hostility and extravagance, and requires that the superseded wife be maintained, failing which the husband incurs a heavy sin (Yājñ 1.73–74); she was also owed a compensatory gift (ādhivedanika), which became part of her strīdhana. The Arthaśāstra likewise requires a husband who takes another wife after waiting the prescribed period to give the first a compensatory payment in addition to her property (AŚ 3.2). These provisions protected the superseded wife’s maintenance, but they confirm that the purpose of marriage in the texts was above all the birth of sons, and that the burden of failing to produce them fell on the woman.

In practice, polygyny was mainly a practice of kings, nobles and the wealthy; inscriptions record kings with several chief queens, and ordinary households were, for economic reasons, largely monogamous. Polyandry, though forbidden by the texts, is not unknown to the tradition: in the Mahābhārata, Draupadī is the common wife of the five Pāṇḍava brothers, and the epic itself treats this as so irregular that it offers several stories to justify it. Polyandrous marriage has also been documented by ethnographers among some communities of the Himalayas and the Nilgiri hills.

Modern law moved towards monogamy. Several provinces prohibited bigamy among Hindus in the 1940s, and the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 made a second marriage during the lifetime of a spouse void and punishable for all Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs. Muslim personal law continues to permit a man to have up to four wives, subject to the Qurʾānic condition of equal treatment, a difference that has figured prominently in debates over a uniform civil code (Chapter 20). The Special Marriage Act of 1954, available to all, is monogamous.

docs.title: 15.14 Reform and Codification
docs.text: The colonial state’s interventions in family law, from the prohibition of satī (1829) to the Sarda Act (1929), were piecemeal and often contested by orthodox opinion, and each was justified by its Indian supporters partly by appeal to the śāstras themselves (Chapters 11 and 19). The comprehensive codification proposed in Ambedkar’s Hindu Code Bill, and enacted in four statutes in 1955–56 after the Bill’s defeat, is the subject of Chapter 20 (Som 1994; Newbigin 2013; Agnes 1999).

docs.title: 15.15 Assessment
docs.text: The family law of the Dharmaśāstras was a sophisticated and internally coherent system for the household of a twice-born man. It provided for the maintenance of dependants, gave women a protected category of property, regulated marriage and inheritance in detail, and embedded the whole in a ritual life that gave meaning to birth, marriage and death. It also excluded Śūdras and women from Vedic learning, made women perpetual dependants of men, condemned widows to austerity, recommended child marriage, and tied women’s sexuality to the purity of caste. Modern apologetics that emphasise the honour paid to women, the Gāndharva marriage or strīdhana, without these facts, misrepresent the system; so do polemics that ignore the variety of custom and the agency women exercised in practice. The modern history of Hindu family law has been, in large part, the history of dismantling the system’s inequalities while retaining some of its forms.

docs.title: 15.16 Summary
docs.text:
• The āśramas and saṃskāras organised the life of the twice-born man; Śūdras and women were excluded from Vedic initiation, and marriage took its place for women.

  • Marriage in the approved forms was the gift of a girl by her father, within varṇa and outside the gotra; the texts recommended child marriage, permitted polygyny, forbade widow remarriage except in Nārada and Parāśara, and did not recognise divorce in the approved forms.

  • Women had a protected category of property (strīdhana) but limited rights of inheritance, generally as a limited estate.

  • Women’s own voices and the legislation of 1829–1956 mark the long process by which this system was challenged and reformed.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Pandey (1969) describes the saṃskāras; Olivelle (1993) the āśramas. Altekar (1956) is a classic, if now dated, account of the position of women; Chakravarti (1993) and Chakravarti (2003) provide the critical framework. Leslie (1989) studies a treatise on the duties of wives, Mani (1998) the satī debate, and Soneji (2012) the devadāsīs. On reform see Kumar (1993), Agnes (1999), Newbigin (2013) and Som (1994).

docs.title: Chapter 16: Custom, Community and Local Justice
docs.text:
Most disputes in pre-modern India were never heard by a king or by a learned Brahmin judge. They were settled within families and lineages, by the elders of castes and villages, by guilds and merchant bodies, by temple authorities and by the councils of tribal communities, according to rules that were for the most part unwritten. The Dharmaśāstras acknowledged this: they recognised the customs of regions, castes and families as authoritative, and they listed family, guild and association among the tribunals entitled to decide cases (Chapter 12). This chapter examines custom as a source of law, the evidence of inscriptions for the working of local assemblies, the caste and village councils known as pañcāyats, the matrilineal and tribal systems that departed most sharply from the śāstras, the fate of custom in colonial courts, and the modern constitutional recognition of local self-government.

It is a subject on which romantic and critical views collide. Local institutions are often celebrated as a tradition of “village democracy” and of consensual justice. They were also, in many places, instruments by which dominant castes and senior men controlled others, and B. R. Ambedkar’s denunciation of the village in the Constituent Assembly (Section 16.3.4) expressed the experience of millions. Both aspects must be kept in view (Davis 2010; Galanter 1989).

docs.title: 16.1.1 The Recognition of Custom
docs.text:
The authority of custom is acknowledged from the earliest Dharmasūtras. Gautama states that the laws of regions, castes and families are authoritative if they are not contrary to the Veda, and that cultivators, traders, herdsmen, money-lenders and artisans are authorities for their own groups (GDh 11.20–21). Baudhāyana lists customs peculiar to the north and to the south and reports the view that each region should follow its own (BDh 1.2.1–4). Manu tells the king to establish the law of each group after examining “the laws of castes, of regions and of guilds, and the laws of families” (Manu 8.41), and to uphold the agreements of villages and guilds (8.219–221). The Arthaśāstra ranks custom (caritra) among the four bases of a lawsuit, below only royal edict (Chapter 12), and advises the conqueror of new territory to maintain the customs of its people (AŚ 13.5) (Lingat 1973).

The later smṛtis also recognised the bodies through which custom was applied. Nārada lists, in ascending order of authority, the family, the guild, the corporation, the judge appointed by the king and the king himself, each competent within its own sphere and each subject to review by the next; Yājñavalkya gives the first four (Nārada 1.7; Yājñ 2.30; Chapter 12). Figure 16.1 sets this hierarchy beside the institutions that the inscriptions and records discussed in this chapter show at work.

Figure 16.1. The hierarchy of tribunals in the later smṛtis (Yājñ 2.30; Nārada 1.7), from the family to the king, with examples of the corresponding bodies known from inscriptions and later records (Chapters 12 and 17). The correspondences are approximate: the texts name types of authority, not particular institutions.

docs.title: 16.1.2 Limits
docs.text: The texts also limit custom. In the theory of the sources of dharma, practice (ācāra) is authoritative only if it is the practice of the “good” or “cultured” (śiṣṭa), defined as learned Brahmins, and only if it does not contradict the Veda or the smṛtis (Chapter 9). Mīmāṃsā authors argued that a custom was valid because it implied a lost Vedic text, so that a custom with a visible worldly motive, such as greed, could not be authoritative. Medieval writers sometimes condemned southern practices, such as marriage with a maternal uncle’s daughter, which southern authors defended. The tension between the universal claims of the śāstras and the authority of local practice was never resolved in theory; in practice, custom governed most of life.

docs.title: 16.1.3 Custom as the Living Law
docs.text: Modern scholars have argued that custom, rather than the smṛtis, was the real law of most Indians. Robert Lingat described the relationship between śāstra and custom as one in which the śāstra provided the general framework and the prestige of tradition, while custom determined most concrete rules (Lingat 1973). Donald Davis, studying medieval Kerala and other regions, has shown how temple authorities, merchant groups, caste assemblies and local rulers produced and applied rules that drew on Dharmaśāstric concepts — dharma, samaya, maryādā — while answering to local interests and customs (Davis 2004); he describes Dharmaśāstra as the jurisprudence that made sense of this world of corporate law-making (Davis 2010).

docs.title: 16.2.1 The Evidence
docs.text: Inscriptions on stone and copper plates are the most important evidence for local institutions in early and medieval India. Land grants record the transfer of villages and fields, often to Brahmins or temples, and specify the rights transferred and the officials to be informed. Temple inscriptions record endowments, the duties of temple servants and the decisions of temple assemblies. Records of village assemblies, especially in the Tamil region, describe their composition and procedures.

docs.title: 16.2.2 The Cōḷa Assemblies and Uttaramerūr
docs.text:
The richest evidence comes from the Tamil country under the Pallava and Cōḷa kings, from the ninth to the thirteenth century. Two kinds of local assembly appear: the ūr, the assembly of ordinary villages of landholders, and the sabhā, the assembly of a brahmadeya, a village granted to Brahmins. Merchant towns had their own bodies (nagaram). These assemblies managed common lands and tanks, collected and remitted revenue, administered endowments, and settled disputes; they worked through committees (vāriyam) for particular tasks — tanks, gardens, justice, the annual supervision of affairs (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

The best-known records are two inscriptions of the reign of Parāntaka I, dated 919 and 921 CE, from Uttaramerūr (near Kanchipuram), a large brahmadeya village. They record the rules adopted by the village sabhā for choosing the members of its committees. The village was divided into thirty wards. To be eligible, a man had to own a specified amount of tax-paying land and a house on his own site, to be between thirty-five and seventy years old, and to know Vedic texts and their exposition; men who had served on a committee in the previous three years, who had failed to render accounts, or who had committed certain sins, and their relatives, were excluded. The names of eligible men in each ward were written on palm-leaf tickets and placed in a pot, from which a young boy drew one ticket — a procedure called kuṭavōlai (“pot-ticket”). Those chosen served for a year on the various committees.

The committees named in the inscriptions included an annual committee, which supervised the general affairs of the village; a garden committee; a tank committee, responsible for the maintenance of the irrigation tank on which the village’s agriculture depended; and a committee for the examination of gold, which certified the purity of the gold used in transactions. Members who were found guilty of misconduct were to be removed, and the rules of eligibility were to apply to future selections.

These inscriptions are a remarkable record of institutional design, with rules on eligibility, rotation, accountability and selection by lot. They have often been described as “democracy” and even as “democracy before the Greeks”. Both descriptions are misleading. Uttaramerūr’s sabhā was an assembly of Brahmin landholders in a village granted to Brahmins; the rules excluded the non-Brahmin cultivators, labourers and artisans who made up most of the village’s inhabitants, and all women; and they date from the tenth century CE, more than a thousand years after Athenian democracy. The lot was used in Athens too, for similar reasons. The Uttaramerūr rules are best understood as the self-government of a privileged corporate body, and as evidence of the sophistication of local institutions under the Cōḷas.

docs.title: 16.2.3 Other Corporate Bodies
docs.text: Inscriptions from many regions record guilds of artisans and merchants, associations of temple servants, Brahmin assemblies (mahājana), and caste bodies making rules for their members, receiving endowments and settling disputes. In western India, merchant associations called mahājan regulated trade and administered charities into the modern period (Chapter 8). Such bodies were the institutional basis of what Davis calls the “jurisprudence of corporate groups” that Dharmaśāstra presupposed (Davis 2010).

docs.title: 16.2.4 Temples as Legal Institutions
docs.text:
From the early medieval period, large temples were among the most important legal institutions of India, especially in the south. They owned land and villages, received endowments of money, cattle and gold, employed priests, cooks, musicians, dancers, accountants and guards, and lent money at interest. Their affairs were managed by committees of Brahmins, local assemblies or royal officers, and their inscriptions record rules for the conduct of rituals, the duties of servants, the investment of endowments and the punishment of those who embezzled temple property. Donald Davis has argued that temples, like guilds and castes, were corporate bodies that made and applied their own law within the framework of Dharmaśāstra (Davis 2010).

Under colonial rule, temples and their endowments became the subject of a large body of litigation and legislation. The courts recognised the deity installed in a temple as a juristic person capable of owning property — a position affirmed by the Privy Council in 1925 — with a human manager (śebait, dharmakartā) acting on its behalf; and provincial legislatures, beginning with Madras in the 1920s, created state boards to supervise the administration of Hindu religious endowments. These arrangements continue, in modified form, in independent India (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 16.3.1 The Word and the Institution
docs.text: Pañcāyat derives from pañca, “five”, and refers to a council of (in principle) five persons — the “five” (pañc) who decide a dispute or a community’s affairs. The proverb that “God speaks through the five” (pañc parameśvar) expresses the authority attributed to such bodies. In practice, the number varied, and the term covers a wide range of institutions: councils of village elders; councils of caste (jāti) elders with authority over all members of the caste in a region; ad hoc arbitration panels chosen by disputing parties; and, from the late nineteenth century, statutory village councils created by colonial and later by Indian governments.

docs.title: 16.3.2 Village Councils
docs.text: Village elders, often drawn from the dominant landholding caste, settled disputes over boundaries, water, debts, family property and minor offences, and represented the village before revenue officials. Their methods were usually conciliatory: they aimed at a settlement acceptable to the parties and to the community rather than a judgment on rights, and they relied on social pressure rather than force. Ethnographers and historians have described these processes in many regions, and have also emphasised that the elders’ authority reflected local structures of power: those without land, and especially the lowest castes, had little voice and often bore the costs of “harmony” (Galanter 1989).

docs.title: 16.3.3 Caste Councils
docs.text:
Caste councils (jāti pañcāyat) regulated the internal affairs of castes: marriage, divorce and remarriage, commensality, occupational rules, ritual observance and the punishment of breaches of caste norms. Their strongest sanction was outcasting (bahiṣkāra, “excommunication”), the exclusion of an offender and sometimes his family from eating, drinking and marrying with other members of the caste — a penalty that could be socially fatal. They could also impose fines, require feasts for the caste, and prescribe penances. Many castes, especially among cultivators, artisans and lower-status groups, allowed divorce and widow remarriage by the decision of their councils, in departure from the Dharmaśāstras.

Caste councils have a dark side, which has been widely documented. They enforced caste boundaries, punished intercaste relationships and resisted the claims of lower castes to equal treatment. In parts of northern India, clan-based councils known as khap pañcāyats have in recent decades issued decrees against marriages within the same clan or village or across caste lines, and some such marriages have ended in so-called “honour killings”. In Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court held that the interference of such assemblies with the marriages of consenting adults is illegal and laid down preventive and remedial measures.

docs.title: 16.3.4 Gandhi and Ambedkar
docs.text:
The village pañcāyat became a central symbol in twentieth-century political thought. M. K. Gandhi, in Hind Swaraj (1909) and many later writings, idealised the self-governing village as the basis of a decentralised, non-violent polity — grām svarāj, village self-rule — in which the pañcāyat would administer justice and the economy would rest on agriculture and village industry. His village was not the village as it was; he insisted that untouchability must be abolished and the village reformed (Gandhi 1909).

B. R. Ambedkar rejected this ideal. Introducing the Draft Constitution in the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948, he said: “What is the village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism? I am glad that the Draft Constitution has discarded the village and adopted the individual as its unit.” For Ambedkar, the village was where caste was most oppressive and where Dalits were most vulnerable; to give it power was to give power to those who dominated it (Constituent Assembly of India 1948). The Constitution as adopted in 1949 compromised: Article 40, among the non-justiciable Directive Principles, directed the state to organise village pañcāyats, but the basic unit of the Constitution was the individual citizen with enforceable rights.

docs.title: 16.3.5 Caste Disputes and the Right- and Left-Hand Divisions
docs.text: Inscriptions and later records show that disputes between castes over status and privileges were a recurrent feature of social life, and that kings and local assemblies were called upon to settle them. In the Tamil country, from about the eleventh century, many castes were grouped into two broad divisions, the “right-hand” (valaṅkai) and “left-hand” (iṭaṅkai) castes, which competed for ritual and social privileges — the right to ride in palanquins, to use certain musical instruments at weddings, to take particular routes in processions. Such disputes were still being brought before the East India Company’s officers in Madras in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They show caste not as a fixed order derived from the śāstras but as a field of continual negotiation, conflict and adjudication, in which local and royal authorities decided claims according to custom and power.

docs.title: 16.3.6 Pañcāyats in the Maratha State
docs.text: The records of the Maratha state under the Peśvās in the eighteenth century provide some of the best evidence for how pañcāyats worked in practice. Civil disputes — over land, debts, inheritance, caste rights and village offices — were commonly referred by government officers to a pañcāyat of the parties’ peers, chosen with their consent; its decision was recorded and enforced by the state. Criminal matters, by contrast, were dealt with by government officials. British administrators in the Deccan after 1818, notably Mountstuart Elphinstone, at first sought to preserve the pañcāyat system, before replacing it with courts on the Company’s model.

docs.title: 16.4 Matriliny in Kerala
docs.text:
The most striking departure from the patrilineal norms of the Dharmaśāstras was the matrilineal system of Kerala and the adjoining Tulu country. Among the Nāyars and several other communities — including some Īḻava groups and the Muslim Māppiḷas of north Malabar, and, in Tulu Nadu, the Bunts under the related aḷiyasantāna system — descent and property passed through women. The basic unit was the taravāṭ, a matrilineal joint family consisting of a woman, her children, her daughters’ children and her brothers, holding property in common under the management of the senior male member (kāraṇavan). A man’s heirs were his sisters’ children, not his own. Marriage took the form of sambandham, a union in which the husband visited the wife in her taravāṭ and had no rights over her property or children. The Nambūtiri Brahmins, by contrast, were patrilineal, and among them only the eldest son married within the caste; younger sons formed sambandham unions with Nāyar women (Arunima 2003).

The Dharmaśāstras had no place for such a system, and British courts at first struggled with it; but they eventually recognised marumakkattāyam as valid custom. From the late nineteenth century, under pressure from reformers within the communities, from economic change and from colonial notions of the “natural” family, the system was transformed by legislation. Laws in Malabar, Travancore and Cochin recognised sambandham as marriage, gave husbands and fathers rights and obligations, and permitted the partition of taravāṭs; the Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act of 1975 finally abolished the joint family system. G. Arunima’s study shows how this transformation, often presented as modernisation, also reduced the independent property rights and social standing of Nāyar women (Arunima 2003).

docs.title: 16.5 Tribal Customary Law
docs.text:
India’s Scheduled Tribes — several hundred communities with their own languages, religions and social organisation — have their own customary laws, transmitted orally and administered by their own institutions. Among the Santals of eastern India, for example, the village headman (mãjhi) and the council of a group of villages under a paragana settle disputes and enforce customary rules on marriage, inheritance and land; the Santal rebellion (hul) of 1855–56 was directed in part against the moneylenders, traders and courts that undermined their institutions. The Khasi of Meghalaya are matrilineal, with ancestral property passing to the youngest daughter, and their villages and clusters of villages are governed by councils (dorbar). The Adi of Arunachal Pradesh hold village assemblies (kebang) that decide disputes and community affairs. Naga villages are governed by councils of elders according to customary law.

Colonial rule often undermined these institutions. The extension of revenue settlements, forest laws and courts into tribal areas exposed communities to moneylenders, traders and landholders from outside, and to the loss of land through debt and litigation. Rebellions such as the Santal hul and the movement led by Birsa Munda among the Mundas of Chotanagpur in the 1890s were in part responses to this process. The colonial state eventually enacted protective tenancy laws, such as the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, which restricted the transfer of tribal land, and recognised customary institutions such as the Munda and Oraon village headmen; independent India extended such protections.

These systems should not be described as variants of Dharmaśāstra, nor romanticised as uniformly egalitarian; like other customary systems, they distribute rights by gender, age and lineage. They are, however, distinct legal traditions with their own principles. The colonial state recognised some of them, for instance by excluding certain hill areas from the ordinary courts, and the Constitution protects them in several ways: the Fifth Schedule provides for the administration of Scheduled Areas in central India, the Sixth Schedule creates autonomous district councils with powers over customary law in parts of the north-east, and Article 371A provides that no Act of Parliament on Naga religious or social practices, customary law and procedure or ownership of land shall apply to Nagaland unless the state’s legislative assembly so decides. The Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act of 1996 (PESA) requires state laws on pañcāyats in Scheduled Areas to respect customary law and the traditional management of community resources.

docs.title: 16.6 Custom in the Colonial Courts
docs.text:
The colonial courts, required to apply “Hindu law” and “Muhammadan law” in matters of succession, marriage and religious usage (Chapter 19), had to decide what weight to give to custom. In a famous judgment of 1868 (Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy), the Privy Council declared that “under the Hindu system of law, clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law”. The courts developed tests for a valid custom: it must be ancient, certain, reasonable, continuous and not opposed to public policy — tests drawn from English law on local customs. In practice, proving a custom was difficult and expensive, and the courts’ preference for written authority tended to favour the textual law of the śāstras as interpreted by Brahmin experts, so that many lower-caste groups were drawn towards Brahmanical norms. Scholars such as Bernard Cohn and Marc Galanter have described this process as the “Brahmanisation” or “textualisation” of Hindu law (Cohn 1996; Galanter 1989).

The Punjab took a different path. The Punjab Laws Act of 1872 directed the courts to apply custom, rather than Hindu or Islamic law, in matters of succession, marriage and other personal relations for the agricultural tribes of the province. Officers compiled records of customary law (riwāj-i-ām) during land settlements, and W. H. Rattigan’s Digest of Civil Law for the Punjab (1880) systematised them. The result was a body of “customary law” that was in part created by the colonial state, and that often limited the rights of women to inherit land in order to keep land within male lineages.

docs.title: 16.7 Local Self-Government in the Constitution
docs.text:
After independence, community development programmes and the recommendations of the Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) led many states to create elected pañcāyat institutions, with uneven results. The Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act of 1992, which came into force in April 1993, gave these bodies constitutional status. It inserted Part IX into the Constitution, providing for a three-tier system of elected pañcāyats at the village, intermediate and district levels; for the gram sabhā, the assembly of all voters in a village, as the base of the system (Article 243A); for regular elections under state election commissions; and for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population and of not less than one-third of seats and chairpersonships for women (Article 243D). Many states have since raised the reservation for women to one-half. The Seventy-fourth Amendment did the same for urban local bodies.

The reservation of seats for women has brought very large numbers of women into elected local office. Research has found that it can change the priorities of local government: a study of village councils in West Bengal and Rajasthan by Raghabendra Chattopadhyay and Esther Duflo found that councils headed by women invested more in the public goods that women in those villages had identified as priorities (Chattopadhyay and Duflo 2004). Other studies have described the obstacles women face, including the exercise of power by male relatives in their name. Statutory pañcāyats, unlike the councils of the past, have no general judicial powers; disputes are handled by the courts, by the lok adālats established under the Legal Services Authorities Act of 1987 to encourage settlement, and by the village courts provided for by the Gram Nyayalayas Act of 2008.

docs.title: 16.8 Legal Pluralism in Modern India
docs.text: Scholars of modern Indian law have described its many coexisting normative orders — state law, religious personal laws, caste and community rules, tribal customary law and the informal settlement of disputes — as a case of legal pluralism. Marc Galanter argued that the colonial and post-colonial state gradually displaced the “indigenous” legal orders of caste and village while also preserving them in modified forms, and that ordinary Indians moved between official and unofficial forums according to their interests and resources (Galanter 1989). Others have emphasised the way in which state law itself creates and shapes “custom” by recognising some practices and not others. The classical recognition of the customs of regions, castes and families is sometimes invoked in these debates as an Indian precedent for pluralism. The precedent is a limited one: the classical pluralism was organised by hierarchy, while modern pluralism must answer to the Constitution’s guarantee of equal rights to every individual, including those whom communities and customs disadvantage.

docs.title: 16.9 Assessment
docs.text: The history of custom and local justice in India shows a legal world far more varied than the Dharmaśāstras alone suggest. Corporate bodies of many kinds made and applied their own rules; matrilineal and tribal systems followed principles of their own; and the śāstras themselves, with their recognition of custom, acknowledged this plurality. The same history shows how local institutions could entrench the power of dominant castes and senior men, and how colonial courts and legislatures transformed custom even as they claimed to preserve it. The modern constitutional settlement — individual rights enforceable against communities, combined with elected local government and protection for tribal customary law — reflects the arguments of both Gandhi and Ambedkar, and the tension between them remains unresolved.

docs.title: 16.10 Summary
docs.text:
• The Dharmaśāstras recognised the customs of regions, castes, families and guilds as authoritative within limits; in practice custom governed most of life.

  • Inscriptions show village and Brahmin assemblies, guilds, merchant bodies and temple authorities making and applying rules; the Uttaramerūr inscriptions (919, 921) record the selection by lot of committees of a Brahmin village assembly — an example of corporate self-government, not of democracy.

  • Caste and village councils (pañcāyats) settled disputes and enforced caste norms, including by outcasting; their coercive side persists in contemporary caste and clan councils.

  • Matrilineal systems in Kerala and the customary laws of tribal communities departed sharply from the śāstras; colonial and post-colonial law first recognised and then transformed them, while the Constitution protects tribal customary law in specified areas.

  • Gandhi idealised the self-governing village; Ambedkar denounced it as a den of caste oppression. The Seventy-third Amendment (1992) gave elected pañcāyats constitutional status, with reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On custom in the Dharmaśāstras, see Lingat (1973) and Davis (2010), and on medieval Kerala Davis (2004); on the Cōḷa assemblies, Nilakanta Sastri (1955). Arunima (2003) studies the transformation of Kerala matriliny; Galanter (1989) and Cohn (1996) the colonial treatment of custom. Chattopadhyay and Duflo (2004) is an influential study of women’s reservation in pañcāyats.

docs.title: Chapter 17: Kingdoms on Record: Charters, Scribes and Statecraft, c. 500–1700
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra and the Dharmaśāstras describe what kings and courts ought to do. For the thousand years between the Guptas and the Mughals, another kind of evidence survives in quantity: the records that kingdoms themselves produced. Tens of thousands of copper-plate charters and stone inscriptions record grants of land, endowments, settlements of disputes and the orders of kings and officials; formularies preserve the models of deeds and letters that scribes copied; and a few historians and royal authors wrote about government from experience. This chapter reads that evidence for what it shows of law and polity in the regional kingdoms of early medieval and medieval India. It describes the copper-plate charter as a legal instrument; the procedure for buying land recorded in the Gupta-period plates of Bengal; the scribes and record-keepers on whom government depended; the Gujarati formulary called the Lekhapaddhati; the medieval Sanskrit treatises on kingship; Kalhaṇa’s history of Kashmir; the Vijayanagara empire with its royal manual of statecraft; the lineage polity of the Rajput kingdoms; the Ahom kingdom of Assam, organised on principles of its own; and the settlements of disputes between communities that kings recorded in stone.

Several related subjects are treated elsewhere and are not repeated here: the debate among historians about the nature of the early medieval state — feudal, segmentary or integrative — in Chapter 5; the fiscal terms of the land grants in Chapter 6; and the village and temple assemblies of the Tamil country in Chapter 16. The records also have their own biases. They were made for those who received land and privileges — Brahmins, temples, monasteries, officials and merchants — and they speak of cultivators, labourers and artisans mainly as the bearers of dues that passed with the land. They are nevertheless the closest view we have of government at work before the Persian archives of the Mughal period (Salomon 1998; Sircar 1965).

docs.title: 17.1 The Charter as a Legal Instrument
17.1.1 What the Law Books Required
docs.text: Yājñavalkya tells the king who has given land or made a permanent endowment (nibandha) to have a written record made, so that future good kings may know of it. The record is to be on cloth or on a copper plate, marked above with the king’s seal; it should name the king’s ancestors and the king himself, state the extent of the gift and describe its boundaries, and bear the king’s own signature and the date, so that the charter (śāsana) is firm (Yājñ 1.318–320). Later smṛtis classify the royal charter among the kinds of document recognised in court (Chapter 12), and Manu lists those who make forged royal charters (kūṭaśāsanakartṛ) among the offenders whom the king should put to death (Manu 9.232). These rules describe, in outline, the charters that survive in large numbers from the fourth century onward.

docs.title: 17.1.2 The Form of a Copper-Plate Grant
docs.text:
A typical copper-plate charter consists of one or more plates strung on a ring that carries the royal seal. Its text follows a pattern that varied by dynasty and period but kept its main parts for more than a thousand years (Figure 17.1). The genealogy in praise-poetry (praśasti) could run, in later charters, to dozens of verses and served the dynasty’s claims to legitimacy; the operative order usually names an auspicious occasion, such as an eclipse, a solstice or a festival, and the religious merit of the king and his parents as the purpose of the gift; the rights and exemptions follow the fiscal formulae described in Chapter 6; and the imprecatory verses (Chapter 5) are followed by an appeal to future kings to maintain the gift.

Figure 17.1. The parts of a typical copper-plate land grant, in the order in which they are inscribed, and (left) a schematic of a set of plates on a seal ring. The pattern is a composite: the order, length and wording of the parts vary by dynasty and period (Sircar 1965; Salomon 1998).

The charter was therefore at once a title deed, a public notice and a political statement. As a title deed it defined the land and the rights, and it was kept by the recipient’s family, sometimes for many centuries; as a notice it informed officials and villagers of their new obligations; as a political statement it recorded the dynasty’s descent, victories and piety. The rights it conveyed were described as perpetual, to last “as long as the moon, the sun and the earth”, and were often granted according to “the rule of the fallow land” (bhūmicchidranyāya), a phrase whose exact sense is debated but which seems to have assimilated the grantee’s title to the right of the person who first brings waste land under cultivation (Sircar 1965; Salomon 1998).

docs.title: 17.1.3 Resumption, Confirmation and Forgery
docs.text: The imprecatory verses were needed because gifts were in fact resumed. Later kings confirmed some earlier grants, sometimes by issuing new plates, and ignored or cancelled others; some charters record that a gift was renewed after the original plates had been lost or destroyed. The value of a charter as evidence made forgery profitable, and epigraphists have identified many spurious plates, some attributed to early kings by much later engravers, others enlarging the boundaries or rights of a genuine grant. The forgers usually betray themselves by anachronistic script, language or titles, and by genealogies that do not fit the dynasty they claim. The smṛtis’ insistence on the seal and the king’s signature, and Manu’s capital penalty, show that the problem was recognised early. In the Tamil country, inscriptions on temple walls served as a public archive of endowments and decisions, and when a temple was rebuilt its earlier inscriptions were sometimes recopied on the new structure so that the record of its rights would not be lost (Nilakanta Sastri 1955).

docs.title: 17.2 Buying Land in Gupta Bengal
docs.text:
A rare view of local administration at work is given by a group of copper plates from northern Bengal, above all the five plates found at Damodarpur (now in Bangladesh), dated in Gupta years that range from the mid-fifth to the mid-sixth century CE. They record not royal gifts but purchases of land by private persons who wished to endow Brahmins or a temple, and the procedure they describe is consistent from plate to plate.

The would-be purchaser applied to the district office (adhikaraṇa) at Koṭivarṣa, the headquarters of a district (viṣaya) in the province (bhukti) of Puṇḍravardhana. The office was headed by the district officer (viṣayapati), appointed by the provincial governor, who sat with a board of four: the chief banker or head of the town’s guilds (nagaraśreṣṭhin), the chief caravan merchant (prathama-sārthavāha), the chief artisan (prathama-kulika) and the chief scribe (prathama-kāyastha). The application named the land wanted and its purpose and offered to pay the price at the rate customary in the district. The record-keepers (pustapāla) then examined their registers and confirmed that the land was fallow and unsettled and yielded no revenue, so that its sale would cause the king no loss and would bring him a share of the religious merit of the gift. The office accepted the price, the land was measured out in the presence of village elders and householders, and the transaction was recorded on copper. The price is stated in gold coins (dīnāra) per unit of land (kulyavāpa); in different plates of the region it is two, three or four dīnāras, perhaps according to locality and the quality of the land. The purchased land was usually held as a perpetual endowment (nīvīdharma), of which the capital could not be alienated and only the yield was enjoyed.

These records show several things that the śāstras do not. The district office was not simply a royal bureaucracy: the representatives of the town’s bankers, merchants and artisans sat beside the king’s officer, so that the leading commercial groups of the district shared in its government (Volume 19 of this series discusses these groups as economic actors). Land was registered, and the registers were consulted before a transfer; the claim that waste land belonged to the king, whose consent was needed for its sale, was put into practice. And the language of merit framed the whole transaction, so that the sale of state land to private donors could be presented as a pious act in which the king shared (Sircar 1965; Singh 2008).

docs.title: 17.3 Scribes and Record-Keepers
docs.text:
Government by charter and register required a class of professional writers. The Arthaśāstra already describes a records office (akṣapaṭala) in which the accounts of departments and the customs of regions, villages, castes and families were registered (AŚ 2.7; Chapter 6). In the Gupta period the word kāyastha appears as the title of a scribe or clerk, as on the Koṭivarṣa board. Over the following centuries it came to name hereditary communities of scribes and administrators in northern and eastern India, whose place in the varṇa order the Dharmaśāstra writers found hard to fix. Other regions had their equivalents, such as the village accountant (karaṇam in Telugu, kaṇakkaṉ in Tamil), who kept the records of fields and dues and in the Telugu country was often a Brahmin, and the hereditary record-keepers of districts in the Deccan (Chapter 18). Their skills passed easily from one regime to another. Under the sultans and the Mughals, Hindu scribes learned Persian and staffed the revenue and accounting departments; under the British they became clerks of the courts and the collectorates.

The power of these men over the records made them objects of suspicion. Yājñavalkya tells the king to protect his subjects when they are oppressed by cheats, thieves, evil-doers, violent criminals and others, “and especially by kāyasthas” (Yājñ 1.336). Kalhaṇa’s history of Kashmir (Section 17.6) is full of invective against the kāyastha officials who, in his view, squeezed the cultivators on behalf of greedy kings, and a century earlier the Kashmiri satirist Kṣemendra had mocked the scribe as a figure of rapacity and fraud in his Narmamālā. The hostility was partly the resentment of Brahmin authors towards a rival literate group; it also reflects a real feature of agrarian government, in which the clerk who measured the field and wrote the assessment held the cultivator’s livelihood in his pen. Kashmir also produced a formulary for such men, the Lokaprakāśa, attributed to Kṣemendra, which contains models of documents and administrative vocabulary; its present text was enlarged in the Sultanate period and contains Persian terms, showing how such handbooks were kept up to date as the language of government changed.

docs.title: 17.4 The Lekhapaddhati: A Scribe’s Formulary from Gujarat
docs.text:
The fullest picture of the documents that medieval government and commerce produced comes from Gujarat. The Lekhapaddhati (“method of documents”), known in a related form as the Lekhapañcāśikā, is a collection of model documents compiled for the use of scribes and preserved in manuscripts of about the fifteenth century. Many of its models carry dates, and most belong to the period of the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) and Vāghelā kings, roughly the tenth to the thirteenth century, though some are later. Its language is a Sanskrit heavily mixed with Old Gujarati administrative and commercial terms. First edited in 1925 and translated into English by Pushpa Prasad, it is one of the very few substantial bodies of non-epigraphic documents surviving from early medieval India (Prasad 2007).

The models fall into two broad groups. The documents of state include royal land grants, orders appointing governors and officials, letters from the king to his officers, and treaties between kings, which set out the terms of alliance or submission and the obligations of each side — the six measures of the Arthaśāstra (Chapter 7) in the form of working instruments. They also name the departments (karaṇa) through which the kingdom was administered, among them offices for trade, for the ports, for customs and for the mint. The private documents include deeds of sale of houses and land, mortgages and pledges, loan agreements with their interest and sureties, deeds of partition, acknowledgements of deposit and letters of many kinds. Their clauses correspond closely to the smṛtis’ requirements for a valid document — the names of the parties and their fathers, the date, the object, the terms and the attesting witnesses (Chapter 12) — and show that the śāstric law of contract and evidence was part of the working knowledge of the scribes who drew up ordinary transactions (Chapter 13).

Among the private documents are deeds for the sale of women as household slaves. They record the purchase, list the domestic and agricultural labour the woman must perform, and secure the buyer’s control over her. Pushpa Prasad has drawn attention to these deeds as evidence of the harsh condition of female slaves in thirteenth-century Gujarat. They are a necessary counterweight to accounts of medieval law drawn only from the śāstras, whose provisions on slavery (Chapter 13) say little about how slaves were actually bought and held.

docs.title: 17.5 Medieval Treatises on Kingship
docs.text:
The nīti tradition continued in the regional courts (Chapter 3), but its most characteristic medieval products were encyclopaedic. Three kinds of work may be distinguished.

The first is the royal encyclopaedia composed in the name of a king. The Mānasollāsa (“Delight of the Mind”, 1131), attributed to the Cālukya king Someśvara III of Kalyāṇa, is arranged in five books of twenty chapters each, on the qualities by which a king gains a kingdom, the means of securing it, and the enjoyments, amusements and sports that it makes possible. Its first two books restate the doctrines of the seven constituents, the six measures and the four means, with practical chapters on forts, the treasury and the army; its later books, on the palace, food, dress, music, painting, horses, elephants and games, present kingship as a courtly culture as much as an art of government. Daud Ali has shown how such texts, read with inscriptions and court poetry, describe a court society whose members were bound to the king by a cultivated ethic of service, refinement and loyalty (Ali 2004).

The second is the rājadharma section of the great Dharmaśāstra digests. Lakṣmīdhara, minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra of Kanauj (r. c. 1114–1155), devoted one of the fourteen books of his Kṛtyakalpataru to rājadharma, gathering verses from the Mahābhārata, the smṛtis and the Purāṇas on the king’s qualities, the consecration, ministers, forts, the treasury, foreign policy and the rites that protect the kingdom. Caṇḍeśvara in fourteenth-century Mithilā (Rājanītiratnākara), Mitra Miśra in seventeenth-century Orchha (the Rājanītiprakāśa, part of his Vīramitrodaya) and Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa for Bhagavantadeva, a Sengar chief of Bhareh near the Chambal (the Nītimayūkha, part of his Bhagavantabhāskara) continued the genre. Their method was that of the digest: to arrange and harmonise authoritative verses, with brief comment, under topical headings. They give little direct information about the kingdoms of their own time, and some were written for rulers who were themselves vassals of the sultans or the Mughals. Yet their concern to define the duties of a king, and the rites of royal consecration and protection, shows that the śāstric model of kingship remained a resource for rulers who wished to present themselves as kings according to dharma.

The third kind is the work written by or for a ruler on the basis of experience. Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s Āmuktamālyada, discussed below, is the outstanding example; the Marathi Ājñāpatra of the early eighteenth century belongs to the same practical genre (Chapter 18). Works of this kind are rare, and for that reason valuable: they show how the categories of the nīti tradition were applied by men who actually governed.

docs.title: 17.6 A Historian’s Kingdom: Kalhaṇa’s Kashmir
docs.text:
Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (“River of Kings”, 1148–49) is the nearest thing in Sanskrit to a political history written from the inside, and Chapter 5 has introduced it as a critic of kings. Its value for the history of polity lies in what it shows of the working of one kingdom over several centuries. Kalhaṇa, the son of a minister, says in his introductory verses that he consulted the works of earlier chroniclers and the inscriptions recording royal foundations and grants, and his eighth and last book, covering his own lifetime, is a detailed and often eyewitness account of court politics.

Several features of the Kashmiri state stand out. Royal power rested on the agricultural surplus of a narrow valley, and the chronicle repeatedly links good government with the protection of cultivators and bad government with their oppression by revenue officers. The landholders called Ḍāmaras, who controlled the countryside with armed followings, appear as a power that kings could neither do without nor fully subdue, and much of Kalhaṇa’s account of the eleventh and twelfth centuries is a story of royal campaigns against them. In the capital, the palace guard known as the Tantrins made and unmade kings in the early tenth century, and Kalhaṇa describes them as virtually selling the throne. Queen Diddā, who ruled first as regent and then in her own name until 1003, appears as a capable and ruthless ruler who held the kingdom together through ministers she raised and destroyed. And the officials of the treasury and revenue — the kāyasthas whom Kalhaṇa detested — appear as the indispensable agents of every regime, devising new exactions for fiscally hard-pressed kings.

Kalhaṇa judges this history by the standards of rājadharma and of karma: kings fall through their own vices and the misdeeds of their ministers, and the good king protects his subjects and honours Brahmins and temples. But his account also gives weight to forces that a purely moral account would ignore — the Ḍāmaras, the guards, the bureaucracy, famine and flood. The chronicle was continued under the sultans by Jonarāja and Śrīvara (Chapter 18) and was translated into Persian at Akbar’s court, so that the Sanskrit tradition of royal history passed into the historiography of the Mughals (Stein 1900).

docs.title: 17.7 Vijayanagara: Empire, Nāyakas and a King’s Advice
17.7.1 The State
docs.text:
The Vijayanagara state, founded around 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Saṅgama family in the aftermath of the Delhi Sultanate’s southern campaigns, became one of the largest kingdoms in the history of the peninsula and survived, in reduced form, after its defeat in 1565 until the mid-seventeenth century. Its kings used the full range of Sanskrit royal titles and also called themselves “sultan among Hindu kings” (hindurāya-suratrāṇa), a title that shows how the political vocabulary of the sultanates had entered southern kingship. Its records — several thousand inscriptions in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit — and the accounts of Portuguese and Persian visitors describe a state in which the king’s power rested on military chiefs (nāyakas) who held territories (amaram) in return for maintaining troops and paying a share of the revenue, while temples, Brahmin settlements and local assemblies continued to manage much of the agrarian economy. Volume 20 of this series describes the military side of this system and Volume 19 the economy.

Historians disagree about how centralised the state was. Burton Stein, extending his segmentary model of the Cōḷa state (Chapter 5), described a kingdom in which the king’s ritual sovereignty, displayed in great festivals such as the Mahānavamī at the capital, held together chiefs whose real power was local; others have stressed the empire’s fiscal reach, its control of the trade in warhorses and its military organisation (Stein 1989). Cynthia Talbot’s study of the preceding Kākatīya kingdom in Andhra shows that the nāyaka relationship already existed there in the thirteenth century, as a personal bond of service between a king and warriors of varied social origins, recorded in inscriptions that celebrate the warriors’ loyalty and their gifts to temples (Talbot 2001). In the Nāyaka kingdoms that succeeded Vijayanagara in the Tamil country — Madurai, Tanjavur and Gingee — a new style of kingship emerged, which V. Narayana Rao, David Shulman and Sanjay Subrahmanyam have described as expressed through lavish giving, court spectacle and a self-confident Telugu court culture, owing more to the values of warriors and merchants than to the Brahmanical model of the śāstras (Narayana Rao et al. 1992).

docs.title: 17.7.2 Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s Āmuktamālyada
docs.text:
The most celebrated ruler of Vijayanagara, Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529), composed in Telugu a long devotional poem, the Āmuktamālyada (“She who gave the garland she had worn”), on the story of the Tamil saint Āṇṭāḷ. Into its fourth canto, within the story of the Vaiṣṇava teacher Yāmuna, who had been a king before he renounced the world, he set some eighty verses on rājanīti. The passage draws on the Sanskrit nīti tradition but speaks with the voice of a practising ruler (Reddy 2010). Among its best-known counsels, it advises the king to increase the prosperity of the kingdom by extending irrigation through tanks and channels and by easing the burdens of poor cultivators; to govern his ports so as to increase the import of horses, elephants, gems, sandalwood and pearls; to attach to himself the foreign merchants who bring horses and elephants, so that their goods do not go to his enemies; to protect, in a manner suited to their customs, people who come from other lands fleeing famine, pestilence or other calamity; and to deal with the forest peoples on the margins of the kingdom by winning their trust rather than by force alone. Other verses concern the choice and supervision of ministers and officials.

Several of these counsels repeat the Arthaśāstra’s concerns — the treasury, the countryside, the forest peoples, the control of officials — but their emphases reflect the circumstances of a sixteenth-century southern empire: dependence on imported warhorses, competition with the Deccan sultanates for the loyalty of merchants and soldiers, and the need to bring new land under the plough. Narayana Rao and Subrahmanyam have argued that such passages, together with Telugu works on nīti reaching back to Baddena’s Nītiśāstramuktāvali of the Kākatīya period, show a distinct body of political thought in early modern South India, concerned with prudent statecraft in a competitive world more than with the ritual order of varṇa (Narayana Rao and Subrahmanyam 2009).

docs.title: 17.8 Lineage and Service: The Rajput Kingdoms
docs.text:
The Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan and central India — Mewar, Marwar, Amber and many smaller states — were organised around the lineage. A ruler was the head of a clan, and much of the land of the kingdom was held by his kinsmen and by the chiefs of allied clans, who owed him military service and attendance at court in return for estates (later called ṭhikānas) that passed from father to son, subject to the ruler’s recognition of each new holder. Sovereignty was in this sense shared within the brotherhood (bhāībandh), and succession disputes, the partition of estates among brothers and the ranking of chiefs at court were the stuff of politics. The ideal that bound the system was loyalty to one’s master (svāmidharma) and the honour of the warrior, celebrated in the genealogies and praise-poetry of the bards (Cāraṇs and Bhāṭs), whose role as keepers of lineage and reputation also made them guarantors of agreements: a bard who stood surety could threaten to wound or kill himself if the agreement was broken, bringing the guilt of his blood on the defaulter.

From Akbar’s reign, most Rajput rulers entered Mughal service as manṣabdārs, often sealed by marriage alliances (Chapter 18). Their ancestral kingdoms were then treated as hereditary assignments (watan jāgīr) within the empire, which allowed them to rule at home much as before while serving the emperor elsewhere. The Mughal connection also brought Persianate methods of record-keeping. Muhaṇot Naiṇsī (1610–1670), minister of the Rāṭhōṛ ruler of Jodhpur, compiled in Rajasthani both a chronicle of the Rajput clans and a survey of the districts of Marwar (Mārvāṛ rā Parganāṃ rī Vigat) that lists villages, their revenue, their principal castes and the history of their holders — an administrative record comparable in purpose, if not in scale, to Abu’l Faẓl’s statistics of the empire. The Rajput polity, with its shared sovereignty, its bonds of loyalty and its compromises with the Mughals, is a further example of how far actual Indian kingdoms departed from the model of a single king ruling through salaried ministers (Kulke 1995; Richards 1993).

docs.title: 17.9 The Ahom State in Assam
docs.text:
At the other end of the subcontinent, the Brahmaputra valley was ruled for six centuries by a dynasty that owed little to the śāstric model of the state. Its history is followed here to its end in the 1820s, beyond the period of this chapter, because the Ahom kingdom outlived the Mughals and has no other place in the book. The Ahoms, a Tai-speaking people, entered the valley under their leader Sukaphā in the thirteenth century and ruled until the Burmese invasions of 1817–1826, after which the valley passed to the British by the Treaty of Yandabo (1826); upper Assam was finally annexed in 1838. The king (svargadeva, “lord of heaven”) ruled with a council of great nobles, among whom three hereditary counsellors — the Burhāgohāin, the Borgohāin and the Borpātrogohāin — held offices reserved for particular Ahom clans, and from the seventeenth century a chief minister, the Borbaruā, and a governor of the lower valley, the Borphukan, were added. Succession was confined to princes without physical blemish, so that rival claimants were sometimes mutilated to disqualify them.

The foundation of the state was the system of compulsory service already mentioned in Volume 20 of this series. Every able-bodied adult man was registered as a paik and grouped with two or three others in a unit (got), one of whose members served the state in turn — as soldier, labourer on roads and embankments, or artisan — while the others cultivated his land; in return each paik held a fixed allotment of rice land from the state. Paiks were organised in larger bodies (khel) under officers whose titles stated the number of men they commanded, from twenty to several thousand. The kingdom thus raised armies and built its great roads and embankments with little use of money, and its registers of men were as important as other kingdoms’ registers of land. The Ahoms also kept chronicles (buraṇjī), first in the Tai Ahom language and later in Assamese, compiled from court records at royal command; they are among the few bodies of pre-colonial Indian historical writing produced by the state itself.

From the seventeenth century the Ahom kings adopted Hindu rites and patronised both Śākta temples and the Vaiṣṇava monasteries (sattras) founded by the followers of Śaṅkaradeva, and Brahmin advisers brought Sanskrit models of kingship to the court. The tensions of this system — the burden of service on the paiks, and conflict between the court and some of the Vaiṣṇava sattras — broke out in the Moāmariā rebellion of the later eighteenth century, which weakened the kingdom before the Burmese invasions (Gait 1906). The Ahom state is a reminder that Indian polities included kingdoms organised on principles of their own, in which labour service and lineage counted for more than the categories of the Arthaśāstra.

docs.title: 17.10 Kings as Arbiters: Settlements in Stone
docs.text:
Inscriptions also record kings acting in the role that the śāstras assign them, as arbiters of disputes between groups, and they show the forms such settlements took. A well-known example is an edict of the Vijayanagara king Bukka I of 1368, found at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa. The Jains of the kingdom had complained of injuries done to them by the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. The king, according to the inscription, summoned the leaders of both communities, placed the hand of the Jains in the hand of the Vaiṣṇavas, and declared that there was no difference between the two faiths: the Jains were to continue their worship with its customary honours, the Vaiṣṇavas were to protect them, and anyone who violated the settlement was to be treated as a traitor to the king and the community. A levy on Jain households was assigned to pay for guards at the Jain shrine and for the repair of temples. The settlement combines the king’s command with an agreement between the parties, and it records the agreement in a public and permanent form.

Other inscriptions record agreements made by communities and given royal sanction. An inscription of 1425 at Virinchipuram, of the reign of Devarāya II, records that the Brahmins of the Paḍaivīḍu kingdom, a province of the Vijayanagara state — Kannaḍa, Tamil, Telugu and Lāṭa (Gujarati) Brahmins of all gotras, sūtras and śākhās — agreed that marriages among them should be made by the gift of the bride alone (kanyādāna), without payment, and that anyone who took or gave gold for a bride would be liable to punishment by the king and expelled from the Brahmin community. Such records show caste and community bodies making rules for their members (Chapter 16) and seeking royal enforcement, and they show the kingdom’s authority working through those bodies rather than over them. They are the concrete form of the śāstras’ instruction that the king should uphold the agreements of castes, guilds and villages (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 17.11 Assessment
docs.text: The records of the regional kingdoms qualify the picture drawn from the śāstras in three ways. First, they show the śāstric law in use: Yājñavalkya’s rules for royal charters and the smṛtis’ requirements for valid documents, debts and pledges were the working knowledge of scribes and officials. Second, they show institutions that the śāstras hardly mention: district offices with merchant members, record-keepers and their registers, hereditary communities of scribes, formularies, treaties drawn up in standard form, and the bonds of service between kings and military chiefs that held the larger kingdoms together. Third, they show the costs of these arrangements to people who appear in the records only as bearers of dues — cultivators transferred with the land, women sold by deed, villagers squeezed by officials — and they preserve critical voices, such as Kalhaṇa’s, that condemned the abuses. Kingship in these centuries drew on the old categories of rājadharma and nīti while adapting them; in the Deccan and the south it shared a vocabulary with the sultanates described in the next chapter.

docs.title: 17.12 Summary
docs.text:
• Copper-plate charters were at once title deeds, public notices and dynastic statements; district offices, record-keepers, scribes and their formularies show the śāstric law of documents in daily use.

  • Medieval works on kingship range from royal encyclopaedias and the rājadharma books of the digests to Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s counsel from experience; Kalhaṇa judged Kashmiri kings by rājadharma while recording the power of landholders, guards and officials.

  • Vijayanagara, the Nāyaka and Rajput kingdoms and the Ahom state rested on bonds of service, shared sovereignty or registered labour rather than on the single king and salaried ministers of the śāstras.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On inscriptions as historical sources, see Salomon (1998) and Sircar (1965). Prasad (2007) translates the Lekhapaddhati; Ali (2004) studies courtly culture and the Mānasollāsa; Stein (1900) remains the standard translation of Kalhaṇa. On Vijayanagara, see Stein (1989); on the Kākatīyas, Talbot (2001); on the Nāyaka kingdoms and South Indian political thought, Narayana Rao et al. (1992) and Narayana Rao and Subrahmanyam (2009); on the Āmuktamālyada, Reddy (2010). On the Ahoms, see Gait (1906). Kulke (1995) collects the main contributions to the debate on the medieval state.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Sharīʿa, Siyāsa and Sovereignty: Islamic Law and the Indo-Persian State, c. 1200–1800
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras were never the only law in India, and for most of the second millennium CE they were not the law of the state.
