The Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 allowed the government to “notify” whole communities — many of them nomadic, pastoral or forest-dwelling groups — as “criminal tribes”, addicted to crime by heredity. Members of notified communities could be required to register, to report to the police, and to live in settlements; they could be punished for leaving without permission. The Act was extended in later years and covered many communities across India. After a committee of inquiry recommended its abolition in 1949–50, it was repealed by the Criminal Tribes Laws (Repeal) Act of 1952, and the communities concerned were “denotified”; but laws on “habitual offenders” and the stigma attached to these groups persisted long after (Singha 1998).

docs.title: 19.6.7 Indian Jurists
docs.text: Indian lawyers and judges became central to this legal order in the later nineteenth century. Kashinath Trimbak Telang and Mahadev Govind Ranade, both judges of the Bombay High Court, combined legal careers with scholarship and social reform; Hari Singh Gour published The Hindu Code (1919), a restatement of Hindu law in code form; and nationalist and reformist lawyers debated how far Hindu law should be reformed by legislation. Their work laid the foundations for the codification of Hindu law after independence (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 19.7 Lawyers, Courts and the National Movement
docs.text:
The colonial legal order created a new profession. A Bengal regulation of 1793 established licensed pleaders (vakīls) for the Company’s courts, and the Legal Practitioners Act of 1879 regulated the grades of pleaders, mukhtārs and revenue agents across British India. The High Courts of 1862 admitted both English-trained barristers and Indian advocates and vakīls, and in 1863 Sambhu Nath Pandit became the first Indian judge of the High Court at Calcutta. Law schools and the universities founded in 1857 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras trained Indian lawyers in English law, while many of the most ambitious went to London to be called to the bar at the Inns of Court. Gandhi (called in 1891), Jinnah, Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Ambedkar were all barristers trained in London.

Law became, in consequence, the profession of the nationalist leadership. W. C. Bonnerjee, the first president of the Indian National Congress (1885), was a Calcutta barrister, and lawyers were prominent among the Congress’s members and leaders thereafter. The courts were also a stage for political conflict. B. G. Tilak was tried for sedition in 1897 and again in 1908, when he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment at Mandalay; Gandhi, tried at Ahmedabad in 1922, pleaded guilty and used his statement to indict the legal order that had convicted him; and the trials of officers of the Indian National Army at the Red Fort in 1945–46, defended by Bhulabhai Desai with Nehru among the counsel, became a national cause. The language of rights, representation and constitutional government that Indian lawyers learned in the colonial courts was turned against colonial rule, and lawyers — Ambedkar, B. N. Rau, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi — were among the principal authors of the Constitution (Chapter 20).

Women entered the profession late and against resistance. Cornelia Sorabji studied law at Oxford in the early 1890s but could not practise as an advocate; in 1916 the Calcutta High Court refused to admit Regina Guha as a pleader on the ground that the law did not contemplate women in that role. The Legal Practitioners (Women) Act of 1923 removed the bar, and Sorabji and others were enrolled in the following years. The profession nonetheless remained overwhelmingly male and drawn from the upper castes for decades after independence, a fact that shaped the interpretation of the personal laws as much as any text.

docs.title: 19.8 Law in the Princely States
docs.text:
British India was not the whole of India. On the eve of independence some two-fifths of the subcontinent’s area and about a quarter of its people lived in more than five hundred princely states, ruled by their own dynasties under treaties that left defence and foreign relations to the British Crown and internal government, within limits, to the ruler. These states had their own courts and laws. Many adopted the Indian Penal Code and other British Indian codes with modifications, and Hyderabad, the most populous, maintained its own high court, codes and establishment of qāḍīs. In personal law most followed the same division between Hindu and Muslim law as British India. But because a ruler could legislate without the delays of the colonial legislature or the need to placate orthodox opinion in the same way, several states went further than British India in social reform.

Baroda under Sayajirao Gaekwad III (r. 1875–1939) passed a law against child marriage in 1904, a quarter of a century before the Sarda Act, and introduced compulsory primary education. Mysore appointed a committee in 1918 to examine the under-representation of non-Brahmins in its public service, and its Hindu Law Women’s Rights Act of 1933 enlarged the inheritance rights of daughters and widows. In Kolhapur, Shahu (r. 1894–1922) reserved half of the posts in his administration for the backward classes in 1902, supported the non-Brahmin movement and the young B. R. Ambedkar, and promoted laws recognising inter-caste marriage. Travancore abolished slavery in the 1850s, legislated on the matrilineal family (Chapter 16) and opened its temples to all Hindus by the proclamation of 1936 (Chapter 20). These measures were cited as precedents in the debates on reservation and on the Hindu Code.

Princely government also had darker sides: arbitrary rulers, heavy revenue demands, the absence of representative institutions in most states, and, in some, the persistence of forced labour and caste disabilities that British India had begun to outlaw. After 1947 the states acceded to India and were merged or integrated, and from 1950 their laws were progressively replaced by the laws of the Union. Their history is nonetheless part of the legal history of India: it shows that the reform of personal and caste law was not the work of the colonial state alone, and that Indian rulers working within the tradition of rājadharma could use royal legislation to change customs that the śāstras had sanctioned.

docs.title: 19.9 Portuguese and French India
docs.text:
Two other European powers ruled small Indian territories with legal systems of their own, and their arrangements show alternatives to the British model. In Goa, conquered by the Portuguese in 1510, the early colonial state was openly confessional: Hindu temples in the conquered districts were destroyed, public Hindu rites were restricted, and the Inquisition established at Goa in 1560 tried converts accused of returning to Hindu or Muslim practices until its final abolition in 1812. In the nineteenth century the approach changed. The Portuguese Civil Code of 1867 was extended to the overseas provinces, and a decree of 1880 codified the “usages and customs” of the Hindus of Goa, preserving rules of Hindu family law within a civil-law framework; among them was a provision, still noted in modern debates, allowing a Hindu husband to take a second wife in specified circumstances of childlessness. Goa’s ancient village associations of landholders (gāvkārī, in Portuguese comunidades), which held and managed village land in common, were also codified and regulated. After Goa’s incorporation into India in 1961 this civil law was retained, which is why Goa is now cited as an example of a common civil code (Chapter 20).

In the French settlements — Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahé, Yanam and Chandernagore — French courts applied French law to Europeans and Hindu and Muslim law to Indians, advised on questions of Indian law by a consultative committee of local jurists. A decree of 1881 allowed Indians to “renounce” their personal status and place themselves under the French Civil Code. Those who did so, the renonçants, were drawn disproportionately from Christian and lower-caste families, for whom renunciation offered escape from caste-based law and, for a time, a place on the electoral roll alongside Europeans. The status of renonçant survived the transfer of the settlements to India in the 1950s. The French option of individual exit from personal law offered, in a colonial form, something like the voluntary civil code that Ambedkar later suggested in the Constituent Assembly.

docs.title: 19.10 Assessment
docs.text: As this chapter and the two before it show, the history of law in India between the thirteenth and twentieth centuries is a history of plural legal orders: Islamic law administered by qāḍīs and shaped by rulers’ regulations; Dharmaśāstra studied by Brahmin scholars and applied, with custom, by caste and village bodies; Sikh and Maratha states with their own institutions; and, finally, the colonial state, which claimed to preserve “native law” while transforming it. The “Hindu law” and “Muslim law” inherited by independent India were products of this last transformation. Understanding that history is a precondition for understanding the debates about personal law and the Uniform Civil Code in the next chapter — and for avoiding the twin errors of treating colonial “Hindu law” as ancient tradition and of imagining that pre-colonial India had a single law that colonialism destroyed.

docs.title: 19.11 Summary
docs.text:
• Hastings’s plan of 1772 directed the Company’s courts to apply “the laws of the Koran” to Muslims and “those of the Shaster” to Hindus in matters of family and religion; translations by Halhed, Jones and Colebrooke supplied the texts.

  • Anglo-Hindu and Anglo-Muhammadan law, built on translations and precedent, textualised, Brahmanised and rigidified the law, and made religion the basis of family law.

  • Anglo-Muhammadan law narrowed Islamic law to personal matters; the Privy Council’s rejection of the family waqf (1894) was reversed by the Act of 1913, the Shariat Act of 1937 set the textual law above contrary custom, and the Act of 1939, drawing on Mālikī doctrine, gave Muslim wives grounds for judicial divorce.

  • Communities that fitted the colonial categories badly, such as the Jains, had to prove their customs case by case; the princely states had their own courts and laws, and some — Baroda, Mysore, Kolhapur, Travancore — went beyond British India in social legislation; Portuguese Goa codified Hindu usages within a civil code, and French India let individuals renounce their personal law.

  • Codes on English models replaced indigenous law in other fields; social legislation and laws such as the Criminal Tribes Act shaped the society inherited by independent India.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On colonial law, see Derrett (1961), Derrett (1968), Cohn (1996), Rocher (1983), Kugle (2001), Singha (1998) and Galanter (1989); on Anglo-Muhammadan law, Kugle (2001) and Fyzee (1949); on the Sikh codes of conduct, McLeod (2003).

docs.title: Chapter 20: The Constitution and the Classical Legacy
docs.text:
The Constitution of India, adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, was in substance a modern liberal-democratic constitution. Its framers drew on the Government of India Act of 1935, on British parliamentary practice, on the constitutions of the United States, Ireland, Canada and other countries, and on the experience of the national movement. It made the individual citizen, endowed with enforceable fundamental rights, the basic unit of the polity, and it declared equality before the law regardless of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. In these respects it broke decisively with the legal order of the Dharmaśāstras, whose law was graded by varṇa and gender.

Yet the classical traditions discussed in this book did not simply disappear. Their vocabulary and symbols were used in the making of the Republic; the codification of Hindu personal law in the 1950s transformed but also preserved parts of the Dharmaśāstric inheritance; and the Arthaśāstra, Manu and the idea of dharma have continued to be invoked, admired and contested in Indian public life. This chapter examines that legacy. It tries to distinguish reception — the ways modern Indians have used and argued about the classical traditions — from derivation, the claim that the classical texts were the source of modern constitutional principles, which the records of the Constituent Assembly do not bear out. Figure 20.1 sets out the main legal milestones of the Republic discussed here.

Figure 20.1. Milestones in the law of equality and of personal law in the Republic, 1950–2024, as discussed in this chapter and in Chapter 16. The entries are evenly spaced; the vertical axis is not a time scale.

docs.title: 20.1.1 Equality and the Abolition of Untouchability
docs.text:
The Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Constitution guarantee equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws (Article 14), prohibit discrimination by the state on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15) and guarantee equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16). Article 17 declares: “ ‘Untouchability’ is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.” Article 25, which guarantees freedom of religion, expressly permits the state to provide for social reform and for “the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus” (Article 25(2)(b)). These provisions were drafted with the legal disabilities of the Dharmaśāstras and of caste custom in view; in substance they negate the varṇa-graded law described in Chapters 10 and 14. Parliament gave effect to Article 17 by the Untouchability (Offences) Act of 1955, later renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act (1976), and by the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989.

The Constitution also provided for affirmative measures: reserved seats in legislatures for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, reservation in public employment and education, and a directive to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections (Article 46). Marc Galanter’s study of these policies remains the classic account (Galanter 1984).

docs.title: 20.1.2 Before the Constitution: Temple Entry and Civil Rights
docs.text: The constitutional abolition of untouchability crowned decades of struggle. Movements for the right of Dalits and other excluded castes to use public roads, tanks, schools and temples were a major feature of social reform in the 1920s and 1930s: the Vaikom satyagraha of 1924–25 in Travancore, which sought the right to use the roads around a temple and was supported by Gandhi and by E. V. Ramasamy; Ambedkar’s Mahad satyagraha of 1927 (Chapter 10); the Kalaram temple entry movement at Nashik from 1930; and the Guruvayur satyagraha of 1931–32. The Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 opened the state’s temples to all Hindus, and several provinces passed temple-entry laws in the following years. These campaigns showed both the depth of resistance to equality and the possibility of change through organised action and law (Zelliot 1992).

docs.title: 20.1.3 Representation: The Poona Pact
docs.text: The question of political representation for the “Depressed Classes” — the contemporary term for the castes regarded as untouchable — was fought out before independence. At the Round Table Conferences in London (1930–32), Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for them, as had been granted to Muslims and others; the British government’s Communal Award of 1932 conceded them. Gandhi, who regarded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes as a division of Hindu society, began a fast unto death in protest. Under intense pressure, Ambedkar agreed to the Poona Pact of September 1932, which replaced separate electorates with seats reserved for the Depressed Classes within joint electorates, in larger numbers than the Award had provided. Ambedkar later regarded the Pact as a defeat. The reserved constituencies of the Constitution descend from this settlement, and the episode remains central to debates about the relationship between Gandhi, Ambedkar and the politics of caste (Zelliot 1992).

docs.title: 20.1.4 Reservation and Its Debates
docs.text: The policies of reservation have been among the most contested features of Indian constitutional law. After the Supreme Court struck down a caste-based reservation in education in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Parliament amended the Constitution in the same year to permit special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for the Scheduled Castes and Tribes (Article 15(4)). The extension of reservation in central government employment to the “Other Backward Classes” on the recommendation of the Mandal Commission (1980), implemented in 1990, provoked fierce protests; in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) the Supreme Court upheld it, while ruling that reservations should not normally exceed fifty per cent and that the “creamy layer” of the backward classes should be excluded. These debates are a modern chapter in the history of caste and law. They show the Constitution using caste categories in order to undo the disadvantages that a caste-based legal and social order had created (Galanter 1984).

docs.title: 20.1.5 Ambedkar’s Warnings
docs.text: B. R. Ambedkar, chairman of the Drafting Committee, was clear that legal equality would not by itself abolish the social order that the śāstras had sanctioned. Moving the Draft Constitution on 4 November 1948, he quoted the historian George Grote on “constitutional morality” and added: “Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated. We must realize that our people have yet to learn it. Democracy in India is only a top-dressing on an Indian soil, which is essentially undemocratic.” In his final speech to the Assembly on 25 November 1949, he warned that on 26 January 1950 India would “enter into a life of contradictions”: in politics there would be equality, in social and economic life inequality (Constituent Assembly of India 1948, 1949). His insistence that political democracy must be accompanied by social democracy — “a way of life which recognizes liberty, equality and fraternity as the principles of life” — drew on his earlier critique of caste and the śāstras (Chapter 10) and on his reading of the Buddha’s dhamma (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 20.2 Dalit Legal and Political Thought after Ambedkar
docs.text: Ambedkar’s critique of the śāstras and his work on the Constitution did not end with his death in 1956. They became the starting point of a body of Dalit political thought, organisation and scholarship that has shaped both the law of caste in the Republic and the way in which the classical texts discussed in this book are read.

docs.title: 20.2.1 Movements
docs.text: The Republican Party of India, founded in 1957 along lines that Ambedkar had planned, carried his politics into electoral competition, though it soon divided. In 1972 young writers in Bombay, among them Namdeo Dhasal, Raja Dhale and J. V. Pawar, founded the Dalit Panthers, taking their name from the Black Panthers of the United States; they joined political militancy to a new Marathi literature of protest and did much to make “Dalit” — “broken”, “ground down” — the name by which the community described itself, in place of the official “Scheduled Castes” and Gandhi’s “Harijan”. In northern India Kanshi Ram organised Dalit and other government employees in BAMCEF (1978) and founded the Bahujan Samaj Party (1984), which sought to unite the “majority” (bahujan) of Dalits, Ādivāsīs, backward castes and religious minorities against upper-caste dominance; its leader Mayawati became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh four times from 1995 (Omvedt 1994; Zelliot 1992).

docs.title: 20.2.2 The Law of Caste in the Republic
docs.text: These movements pressed the state to give effect to Article 17. The Untouchability (Offences) Act of 1955, renamed and strengthened as the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976, proved weak against the violence that met Dalit assertion, and Parliament enacted the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in 1989, which defined a range of “atrocities”, provided for special courts and restricted anticipatory bail. The Act was widened in 2015. In Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra (2018) the Supreme Court introduced safeguards against arrest under it; after nationwide Dalit protests Parliament restored the earlier position by inserting section 18A, which the Court upheld in Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020). A further question concerns religion. The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order of 1950 confined Scheduled Caste status to Hindus; it was extended to Sikhs in 1956 and to Buddhists in 1990, but Dalits who are Christians or Muslims remain outside it, an exclusion that Dalit organisations have long contested. The question shows how a category created to undo the effects of a Brahmanical social order is still defined by religion.

docs.title: 20.2.3 Scholarship
docs.text:
Dalit and Dalit-Bahujan scholars have also changed the terms in which caste is studied. The political theorist Gopal Guru has made humiliation a central category of social and political theory, and, with the philosopher Sundar Sarukkai, has asked who in Indian social science is allowed to theorise and whose experience is treated only as data (Guru 2009; Guru and Sarukkai 2012). Guru’s argument that “Dalit women talk differently” — that their experience of caste and patriarchy is represented neither by upper-caste feminism nor by male-led Dalit politics — opened a Dalit feminist literature, which Sharmila Rege developed through women’s life narratives (Guru 1995; Rege 2006). Kancha Ilaiah’s Why I Am Not a Hindu (1996) set the culture and knowledge of the labouring Dalit-Bahujan castes against what he called Brahmanical Hinduism (Ilaiah 1996). Anand Teltumbde has argued that the constitutional categories of reservation and protection have left caste violence and economic subordination largely intact (Teltumbde 2018), and Sukhadeo Thorat and Katherine Newman have documented discrimination in modern labour, credit and housing markets (Thorat and Newman 2010). Historians have traced the longer story: Gail Omvedt the Dalit movement under colonial rule, and Anupama Rao the way in which Dalits in western India became political subjects through the law’s categories of rights, representation and violence (Omvedt 1994; Rao 2009).

For the history of polity and law, this scholarship matters in two ways. It insists that the śāstras be read from the standpoint of those whom they excluded, which is one reason why this book sets out their provisions on varṇa and untouchability with their references rather than in paraphrase (Chapters 10 and 14). And it shows that the break with hierarchy described at the beginning of this chapter was not completed in 1950: it remains, as Ambedkar warned, a task of social as well as legal change.

docs.title: 20.3 The Directive Principles
docs.text:
Part IV of the Constitution, the Directive Principles of State Policy, sets out goals that are not enforceable in the courts but are declared to be “fundamental in the governance of the country”. They were modelled in part on the Irish Constitution of 1937, and they reflect the socialist, Gandhian and liberal currents of the national movement. They direct the state to secure a social order based on justice, social, economic and political (Article 38); adequate means of livelihood for all, the prevention of the concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work and the protection of children (Article 39); the organisation of village pañcāyats (Article 40); the right to work, to education and to public assistance in old age, sickness and disablement (Article 41); a living wage (Article 43); the promotion of the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, especially the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Article 46); the prohibition of intoxicating drinks (Article 47); the organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry on modern lines and the prohibition of the slaughter of cows and calves (Article 48); and a uniform civil code (Article 44).

Popular writing sometimes presents these principles as a modern form of rājadharma, matching each Article with a verse of the Arthaśāstra or Manu. Such parallels are not supported by the records of the Constituent Assembly, whose debates on the Directive Principles drew on modern constitutional models and on the programmes of the national movement. Some provisions — the pañcāyats, prohibition and the protection of cattle — do reflect Gandhian and Hindu sentiment in the Assembly; the protection of the weaker sections reflects Ambedkar’s concerns. The ideal that a ruler should seek the welfare of his people is ancient and widespread; the specific programme of Part IV is a twentieth-century one (Austin 1966). Nor did the new rights remain the property of lawyers and legislators. Rohit De has shown how, in the Republic’s first decade, ordinary citizens — butchers, traders, sex workers and others — went to court under the fundamental rights to challenge measures such as prohibition and bans on cow slaughter, some of them adopted in the name of the Directive Principles, so that the Constitution became a part of everyday life (De 2018).

docs.title: 20.4 Symbols of the Republic
docs.text:
The Republic adopted classical symbols. Its national emblem, adopted on 26 January 1950, is an adaptation of the lion capital of the Aśokan pillar at Sarnath, with the motto satyam eva jayate, “truth alone conquers”, from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.1.6). The wheel at the centre of the national flag, adopted in July 1947, is the wheel of dharma from the same capital. The original manuscript of the Constitution was calligraphed by hand and illuminated by artists working under Nandalal Bose of Santiniketan, with scenes from Indian history and mythology — from the Indus civilisation and the Vedic hermitage to the Buddha, Aśoka, Vikramāditya’s court, Akbar, Śivājī, Guru Gobind Singh and Gandhi.

The name of the country was also debated. Article 1 of the Constitution begins: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” Members of the Constituent Assembly proposed various names — Bharat, Bharatavarsha, Hind, Hindustan — and the compromise formula recognised both the English name and the Sanskrit name with its Purāṇic associations.

The choice of Aśokan symbols was deliberate. Jawaharlal Nehru and others saw in Aśoka a model of a ruler who had combined power with ethical restraint and religious tolerance, and the symbols linked the new state to an Indian past that was neither specifically Hindu nor Brahmanical. These are acts of reception by a modern state; they tell us how the founders wished the Republic to be understood, not that the Constitution derived its principles from Aśoka.

docs.title: 20.5.1 The Hindu Code Bill
docs.text: The most direct encounter between the Constitution’s principles and the Dharmaśāstric inheritance was the codification of Hindu personal law. A Hindu Law Committee chaired by B. N. Rau prepared a draft code in the 1940s. As Law Minister after independence, Ambedkar took up the project: his Hindu Code Bill proposed to replace the textual law of the Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga, as interpreted by the courts, with a single code providing for monogamy, divorce, the abolition of caste restrictions on marriage and adoption, and equal inheritance for daughters. It met fierce opposition, inside and outside Parliament, from those who saw it as an attack on Hindu tradition. In 1951 the government withdrew it, and Ambedkar resigned from the cabinet, citing the failure to enact it among his reasons (Som 1994; Newbigin 2013).

docs.title: 20.5.2 The Acts of 1955–56
docs.text:
After the first general election, the government enacted the substance of the Bill in four statutes. The Hindu Marriage Act (1955) made monogamy compulsory, allowed divorce on specified grounds, and recognised marriages between persons of different castes; it retained the ceremonies of customary Hindu marriage, providing that where the seven steps (saptapadī) are part of the rite, the marriage is complete when the seventh is taken (Chapter 15). The Hindu Succession Act (1956) gave daughters, widows and mothers equal shares with sons in a man’s separate property and made women absolute owners of their property, but it preserved the Mitākṣarā coparcenary in which only males had birthrights. The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act (1956) and the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act (1956) completed the scheme.

Reba Som and Eleanor Newbigin have shown that the result was a compromise: the codes extended a single law to all who counted as “Hindus” — including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs — and introduced major reforms, but they also retained the joint family and the coparcenary and thus the economic advantages of sons (Som 1994; Newbigin 2013). Flavia Agnes has argued that the reforms did less for women than their reputation suggests and that many of their benefits were limited to the middle classes (Agnes 1999). The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act of 2005 made daughters coparceners by birth with the same rights as sons, and in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) the Supreme Court held that this right does not depend on the father having been alive when the amendment came into force (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 20.5.3 Continuity and Change
docs.text: The Hindu codes thus both broke with and continued the Dharmaśāstric tradition. They abolished its varṇa distinctions, its polygyny, its denial of divorce and its exclusion of daughters from inheritance; they retained its sacramental understanding of marriage, its joint family and, until 2005, its male coparcenary; and they continued to treat religion as the basis of family law. Judges and lawyers still cite Dharmaśāstra texts and their colonial interpretations in some areas — for example, in cases about Hindu religious endowments, the status of deities as legal persons, and customary marriage ceremonies — but the governing law is statutory.

docs.title: 20.6 Personal Law and the Uniform Civil Code
20.6.1 A Plural System
docs.text: India’s personal law system is a legacy of the colonial division of family law by religion (Chapter 19). Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs), Muslims, Christians and Parsis are governed in marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption and succession by separate bodies of law, some codified and some uncodified, while the Special Marriage Act of 1954 provides a civil alternative open to all. Goa has its own civil code, inherited from Portuguese rule. Scheduled Tribes are often governed by custom (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 20.6.2 Muslim Personal Law after 1947
docs.text: Independent India retained the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act of 1937 and the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act of 1939 (Chapter 19). Muslim marriage, divorce, maintenance and inheritance therefore continued to be governed by a largely uncodified body of Ḥanafī law — and, for Shīʿī Muslims, of Twelver law — as interpreted by the courts and supplemented by statute. Religious and charitable endowments were placed under state boards by the Wakf Act of 1954, which was replaced by the Waqf Act of 1995 and substantially amended in 2025. The All India Muslim Personal Law Board, founded in 1973, became the most prominent voice of those who held that the personal law was a matter for the community and its scholars rather than for Parliament, and the controversies over maintenance and triple ṭalāq described below were in part disputes over that claim. Muslim women’s organisations and reformers have meanwhile sought change both from within the tradition and through the courts. The history illustrates a general feature of Indian personal law: the state and the religious communities have both claimed authority over bodies of law that were themselves shaped to a large extent by the colonial courts.

docs.title: 20.6.3 Civil Marriage and Choice
docs.text: Alongside the religious personal laws, the Special Marriage Act of 1954 allows any two persons, irrespective of religion, to marry by civil registration, and marriages under it are governed by secular rules of divorce and succession. The Act extended a colonial statute of 1872 that had been available only to those who declared that they professed no religion. It has been the main legal route for interfaith marriages, though its requirement of public notice before the marriage has been criticised for exposing couples to harassment. The courts have repeatedly affirmed the right of adults to marry a person of their choice, against the opposition of families and communities (Chapter 16). The contrast with the Dharmaśāstras, in which marriage was arranged by fathers within the bounds of varṇa and gotra, is complete.

docs.title: 20.6.4 Article 44
docs.text:
Article 44, among the non-justiciable Directive Principles, provides that “the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” Where to place the clause was settled early. In 1947 the Assembly’s sub-committee on fundamental rights decided by a majority that a uniform civil code should not be a justiciable right; Minoo Masani, Hansa Mehta and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur dissented, arguing that personal laws based on religion stood in the way of national unity and of equality for women (Austin 1966).

When the draft article (then numbered 35) came before the Constituent Assembly on 23 November 1948, Mohamed Ismail Sahib, Naziruddin Ahmad, Mahboob Ali Baig and B. Pocker Sahib moved amendments to protect the personal law of any group or community from change without its consent. They argued that personal law was part of religious observance, that the freedom of religion guaranteed elsewhere in the draft would otherwise be weakened, and that a code imposed by the majority would breed discontent among the minorities. K. M. Munshi replied that the Shariat Act of 1937 had itself overridden the customs of the Khojas and Cutchi Memons, that countries with Muslim majorities such as Turkey and Egypt did not exempt their minorities from a common civil law, and that the clause would equally require the reform of Hindu law, which many Hindus resisted. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar pointed to the uniform criminal and commercial law that India already had. Ambedkar, closing the debate, observed that India already had a uniform law in almost every field except marriage and succession, that until the 1930s Muslims in the North-West Frontier Province and elsewhere had followed customary rules of succession close to Hindu law, and that the article only required the state to “endeavour”. A future Parliament, he suggested, might make a code applicable at first only to those who declared their willingness to be bound by it. The amendments were rejected and the article adopted (Constituent Assembly of India 1948).

The debate set the terms of the later controversy. Both sides treated the Hindu Code then being prepared as part of the same question, so that the reform of Hindu law in 1955–56 (Section 20.5) was in one sense a partial, community-by-community step towards the goal of Article 44, and in another a reason why Muslims came to see the demand for a uniform code as directed at them. Ambedkar’s idea of a voluntary code was realised in part by the Special Marriage Act of 1954, described above.

docs.title: 20.6.5 Courts and Controversies
docs.text: The tension between personal law and constitutional equality has produced some of the most contested judgments in Indian legal history. In Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman could claim maintenance from her former husband under the general provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and remarked on the desirability of a uniform civil code; the political reaction led Parliament to pass the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act of 1986, which was widely seen as reversing the decision. In Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001), the Court upheld the 1986 Act but interpreted it to require a reasonable and fair provision for the divorced wife’s future. In Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995), it held that a Hindu husband could not escape the prohibition of bigamy by converting to Islam. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), a majority of the Court held the practice of instant “triple ṭalāq” unconstitutional or invalid, and Parliament subsequently made it an offence. Cases concerning women’s entry into temples, such as the Sabarimala case of 2018, raised similar questions about the relation between religious practice and equality within the Hindu fold.

docs.title: 20.6.6 The Debate
docs.text:
Supporters of a uniform civil code argue that equality before the law and gender justice require a single family law for all citizens, and that personal laws in all communities discriminate against women. Opponents argue that a uniform code imposed by a majority would threaten minority identities and that reform should come from within communities. Feminist scholars such as Flavia Agnes have criticised both the majoritarian appropriation of the uniform code demand and the conservatism of community leaderships, and proposed reforms that would secure women’s rights across personal laws (Agnes 1999). The political theorist Ayelet Shachar has proposed “transformative accommodation”, in which communities retain authority over some matters while individuals can invoke state law to protect their rights (Shachar 2001). Narendra Subramanian’s comparative history of the personal laws since independence shows that each of them — Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Parsi — has been reshaped through negotiation between the state, community leaders and reformers within the community, so that the choice has never been simply between an unchanged religious law and a uniform code (Subramanian 2014).

Official bodies have reached different conclusions. The Law Commission of India, asked by the government in 2016 to examine the question, issued a consultation paper in 2018 which concluded that a uniform civil code was “neither necessary nor desirable at this stage” and recommended instead that discriminatory provisions be removed from each personal law, with reforms such as equal rights of inheritance and a common minimum age of marriage; its successor commission invited the public’s views afresh in 2023. Goa’s civil code, derived from the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867 and retained after 1961, is often cited as a working model, though it too contains provisions specific to particular communities. In 2024 the state of Uttarakhand enacted a uniform civil code for its residents, excluding Scheduled Tribes; in force from January 2025, it prescribes common rules of marriage, divorce and succession and requires the registration of marriages and of couples living together outside marriage. Its supporters present it as the fulfilment of Article 44; its critics object to its registration requirements and question whether a state law can achieve uniformity. The national debate continues.

Proponents of both positions sometimes appeal to the classical tradition — to the Dharmaśāstras’ recognition of regional and community custom as a model of pluralism, or to the ideal of a single dharma for all. Neither appeal is straightforward. The pluralism of the śāstras was a hierarchical pluralism, in which different groups had different rights because they had different status; the “single dharma” was the dharma of the varṇa order. The modern debate is about how a democratic state committed to equal citizenship should accommodate religious and cultural diversity, a question the classical texts did not ask.

docs.title: 20.7 Religion, Endowments and the State
docs.text:
A further area in which the Constitution engaged with the classical inheritance is the relationship between the state and religious institutions. Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health, and permits the state to regulate the secular activities associated with religious practice and to provide for social reform. Article 26 guarantees religious denominations the right to manage their own affairs in matters of religion and to own and administer property in accordance with law. In the Shirur Mutt case (Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, 1954), the Supreme Court held that what constitutes an essential part of a religion is to be ascertained from the doctrines of that religion itself, and that the state may regulate the secular administration of religious institutions but not their essential religious practices. The “essential practices” test that developed from this case has required courts to decide questions about Hindu and other religious traditions — for instance, whether a particular rule of temple worship or entry is essential to the religion — and has drawn them into the interpretation of texts and customs.

Several states continue to administer large Hindu temples through statutory boards, a practice inherited from the colonial period, while the endowments of other religions are governed by their own statutes, such as the Waqf Act. The arrangement illustrates the peculiar position of Indian secularism, which neither separates state and religion completely nor establishes a state religion, but regulates and reforms religious institutions in the name of equality and public order (Galanter 1989).

docs.title: 20.8 The Courts and the Classical Texts
docs.text:
Indian courts have on occasion referred to the classical texts, and some judges have written about dharma in speeches and essays. Such references are usually illustrative: a judge may quote Manu or the Mahābhārata on the duty of the king to protect his subjects, or on truth in testimony, to adorn a judgment that rests on constitutional and statutory grounds. They do not show that constitutional doctrines such as the “basic structure” of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973) or the expansive interpretation of the right to life and personal liberty (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978) were derived from Dharmaśāstra; those doctrines rest on constitutional reasoning and on comparative constitutional law. Claims that particular judges based landmark decisions on concepts such as rājadharma or the ātman should be treated with caution unless the passages can be identified in the judgments.

Courts have also confronted classical norms directly. The Supreme Court’s decision on adultery (Section 20.11) rejected a conception of the wife as her husband’s property that the colonial code had shared with the Dharmaśāstras, and its judgments on khap pañcāyats (Chapter 16) and on untouchability have set constitutional limits on the authority of caste and custom.

docs.title: 20.9 Kauṭilya in Modern India
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra has had a remarkable modern career. After its rediscovery (Chapter 3), nationalist historians cited it as proof that ancient India had possessed a sophisticated science of government, and Max Weber’s remark comparing it with Machiavelli made it known in European political thought. In independent India, Cāṇakya became a national symbol of political wisdom: the diplomatic enclave in New Delhi is named Chanakyapuri, and his name is attached to institutes, awards and conferences. In recent decades, the Arthaśāstra has been studied in courses on strategic thought and international relations, and Roger Boesche and others have presented Kauṭilya as an early political realist (Boesche 2002). Popular management literature presents “Kautilyan” principles of leadership.

These uses are part of the text’s reception history and are legitimate subjects of study. They often, however, rest on the traditional dating of the text to the Mauryan period and on a selective reading that emphasises its realism and its welfare provisions while passing over its espionage, coercion and hierarchy. The scholarly understanding of the Arthaśāstra as a composite text of c. 50 BCE–300 CE, revised to accommodate dharmaśāstric norms (Chapter 3), and the attention of historians such as Upinder Singh to its violence (Singh 2017), provide a necessary corrective. It is one thing to find the text illuminating, another to read modern realism, the welfare state or the mixed economy into it.

docs.title: 20.10 Dharma, Rāmarājya and Modern Politics
docs.text:
The language of dharma and kingship has also been used in modern political argument. M. K. Gandhi described his ideal of a just and non-violent polity as Rāmarājya, explaining that he meant not Hindu rule but a rule of righteousness, open to people of all faiths. Ambedkar, by contrast, criticised the figure of Rāma for his treatment of Sītā and of Śambūka (Chapter 5), and many Dalit and rationalist writers have rejected the ideal of Rāmarājya as a nostalgia for caste society. Hindu nationalist movements have invoked dharma and Rāma in a different spirit, as symbols of national and religious identity. The Constitution’s own language is secular: the word dharma does not appear in its operative provisions, and the word “secular” was added to the Preamble in 1976. The forty-second amendment of the same year also added a list of “fundamental duties” of citizens (Article 51A), which some writers have compared with the classical language of duty, although these duties fall on every citizen alike and not by varṇa or sex.

These uses of the past are part of contemporary politics, and this book does not take sides in them. Its concern has been to establish, as accurately as possible, what the classical texts said and how they were used historically, so that modern arguments about them can at least proceed from a sound understanding of their content.

docs.title: 20.11 Criminal Law after Independence
docs.text:
Independent India retained the colonial criminal law — the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Indian Evidence Act of 1872 — and amended it piecemeal. Several of the most important changes concerned matters that the Dharmaśāstras had also regulated, and they show how far the modern law has moved from the classical assumptions about gender, caste and sexuality discussed in earlier chapters.

The law of sexual violence was transformed in stages. Public protest after the Supreme Court’s acquittal of two policemen accused of raping a young tribal woman in the Mathura case (1979) led to amendments in 1983 that, among other things, shifted the burden of proof in custodial rape. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) the Court laid down guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, later replaced by a statute of 2013. After the gang rape and murder of a young woman in Delhi in December 2012, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act of 2013 widened the definition of rape and introduced new offences. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act of 2005 provided civil remedies against violence within the home. These measures rest on the premise, foreign to the Dharmaśāstras, that a woman’s bodily autonomy is a right that the law must protect against her husband and family as well as against strangers.

The courts also struck down provisions that had embodied older moral assumptions. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court held the offence of adultery, which had punished only the man who had relations with another man’s wife and treated the wife as her husband’s property, to be unconstitutional (Chapter 14). In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) it held that section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial provision criminalising “carnal intercourse against the order of nature”, could not be applied to consensual sexual relations between adults; in National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) it recognised the right of transgender persons to self-identification. Laws against caste atrocities (Section 20.1) belong to the same development.

In 2023 Parliament replaced the three colonial codes with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, which came into force on 1 July 2024. The new codes retain much of the structure and substance of the old, while reorganising and renaming offences; their supporters presented them as a decolonisation of the criminal law, and their critics questioned how far they departed from the colonial model. The names, drawn from Sanskrit, illustrate once more the use of the classical vocabulary of nyāya and rakṣā to frame modern legislation — a vocabulary whose classical contents, as this book has shown, were very different.

docs.title: 20.12 Women in the Republic
docs.text:
The Dharmaśāstras’ maxim that a woman is not fit for independence (Manu 9.3) stood in sharp contrast to the political order created in 1950. The Constitution granted the vote to every adult citizen, women and men alike, without the property and educational qualifications that had limited the franchise — including the limited franchise extended to some women in the provinces from the 1920s — under colonial rule. Fifteen women sat in the Constituent Assembly. Among them, Hansa Mehta also served on the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, where she is credited with securing the wording “all human beings” in place of “all men” in the first article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; Dakshayani Velayudhan, the only Dalit woman in the Assembly, spoke for the abolition of untouchability and for a constitution grounded in the people’s own needs.

Formal equality was followed, slowly, by measures to increase women’s representation. The amendments of 1992 reserved one-third of the seats in rural and urban local bodies for women (Chapter 16). The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act of 2023 provides for the reservation of one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and the state legislative assemblies for women, to take effect after the delimitation of constituencies following the next census. The persistence of low female representation in legislatures for more than seventy years after 1950, and the long campaign required for this amendment, show how far political equality for women depended on deliberate legal change rather than on any inheritance from the classical ideals of rājadharma, in which political authority was in principle male (Agnes 1999).

docs.title: 20.13 Conclusion
docs.text:
The classical Indian traditions of polity and law were among the most elaborate intellectual achievements of the pre-modern world. The Arthaśāstra analysed the resources of the state and the relations between states with a precision few ancient texts can match; the Dharmaśāstras developed a law of procedure, evidence, contract and inheritance of real technical sophistication; Buddhist and Jain thinkers offered alternative accounts of kingship and of the duties of rulers; Islamic jurists and Mughal administrators built a second great legal tradition on Indian soil; and custom, community and local institutions governed the lives of most people. These traditions were also, in central respects, systems of hierarchy and coercion, in which rights and penalties depended on birth and sex and the power of the king and of dominant groups was legitimated by religion.

Modern India’s Constitution chose a different foundation: the equal citizen with enforceable rights. It retained classical symbols, codified parts of the classical law and left room for custom and community, but it subordinated all of them to the principle of equality. The task of reading the classical traditions today is therefore not to find in them the source of modern values, but to understand them as they were — their achievements and their exclusions together — and to judge, in the light of the values the Constitution affirms, what in them deserves to be remembered and what deserves to be left behind.

docs.title: 20.14 Summary
docs.text:
• The Constitution of 1950 made the individual citizen with enforceable rights the basis of the polity, guaranteed equality before the law regardless of caste and sex, and abolished untouchability — negating the varṇa-graded law of the śāstras.

  • Ambedkar warned that political equality would coexist with social inequality; the Dalit movements and scholarship that followed him have shaped the law of caste and the reading of the śāstras.

  • The Republic’s classical symbols are acts of reception, not evidence that its principles derived from the classical texts.

  • The Hindu Code of 1955–56 transformed the Mitākṣarā and Dāyabhāga law while preserving parts of it; personal law remains divided by religion, and the uniform civil code is still debated.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the making of the Constitution, see Austin (1966), and on its first decade in the courts De (2018); on affirmative action and caste, Galanter (1984); on law and society, Galanter (1989). Dalit political thought after Ambedkar can be approached through Omvedt (1994), Guru (2009), Rao (2009) and Teltumbde (2018). The Hindu Code is studied by Som (1994) and Newbigin (2013); women’s rights and personal law by Agnes (1999) and Subramanian (2014); theories of accommodation by Shachar (2001). Menski (2003) surveys modern Hindu law; Lubin et al. (2010) includes chapters on law and religion in modern India.

A ruler’s hereditary home territory under the Mughals (ch. 17) yogakṣema Acquisition and secure possession; welfare (ch. 5) zabt (Pe.) Mughal assessment of revenue in cash on measured land (ch. 18) zawābiṭ (Ar.) State regulations made by a Muslim ruler (ch. 18)

docs.title: Persons
docs.text:
Brief notes on authors, rulers, jurists, reformers and scholars mentioned in this volume. Dates are approximate where marked; for legendary or traditional figures, the notes describe the tradition. Chapter references are to the chapters in which each person is chiefly discussed.

Person Note Authors and figures of the classical tradition Manu Mythical first man and law-giver, to whom the Mānava Dharmaśāstra is attributed; the text itself is a work of c. 2nd c. CE (ch. 10). Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya, Viṣṇugupta) Traditionally the minister of Candragupta Maurya and author of the Arthaśāstra; the text as we have it is composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE (ch. 3). Yājñavalkya Upaniṣadic teacher, to whom a smṛti of c. 4th–5th c. CE is attributed (ch. 11). Nārada Divine sage to whom the first purely legal smṛti (c. 5th–6th c.) is attributed (ch. 11). Bṛhaspati, Kātyāyana Names attached to lost law books of c. 6th–7th c., known from quotations (ch. 11, 12). Kāmandaka Author of the Nītisāra, a verse digest of polity, c. 500–700 CE (ch. 3). Medhātithi Author of the oldest complete surviving commentary on Manu, 9th–10th c., probably in Kashmir (ch. 9, 10). Viśvarūpa Author of the Bālakrīḍā, the earliest surviving commentary on Yājñavalkya, c. 9th c. (ch. 11). Vijñāneśvara Jurist at the court of Vikramāditya VI at Kalyāṇa; author of the Mitākṣarā, c. 1100–1120 (ch. 11). Jīmūtavāhana Bengali jurist, author of the Dāyabhāga, 12th c. (ch. 11). Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa Author of the Smṛticandrikā, a digest respected in the south, c. 1200 (ch. 11). Mādhava Scholar and minister at Vijayanagara, author of the commentary on Parāśara known as the Parāśaramādhavīya, 14th c. (ch. 11). Vācaspati Miśra Jurist of Mithilā, author of the Vivādacintāmaṇi and other digests, 15th c.; not to be confused with the earlier philosopher of the same name (ch. 11). Mitra Miśra Author of the Vīramitrodaya, composed for the Bundela king Vīrasiṃha of Orchha, 17th c. (ch. 11). Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa Author of the Bhagavantabhāskara, of which the Vyavahāramayūkha is a part, 17th c. (ch. 11). Lakṣmīdhara Minister of Govindacandra of Kanauj; compiler of the Kṛtyakalpataru, 12th c. (ch. 9). Caṇḍeśvara Minister in Mithilā; author of digests on law and on royal policy, 14th c. (ch. 3, 9). Kullūka Bhaṭṭa Author of the Manvarthamuktāvalī, the most widely used commentary on Manu, perhaps 13th–15th c. (ch. 10). Somadeva Sūri Digambara Jain monk, author of the Nītivākyāmṛta and Yaśastilaka, 10th c. (ch. 8). Jinasena Digambara Jain author of the Ādipurāṇa, 9th c. (ch. 8). Hemacandra Jain scholar at the court of Kumārapāla of Gujarat, 12th c. (ch. 8). Kalhaṇa Kashmiri poet, author of the Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148–49) (ch. 5, 17). Kṣemendra Kashmiri poet and satirist, 11th c.; mocked the scribes of Kashmir; a formulary, the Lokaprakāśa, is attributed to him (ch. 17). Muhaṇot Naiṇsī (1610–1670) Minister of Jodhpur; compiler of a chronicle of the Rajputs and a survey of the districts of Marwar (ch. 17). Megasthenes Envoy of Seleucus to the court of Candragupta Maurya, c. 300 BCE; his Indika survives only in quotations by later Greek and Latin writers (ch. 3, 6, 7). Kālidāsa Sanskrit poet and dramatist, c. 4th–5th c. CE; author of the Raghuvaṃśa and Abhijñānaśākuntala (ch. 7). Bāṇa Court poet of Harṣa, 7th c.; author of the Harṣacarita and Kādambarī, in which a character condemns Kauṭilya’s teaching (ch. 3). Basavaṇṇa Twelfth-century minister and poet-saint in the Kannada country, leader of the Vīraśaiva movement, whose vacanas rejected caste privilege (ch. 1). Guru Nānak (1469–1539) First Guru of the Sikhs, who rejected the religious authority of caste (ch. 1). The Buddha Founder of Buddhism; c. 480–400 BCE on the short chronology now widely accepted (traditional Theravāda dates 624–544 BCE) (ch. 8). Mahāvīra Twenty-fourth Jina of the Jains, an older contemporary of the Buddha (traditional Śvetāmbara dates 599–527 BCE) (ch. 8). Nāgārjuna Buddhist philosopher, c. 2nd c. CE, to whom the Ratnāvalī, a letter of counsel to a king, is attributed (ch. 8). Bhavabhūti Sanskrit dramatist, early 8th c.; his Uttararāmacarita makes Rāma recoil from killing Śambūka (ch. 5). Raghunandana Bengali jurist, 16th c.; author of the Smṛtitattva (ch. 9, 11). Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa Scholar of the Bhaṭṭa family of Banaras; author of the Nirṇayasindhu (1612) (ch. 9, 18). Gāgā Bhaṭṭa Banaras scholar who consecrated Śivājī as king in 1674 (ch. 18). Tryambakayajvan Author of the Strīdharmapaddhati at the Thanjavur court, 18th c. (ch. 10, 15). Jagannātha Tarkapañcānana Bengali paṇḍit who compiled the Vivādabhaṅgārṇava at the instance of William Jones, translated by Colebrooke (ch. 19). Rulers Candragupta Maurya Founder of the Mauryan empire, r. c. 321–297 BCE (ch. 3). Aśoka Mauryan emperor, r. c. 268–232 BCE; author of the Rock and Pillar Edicts (ch. 8). Khāravela King of Kaliṅga, c. 1st c. BCE; patron of Jain ascetics (ch. 5, 8). Samudragupta Gupta emperor, 4th c. CE; Allahabad pillar inscription (ch. 5, 7). Harṣa King of Kanauj, r. c. 606–647 (ch. 5, 7). Kumārapāla Caulukya king of Gujarat, r. 1143–1172; patron of Hemacandra (ch. 8). Akbar Mughal emperor, r. 1556–1605 (ch. 18). Aurangzeb Mughal emperor, r. 1658–1707; commissioned the Fatāwā-i ʿĀlamgīrī (ch. 18). Śivājī Founder of the Maratha state, crowned 1674 (ch. 18). Ranjit Singh Sikh ruler at Lahore, r. 1801–1839 (ch. 18). Prabhāvatīguptā Daughter of Candragupta II, Vākāṭaka queen and regent for her sons, c. 400 CE (ch. 5, 7). Diddā Queen of Kashmir, regent and then ruler in her own right until her death in 1003 (ch. 5, 17). Rājarāja I Cōḷa king, r. 985–1014; builder of the Rājarājeśvara temple at Thanjavur (ch. 5). Mārttāṇḍa Varma King of Travancore, r. 1729–1758; dedicated his kingdom to the deity Padmanābha in 1750 (ch. 5). Raḍiyya (Raziya) Sultan of Delhi, r. 1236–1240 (ch. 5). Rudramā Devī Kākatīya ruler of the eastern Deccan, later 13th c. (ch. 5). Kṛṣṇadevarāya Vijayanagara emperor, r. 1509–1529; author of the Telugu Āmuktamālyada (ch. 3, 5, 17). Ahilyabai Holkar Ruler of the Maratha state of Indore, r. 1767–1795 (ch. 5). Someśvara III Cālukya king of Kalyāṇa, r. 1126–1138; the Mānasollāsa (1131) is attributed to him (ch. 3, 17). Bukka I Vijayanagara king, r. c. 1356–1377; settled a dispute between Jains and Śrīvaiṣṇavas in 1368 (ch. 17). Muḥammad b. Tughluq Sultan of Delhi, r. 1325–1351 (ch. 18). Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq Sultan of Delhi, r. 1351–1388; author of the Futūḥāt-i Fīrūzshāhī (ch. 18). Jahāngīr Mughal emperor, r. 1605–1627; his memoirs record his ordinances of justice (ch. 18). Nūr Jahān (d. 1645) Wife of Jahāngīr from 1611; issued orders under her own seal and had coins struck in her name (ch. 18). Shahu of Kolhapur Ruler of Kolhapur, r. 1894–1922; reserved posts for the backward classes in 1902 (ch. 19). Islamic and Persian writers Ziyāʾ al-Dīn Baranī Historian and political writer of the Delhi Sultanate (c. 1285–1357); Fatāwā-yi Jahāndārī (ch. 18). Abu’l Faẓl Minister and historian of Akbar; Akbarnāma and Āʾīn-i Akbarī (ch. 18). Shaykh Niẓām Burhānpūrī Head of the board that compiled the Fatāwā-i ʿĀlamgīrī (ch. 18). Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī (1201–1274) Persian philosopher and scientist; author of the Akhlāq-i Nāṣirī (ch. 18). Todar Mal (d. 1589) Revenue minister of Akbar; architect of the zabt system (ch. 18). Ibn Baṭṭūṭa (1304–c. 1368) Moroccan traveller and Mālikī jurist; qāḍī at Delhi under Muḥammad b. Tughluq (ch. 18). Shāh Walī Allāh (1703–1762) Scholar of Delhi; author of the Ḥujjat Allāh al-bāligha (ch. 18). Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī (1863–1943) Deobandi scholar whose treatise on a wife’s right to divorce informed the Act of 1939 (ch. 19). Syed Ameer Ali (1849–1928) Jurist and judge of the Calcutta High Court; writer on Muslim law (ch. 19). Colonial administrators and scholars Warren Hastings (1732–1818) Governor and Governor-General of Bengal; Judicial Plan of 1772 (ch. 19). Nathaniel Brassey Halhed (1751–1830) Translator of A Code of Gentoo Laws (1776) (ch. 19). William Jones (1746–1794) Judge and Orientalist; translator of Manu (1794) (ch. 10, 19). Henry Thomas Colebrooke (1765–1837) Translator of the Digest (1797–98) and Two Treatises (1810) (ch. 11, 19). Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800–1859) Law Member; chief author of the draft Indian Penal Code (ch. 14, 19). R. Shamasastry (1868–1944) Librarian at Mysore; discoverer, editor and translator of the Arthaśāstra (ch. 3). Mountstuart Elphinstone (1779–1859) Commissioner of the Deccan after 1818 and governor of Bombay (ch. 16). Georg Bühler (1837–1898) Indologist; translator of Manu and other smṛtis in the Sacred Books of the East (ch. 1, 10). Julius Jolly (1849–1932) Indologist; translator of Nārada and Bṛhaspati; historian of Hindu law (ch. 1, 11). Reformers and critics Rammohun Roy (1772–1833) Bengali reformer; campaigned against satī (ch. 15). Īśvaracandra Vidyāsāgar (1820–1891) Sanskrit scholar and reformer; campaign for widow remarriage (ch. 15). Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) Anti-caste reformer; Gulamgiri (1873) (ch. 10, 15). Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) Teacher and poet; co-founder of schools for girls in Pune (ch. 15). Tarabai Shinde (c. 1850–1910) Author of Strī-Puruṣ Tulanā (1882) (ch. 15). Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) Scholar and reformer; The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887) (ch. 15). Rukhmabai (1864–1955) Litigant in a celebrated restitution-of-conjugal-rights case; later a physician (ch. 15). Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856–1920) Nationalist leader, opponent of the Age of Consent Bill of 1891 (ch. 11). Hansa Mehta (1897–1995) Member of the Constituent Assembly and of the UN Commission on Human Rights (ch. 20). Dakshayani Velayudhan (1912–1978) The only Dalit woman in the Constituent Assembly (ch. 20). M. K. Gandhi (1869–1948) Leader of the national movement; Hind Swaraj (1909) (ch. 16, 20). E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar) (1879–1973) Leader of the Self-Respect Movement (ch. 10, 20). Muthulakshmi Reddy (1886–1968) Physician and legislator; campaigned against temple dedication (ch. 15). Kashinath Trimbak Telang (1850–1893) Lawyer, scholar and judge of the Bombay High Court (ch. 19). Mahadev Govind Ranade (1842–1901) Judge of the Bombay High Court and social reformer (ch. 19). Hari Singh Gour (1870–1949) Lawyer; author of The Hindu Code (1919) (ch. 19). B. N. Rau (1887–1953) Jurist; chairman of the Hindu Law Committee and constitutional adviser to the Constituent Assembly (ch. 20). Jawaharlal Nehru (1889–1964) First Prime Minister of India (ch. 20). B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956) Jurist, scholar and Dalit leader; chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution; burned the Manusmṛti at Mahad (1927) (ch. 8, 10, 16, 20). Modern scholars K. P. Jayaswal (1881–1937) Historian; Hindu Polity (1924) (ch. 1, 2). P. V. Kane (1880–1972) Sanskritist and lawyer; History of Dharmaśāstra (1930–62) (ch. 9). R. P. Kangle Editor and translator of the Arthaśāstra (1960–65) (ch. 3). Robert Lingat French scholar of Indian law; The Classical Law of India (ch. 9). J. D. M. Derrett Scholar of Hindu law and its colonial administration (ch. 9, 19). R. S. Sharma Historian of ancient Indian political ideas and of the Śūdras (ch. 2, 4, 10). Patrick Olivelle Editor and translator of the Dharmasūtras, Manu, Yājñavalkya and the Arthaśāstra (ch. 3, 9, 10). Uma Chakravarti Historian of early Buddhism and of caste and gender (ch. 8, 10, 15). Ludo Rocher (1926–2016) Scholar of Dharmaśāstra and of its colonial reception (ch. 9, 19). Richard W. Lariviere (b. 1950) Editor and translator of the Nāradasmṛti (ch. 11, 12). Thomas R. Trautmann (b. 1940) Historian of the Arthaśāstra, of Dravidian kinship and of colonial knowledge of India (ch. 3, 6). Marc Galanter (b. 1931) Scholar of modern Indian law, legal pluralism and compensatory discrimination (ch. 16, 20). Donald R. Davis, Jr. Historian of Dharmaśāstra as a legal tradition, including medieval Kerala (ch. 9, 12). U. N. Ghoshal (1886–1969) Historian of Indian political ideas (ch. 1, 5). Romila Thapar (b. 1931) Historian of early India; Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961) (ch. 3, 8). Bernard S. Cohn (1928–2003) Anthropologist and historian of colonial knowledge and law (ch. 16, 19). Muzaffar Alam (b. 1947) Historian of Islamic political thought and the Mughal state (ch. 18). Steven Collins (1951–2018) Scholar of Pali Buddhism; translator of the Aggañña Sutta (ch. 8). Upinder Singh (b. 1959) Historian of early India; Political Violence in Ancient India (2017) (ch. 3, 5, 14). Mark McClish Historian of the Arthaśāstra and its relation to Dharmaśāstra (ch. 3, 9).

docs.title: Guide to the Principal Sources
docs.text:
This guide lists the principal primary texts discussed in this volume, with their approximate dates and the editions and translations used or recommended. Full details are given in the select bibliography. Verse and chapter numbers in the text follow the editions named here; other editions may number some verses differently.

Text Date Editions and translations; remarks Vedic and epic Ṛgveda c. 1500–1200 BCE (core) Translation: Jamison and Brereton (2014). Hymns on ṛta, Varuṇa, kingship and the assembly (ch. 2). Brāhmaṇas, Upaniṣads c. 1200–500 BCE Royal rituals, early uses of dharma, kings as patrons (ch. 2). Mahābhārata, Śānti Parvan c. 400 BCE–400 CE Critical edition (Poona); translation of Book 12, part one: Fitzgerald (2004). Rājadharma and Āpaddharma (ch. 5, 7). Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki c. 400 BCE–400 CE Critical edition (Baroda). Ideal kingship; Rāmarājya (ch. 5). Arthaśāstra and nīti Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya c. 50 BCE–300 CE First edition and translation: Shamasastry (1909, 1915); critical edition, translation and study: Kangle (1960); translation: Olivelle (2013); selections: McClish and Olivelle (2012); topical version: Rangarajan (1992) (ch. 3–7). Kāmandaka, Nītisāra c. 500–700 CE Verse digest of Kauṭilyan polity (ch. 3, 4). Tirukkuṟaḷ, Poruṭpāl c. 5th c. CE Tamil couplets on polity (ch. 4, 5). Somadeva Sūri, Nītivākyāmṛta 10th c. Jain aphorisms on polity (ch. 8). Someśvara III, Mānasollāsa 1131 Royal encyclopaedia of government and courtly life; see Ali (2004) (ch. 3, 17). Kalhaṇa, Rājataraṅgiṇī 1148–49 Translation: Stein (1900) (ch. 5, 17). Lekhapaddhati c. 10th–15th c. Gujarati formulary of model documents; translation: Prasad (2007) (ch. 17). Kṛṣṇadevarāya, Āmuktamālyada (Telugu) early 16th c. Translation: Reddy (2010); see Narayana Rao and Subrahmanyam (2009) (ch. 17). Copper-plate charters and inscriptions 4th c. onwards Guides: Sircar (1965; Salomon 1998) (ch. 6, 16, 17). Buddhist and Jain Dīgha Nikāya (Pali) 5th c. BCE onwards Aggañña, Cakkavatti-sīhanāda, Kūṭadanta and Mahāparinibbāna Suttas; Aggañña translated by Collins (1993) (ch. 8). Vinaya Piṭaka (Pali) 4th c. BCE onwards Translation: Horner (1938) (ch. 8). Inscriptions of Aśoka c. 268–232 BCE Hultzsch (1925); study: Thapar (1961) (ch. 8). Jinasena, Ādipurāṇa 9th c. Jain account of the first king and the varṇas; see Jaini (1979) (ch. 8). Dharmaśāstra Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana, Vasiṣṭha c. 3rd–1st c. BCE Translation: Olivelle (1999) (ch. 9). Manusmṛti c. 2nd c. CE Critical edition and translation: Olivelle (2005); translations: Bühler (1886), Doniger and Smith (1991); Medhātithi’s commentary: Jha (1920); first English translation: Jones (1794) (ch. 10). Yājñavalkyasmṛti c. 4th–5th c. CE Translation: Olivelle (2019) (ch. 11). Nāradasmṛti c. 5th–6th c. CE Critical edition and translation: Lariviere (1989); earlier translation: Jolly (1889) (ch. 11). Bṛhaspati, Kātyāyana c. 6th–7th c. CE Known from quotations; fragments of Bṛhaspati translated in Jolly (1889) (ch. 11, 12). Vijñāneśvara, Mitākṣarā c. 1100–1120 Inheritance chapter translated in Colebrooke (1810) (ch. 11). Jīmūtavāhana, Dāyabhāga 12th c. Translation: Rocher (2002); earlier: Colebrooke (1810) (ch. 11). Medieval digests (nibandha) 12th–18th c. See Table 9.1 and Kane (1930) (ch. 9). Burmese dhammasattha (Pali, Burmese, Mon) 13th–19th c. See Lammerts (2018); Hooker (1978) for Southeast Asia (ch. 9). Islamic and colonial al-Marghīnānī, al-Hidāya (Arabic) 12th c. Ḥanafī manual; English version from a Persian rendering by Charles Hamilton (1791) (ch. 18, 19). Fatāwā-yi Tātārkhāniyya (Arabic) 14th c. Ḥanafī rulings compiled under Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (ch. 18). Baranī, Fatāwā-yi Jahāndārī 14th c. See Alam (2004) (ch. 18). Fatāwā-i ʿĀlamgīrī 1660s–1670s See Guenther (2003) (ch. 18). Jahāngīr, memoirs (Jahāngīrnāma) early 17th c. Translation: Thackston (1999) (ch. 18). Vivādārṇavasetu 1773–1775 English version: Halhed (1776); see Rocher (1983) (ch. 19). Vivādabhaṅgārṇava 1790s English version: Colebrooke (1798) (ch. 19). Constituent Assembly Debates 1946–1949 Constituent Assembly of India (1948, 1949) (ch. 16, 20).
